## `Tensile/Lowering/` — the GIR lowering stack, in full

This report describes every module, class, function and method in the Python package rooted at
`Tensile/Lowering/`: what each piece exists to solve, how it computes its answer, and why it is
built the way it is. It is written to be read with nothing but this text and the source tree.

### 0. How to read this report

**Self-containment.** Every concept used here is defined here. Where the source code cites an
external design document by section number, this report restates the concept in full instead of
forwarding the citation. Where the source cites an internal work-item id (spelled `#NNN` in
docstrings — e.g. `#235`, `#183`), this report keeps at most a bare parenthetical as *provenance*
for readers who have the tracker open; **no claim in this report requires reading one**, and each
historical defect referenced is described in place.

**Citations.** Source locations are `path:line`, repo-relative to `tensilelite/Tensile/`. All line
numbers in this document were read off the files at the time of writing; if the file has since
moved, search for the quoted identifier.

**Section numbering.** `§N` in this document always refers to a section *of this document*. There
is no other numbering scheme in use here.

**Scope of the package.** 10,857 lines across 48 `.py` files (4 of which are `__init__.py`),
containing 271 module-level `def`/`class` definitions plus 164 nested methods and closures — 435
named things (counted by walking the AST of every file, not by grep). §19 is a complete index;
every one of them is described somewhere above it.

**Reading order.** §1 is the idea and the vocabulary. §2 is the map. §3–§5 are the IR itself.
§6 is the analyses, §7 the passes, §8 the verifier. §9–§11 are the emission and debug surfaces.
§12–§13 are the two ends (LoopIR in, rocisa out). §14–§15 are the pure geometry and the
off-IR checkers. §16 is how the package is tested, §17 the failure catalogue, §18 the gaps.

---

### 1. The idea: why there are two intermediate representations

#### 1.1 The division of labour

The `UseLoopModel` code-generation path has three layers.

**Layer 1, LoopIR** (produced by `Tensile/LoopModel/`, outside this package) states *what the
schedule is*: which operations exist, at which loop level, in what order, and how far ahead of
their consumers they run. It is a **tree**, it is **rolled** (one node per *kind* of operation, not
one per dynamic instance), and its buffer indices are **formulas** — an expression like
`(k + 2) mod 2` — rather than numbers.

**Layer 2, GIR** (this package) is where the physical consequences of that schedule are worked out.
Four questions dominate, and they are all the same *kind* of question:

1. Which of the *S* rotating LDS buffers does *this particular* access actually touch?
2. At which instruction does the LDS **read pointer** have to be flipped to the next buffer?
3. At which instruction does the **global read address** have to advance to the next reduction
   chunk?
4. Where do **barriers** go?

Each is "one physical register or resource must hold the right value at this program point". That
is a **compiler dataflow problem**, not a scheduling problem. And you cannot ask "does this value
reach that point?" of a tree whose indices are symbolic formulas: there is no *point* to reach, and
no *value* to propagate. So GIR is a **control-flow graph in SSA form** — the software-pipeline
stages are unrolled into real basic blocks, and each rotating buffer generation is an explicit named
SSA value with a phi at the loop header. All four questions then become textbook fixpoints.

**Layer 3, rocisa** turns each resolved GIR action into machine instructions. It decides *how* (a
buffer swap becomes an `s_xor` on a descriptor, or a `v_xor` on an address register), never *what*
or *where*.

That is the whole reason for two IRs. Not layering for its own sake: the questions genuinely change
form between the tree and the graph.

#### 1.2 The one pattern everything in `gir/` follows

```
    analysis  ──►  plan  ──►  placement  ──►  apply
   (IR frozen)             (IR frozen)      (the ONLY body mutator)
```

**No analysis touches the IR.** Each returns a *plan*: a list of `PendingMark` objects, each saying
"a pointer flip has to happen somewhere between *here* and *there*". A separate stage
(`PlacementPass`) picks a concrete point inside each range. One pass — `ApplyMarksPass`, and only
it — inserts the resulting `Mark` nodes into block bodies.

Three layers rather than one, because **an insertion has a legal *range*, not a correct point.** A
read-pointer flip may sit anywhere after the last use of the old buffer and before the first use of
the new one. Baking an index into the analysis is premature realization; it is the mistake the
first version of this code made, and it is what made it impossible to change placement policy
(earliest vs. midpoint) without rewriting the analysis.

There is one deliberate exception to "no analysis touches the IR", and it is *structural*, not a
body edit: `ScaffoldShapePass` (§11.3) is allowed to change the CFG. It is the first stage and the
only one with that permission, and `StructuralPass` (`gir/passes/base.py:33`) is a distinct base
class precisely so the permission is typed rather than conventional.

#### 1.3 The recurring problem shape

Two of the analyses — LDS read-pointer placement (`swap_regions.py`) and global-read-address
advance placement (`gr_increment.py`) — are literally the same problem for a different register:
**one register, a required value at each access, and exactly one kind of instruction that changes
it.** That is the classic code-motion pair (a forward *availability* fixpoint and a backward
*anticipation* one), so both are solved by one module, `value_placement.py` (§7.2), and the rule
cannot drift between them.

#### 1.4 Glossary

These terms are used throughout the source and throughout this report. Several of them collide with
ordinary English or with each other; the collisions are called out.

| term | meaning here |
|---|---|
| **operand** / **op-class** | A logical tensor role in the GEMM: `A`, `B`, `acc`, and on a microscaling kernel the scale tensors `MXSA`/`MXSB`. Interchangeable in this package. Names are *data*, never literals in the algorithms. |
| **agent** | An independently-scheduled execution stream — in practice a **wave**. Two accesses are *same-agent* if one wave issues both, *cross-agent* otherwise. Program order plus a completion counter orders same-agent accesses for free; only cross-agent pairs need a barrier. |
| **hop** | One step of an operand's data trajectory. Two hops matter: the **copy hop** `global → shared` (LDS), and the **read hop** `shared → register`. A one-hop operand goes `global → register` directly. |
| **movement** / **unit** | The identity of a *copy*. Because a fusion can merge several op-classes into one cooperative load instruction, a copy is named by a **member tuple** — `('A',)` unfused, `('A','B')` when one aliased descriptor serves both. A *read*, by contrast, is per op-class and names a bare operand string. This asymmetry is the model, not an inconsistency; see `gir/refs.py` (§5.2). |
| **generation** | Which buffer of a rotating ring an access touches. The one SSA value class in GIR (`Gen`). |
| **ring** (`S`) | The depth of a rotating buffer set. `S = 1` means in-place (the generation never changes); `S = 2` is double buffering. |
| **chunk** | One reduction-axis slab of work — one iteration's worth of `K`. The steady loop consumes one (or, with a multi-block body, several) chunks per trip. |
| **region** — *two unrelated meanings* | (a) **Storage region**: when an operand's LDS tile is *split* into `n` storage-disjoint pieces, each piece is a region. Used by `lds_hazards`, `mem_tokens`, `region_increment`, `lds_geometry`. (b) **Placement region** (`gir/region.py`): the legal *window* in which a `Mark` may be inserted. The two never appear in the same expression, but they do appear in the same file list — read the type, not the word. |
| **Φ fuse** | A merge of several copy movements into one cooperative instruction with **one completion event**. The fused group's members are paired *by index*: piece *j* of A moves with piece *j* of B, even if they are split on different axes. |
| **quantum** | The set of axes one *instruction* covers. A wide `ds_load` that fills two logical tiles has a quantum of two along that tile axis. Those axes are deliberately **absent** from the hop's coordinate set, and re-inserted where an analysis needs the individual locations (`refs.covered_coords`). |
| **ord** | The loop-order word — the sequence of inner modes from outermost to innermost. Carried into GIR as `Program.meta['inner_order']`. |
| **peel** / **M** | The prologue/drain depth. With peel depth `M`, the prologue issues `M` chunks' worth of copies before the loop, and a matching `M`-step drain finishes them after. |
| **T** | The runtime trip symbol: the total number of reduction chunks. Never a compile-time number. |
| **θ (theta)** | The schedule *decision object* produced by layer 1: which op-class instances exist, at which level, in which order. GIR consumes it and never re-derives it. Where this report says "a θ fact" it means "a fact carried in `Program.meta`, decided upstream". |
| **fence** | A proc-scoped ordering point. GIR models it as a `Mark`, not as an `s_barrier`; layer 3 decides the instruction. |
| **model-only block** | A block GIR reasons over that **no backend emits**. The kept short-trip arm is the case. |
| **act** | One entry in the flat emission plan: `EmitAction(kind, at)` (`gir/emit_plan.py:46`) — a `kind` string plus an `at` dict of *already-resolved integers*. An act holds **no** node reference and no way back to the IR; it is the entire interface between the ordering layer and the leaf emitters, and there are exactly eight kinds. This is the report's central emit-layer noun; §13.1 and §13.3 give the full treatment and §14.7 restates it where the renderer needs it. Note the arithmetic: one *read act* is not one instruction — it decomposes into N `ds_read`s spaced by the lane interleave (§17.9). |
| **TDM** (**T**ensor **D**ata **M**over) | The gfx1250 hardware block that moves a tile from global memory into LDS from a *descriptor* (base, dims, strides) rather than from a per-lane address. It is the only copy mechanism this lowering emits: every "copy hop" in this report is a TDM load, `Solution.py` rejects `UseLoopModel` unless `TDMInst=3` (TDM on both A and B), and "the descriptor" always means the TDM descriptor. What makes it matter to GIR rather than to the backend is that a descriptor is *stateful* — advancing to the next reduction chunk (§7.4) and stepping between storage regions (§7.5) are edits to a live register, so where those edits go is a dataflow question. |
| **PGR** / **PLR** | The two prefetch-depth kernel parameters, `PrefetchGlobalRead` and `PrefetchLocalRead`. **PGR** is how many reduction chunks the *copy* hop runs ahead — it is what sets the peel depth `M`. **PLR** is how many chunks the *read* hop runs ahead within the register ring. "PGR2/PLR1" throughout this report names one point of the configuration matrix. Under `UseLoopModel` PGR is 1 or 2 (0 and ≥3 are rejected upstream) and PLR is 0–3. |
| **`Access`** — *two unrelated classes* | `lds_hazards.Access` (`gir/analyses/lds_hazards.py:77`, §9.3) is a shared-space touch: block, position, operand, generation, regions, agent. `value_placement.Access` (`gir/analyses/value_placement.py:68`, §7.2.2) is a point in the pointer-placement problem: block, index, and the value the pointer must hold there. They share a word and nothing else, and only the first is exported (`gir/analyses/__init__.py:28`) — so a bare `Access` in an import list is always the hazard one. See the duplicate-name table in §2.3. |

### 2. Package map, module inventory and public API

#### 2.1 Layer map

```
θ ──emit_mainloop──► LoopIR tree + ledger              (Tensile/LoopModel/, layer 1)
        │  loopir_to_gir.lower_to_gir                  unroll the pipeline stages into a CFG,
        ▼                                              attach the Gen SSA
      GIR  ──run_pipeline──► finalized GIR             shape → reg → tokens → collect → place
        │                                              → apply → record
        │  gir.emit_plan.plan_block                    pure: CFG → an ordered list of EmitActions
        ▼
   gir_to_rocisa.GirToRocisa + leaves.LeafEmitters     the thin rocisa adapter (layer 3)
        ▼
   KernelWriterAssembly
```

`build_gir()` (`loopir_to_gir.py:882`) is the single entry point that runs the top two arrows
exactly once per kernel; the three stage forks in `KernelWriter` then only *ask* the emitter for
their block.

#### 2.2 Complete module inventory

All 48 code modules (line counts measured, not estimated) — 10 in `gir/`, 15 in `gir/analyses/`,
13 in `gir/passes/`, 10 at the top level, 10,857 lines in total. The four tables below are the
whole of `ls *.py gir/*.py gir/passes/*.py gir/analyses/*.py`; nothing is omitted.

**The three prose documents that are not code.** The directory also holds
`lowering-design.md` (75,570 B), `GIR_IMPLEMENTATION_GUIDE.md` (21,123 B) and
`SGPR_INTEROP_REPORT.md` (18,499 B), and `__init__.py:4` still points at the first of them as
"the whitepaper". Their status, stated once so nobody has to guess: **this report supersedes all
three as the description of what the code does today.** `lowering-design.md` is the *design note
written before the code existed* — it is the record of the intent (why two IRs, what layer 2 owes
layer 3) and its section numbering is the one still quoted in a few `gir/render.py` format strings
(see §14.1); it is not maintained against the source and several of its module descriptions are
stale. `GIR_IMPLEMENTATION_GUIDE.md` is a short orientation note that predates this report and is
strictly a subset of it; its line counts for the two renderers are known to be out of date.
`SGPR_INTEROP_REPORT.md` records one investigation (which SGPRs the GIR path shares with the
scaffold) and is a historical artefact, not a specification. **Nothing in this report defers to any
of the three**: every fact below was taken from the source, and where any of them disagrees, they

#### 2.3 Public API — what is supported surface, and what is not

There are four export lists, and they are deliberately different sizes. The counts below were
taken by parsing each `__all__` literal, not by eye.

- **`Tensile/Lowering/__init__.py:14`** exports exactly **four** names:
  `lower_to_gir`, `lower_params_to_gir`, `build_gir`, `gir_text`. This is the surface
  `KernelWriter` uses. Anything a consumer outside this package needs should arrive through one of
  these four.
- **`gir/__init__.py:31-49`** exports **62** names — the whole graph vocabulary, the analyses, the
  passes, the verifier, the renderer, the plan and the five dataflow checks. This is the surface
  the *tests* and the *emitter* use. It is internal to the lowering stack, but it is stable enough
  that the unit test suite imports from it directly (`test_gir.py:21-26`).
- **`gir/analyses/__init__.py:36-47`** exports **42** names. Only 18 of them are re-exported by
  `gir/__init__.py`; **24 are not**, and a consumer that wants one of those must import from
  `gir.analyses` directly. The 24 are, in full:

  ```
  Access  Break  FOLD  FoldVerdict  Linear  LoopShape  LoopShapeInfo  NA  POST  PRE
  PROC_SCOPES  RAW  RegionIncrementRegions  SPLIT  ShortPathFold  UNSOUND
  UniformPlacement  UniformViolation  Unresolved  WAR  WAW
  reduction_coverage_violations  region_of  walk_violations
  ```

  **Two of those twenty-four are renamed aliases**, and both deserve saying out loud because the
  name in the export list is not the name in the source file. `LoopShapeInfo` is
  `loop_shape.Loop` (`gir/analyses/__init__.py:33`), renamed on export so it cannot be confused
  with `nodes.Loop`-shaped control flow — that one is explained where the class is, in §6.4.5.
  `UniformViolation` is `uniform_placement.Violation` (`gir/analyses/__init__.py:34`), renamed for
  exactly the same reason: "Violation" alone is far too generic for a package that also produces
  `walk_violations` (region walk, §7.5), `reduction_coverage_violations` (loop covering, §6.4.8)
  and the verifier's `G-*` messages. **What it is:** one record of the liveness failure
  `UniformPlacement` (§10.17–§10.21) exists to catch — a proc-scoped selector, e.g. a fence or a
  block-scoped guard, that some agent of its own scope does not reach. Reaching it on only *some*
  waves is a hang, not a miscompare, which is why it gets a typed record rather than a boolean.
  It is exported so a caller can inspect the failure instead of just being told there was one;
  today `verify_gir` is the only caller and it renders the record into a `G-UNIFORM` message. As
  §19.2.8 (S8) records, the analysis is structurally inert on programs this lowering currently
  produces, so in practice the list is always empty — the type is there for wave specialization.

  Three whole subsystems are in that list — `ShortPathFold` (§10.1), `LoopShape` (§6.4) and
  `UniformPlacement` (§10.17) — even though `verify_gir` itself depends on all three — it calls `LoopShape` and `UniformPlacement` directly, and reads the `prog.meta["short_loop"]` record the `ShortPathFold`-driven pass leaves behind. That is not a
  policy so much as accretion: `gir/__init__.py`'s `__all__` was written when the analyses package
  held five modules and nobody has extended it since. The honest reading is that
  `gir/__init__.py` is the *older* surface, not a deliberately narrowed one, and a future
  maintainer adding an analysis should decide explicitly whether it belongs upward rather than
  copying the current omission.
- **`gir/passes/__init__.py:32-36`** exports **15** names: the two base classes, the ten pass
  classes, `folded`, and `pipeline` / `run_pipeline`.

**Names that mean two different things in two different files.** Each of these is described where
it lives, but nowhere else does the report warn that the *word* is overloaded, and a
`grep -rn 'def _ring_of'` returns two answers that are not variants of one another. Collected
once, so a reader who arrives by grep is not misled:

| name | file A | file B (and C) | are they related? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Access` | `lds_hazards.py:77` — a shared-space touch (block, pos, operand, generation, regions, agent), §9.3 | `value_placement.py:68` — a point in the pointer-placement problem (block, index, required value), §7.2.2 | **No.** Only the hazards one is exported (`gir/analyses/__init__.py:28`), so a bare `Access` in an import list is unambiguous — but inside `gir/analyses/` it is not |
| `_ring_of` | `lds_hazards.py:180` — the *LDS* ring depth read off a `Ref` | `swap_regions.py:104` — the ring depth of a **(hop, unit)** pair, which for the read hop is the *register* ring | **No.** Different rings. Merging them was tried and is wrong: the read hop's two rings are genuinely different numbers (§7.3.2) |
| `_generation` (**three** copies) | `quantum.py:101` — the generation tuple of an `at` dict | `passes/tokens.py:97` — the concrete generation of a `(ref, gen)` pair; and `short_path.py:171` — the same, but resolved in a *named frame* (the `base=` parameter, which is the §10.7 fix) | Same *concept*, three different inputs. `short_path`'s is the one with the frame parameter and the only one that can be wrong |
| `_topo` | `gr_increment.py:255` (live) | `swap_regions.py:178` (**dead** — reachable only through the unused local at `:244`) | **Yes — near-identical Kahn sorts**, behaviourally identical — same indegree init, same FIFO `ready.pop(0)`, same `seen` guard, and both append the unordered remainder; only the variable names and docstrings differ. §7.6 recommends deleting the dead copy and moving the live one into `cfg.py` beside `successors` |
| `_units` | `gr_increment.py:155` (a nested function, keyed by order) | `swap_regions.py:138` (module level, keyed by hop) | Same idea, different key. The hop parameter is the whole difference: `swap_regions` runs the problem twice, once per hop |
| `_kind` | `lds_hazards.py:316` — classify a producer/consumer pair as RAW/WAR/WAW | `short_path.py:101` — the *instruction* kind of a node, for correspondence | **No.** Unrelated questions that happen to be spelled the same |
| `_targets` | `passes/fold_short_path.py:197` | `passes/early_exit.py:112` | **Yes — duplicates**, and both are stale copies of `nodes.successor_labels`; §19.4.1 says to delete them |
| `shared_refs` | `refs.py:27` — filter *one instruction's* `Ref` list down to the shared-space ones, `(refs) -> tuple` | `mem_tokens.py:115` — a generator over the *whole program*, yielding `(block, inst, ref, is_write)` | Same word, different arity, and **the second does not call the first**: it re-implements the space test inline because it also needs the write flag. Its docstring says it mirrors `lds_hazards._shared_accesses`, which is the third walk of the same shape (that one builds the richer `Access` record) |

One name the report deliberately does *not* list here: `Unresolved`. There is exactly one
(`lds_hazards.py:138`); it is not overloaded.

One inconsistency worth recording, because it is the sort of thing that goes unnoticed without a
documented API section: `gir/__init__.py:12` **imports** `Trips` and `LoopBack` from `.nodes` but
the terminator row of `__all__` (`gir/__init__.py:33`) omits both. They are importable
(`from ...gir import LoopBack` works, and `test_gir.py:20` imports them from `gir.nodes`) but they
are not advertised. Since `LoopBack` is now the terminator on every steady loop (§3.5) and `Trips`
is the trip-count node, both belong in `__all__`. That is a one-line fix nobody has made.

reached from `KernelWriter.py` (`:3782`, `:3802`, `:3883`, `:11500`), whose row below records only
its `tdm_split` use. Measured, not
recalled:

| importer | what it takes | why here |
|---|---|---|
| `Components/LraTileAssignment.py:35` | `lds_geometry.region_row_elems` | the reason is recorded at `lds_geometry.py:118-124` — the alternative home, `Tensile/Common/`, imports rocisa in its package `__init__`, which would make this arithmetic un-unit-testable in the pure-Python environment |
| `Components/LocalRead.py:37` | `lds_geometry.region_row_elems` **and `fold_inner_offset`** (`:762`, `:1683`) | the scaffold read path must produce the *same* address the GIR read leaf does; `fold_inner_offset` (§17.11) is the piecewise in-region offset and this is its only non-`Lowering` consumer |
| `Component.py:75, 237` | `tdm_split.split_of` | one gate: is this operand region-split at all |
| `KernelWriterAssembly.py:116` | `tdm_split.split_of` / `any_split` / `derive` — 12 call sites (`:1023`, `:7603`, `:11352`, `:11387`, `:11470`, `:11500`, `:19125`, `:19127`, `:19413`, `:19510`, `:20364`, `:20440`) | the descriptor and address emission on the *scaffold* path |
| `KernelWriter.py:81, 11422` | `tdm_split.any_split` | one shape decision |
| `SolutionStructs/Solution.py:42` | `tdm_split.split_factors` / `split_of` / `wave_region_span`, re-exported as `tdmSplitFactors` / `tdmSplitOf` (`:178-179`) and used by the gates at `:1065-1076`, `:5040`, `:5091` | the parameter validation must reject exactly what the geometry cannot express |
| `LoopModel/bridge.py:45, 121, 129-130` | `tdm_split.split_factors`, `tdm_split.wave_region_span` | layer 1 must model the same split the kernel was accepted with — see the import-cycle note below |

`Solution.py:175` states the rule that makes this acceptable: `tdm_split.py` **imports nothing**,
so `Components/`, `Lowering/` and `SolutionStructs/` can all depend on it without creating a cycle.
`lds_geometry.py` imports only `tdm_split`. Any future upward-reachable module must keep that
property.

**One genuine cycle, broken by a lazy import — do not "clean this up".**
`Tensile/Lowering/__init__.py` imports `loopir_to_gir`, which imports `..LoopModel`; so
`LoopModel/bridge.py` cannot import `Tensile.Lowering` at module scope without closing a cycle at
interpreter start-up. It therefore does the import **inside the function**, and says so:

```python
# LoopModel/bridge.py:42-45
# LAZY, and it has to be: `Tensile.Lowering.__init__` imports `loopir_to_gir`, which imports
# this package, so a module-level import here closes a cycle.  `tdm_split` itself imports
# nothing — the cycle is entirely in the parent package's `__init__`.
from ..Lowering import tdm_split as _tdm_split
```

Hoisting those four lines to the top of `bridge.py` breaks `import Tensile.Lowering` outright, and
the failure surfaces as an unrelated-looking `ImportError` during `KernelWriter` construction. The
layer map of §2.1 shows the *data* dependency as one-directional, and it is; this is a Python
packaging artefact of `Lowering/__init__.py` eagerly importing the front end. The clean fix, if
anyone wants one, is to make `Tensile/Lowering/__init__.py` lazy about `loopir_to_gir` rather than
to move the import in `bridge.py`.

---

### 3. `gir/nodes.py` — the node set (511 lines, 19 top-level names)

#### 3.1 Concept: what a GEMM-dataflow IR must and must not say

GIR is a **semantic** IR. Its rule, enforced by the verifier's `G-SEMANTIC` check
(`gir/verify.py:149`), is that no node may carry a *physical* field: no address, no VGPR colour, no
vector width, no byte offset. A buffer swap is the *fact* "the read generation changes here", never
an `s_xor`. The reason is not purity for its own sake — it is that the same fact has different
realizations on different back ends (a descriptor `s_xor`, an address-register `v_xor`, or nothing
at all when the scheduler re-derives it), and a node that names one of them cannot be reused by the
others.

The module imports nothing but `dataclasses` (`gir/nodes.py:25-26`). Every other file in `gir/`
transitively depends only on the standard library, which is what makes the whole analysis stack
runnable under a plain `pytest` with no compiled `rocisa` present.

The vocabulary splits into five groups, which is also the file's own section layout:

| group | nodes | what it answers |
|---|---|---|
| nouns | `Tile`, `Gen`, `Ref` | *what data*, *which buffer generation*, *one use of it* |
| verbs | `Move`, `Mma` | *one data movement hop*, *one multiply-accumulate* |
| point | `Mark` (+ `MARK_KINDS`) | *a semantic fact at a program point* |
| control | `Bound`, `Pred`, `Goto`, `CondGoto`, `Trips`, `LoopBack`, `Return`, `CondChain` | the CFG terminators |
| graph | `successor_labels`, `Block`, `GenPhi`, `GenXfer`, `Program` | the CFG itself |

#### 3.2 The nouns

**`Tile` (`gir/nodes.py:33`)** — a logical operand fragment, frozen and hashable. Fields:
`operand` (an open set of names: `'A'`, `'B'`, `'acc'`, `'MXSA'`, `'meta'`, …), `space`
(`'global'` | `'shared'` | `'register'`), `coord` (a tuple of `(mode, value|None)` pairs), and
`shape` (a tuple of `(kind, n)` size records — a *size*, never an address).

The invariant on `coord` is that it never contains the reduction-loop induction variable, spelled
`'iter'`. That is `G-NOITER` (`gir/verify.py:135`). The reason is structural: the cross-trip
relation lives in the `Gen` phi, and a coordinate that also carried the trip index would give the
IR two ways to say the same thing, which diverge.

Two methods, both one-liners:
- `Tile.coord_map()` (`:49`) — `dict(self.coord)`, so a consumer can index by mode name.
- `Tile.shape_map()` (`:52`) — `dict(self.shape)`.

**`Gen` (`gir/nodes.py:57`)** — the **one SSA value class in GIR**: a loop-carried buffer
generation. Two integer fields, `id` and `ring`. `id` distinguishes independently-rotating buffer
sets (A-shared vs B-shared); `ring` is the depth `S` (1 = in place). A `Gen` is *defined* by a
`GenPhi` at a loop header and *transferred* across the back edge by a `GenXfer`.

That there is exactly one SSA value class is the design's central simplification. Registers are
*not* SSA here — they are named by a concrete `(group, slot)` decided upstream — because the
register rotation width is a schedule decision this layer only validates (§6.5). Making the LDS
generation the sole SSA value is what lets the reaching-value analysis (§6.2) be nine lines of
transfer function.

**`Ref` (`gir/nodes.py:70`)** — a *use* of a `Tile` inside an instruction, and the widest node in
the file. Its ten fields split into four independent groups, and the groups are mutually exclusive
in practice but not by type:

```
tile                       which fragment
gen, gdelta                loop-carried shared residence: generation `gen` offset by `gdelta`
abs_gen                    ABSOLUTE shared residence: a concrete pinned generation int
group, slot, reg_ring      register residence: partition index, rotation slot, rotation width W
covers                     the movement-quantum footprint: ((axis, extent), ...)
size_regs, size_bytes      sizes
```

The `gen`/`abs_gen` split is the peel/steady distinction made structural. A prologue fill or a
short-arm access knows *exactly* which buffer it touches — its chunk index is a compile-time
constant — so it carries `abs_gen=<int>` and no `Gen`. A steady or drain access does not: its
buffer depends on the trip parity, a runtime value, so it carries `gen` plus a `gdelta` offset and
the concrete generation is *computed* by `GenReaching`. Mixing them would force every consumer to
ask "is this number a generation or a slot?" — which is exactly the confusion the renderer had to
be taught to spell apart (§14.8).

`reg_ring` is `W`, the register rotation width. GIR **consumes** it — it is read off the upstream
slot expression's modulus — and `RegBandAnalysis` (§6.5) only validates it. Deciding `W` here
would create a second authority that can disagree with the scheduler.

`covers` is the second half of a subtraction whose first half happens upstream. When one
instruction moves several tiles at once (a wide `ds_load` that fills two logical tiles), the axis
it spans is *removed* from the read's coordinate set upstream — so the definition names one
location while every consumer names all of them. `covers` records the removed axes and their
extents, and `refs.covered_coords` (§5) re-inserts them for the analyses that track locations. The
alternative — emitting one `Ref` per covered coordinate — was tried and rejected: it files *N*
residencies against a single completion event, so a single `Await` looks like it discharges only
one of them.

#### 3.3 The verbs

**`Move` (`gir/nodes.py:108`)** — the *only* data-movement verb: one hop down the memory hierarchy.
`srcs` and `dsts` are tuples of `Ref`; the hop is identified by the spaces, never by a flag:

- shared appears in `dsts` → this is a **copy** (global → shared).
- shared appears in `srcs` and a register in `dsts` → this is a **read** (shared → register).
- global in `srcs`, register in `dsts`, no shared at all → a direct-to-register (one-hop) read.

`deps` carries the dependence edges inherited from the schedule as `(name, counter, kind)` triples.
`token` is the *semantic completion class* stamped by `TokensPass` (§11.8) — "which logical buffer
did this fill or drain". `token_ids` is the *backend storage name(s)* from `MemTokenAssignment`
(§8.1). These two are deliberately different questions: one names **what completed**, the other
**which storage**. A Φ-fused copy has *one* completion token and *several* storage ids, and
collapsing them is a bug this file's docstring records at `:118-123`.

**`Mma` (`gir/nodes.py:133`)** — the compute verb, with an **open operand set**. `srcs` is a tuple
of register `Ref`s, and operand identity is read off `Ref.tile.operand`; there is no `role`
vocabulary and no `a`/`b` field. A plain kernel has `srcs = (A, B)`; a microscaling kernel has
`(A, B, MXSA, MXSB)`; a sparse one `(A, B, meta)`. `dsts` is the accumulator. `coord` is the
instruction's own position over the mode set, and `block` is the hardware WMMA block-group tag.

#### 3.4 `Mark` and the closed kind set

**`MARK_KINDS` (`gir/nodes.py:157-158`)** is a **closed set of seven**:

```
phase_boundary   fence   swap   gr_increment   region_increment   gsu_guard   gl2_prefetch
```

**`Mark` (`gir/nodes.py:162`)** carries `kind` and a kind-specific `at` payload dict. The payload
schema per kind is enforced by `G-MARK` against `_MARK_SCHEMA` (`gir/verify.py:75-95`):

| kind | required `at` keys | source |
|---|---|---|
| `phase_boundary` | `phase` | the lowering, at each block head |
| `fence` | `buffers`, `scope`, `kinds`, `edges` (+`tokens` by `G-TOKEN`) | `FenceRegions` (§8.13) |
| `swap` | `hop`, `gen_from`, `gen_to`, **and** `operand` (read hop) or `unit` (copy hop) | `SwapRegions` (§7.3) |
| `gr_increment` | `unit` (+`chunks`, `to_chunk` in practice) | `GrIncrementRegions` (§7.4) |
| `region_increment` | `unit`, `steps`, `from_region`, `to_region` (+`axis_steps`) | `RegionIncrementRegions` (§7.5) |
| `gl2_prefetch` | `depth`, `block` | `Gl2PrefetchRegions` (§7.7) |
| `gsu_guard` | `variant` | not produced today; reserved |

`gl2_prefetch` is the only row that names **no subject at all** — no `operand`, no `unit` — and that
absence is the fact rather than an omission. The L2 warm-up runs off its own address VGPRs and its
own increment SGPRs, never touches a TDM descriptor, and feeds nothing in the trip that issues it,
so there is no movement for it to hang off. A `unit` key here would be a claim that some movement's
pointer moved, and the region/token analyses would be entitled to believe it.

The `swap` row is the one the schema table cannot express, because the required key depends on the
value of another key. `_check_marks` (`gir/verify.py:398`) special-cases it at `:410-419`: a read
swap must name an op-class under `operand`, a copy swap must name a Φ movement's member tuple under
`unit`. That distinction is the model, and the check exists because labelling a fused copy swap
with a bare operand name is exactly how the other members went unnoticed.

There is no `barrier` Mark kind and never was. The comment above the tuple
(`gir/nodes.py:150-156`) states the reason: GIR carries the *ordering obligation*, and whether it
becomes an `s_barrier`, a wait-count, or nothing at all is the back end's decision from the target
configuration. On the path where the downstream scheduler re-derives every barrier, a GIR-emitted
one would be discarded, so presuming the realization in the node name would have been wrong on that
path. **That comment is itself stale and should be corrected:** it says "`await` replaces the
never-created `barrier` kind", but the kind in `MARK_KINDS` is spelled `fence`, and `await` appears
nowhere in the tuple. The reasoning is right; the name in the prose is one rename behind. Fixing
the word is a one-line change nobody has made.

#### 3.5 The control-flow terminators

Five terminator types plus two helper value types. The design principle is that GIR **describes**
control flow rather than **implementing** it: a loop states its trip count, not a comparison.

**`Bound` (`gir/nodes.py:181`)** — the right-hand side of a terminator predicate: `var + const`,
or the bare constant when `var` is empty. `Bound.render()` (`:194`) formats it. Deliberately *not*
the upstream index-expression language (mixed-radix terms, moduli, chunk carries): those describe
*data* coordinates, never a control-flow test, and duplicating them would give GIR a second formula
language to keep in sync. `_gir_bound` (§15.2.1) raises rather than lowering a richer expression.

**`Pred` (`gir/nodes.py:203`)** — a structured symbolic predicate `lhs op rhs`, read **by field**.
`__post_init__` (`:220`) validates `op` against `_PRED_OPS = (">=", ">", "==", "<", "<=", "!=")`
(`:177`). `render()` (`:224`) formats it. `label` is a downstream scaffold hint, attached by
`ScaffoldMapPass` (§11.6) and advisory: a back end with its own loop scaffold routes on the label,
a from-scratch back end lowers `render()` and ignores it.

It used to be a free-form string. The multi-exit header and the drain-multiplicity matrix both need
to ask "which counter does this test, and against what?", and answering that by parsing
`'iter < T - 2'` is how a structured question gets a fragile answer.

**`Goto` (`gir/nodes.py:229`)** — unconditional, one `target`.

**`CondGoto` (`gir/nodes.py:235`)** — `pred`, `t_target`, `f_target`. The steady back edge is not one of these: it is
`LoopBack` (below), and the node's own docstring — which still says "there is no separate loop-back
primitive" — is one change behind. What remains true either way is that "is this a back edge?" is a
*graph property*, answered by dominance (§6.1), not by a node type.

**`Trips` (`gir/nodes.py:248`)** — a loop's dynamic trip count, `(var - sub) // div`.
`render()` (`:272`). This node is the answer to a specific past defect. A trip count is what the
model states — the steady region is a *range* — while a comparison is one *encoding* of it, and
decoding the encoding needs three facts that live outside the node: where the counter starts, which
way it steps, and where the test sits. None are shared with the back end, whose loop counter is
initialized to the count and **decrements**. Holding the comparison meant every reader re-derived
the count from assumptions, and two off-by-ones came from exactly that.

`div` is why `Trips` is not `Bound` renamed: a multi-block steady chain consumes `div` chunks per
trip and therefore runs `(T - M) // div` times, a statement `var + const` cannot make at all.

**`LoopBack` (`gir/nodes.py:279`)** — the loop terminator: run `body` for `trips` iterations, then
go to `exit_target`. `label` is the scaffold hint (there is no `Pred` on this edge to hang it on).
The CFG shape is unchanged from the `CondGoto` it replaced — the same two successors — so
dominance, back-edge detection and every traversal behave identically.

**`Return` (`gir/nodes.py:296`)** — a sink with **no successors**. Some drain variants finish the
kernel in place. Modelling that as `Goto('end')` would be indistinguishable from a fall-through to
the common exit — `'end'` is a pseudo-target every analysis filters out — so a pass could
"helpfully" retarget the edge. A distinct node makes the sink explicit, and `verify_gir` accepts a
terminator with no targets *only* for this node (`gir/verify.py:346`).

**`CondChain` (`gir/nodes.py:309`)** — an **ordered** chain of guarded exits plus a default. Its
`__post_init__` (`:331`) rejects an empty `arms` tuple and any arm that is not a `(Pred, target)`
pair. This is the shape a loop header needs when several typed early exits test the *same* counter
against different bounds — with peel depth `M`, a trip count `T <= M` enters a partially-drained
drain variant instead of the steady loop. The arms are a tuple and never a set because the first
satisfied arm wins.

It is one terminator rather than a fan of single-exit blocks so the header stays **one block**: its
phis, transfers and body belong to the header, and splitting it would force every analysis to
re-join the pieces. A one-arm `CondChain` is exactly a `CondGoto`; the two-way form is kept as the
common shape rather than folded away.

#### 3.6 The graph

**`successor_labels(blk)` (`gir/nodes.py:342`)** — *the* successor list of a block, and the single
authority every CFG walk uses. It lives next to the terminator definitions because a second copy of
the switch is a silent wrong answer waiting for the next terminator kind: `Program.walk_rpo` used
to carry its own that handled only `Goto`/`CondGoto`, so a `CondChain` header or a `Return` sink had
*no* successors as far as reverse-postorder was concerned, and the generation analysis then visited
blocks in the wrong order. Targets come back in program-significant order (a chain's arms first, in
arm order, then its default) and are **not** filtered against `prog.blocks` — the caller decides
whether to drop the `'end'` pseudo-target.

**`Block` (`gir/nodes.py:370`)** — one software-pipeline phase as a basic block. `phase` is both
the classification and the label, over the domain

```
'prologue' | 'steady{n}' | 'drain{n}' | 'short{n}' | 'tail'
```

(`gir/nodes.py:373`; the first steady block is spelled `'steady'` with no index, and copies 1..n-1
are `'steady1'`…). `short{n}` is the degenerate arm taken when the trip count does not exceed the
peel depth; it exists until `FoldShortPathPass` rules on it and is then either deleted or kept as a
real second path (the decision is §10.1–§10.16, the mutator §11.4). Other fields: `loop`, `preds`,
`succs`, `phis` (list of `GenPhi`),
`xfers` (list of `GenXfer`), `body` (a list of `Move` | `Mma` | `Mark` in program order), `term`,
and `role` (the wave role; `'all'` everywhere today).

Four fields deserve their own explanation because they are the block's **frame**, and they are what
make cross-block reasoning possible at all:

- **`gen_rel`** — the reduction-chunk position this block's `Ref.gdelta` values were computed
  against; `None` means the block's refs carry absolute generations instead. A frame-free
  requirement is `ref.gdelta - gen_rel`.
- **`chunk_base`** — the block's position on the *global* reduction-chunk timeline, with the first
  steady trip at 0. An edge's chunk delta is the difference of its endpoints' bases (plus, on a
  back edge, the trip's own chunk count, which the block's `GenXfer.adv` states).
- **`path_chunk_base`** — `{predecessor: chunk_base on that path}`. A block reached by two paths
  can sit at two *different* positions on the timeline, and one integer cannot say so. The folded
  short-arm entry edge is the case: on the long path the first drain block runs one chunk past the
  last steady trip, but on the folded path it handles chunk 0 — the position the short arm it
  replaced had. Without this, subtracting two per-block integers made the folded join look like an
  unsplittable critical edge when the two paths in fact agree.
- **`model_only`** — the block is one GIR reasons over that **no back end emits**. Because the
  emitter requests blocks by phase name, an unemitted block is otherwise indistinguishable from a
  forgotten one, and any `Mark` an analysis places in it is silently discarded. `G-EMIT` (§12.1) turns
  that discard into an explicit counted fact.

`Block.label` (`:431`) is a property returning `phase`.

**`GenPhi` (`gir/nodes.py:436`)** — `gen = φ(entry_val, back_edge_val)` at a loop header. Only
`entry_val` is stored; the back-edge value is derived from the matching `GenXfer`.

**`GenXfer` (`gir/nodes.py:447`)** — a back-edge transfer `v' = (v + adv) % ring` for one `Gen`.
It names its `gen` so the reaching analysis can key transfers per back edge rather than assuming a
single `xfers[0]`.

**`Program` (`gir/nodes.py:459`)** — the whole main loop as one minimal CFG. `blocks` is an
insertion-ordered `{label: Block}`; `entry` is the entry label; `tiles` is an optional interned
tile table (empty in practice); `params` holds presets the analyses read; `meta` holds the schedule
facts (the lowering writes **17** keys, and one further key is read but never written — §15.8
enumerates all 18); `version` is bumped by any mutation so cached analyses invalidate; `pending`
holds the `PendingMark` plan between the collect and apply passes.

Four methods:
- `add_block(blk)` (`:477`) — insert by label, return the block.
- `block(label)` (`:481`) — lookup, `KeyError` if absent.
- `bump()` (`:484`) — `version += 1`. Every mutating pass must call it.
- `walk_rpo()` (`:487`) — reverse postorder over the CFG following terminators, so a block is
  yielded after its non-back-edge predecessors. Implemented as a recursive post-order with an
  ordinary `seen` (visited) set that prunes any already-visited successor — back, cross and forward edges alike — then reversed. Blocks unreachable from the entry are appended in
  insertion order, defensively, rather than dropped.

**Complexity.** `walk_rpo` is O(V + E) with V = blocks (typically 4–12: one prologue, 1–2 steady, M
drains, up to M short) and E ≈ 2V. Every CFG walk in the package is at this scale, which is why
none of them is worth optimizing; the costs that matter are all O(accesses²) and live in §9.

**Extension notes.** Adding a terminator kind requires touching at least six places — two beyond the successor switches: `loop_shape._exit_tester` (`gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:117`), which computes its own exit-target list and yields `()` for any kind it does not recognize (so `LoopShape` finds no exit tester and `G-TRIP` is silently skipped), and `render._term_line` (`gir/render.py:152`), which falls through to `"term: <none>"`. The four successor switches are:
`successor_labels` (`gir/nodes.py:342`), `verify._term_targets` (`gir/verify.py:337`),
`fold_short_path._targets` (`gir/passes/fold_short_path.py:197`) and `early_exit._targets`
(`gir/passes/early_exit.py:112`). The last three are duplicates of the first and should be
collapsed into it; they exist because each was written before `successor_labels` was extracted, and
the two pass-local copies do not handle `Return` or (in `fold_short_path`'s case) `CondChain`.
That is latent: neither pass currently runs on a program containing those, but a future one will.
Collapsing them is a safe, mechanical improvement.

#### 3.7 What is wrong with this node set

Everything above says what the nodes *are*. This subsection says what a maintainer should be
unhappy about, and which alternatives were considered and rejected. Nothing here is a bug report —
each is a design commitment with a cost.

**1. The nodes are mutable, and that is load-bearing in both directions.** `Move`, `Mma` and
`Mark` are ordinary mutable dataclasses: passes edit `body` lists in place, `TokensPass` stamps
tokens onto existing `Move`s, `ApplyMarksPass` splices. The benefit is that a pass is a dozen
lines and there is exactly one `Program`. The cost shows up three separate places in this report:
the nodes are **unhashable in practice** (a `Hazard` holds a `Move`, so `_cover` must key on
integer indices — §8.15), analyses must key side tables on `id(node)` (and then retain `prog` so
the ids cannot be recycled — §6.6 observation 3), and correctness depends on a hand-maintained
`version` counter that every mutator must remember to `bump()`. **The alternative** — an immutable
IR with a rebuild-per-pass discipline, like the functional half of MLIR — would delete all three
problems and cost a full graph copy per pass. At 4–12 blocks and a few hundred instructions that
copy is genuinely cheap (§20.14 measures the node set's own cost as a small fraction of the
budget), so this is *not* an obviously wrong trade to revisit; what makes it a large change rather
than a small one is that `PendingMark` anchors are node identities, so an immutable IR needs
stable ids as a separate concept. Do not attempt it piecemeal.

**2. There is no explicit `Copy` versus `Read` node — both are `Move`.** A `Move` is distinguished
by the *space* of its refs (`shared` destination = a copy hop, `shared` source = a read hop), not
by its class. This is why `refs.py` (§5) has to exist at all, and why "which movement is this"
was answered three different ways in three modules before `copy_unit` was extracted. **The
alternative** — two node classes — was rejected because a fused copy and a split read are the
*same* node shape with different ref sets, and the analyses that matter (hazards, tokens, fences)
genuinely want to iterate "every shared touch" without a type switch. The residual cost is that
the distinction is a *derived* property, and every new consumer must be told to derive it through
`refs.py` rather than by inspecting `srcs`/`dsts` itself. That instruction is easy to miss.

**3. `Mark` is a stringly-typed union.** One class carries six unrelated payload shapes,
discriminated by `kind` against the closed `MARK_KINDS` tuple (`:157`) and validated by a schema
table in the *verifier* (`verify.py:75`) rather than by the type system. A `swap` Mark and a
`fence` Mark share no fields. **The alternative** — six dataclasses with a common base — is what a
statically-typed IR would do, and it would move the schema check from run time to construction
time. It was rejected for a concrete reason: every consumer of a Mark (placement, apply,
emit_plan, the renderer, the backend dispatch) switches on the kind *anyway*, so six classes would
add six imports and six `isinstance` arms without removing a single switch — and the one thing the
union buys, a uniform `PendingMark` currency that placement can carry without knowing what it is,
is exactly the property the placement pipeline is built on. The honest cost is that adding a kind
means touching four sites in three files (§19.4.7) and forgetting the schema entry produces a
run-time error rather than a type error.

**4. Five terminator dataclasses, and the successor switch has been duplicated three times.**
The set is `Goto`, `CondGoto`, `LoopBack`, `Return`, `CondChain` — `Trips` is *not* a terminator but
the trip-count operand carried inside `LoopBack.trips` (built only at `loopir_to_gir.py:116`, and
absent from `successor_labels`'s switch). `LoopBack` is the loop-back form, and it names a dynamic
trip count via its `Trips` rather than a counter comparison (#228/#231); `CondChain` is a
multi-exit generalization of `CondGoto`. A tighter design would be *one*
terminator with a list of `(predicate, target)` arms and a default, of which all five are special
cases. That was not done because each carries different *verifiable* structure (`CondChain`'s
`__post_init__` at `:331` rejects malformed arm lists; `Trips` carries the trip symbol the loop
shape analysis reads), and collapsing them would move those checks into one function of many
cases. The measurable cost of the current shape is the duplication named in the extension notes
above: three copies of one switch, two of them already incomplete. **If you change anything in
this file, collapse those three first** — it is the highest-value ten-line change in the package.

**5. `Program.tiles` is dead; `Program.params` is a bag but no longer an empty one.** `tiles` is an
interned tile table that is empty in every program this lowering builds. `params` is an untyped dict
of presets the analyses were meant to read by string key. **As of #216 it has exactly one reader and
one writer**: `KernelWriter._loopModelGirProgram` writes `{"PrefetchGL2": kernel["PrefetchGL2"]}`
and `Gl2PrefetchRegions` reads it back through `Gl2PrefetchRegions.PARAM` (§7.7). Before that it was
written once and never read, i.e. as dead as `tiles`.

`meta` is the *documented* fact channel (§15.8) and `params` was the undocumented one. A reader
could not tell from the class which of the two a new fact belongs in. The rule that is actually
followed — and that #216 is the first case to exercise — is: **`meta` is what θ DERIVED, `params` is
what the TARGET PRESET.** GL2 is the clean example of the second: the prefetch stages nothing, files
no residency and has no completion class, so there is no operand for it to be and θ must not learn
the word `PrefetchGL2` (#163). The key is a class constant rather than a bare string precisely
because a typo in a bag-of-strings channel is an analysis that is silently inert forever. That rule
should be in the docstring and still is not.

**6. What the node set cannot say at all.** There is no store/global-write node (so the epilogue
is unmodelled — §19.5.1), no node for a register-space rotation independent of a movement, and no
way to express a `Move` whose extent is a runtime value rather than a compile-time tile. Each of
those is a real limitation with an owner in §19.5, and each would be a *node* change rather than
an analysis change — which is why they are listed here as well as there.

---

### 4. `gir/region.py` and `gir/analysis.py` — the two pieces of infrastructure

#### 4.1 `gir/region.py` (67 lines) — the insertion model

**The idea.** A `Mark` has a legal placement **range**, not a single correct point. A read-pointer
flip may sit anywhere after the last access using the old generation and before the first access
using the new one. Baking a body index into an analysis is premature realization, and it is what
made it impossible to change placement policy without rewriting the analysis.

Two module constants are **anchor sentinels**: `BLOCK_ENTRY = "<entry>"` (`:27`) and
`BLOCK_EXIT = "<exit>"` (`:28`). Two are **placement policies**: `EARLIEST = "earliest"` (`:31`)
and `MIDPOINT = "midpoint"` (`:32`).

**There are exactly two policies.** There is no third, and no `PINNED`: a fence's Region is not a
distinct policy, it is a *degenerate window* — `after = body[slot-1]`, `before = body[slot]` —
built by `fence_regions._region_at` (`gir/analyses/fence_regions.py:247`) and carried with the
default `EARLIEST`, which on a one-slot window resolves to that slot. A maintainer searching for a
`PINNED` symbol will find only prose (`gir/passes/collect_pending.py:12`,
`gir/analyses/fence_regions.py:248`), and the prose means "the window is degenerate", not "there is
a third policy".

**`Region` (`gir/region.py:36`)** — frozen: `block` (a label), `after` (place strictly after this
anchor), `before` (place strictly before it), `policy`. The anchors are **opaque node references**,
not indices, which is what lets a Region survive other Marks being inserted into the same body
before it is resolved. A Region may in principle span a block edge; in practice every producer
today emits a single-block window.

The policy travels with the Region because it differs by *what the Mark mutates*, so a single
global policy in the placement pass would be wrong:

- **`EARLIEST`** — every write-descriptor change (`gr_increment`, `region_increment`, and the
  copy-hop `swap`). The descriptor feeds the load, so every cycle between the update and the load
  it feeds is overlap.
- **`MIDPOINT`** — the LDS read pointer only, midway between the last use of the old generation
  and the first use of the new. It is bounded by two *different* resources, so it is not the
  descriptor rule and must not be slammed to either edge.
- **`MIDPOINT` again, for a different reason** — the `gl2_prefetch` pair (#216, §7.7). Its window
  is `BLOCK_ENTRY..BLOCK_EXIT` and **every point in it is correct**, because nothing in the trip
  consumes what it fetches. So this is the only policy choice in the package that is purely a
  COST decision: at block entry the prefetch block would contend with the trip's own TDM copy for
  memory-pipe slots to fetch data nobody wants for `PGR+GL2` chunks, and mid-body is where that
  pipe has slack. It is therefore the one placement worth *measuring* rather than settling by
  argument — and since the window is computed either way, moving the pick is one line.

**`PendingMark` (`gir/region.py:59`)** — mutable: `mark` (a `nodes.Mark`), `region`, and `anchor`
(`None` until `PlacementPass` fills it, then a `(block_label, node_or_sentinel)` pair).

**Trade-off.** The three-layer split (analysis → plan → placement → apply) costs one extra
list-of-objects pass over the program and makes the flow harder to follow than a single walker that
inserts as it goes. It buys: (a) the analyses stay pure and therefore trivially cacheable and unit
testable; (b) placement policy is a one-line change; (c) an analysis cannot corrupt the body it is
reading. The one thing it does *not* buy is protection against two analyses placing conflicting
Marks in the same window — nothing checks that today, and it is the obvious next invariant.

#### 4.2 `gir/analysis.py` (59 lines) — the analysis base and manager

**`Analysis` (`gir/analysis.py:24`)** — a base class with two members: a `cache_key` property
(`:32`) defaulting to the class name, and `run(self, prog, am)` (`:36`) which subclasses override
and which must be **pure**. A parameterized analysis overrides `cache_key` to fold its parameters
in so distinct parameterizations cache separately. **Three** analyses override it today, and all
three do so only to pin a stable name independent of the class name — none of them is actually
parameterized: `DepDefuseAnalysis` → `"DepDefuse"` (`gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py:45`),
`RegBandAnalysis` → `"RegBand"` (`gir/analyses/reg_band.py:40`), and `GrIncrementRegions` → its own
name (`gir/analyses/gr_increment.py:119`). The other eleven analyses take the default. Since the
default is already the class name only for `GrIncrementRegions`, only that one override is a no-op in effect — `DepDefuseAnalysis` → `"DepDefuse"` and `RegBandAnalysis` → `"RegBand"` do change the key, since the class names are `DepDefuseAnalysis` and `RegBandAnalysis`; they exist
so a rename of the class does not silently change a cache key that a test or a dump keys on.

**`AnalysisManager` (`gir/analysis.py:40`)** — lazy, cached, invalidated.

- `__init__` (`:45`) — an empty dict.
- `get(analysis, prog)` (`:48`) — keyed on `(analysis.cache_key, prog.version)`, so a pass that
  mutates and bumps the version transparently invalidates every stale result. Takes an
  **instance**, not a class, which is what makes parameterized analyses possible.
- `invalidate(names=None)` (`:55`) — clears everything. `names` is accepted and ignored: the
  version bump already makes stale entries unreachable, so this is only about keeping the dict
  small. Finer per-name invalidation can key on `names` later.

**Complexity and cost.** The cache is a plain dict, and because the key includes the version, a
mutating pass leaves the old entries as garbage until `invalidate()` runs. `run_pipeline` calls
`invalidate()` after *every* pass (`gir/passes/pipeline.py:67`), which is coarse: it throws away
`Dominators` and `BackEdges` even after a pass that touched only bodies. On a 12-block CFG that is
free; on a hypothetical grid-stride or persistent-loop program with many more blocks it would not
be, and the fix is exactly what the docstring proposes — have each pass return the names it
invalidated (the `Pass.run` contract already says it does) and honour them here. Today
`ApplyMarksPass` returns `("body",)` and `TokensPass` returns `("tokens",)`, but nothing consumes
either.

#### 4.3 Weaknesses of the insertion model and the manager, and the alternatives

These two files are 126 lines together and carry the whole extensibility story, so their
trade-offs are worth stating rather than leaving to be inferred.

**The `Region` is a *window*, and the policy that collapses it lives somewhere else.** An analysis
answers "anywhere in `(after, before)`" and `PlacementPass` (§11.10) picks the point — earliest
for a TDM descriptor edit, midpoint for an LDS read swap. That separation is the reason a
placement policy could be changed without touching a single analysis, and it is right. The two
costs are real, though. First, **the window is not verified**: a malformed window (`hi < lo`)
falls back to `region.before` instead of raising, which is S11 in §19.2.8 — an analysis that
computed its window backwards produces a plausible placement rather than an error. Second, the
window is expressed as *node identities* in a *named block*, and nothing checks that the anchor
node is actually in that block; S1 and S12 together mean a Region naming a node in the wrong block
silently lands the Mark at the end of some other block. **The alternative** — a Region expressed
as `(block, slot_lo, slot_hi)` integer slots rather than node anchors — would make both failures
structurally impossible, and was rejected because slots are invalidated by every insertion while
node identities survive them. That reasoning is sound *given* mutable nodes (§3.7 item 1); it is
another thing an immutable IR would change. The assertion named in S1 —
`assert pm.anchor[0] == pm.region.block` — will NOT catch it: `PlacementPass._resolve` builds the
anchor as `(region.block, …)` on every path, so that equality holds by construction. The check has to
sit where the failure actually is: `_slot` (`placement.py:53-56`) and `ApplyMarks._anchor_index`
(`apply_marks.py:53-54`) must raise instead of silently returning `0`/`len(body)` when the anchor node
is not found in the body.

**`invalidate(names=None)` accepts a parameter it ignores, and the honest reading is that
per-name invalidation was designed and never needed.** Three things make it free to leave alone:
the cache key already contains `prog.version`, so a stale entry is *unreachable* rather than
wrong; the CFG is 4–12 blocks; and the analyses that would be re-run are the cheap ones. The
alternative — honour the returned names — is about ten lines and is written out in §19.5.2 (S5)
and §20.20. **Do not do it speculatively.** The reason is not cost, it is that a *partial*
invalidation is a correctness surface: today the only way to get a stale result is to mutate
without bumping the version, which one grep finds; with per-name invalidation, a pass that
invalidates the wrong name set produces a stale-but-reachable result, which nothing finds. If the
persistent-loop work (§19.5.1) makes V an order of magnitude larger and this becomes a measurable
cost, the safe form is to keep the version key *and* the name filter, so a wrong name set is a
performance bug rather than a correctness one.

**The manager takes an instance, not a class, and nothing enforces purity.** Taking an instance is
what makes a parameterized analysis expressible at all, and the `cache_key` property is the seam.
But `run(self, prog, am)` is only *documented* to be pure — an analysis that mutated `prog` would
be cached under the pre-mutation version and would poison every later `get`. Three cheap guards
were considered: hashing the program before and after (too expensive to do per call, and the nodes
are unhashable — §3.7 item 1), snapshotting `prog.version` around the call and asserting it did
not change (**cheap, one line, and not implemented** — this is the one worth adding), and making
`run` take a read-only proxy (a large change for a discipline that has not yet been violated).

**What is *not* a weakness, and is worth saying because it looks like one.** The cache is
unbounded and never evicts. That is deliberate: one `Program` is built per kernel and discarded,
so the manager's lifetime is a single lowering; a cache with an eviction policy would add a knob
whose only effect is to make a repeated `get` occasionally slow.

---

### 5. `gir/refs.py` (155 lines) — the shared `Ref` accessors

#### 5.1 The idea: a read is per op-class, a copy is per movement

This is the smallest module in the package and the one that encodes the deepest asymmetry. Three
other modules need the same answer to "which operand(s) does this `Move`'s shared hop belong to",
and each of them used to compute it by taking the first shared `Ref`. That is wrong for a
**Φ-fused** movement, which carries one `Ref` *per member*.

The distinction:

- A **read** is per op-class. A's read and B's read are different instructions at different
  addresses; their unit is a singleton by construction.
- A **copy** is per **movement**. A fuse merges several global→shared op-classes into one
  cooperative instruction with one completion class, so its identity — and the identity of the
  pointer it advances and swaps — is the **group**.

Two module constants: `SHARED = "shared"` (`:23`), `REGISTER = "register"` (`:24`).

#### 5.2 The functions

**`shared_refs(refs)` (`gir/refs.py:27`)** — every `Ref` in `refs` residing in shared space, in
order. One line.

**`first_shared_ref(refs)` (`gir/refs.py:32`)** — the single shared `Ref`, or `None`. For the
**read** hop, where the source is one op-class's shared tile and a second shared source would be a
different movement, not a member of this one.

**`_rotation_state(ref)` (`gir/refs.py:44`)** — the rotation state a shared `Ref` names, as a
comparable key: `(gen.ring or None, gdelta, abs_gen)`.

Deliberately **not** the `Gen` itself. `Gen.id` distinguishes independently-staged buffer sets, and
a fused movement fills *both*: A's LDS region and B's are different memory, so different ids is the
correct model, not a discrepancy. What makes them one pointer is that they rotate in **lockstep** —
same ring depth, same offset — so a single register value serves every member at every point.
Comparing ids would reject every real fuse; comparing the rotation state is the actual soundness
condition.

**`copy_unit(inst)` (`gir/refs.py:58`)** — the module's centrepiece. Returns
`(members, refs)` for a global→shared copy `Move`, or `(None, None)`.

```
copy_unit(inst):
    if inst is not a Move:            return (None, None)
    refs = shared_refs(inst.dsts)
    if refs is empty:                 return (None, None)
    states = { _rotation_state(r) for r in refs }
    if |states| > 1:                  RAISE          # one pointer is false
    return (tuple(r.tile.operand for r in refs), refs)
```

`members` is `('A',)` unfused, `('A','B')` for the fused group. The lockstep check is the point: if
the members disagree on rotation, "one pointer" is false and every downstream conclusion (one swap,
one increment) is unsound. Naming the movement by `refs[0].tile.operand` instead happens to give
the right *instruction count* when the descriptor really is aliased, and is simply wrong the moment
a fused group keeps two pointers. Being right by accident is not the same as being modelled.

**`read_operand(inst)` (`gir/refs.py:95`)** — the operand of a shared→register read `Move`, or
`None`. Requires both a shared source and at least one register destination, which is what excludes
a copy and a direct-to-register global read.

**`covered_coords(ref, extent=None) -> tuple` (`gir/refs.py:105`)** — every coordinate one
reference fills: the movement quantum's absorbed axes, re-inserted.

```
covered_coords(ref):
    axes = ref.covers or ()
    if not axes:      return (ref.tile.coord,)          # every ordinary read
    named = {a for a,_ in ref.tile.coord}
    out = [ref.tile.coord]
    for (name, ext) in axes:
        if name already in named or ext <= 1:  continue  # no-op, not an error
        out = [ c + ((name, v),) for c in out for v in range(ext) ]
    return tuple(out)
```

Three properties are load-bearing:

1. **It is useless alone.** Because the axis is gone from the read's presence upstream, the
   definition's coordinate does not name it while every consumer's does. This cross product is what
   makes the one definition readable as filling all of them. Applying the upstream subtraction
   without this is measurable, not subtle — the short-arm analysis reports "16 consumers read a
   location the arm never writes" at the microscaled-fp8 shape.
2. **It is a re-insertion, not a preimage.** An earlier form kept the axis in the coordinate and
   asked the merge map for `{t : carrier(t) == carrier(self)}`. That is the same set, but it can
   only be computed while the coordinate still exists — and the whole point of the quantum is that
   it does not.
3. **One definition, many locations — not many definitions.** The instruction is a single
   completion event, so the IR keeps a single `Ref`; what expands is the set of places an analysis
   considers written.

The `extent` parameter is accepted and unused in the current body; it is a vestige of the preimage
form.

**`_tile_axis_of(coord)` (`gir/refs.py:142`)** — the last coordinate entry, as `(name, value)`, or
`(None, None)` when the coord is empty. The tile coordinate is appended last by convention.
**Currently unreferenced** anywhere in the package (`grep -rn _tile_axis_of` finds only the
definition) — dead since the preimage form was removed, and a candidate for deletion along with
`_extent_hint` and `covered_coords`'s `extent` parameter.

**`_extent_hint(ref) -> int` (`gir/refs.py:150`)** — `max(1, size_regs) * 8`, a bound on the tile
values to scan for a preimage. Also **unreferenced** today, same vestige.

**Complexity.** `covered_coords` is O(∏ extents) in the covered axes, which is 1 for A and B (no
`covers`) and 2 for the merged scale reads. `copy_unit` is O(|dsts|), at most 2. This module is
never a cost.

#### 5.3 Weaknesses, dead code and extension notes

155 lines, eight functions, and it is the smallest file in the package that anything can go
seriously wrong in — because it answers *identity* questions, and a wrong identity is a wrong
analysis everywhere downstream rather than a local error.

**Two of the eight functions are dead, and both for the same reason.** `_tile_axis_of` (`:142`)
and `_extent_hint` (`:150`) are unreferenced anywhere in the tree, and `covered_coords`' `extent`
parameter (`:105`) is accepted and unused. All three are vestiges of the *preimage* formulation
that `covered_coords` replaced: the old code kept the absorbed axis in the coordinate and asked
"which tiles map to my carrier", which needed the tile axis and a bound on the values to scan. The
re-insertion form needs neither. **Delete all three together** — that is the whole cleanup, it has
no dependants, and leaving them invites someone to reconstruct the preimage form from the parts
that are still lying around. Recorded as S6 in §19.2.8.

**The asymmetry is the design, and it is the thing most likely to be "fixed" by mistake.** A copy
is named by a member *tuple* and a read by a bare operand *string*. It reads like an
inconsistency, and the temptation is to make reads return `('A',)` for symmetry. Do not: the
tuple exists because a Φ fuse merges op-classes into one instruction with **one completion event**
and therefore one pointer, and a read has no such merging — two reads of A and B are two
instructions, two completions, two register destinations. Making them symmetric would make the
type say a fuse is possible where it is not, and `copy_unit`'s lockstep check (the one thing
standing between a fused pointer and silent corruption) would have nothing to guard. §8.2 and
§13.5 both depend on the distinction being visible in the type.

**`copy_unit` raises, and that is the only place in this file that can.** If the members of one
copy disagree on rotation state, "one pointer" is false and it raises rather than picking a
member. Two things follow. First, **every caller must be prepared for a raise** — today they all
are, because the raise is unreachable on any program the lowering builds (θ only fuses lockstep
movements), which means it is also **untested against a real program**: the fixture that exercises
it is synthetic. Second, the raise is the *only* enforcement of the lockstep precondition
anywhere; there is no verifier invariant for it. If you ever make fusing a decision GIR takes
rather than one it inherits, that raise must become a `G-*` check first.

**What this file cannot express, and where it will bite.** `_rotation_state` compares
`(ring, gdelta, abs_gen)`, which is exactly right for "do these rotate together" and says nothing
about *where* they live. Two members that rotate in lockstep but sit in unrelated LDS regions are
one pointer by this test — correct today, because a fused descriptor is genuinely one descriptor
— but it means the file cannot answer "may these two be fused?" as a *question*, only "are these
two consistent with having been fused?". The distinction matters for #216 (a third pointer for the
GL2 prefetch path), which will want the first question.

**Extension notes.** Adding an accessor here is cheap and almost always the right move when two
modules disagree about a ref-derived fact: that is the file's whole history — `copy_unit` exists
because three modules had three answers to "which movement is this". The rules: (1) take the
*instruction* or the *ref list*, never the program, so the function stays testable without a CFG;
(2) return `(None, None)` for "not applicable" and raise only for "the IR is inconsistent" —
`copy_unit` is the model for both halves; (3) import only `..nodes`, so `refs.py` stays at the
bottom of the dependency graph where every analysis can reach it; and (4) if the new accessor
derives a fact an analysis currently computes inline, delete the inline copy in the same change,
or you have added a third answer rather than removing a second.

---

### 6. `gir/analyses/` I — the foundational analyses

`gir/analyses/` holds fifteen modules plus the package `__init__`. This section covers the five
that everything else stands on: `cfg.py`, `gen_reaching.py`, `dep_defuse.py`, `reg_band.py` and
`loop_shape.py`. Here, in order: **§6.1** `cfg.py`, **§6.2** `gen_reaching.py`, **§6.3**
`dep_defuse.py`, **§6.4** `loop_shape.py`, **§6.5** `reg_band.py`, closing with a comparison table
at **§6.6**.

**Where the other ten analyses are.** They are large enough that each got its own top-level
section rather than a subsection here, and every reference in this report points at the section
that actually holds the text:

| module | question it answers | section |
|---|---|---|
| `value_placement.py` | the shared AVAIL/ANTIC solver both pointer analyses run on | §7.2 |
| `swap_regions.py` | where the LDS buffer pointers flip | §7.3 |
| `gr_increment.py` | where the global-read address advances | §7.4 |
| `region_increment.py` | where the descriptor steps between storage regions | §7.5 |
| `mem_tokens.py` | the LDS memory-token (alias-class) numbering | §8.1–§8.12 |
| `fence_regions.py` | the minimal fence cover over the cross-agent hazards | §8.13–§8.23 |
| `lds_hazards.py` | RAW/WAR/WAW over the shared space, with trip distance | §9 |
| `short_path.py` | may the degenerate short-trip arm be folded away? | §10.1–§10.16 |
| `uniform_placement.py` | does every agent of a fence's scope reach it? | §10.17–§10.21 |

#### 6.0 What "foundational" means here, and the standard these five are held to

Two of these five are consumed by nearly everything downstream. `Dominators` and `BackEdges`
(§6.1) give every other analysis its notion of "loop" without any node in the IR claiming to be
one. `GenReaching` (§6.2) turns the IR's single SSA value — the rotating LDS buffer generation —
into a concrete integer per access, and five separate consumers (`TokensPass`,
`MemTokenAssignment`, `LdsHazards`, and through them `FenceRegions` and the verifier's token
check) read nothing else to decide which physical buffer an instruction touches. The other three
are narrower: `DepDefuse` (§6.3) indexes facts the lowering already attached, `RegBand` (§6.5)
cross-checks one integer per operand group, and `LoopShape` (§6.4) derives the loop's shape and
trip count from the CFG so the verifier can check that the pipeline covers the reduction exactly
once.

This package has been burned, more than once, by a module that used dataflow *vocabulary* for what
was structurally a pattern match. The canonical instance is recorded in the source itself: the
global-read-address analysis (`gr_increment.py`, §7.4) carried a docstring asserting it was "a
reaching-definition over the WHOLE CFG" while its body was the rule *"if this block is a loop
header and its back edge carries a generation transfer, emit one Mark per copy"*. With a
multi-block steady body those two filters become mutually exclusive — the non-header copies fail
the first, and the header fails the second because the back edge leaves the *last* body block, not
the header — so the analysis emitted **zero** increments in every steady block, the global address
never advanced, and every trip re-fetched the same tiles (`gir/analyses/gr_increment.py:15-23`).
It produced no results at all under a shape it had not anticipated, and nothing in its name or its
docstring said so.

So this section states, for every one of the five, and separately:

| | what is asked |
|---|---|
| **domain / lattice** | what the values are, and how they order |
| **direction** | forward, backward, or none |
| **transfer function** | what one program point does to a value |
| **meet** | how values from several predecessors combine |
| **fixpoint** | is it iterated, and why does it terminate |
| **complexity** | big-O, and the practical value of *n* |

And where the honest answer is *"this is not a dataflow analysis"*, that is said in those words.
Two of the five are not:

| module | class | honest classification |
|---|---|---|
| `cfg.py` | `Dominators` | a **real** iterative dataflow fixpoint (forward, meet = ∩) |
| `cfg.py` | `BackEdges` | a **derived relation**: one O(E) scan over the dominator result, no fixpoint |
| `gen_reaching.py` | `GenReaching` | a **real** forward dataflow, on a flat (constant-propagation-shaped) lattice — but solved in *one* reverse-postorder sweep rather than by iteration, for a reason given in §6.2.5 |
| `dep_defuse.py` | `DepDefuseAnalysis` | **not** an analysis: an index over facts already on the nodes. No lattice, no direction, no fixpoint. It is honest about this in its own docstring ("it only reads `deps` already on the nodes") |
| `reg_band.py` | `RegBandAnalysis` | **not** an analysis: a must-agree fold over one integer per key, whose "conflict" lattice element is spelled as a raised exception rather than a value |
| `loop_shape.py` | `LoopShape` | a **structural derivation** over the natural loop plus an exact linear-arithmetic check. It contains one transitive-closure computation (`_loop_blocks`) but no lattice and no meet |

Being in the last three categories is not a defect; it is a defect only when the module *claims*
otherwise. None of these three does.

#### 6.1 `cfg.py` (106 lines) — dominators and back edges

##### 6.1.1 Concept: a loop is a graph property, not a node kind

GIR has no loop node. `Block.loop` is a bool that the lowering sets, `Block.phase` is a string
that starts with `'steady'`, and neither is trusted by anything that needs to know where the loop
is. The single authority is **dominance**: a CFG edge `src → target` is a back edge exactly when
`target` dominates `src` (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:96-106`).

The reason is stated in the module docstring (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:6-8`) and it is forward-looking
rather than aesthetic. A future *persistent* or grid-stride kernel wraps the whole main loop —
prologue, steady, drain — in a second outer loop over work tiles. That outer loop has a header, a
latch and a back edge exactly like the reduction loop does, and it has no `phase` name and no
`loop` flag that the current lowering would set. An analysis that finds loops by dominance admits
it with **no code change**; an analysis that finds them by `blk.loop` or by `phase.startswith`
silently reports one loop where there are two. The same argument already pays off inside the
current shape: a multi-block steady chain (`loop_copies = n`, three fall-through blocks sharing
one back edge) is one loop with one header, and `blk.loop` set on all three would say three.

The module imports only `gir/nodes.successor_labels` and the `Analysis` base
(`gir/analyses/cfg.py:13-14`) — no other analysis, so it is the root of the intra-package
dependency graph.

##### 6.1.2 `successors(prog)` (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:17`)

```
successors(prog) -> {label: [successor labels present in prog.blocks]}
```

A plain function, **not** an `Analysis` — it is cheap, it is needed by callers that have no
`AnalysisManager` in hand, and caching a dict comprehension over twelve blocks would cost more
than recomputing it. It delegates the terminator switch to `nodes.successor_labels`
(`gir/nodes.py:342`, described in §3.6) and adds exactly one thing: it **filters targets against
`prog.blocks`**, which drops the pseudo-target `'end'`. `successor_labels` deliberately does not
filter, because a verifier wants to see a dangling target; a graph walk wants it gone. Splitting
the responsibility this way is why there is one switch and not two.
