Its callers are `Dominators.run` here — `BackEdges.run` is *not* one, it calls `successor_labels` directly and applies the `prog.blocks` filter inline (§6.1.6) — plus `gr_increment.py:59`, `fence_regions.py:46`,
`swap_regions.py:68`, `lds_hazards.py:65`, `uniform_placement.py:63` and — through a
function-local import — `loop_shape._loop_blocks` (`gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:90`). That local
import is not laziness for a cycle: `loop_shape` already imports `BackEdges` from `.cfg` at module
scope (`:45`), so there is no cycle to avoid and the local import is simply inconsistent. Hoisting
it to the module header is a safe one-line cleanup.

**Complexity.** O(V + E). V is the block count — 4 to 12 in every kernel this package produces
(one prologue, one or two steady, `M` drains, up to `M` short-arm blocks, occasionally a tail) —
and E ≈ 2V because every terminator has at most two targets except a `CondChain`, whose arm count
is bounded by `M`.

##### 6.1.3 `Dominators` (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:23`) and `Dominators.run` (`:27`)

The textbook iterative dominator computation. Result: `{label: set(labels that dominate it)}`,
where by convention every block dominates itself.

**Domain / lattice.** For each block, an element is a *set of block labels*. The lattice is the
powerset of `prog.blocks` ordered by **superset**: `⊤` is the full label set (`all_set`, "we know
nothing yet, so assume every block might dominate"), `⊥` is the empty set. Larger sets are higher.
The solution is the **greatest** fixpoint reachable from the initial assignment, which is why the
iteration only ever *shrinks* sets.

**Direction.** Forward — information flows from predecessors to successors.

**Meet.** Set **intersection** over the predecessors. A block is dominated by `d` iff *every*
path from the entry passes through `d`, and intersection is exactly the "every path" quantifier.

**Transfer function.** `f_n(X) = {n} ∪ X`. Adding the block itself is the only thing a block does
to the incoming set; there is no kill.

**Initialisation.** `dom(entry) = {entry}` and `dom(n) = all_set` for every other `n`
(`gir/analyses/cfg.py:37`). The optimistic (⊤) initialisation of the non-entry blocks is what
makes the greatest fixpoint reachable; initialising to `∅` would produce the trivial and useless
least fixpoint `dom(n) = {n}`.

```
Dominators.run(prog):
    succ  = successors(prog)                       # 'end' already dropped
    preds = invert(succ)                           # {label: [predecessor labels]}
    dom[entry]      = {entry}
    dom[n != entry] = all_labels                   # TOP
    repeat until no change:
        for n in labels (INSERTION ORDER):
            if n == entry: continue
            inter = intersection over p in preds[n] of dom[p]
            if preds[n] is empty: inter = {}        # unreachable block
            new = {n} | inter
            if new != dom[n]: dom[n] = new; changed = True
    return dom
```

**Fixpoint and termination.** The transfer and meet are monotone, and every update strictly
shrinks a finite set (`new != dom[lab]` can only fire on a decrease, because `{n} ∪ ∩preds` can
never grow once the predecessors have stopped growing). The total descent is bounded by
`V` blocks × `V` labels = V² element removals, so the round-robin loop runs at most O(V) sweeps.

**Complexity.** O(V) sweeps × O(E) meets × O(V) per set operation = **O(V²·E)** worst case, with a
practical V of 4–12 and E of roughly 2V, so a handful of microseconds. It is called once per
`AnalysisManager` per `Program` version and shared by `BackEdges`, `FenceRegions`
(`gir/analyses/fence_regions.py:263`) and, transitively, everything that asks for `BackEdges`.

**Three honest observations about the implementation.**

1. **It iterates in insertion order, not reverse postorder.** Sweeping in RPO is the standard and
   free improvement: it makes the round-robin converge in one pass plus one confirming pass on a
   reducible CFG, instead of up to `depth+2`. `Program.walk_rpo()` already exists
   (`gir/nodes.py:487`) and returns exactly the order wanted. At V = 12 the difference is
   unmeasurable, which is why nobody has done it; at V in the hundreds — the persistent-loop shape
   the module docstring anticipates — it is the first thing to change.

2. **The guard `rp = [p for p in preds[lab] if p in dom]` (`:45`) is vestigial.** `dom` is
   initialised with a key for *every* label and `preds` is built only from labels that exist in
   `prog.blocks`, so `p in dom` is unconditionally true. It is a leftover from a version that
   populated `dom` incrementally. Harmless, but it reads as if unreachable predecessors were being
   handled, and they are not — see the next point.

3. **An unreachable block gets `dom = {itself}`, not `⊤`.** With `preds[lab]` empty the code sets
   `inter = ∅` and hence `new = {lab}` (`:50-52`). Formally, an unreachable block should keep the
   ⊤ value (everything dominates it vacuously). The chosen answer is the more useful one for the
   one consumer that could care: a self-loop on an unreachable block still reports as a back edge,
   because `lab ∈ dom[lab]` holds. It is a deliberate deviation from the textbook, undocumented in
   the source, and worth a comment.

**A faster data structure, if it ever matters.** Two options, in increasing order of effort.
(a) Represent each dominator set as a Python `int` bitmask over a fixed label indexing; `&` on
integers replaces `set.__and__` and the inner loop becomes a single machine word operation for any
V ≤ 64. (b) Replace the set formulation entirely with the immediate-dominator formulation
(iterating over `idom` pointers and walking up the tree to intersect), which is O(E·log V) in
practice and gives you the dominator *tree* for free — useful if a future pass needs "the nearest
common dominator of these two blocks", which the current set representation answers only by
intersecting and then finding the deepest member.

##### 6.1.4 `BackEdge` (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:59`) and `BackEdge.__init__` (`:63`)

A plain (non-dataclass) three-field record:

```
BackEdge.src     : str          block LABEL the back edge leaves from (the latch)
BackEdge.header  : str          block LABEL it targets (the loop header)
BackEdge.xfers   : list[GenXfer]  a COPY of the src block's xfers list
```

`xfers` is the design point. A `GenXfer` (`gir/nodes.py:447`) is the statement
`v' = (v + adv) % ring` for one generation across one back edge, and it lives on the *latch*
block. Carrying the list on the edge object means `GenReaching` can ask "what transfers apply when
I leave this block?" and get the answer per edge, instead of reaching into `blk.xfers[0]` and
assuming a block has exactly one back edge with exactly one transfer. That assumption is false the
moment a block latches two loops (the persistent shape) or stages two operands on independently
sized rings. The list is copied (`list(blk.xfers)`, `:105`) so a later mutation of the block does
not retroactively change an already-computed analysis result — though in practice the version bump
would have invalidated it anyway.

##### 6.1.5 `BackEdgeSet` (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:69`) — the query surface

A thin wrapper over `list[BackEdge]` with four members.

- **`__init__(edges)` (`:70`)** — `self._edges = list(edges)`; materialises whatever iterable it
  is handed.
- **`__iter__()` (`:73`)** — iterate the edges. This is how nearly every consumer uses it:
  `{be.header for be in back}` in `SwapRegions` (`gir/analyses/swap_regions.py:230`),
  `{(be.src, be.header) for be in back}` in `GrIncrementRegions`
  (`gir/analyses/gr_increment.py:125`), `{be.src for be in back}` in `ScaffoldMapPass`
  (`gir/passes/scaffold_map.py:59`), and `for be in am.get(BackEdges(), prog)` in `LoopShape`
  (`gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:149`).
- **`leaving(label)` (`:76`)** — back edges whose **source** is `label`. One caller:
  `GenReaching.run` (`gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py:134`), which needs the transfers that apply
  when control leaves a block.
- **`entering(label)` (`:87`)** — back edges whose **target (header)** is `label`. **Currently has
  no caller anywhere in the tree** (verified by grep over all of `Tensile/`). It is the natural
  counterpart of `leaving` and is kept for symmetry; a maintainer should know it is untested by
  use.
- **`is_back_edge(src, target)` (`:91`)** — membership test, O(|edges|) by linear scan. **Also has
  no caller.** If either of these two ever acquires a hot caller, back the set with a
  `{(src, header)}` frozenset — most consumers already build exactly that set themselves, so a
  fourth accessor returning it would remove three duplications.

**The naming defect this class records.** `leaving` used to be called `headed_by`, and it filtered
on `be.src` the whole time. For the single-block steady loop `src == header`, so the name and the
behaviour coincided and nothing showed. With a multi-block steady body they diverge: the back edge
leaves the *last* copy while the header is the *first*, so `headed_by(header)` returned the empty
list — the exact opposite of what its name promised. `GrIncrementRegions` asked
`headed_by(header)`, got nothing, and emitted no global-read-address increments at all
(`gir/analyses/gr_increment.py:22-23`, and the docstring on `leaving` itself at
`gir/analyses/cfg.py:82-84`). The rename is the fix, and the docstring is deliberately blunt about
it because the next accessor added here will face the same temptation.

##### 6.1.6 `BackEdges` (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:95`) and `BackEdges.run` (`:99`)

```
BackEdges.run(prog, am):
    dom = am.get(Dominators(), prog)
    for (lab, blk) in prog.blocks.items():
        for s in successor_labels(blk):
            if s in prog.blocks and s in dom[lab]:
                emit BackEdge(src=lab, header=s, xfers=list(blk.xfers))
    return BackEdgeSet(edges)
```

**Classification.** Not a fixpoint — a single O(E) scan over an already-computed dominator
relation, with a dictionary lookup and a set membership per edge. Its cost is entirely the
`Dominators` it demands, which the `AnalysisManager` has usually already cached.

**Ordering.** Edges come out in `prog.blocks` insertion order, then in successor order within a
block. Every consumer treats the result as a set, so this is not load-bearing — but it is stable,
which is what makes GIR dumps reproducible.

**Note it calls `successor_labels` directly (`:103`), not the local `successors` helper.** That
means it does *not* pre-filter, and instead applies the `s in prog.blocks` test inline. The two
are equivalent; the direct call avoids materialising the whole successor dict a second time when
`Dominators` has already built one. It is a micro-optimisation that also creates a second place
where the `'end'` filter is spelled out.

##### 6.1.7 What the tests pin

`test_gir.py` never tests `Dominators` or `BackEdges` in isolation; it tests them through the CFG
shapes that historically broke them, which is the more useful contract:

- **A multi-exit header must not confuse back-edge detection.**
  `test_condchain_arms_are_ordinary_forward_edges` (`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:1039`) builds a header
  whose terminator is a two-arm `CondChain` into two drain variants with a default into the steady
  loop, then asserts both that `successors(prog)["head"] == ["d0", "d1", "steady"]` — arm order
  preserved, because the first satisfied arm wins and a set would lose that — and that
  `{e.header for e in BackEdges} == {"steady"}`. Before `successor_labels` was extracted, a
  `CondChain` had no successors as far as the traversal was concerned.
- **A `Return` sink contributes no edges.** `test_return_is_a_sink_with_no_successors`
  (`:1179`) asserts `successors(prog)["drain0"] == []`, and
  `test_return_renders_and_survives_dominance` (`:1191`) asserts that `BackEdges` and `Dominators`
  simply skip a terminator with no targets rather than raising.
- **A multi-block steady chain is ONE loop with ONE back edge.**
  `test_loop_copies_chain_shape` (`:1103`, parameterised over `n ∈ {1,2,3}`) asserts
  `[(e.src, e.header) for e in BackEdges] == [(f"steady{n-1}", "steady")]` — the shape whose
  misreading produced the zero-increment defect above.
- **A tail loop is a legitimate second loop region.**
  `test_tail_loop_is_an_accepted_second_loop_region` (`:1238`) asserts
  `{e.header for e in BackEdges} == {"steady", "tail"}`, and the verifier's own CFG check excludes
  the tail *by phase* so that the reduction-loop header count stays exactly one
  (`gir/verify.py:203-210`).

##### 6.1.8 Alternatives weighed, and extension notes for `cfg.py`

**Why the iterative bit-vector dominator solver, and not Lengauer–Tarjan or Cooper–Harvey–Kennedy.**
`Dominators.run` is the textbook iterative fixpoint: initialise every block to "all labels",
sweep in insertion order intersecting predecessors' sets, repeat until nothing changes. Its cost
is `O(V²·E)` in the worst case and it allocates a set per block per round. The two standard
alternatives are strictly better asymptotically — Lengauer–Tarjan is near-linear, and
Cooper–Harvey–Kennedy's immediate-dominator form is `O(V·E)` with tiny constants and about twenty
lines. Neither is here, and the reasoning is not "nobody got around to it":

- **V is 4–12.** One prologue, one or two steady blocks, `M` drains, up to `M` short blocks. At
  those sizes the iterative solver converges in two or three rounds and costs microseconds; §20.4
  measures the round counts directly. An asymptotic win on a twelve-node graph is not a win.
- **The set-of-labels form is what the *consumers* want.** `BackEdges` needs the dominance
  *relation* (`is x dominated by y`) on arbitrary pairs, and the verifier's CFG checks ask the
  same question. Cooper–Harvey–Kennedy computes the immediate-dominator *tree*, from which the
  relation is a walk up the tree — correct, but it turns a set membership into a loop, and the
  relation is queried far more often than it is built.
- **Insertion order is not RPO, and that is the part to watch.** The sweep visits blocks in
  `prog.blocks` insertion order. For the shapes this lowering builds, insertion order *is* a
  topological order of the forward edges, so convergence takes the minimum number of rounds. It
  is not guaranteed to be, and nothing checks it: a future pass that inserts a block out of order
  costs extra rounds (never a wrong answer — the fixpoint is order-independent). §6.6 observation
  1 names this as one of exactly two things that move if V grows by an order of magnitude, and the
  fix is one line: iterate `prog.walk_rpo()` instead of `prog.blocks.values()`.

**The honest summary:** the current solver is the right choice *today* and the wrong choice at
V ≈ 100. The trigger to revisit it is the persistent / grid-stride loop (§19.5.1), not a profile.

**Extension notes.** If you add a graph question — "which blocks are in this loop", "is this edge
critical", "what is the immediate dominator" — it belongs **in `cfg.py`**, and this is one of the
few placement rules in the package that is not a preference: `cfg.py` imports only `..nodes` and
`..analysis`, so it sits at the root of the analysis dependency graph, and importing any sibling
analysis into it would create a cycle. Three specific notes:

1. **Ask `successor_labels` (`gir/nodes.py:342`), never a local switch.** `cfg.successors` is a
   thin wrapper over it precisely so there is one authority; §19.4.1 records that three other
   copies of that switch exist and two are already incomplete.
2. **Do not filter unreachable blocks silently.** `walk_rpo` appends them defensively rather than
   dropping them, and `Dominators` gives an unreachable block the full label set. Both are
   deliberate: an unreachable block in this IR means a pass built one, which is a defect to be
   *seen*, not tidied away.
3. **A new derived relation should say it is derived.** `BackEdges` is one `O(E)` scan over the
   dominator result with no fixpoint, and §6.0's table classifies it as such. Anything similar —
   loop nesting depth, exit edges — is the same shape, and the classification belongs in the
   docstring for the reason §6.0 gives at length.

#### 6.2 `gen_reaching.py` (138 lines) — the concrete generation each access uses

##### 6.2.1 What a generation number *is*

An operand staged through LDS does not get one buffer; it gets a **ring** of `S` buffers, used
round-robin so that the copy filling chunk *k+1* does not overwrite the buffer the reads of chunk
*k* have not finished with. A **generation** is the index of one buffer in that ring: an integer
in `[0, S)`. Equivalently, it is the residue class of the reduction-chunk index modulo `S`. With
`S = 2` (double buffering) chunk 0, 2, 4 … live in generation 0 and chunk 1, 3, 5 … in generation
1; with `S = 1` every chunk lives in generation 0 and there is no rotation at all.

The generation is the **only** SSA value class in GIR (§3.2). It is loop-carried: defined by a
`GenPhi` at the loop header, advanced across the back edge by a `GenXfer` stating
`v' = (v + adv) mod ring`, and used by every `Ref` that names a shared residence. That is what
makes the question "which buffer does this instruction touch?" a textbook reaching-value problem
rather than an index-arithmetic exercise — and it is why the tree-shaped LoopIR could not answer
it: in the tree the buffer index is the *formula* `(k + 2) mod 2` over a loop variable that has no
program point, so there is no point at which to say "here, the value is 1".

##### 6.2.2 The three distinct things a value's residence can say

This distinction is the single most confusable thing in the IR, and the debug dump had to be
changed to spell the three apart after they were being read for one another
(`gir/render.py:25-41`). A `Ref` may carry any combination of:

1. **An SSA generation *identity*** — `ref.gen` (a `Gen` object) together with the constant offset
   `ref.gdelta`. The dump prints this as **`gen#<id>[v+<δ>]`**. It answers *"which phi feeds this,
   and how far past that phi's value does this access sit?"*. It is **not a number**: `v` is the
   loop-carried value, unknown at compile time in the general case. `Gen.id` distinguishes
   independently-rotating buffer sets — A's LDS ring and B's LDS ring are different memory and get
   different ids — and `Gen.ring` is `S`.

2. **A concrete generation *value*** — `ref.abs_gen`, an integer. The dump prints this as
   **`gen@<n>`**. A prologue peel access, or a short-arm access, knows exactly which buffer it
   touches because its chunk index is a compile-time constant. Such a `Ref` carries no `Gen` at
   all. This is the *only* residence field that is a physical buffer index straight out of the
   lowering.

3. **A register residence** — `ref.group`, `ref.slot`, `ref.reg_ring`. The dump prints this as
   **`reg(g<group>,s<slot>/W<ring>)`**. This is the *other* rotation in the kernel and it is
   unrelated to the LDS ring: registers rotate with width `W` (`ref.reg_ring`, §6.5) over slots
   `0..W-1` within a partition `group`. `W` is printed beside the slot precisely because `s1` of a
   2-deep ring and `s1` of a 4-deep ring are different residences and were indistinguishable.

The renderer used to spell (1) as `gen0[v]` and (2) as `gen=0` — one character apart, in the same
dump, for an SSA identity and a concrete integer — and to chain the three as `if/if/if` with early
returns, so a `Ref` that carried *both* a generation and a register residence showed only the
first. A shared read's destination register was therefore invisible whenever its source generation
was pinned. Both are fixed (`gir/render.py:29-41`).

**And `GenReaching` produces a fourth thing that the dump does not print**: for a `Ref` of form
(1), the *resolved* concrete generation `(entry_value_of_gen + gdelta) mod ring`. That number is
the analysis's whole output. It is what `TokensPass` stamps and what `LdsHazards` compares, and it
is **not** a field on the `Ref` — asking for it always means going through `Reaching.of(ref)`.
Keeping it off the node is deliberate: it is a *derived* fact that depends on which block the
instruction sits in, and a field would invite someone to read it without the frame.

##### 6.2.3 The result object: `Reaching` (`gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py:22`)

The analysis returns a `Reaching`, not a raw dict, and the reason is the keying. The internal maps
are **identity-keyed** — `id(ref)` — because a `Ref` is not hashable in a way that distinguishes
two structurally identical uses in different blocks, and because two `Ref`s with the same fields in
the *same* block are genuinely the same use. Identity keys are only valid while the keyed objects
are alive: CPython reuses `id()` values after garbage collection, so a stale `by_ref` map applied
to a freshly allocated `Ref` would silently return a *different* instruction's generation. The
mitigation is `Reaching._prog` (`:27`), a reference to the `Program` held purely so the `Ref`s
reachable from `prog.blocks[…].body[…].srcs/dsts` cannot be collected for the result's lifetime.

That mitigation is sound but not free-standing, and a maintainer should know its edge: it protects
against *collection*, not against *replacement*. If a pass deleted a `Move` from a body and a new
`Ref` happened to land on the freed id, a `Reaching` computed before the deletion would be wrong.
Nothing does that today — `ApplyMarksPass` only *inserts* `Mark`s — and any mutation bumps
`prog.version`, which makes the `AnalysisManager` key miss and the stale result unreachable
(§4.2). The identity keying is nevertheless the sharpest edge in this file, and it is exactly the
pattern the package's own convention says to encapsulate behind a result API. `Reaching` **is**
that encapsulation: no caller sees `id(...)`.

The four members:

- **`Reaching.__init__(prog, by_ref, by_xfer, relative_blocks=())` (`:26`)** — stores the program,
  the two maps, and freezes the relative-block set. Shapes:

  ```
  by_ref   : {id(Ref) -> int}                      the concrete generation that Ref uses
  by_xfer  : {(block_label, Gen.id) -> int}        the NEXT trip's entry generation for that Gen
  _relative: frozenset[str]                        block labels whose entry frame is arbitrary
  ```

- **`Reaching.of(ref)` (`:32`)** — the concrete generation `ref` uses, or `None` if the `Ref`
  carries no generation at all (a global source, or a register-only destination). The docstring
  (`:33-38`) carries the caution that makes this API usable: **for a block reported by
  `is_relative`, the returned value sits on an arbitrary base.** It is meaningful only *relative to
  other values in the same block*, never as an absolute buffer identity, and never comparable
  across blocks. A consumer needing an absolute generation must check the flag and widen or refuse.

- **`Reaching.is_relative(block_label) -> bool` (`:41`)** — true when that block's entry
  generations could not be merged from its predecessors.

- **`Reaching.xfer(block_label, gen)` (`:46`)** — the next-trip entry generation for the back edge
  leaving `block_label`, for the `Gen` object `gen`. Keyed by `gen.id`, so a program with two
  independently-rotating rings gets two answers from one block. **No caller in the tree today**;
  it is the counterpart of `of()` for the loop-carried edge and exists because the information is
  computed anyway during the sweep. If you are pruning, this and the `by_xfer` map it fronts are
  the candidates — but note that any future analysis that wants to reason across a trip boundary
  (a loop-carried hazard that needs the *next* trip's buffer, say) will want exactly this.

##### 6.2.4 The lattice, the meet, and where relativity comes from

**Domain.** Per block, a map `Gen -> int`, i.e. one *concrete generation* per independently
rotating buffer set. Per `Gen`, the value domain is a **flat lattice** — a constant-propagation
lattice — with:

```
                          TOP  ("no information yet": the Gen is absent from the map)
                        /  |  \
                       0   1   ...  ring-1        the concrete generations
                        \  |  /
                         BOTTOM  ("no compile-time constant exists")
```

**The implementation does not spell `BOTTOM` as a symbol.** It spells it as the pair
*(value = `RELATIVE_BASE`, block flagged relative)* — `RELATIVE_BASE = 0`
(`gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py:66`). That is a real design decision with a real cost and a real
benefit, and both should be understood before touching it. The cost: `0` is also a perfectly
legitimate concrete generation, so the value alone cannot tell you which case you are in — you
*must* consult `is_relative`, and a consumer that forgets gets a plausible-looking wrong answer.
The benefit: everything downstream that only needs the *relative* distinction inside a block
("this access and that access are on different buffers") keeps working unchanged, because
consistent offsets from an arbitrary base preserve differences. Given that the dominant consumer —
the LDS memory token — is documented as a *logical* buffer name whose only requirement is the
this-buffer-vs-other-buffer distinction, that is the right trade. It is nevertheless the place a
future reader will be misled, and naming `RELATIVE_BASE` a sentinel object rather than the integer
`0` would make the misuse a `TypeError` instead of a wrong number.

**Meet.** Agreement-or-bottom over the known predecessors, per `Gen`:

```
meet(v1, ..., vk) = v          if k == number of known preds and all vi equal v
                  = BOTTOM     otherwise   (disagreement, OR a pred that supplies nothing)
```

Note the second disjunct: a `Gen` that *some* predecessor supplies and another does not is bottom,
not "inherit the one that has it". That is correct — an unsupplied `Gen` on one path means the
value entering along that path is unknown, which is exactly disagreement.

**Direction.** Forward.

**Transfer.** Two rules, both at `gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py:129-137`:

```
for a Ref with a Gen:        of(ref)  = (entry[ref.gen] + ref.gdelta) mod max(1, ref.gen.ring)
for a Ref with abs_gen:      of(ref)  = ref.abs_gen                     (no frame involved)
for a back edge's GenXfer:   xfer[b,g]= (entry[xf.gen] + xf.adv) mod max(1, xf.ring)
```

`max(1, ring)` guards a `ring` of 0, which the lowering should never produce; it turns a
would-be `ZeroDivisionError` into the ring-1 (in-place) answer. It does *not* guard a `None` ring:
`max(1, None)` raises `TypeError` in Python 3, so that half already fails loudly (and `ring` is
declared `int` on both `Gen` and `GenXfer`, so it should never be `None` anyway). Defensive, and arguably it should
raise instead — a ring of 0 is a lowering defect, and the package's stated rule is *report, never
silently resolve*.

##### 6.2.5 `_resolve_phi_entry(blk)` (`gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py:51`) — the cycle cut

```
_resolve_phi_entry(blk) -> {phi.gen: phi.entry_val for phi in blk.phis}
```

One line, and the most consequential one in the file: **a loop header's entry map is *declared*,
not merged.** A `GenPhi` (`gir/nodes.py:436`) stores only `entry_val`, the generation on the
loop-*entry* edge; the back-edge value is not stored at all. By keying the header on `entry_val`,
the analysis breaks the only cycle in the dataflow graph, and that is why **the whole analysis is
a single reverse-postorder sweep with no iteration** (§6.2.7).

The docstring (`:52-60`) is explicit that this **fixes a representative trip, not an invariant**,
and the reader must take that seriously. With `ring = 2` and `adv = 1`, trip 0 enters the header at
generation 0 and trip 1 at generation 1. `entry_val` names the first of those. So `of()` inside a
steady block is *the generation on the representative (first) trip*, and its absolute value is
therefore not a property of the static instruction. What **is** invariant is the *difference*
between two accesses in the same block: `gdelta` offsets are exact regardless of which trip you
are on, because both are shifted by the same unknown.

An earlier revision of this docstring asserted the equality — that `entry_val` was the value on
every trip — which is false and which invited reading `of()` as an absolute generation. It is
retracted in place, which is the right way to handle a wrong comment: deleting it would leave the
next reader free to re-derive the same mistake.

The sound consumers are the ones whose question is relative. The LDS memory token is a *logical*
buffer name; a token's only requirement is that two accesses to the same physical buffer get the
same name and two accesses to different buffers get different names, **within a body**. A uniform
shift of every generation by the unknown trip parity preserves both. A consumer whose question is
absolute — "is this the buffer the prologue filled?" — is not served, and §6.2.6 is about the one
that asked.

##### 6.2.6 `_entry_of(blk, entries, relative=())` (`gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py:69`)

The meet, implemented. Returns `(entry_map, is_relative_bool)`.

```
_entry_of(blk, entries, relative):
    if blk.phis:                                  # a loop header DECLARES its entry
        return _resolve_phi_entry(blk), False

    known = [entries[p] for p in blk.preds if p in entries]     # visited preds only
    if not known:
        return {}, bool(blk.preds)     # entry block: {} and NOT relative;
                                       # a block with preds but none visited: relative

    merged   = {}
    relative_here = any(p in relative for p in blk.preds if p in entries)   # TRANSITIVITY
    for gen in union of the keys of `known`:
        vals = [m[gen] for m in known if gen in m]
        if len(vals) == len(known) and all equal:
            merged[gen] = vals[0]              # a real merged value
        else:
            merged[gen] = RELATIVE_BASE        # no compile-time merge exists
            relative_here = True
    return merged, relative_here
```

Four things this encodes, each of which was a defect before it was:

**(a) The disagreement is real, not a modelling slip.** `drain0` has two predecessors: the last
steady block, and the prologue (on the degenerate path where the trip count does not exceed the
peel depth so the steady loop never runs). The generation the steady loop leaves behind is
**trip-parity dependent** — a runtime value — so *no* compile-time constant is the merged value.
This is not a case to be smoothed over; it is a genuine ⊥.

**(b) Returning `{}` and calling it "nothing to merge" was the original bug.** That silently based
everything at 0 and documented it as a fact rather than a placeholder, so a consumer could not
distinguish a merged generation from a fabricated one. One did read it as absolute, and produced a
spurious buffer swap in the drain (`:78-82`). The fix has two halves — flag it, *and* teach the
consumer that needed an absolute value to compute frame-free requirements instead (which is what
`SwapRegions` now does).

**(c) The "exactly one known predecessor → inherit" case needs no special handling.** One
predecessor trivially agrees with itself, so the general merge covers the fall-through chain of a
multi-block steady body for free (`:86-87`). Deleting the special case removed a divergent second
derivation.

**(d) Relativity is TRANSITIVE, and it was not.** This is the subtlest of the four. `drain1`'s only
predecessor is `drain0`; `drain0` is relative because its own two predecessors genuinely disagree.
Under rule (c), `drain1`'s single predecessor "trivially agrees with itself", the merge succeeds,
and the flag was dropped — so `drain1` reported `is_relative = False` while sitting on the very
same arbitrary base it inherited, and a consumer reading `of()` as an absolute buffer id got no
warning (`:89-95`). The `any(p in relative …)` seed at `:103` is the fix. The contract
*"`of()` is absolute unless flagged"* only actually holds along a chain because of that one line.

One asymmetry worth noting in the `not known` branch (`:99-101`): it returns `bool(blk.preds)` as
the relative flag. The *entry* block has no predecessors and is correctly not relative (its refs
carry `abs_gen`, so there is nothing to be relative about). A block that has predecessors but none
of them visited yet is flagged relative — a conservative and correct answer, but one that can only
arise if the RPO walk fails to order a block after its non-back-edge predecessors, i.e. on an
irreducible CFG. That case is unreachable today and unpinned by any test.

##### 6.2.7 `GenReaching` (`gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py:114`) and `GenReaching.run` (`:115`)

```
GenReaching.run(prog, am):
    back = am.get(BackEdges(), prog)
    by_ref, by_xfer, entries, relative = {}, {}, {}, set()

    for blk in prog.walk_rpo():                       # ONE sweep, reverse postorder
        entry, is_rel = _entry_of(blk, entries, relative)
        entries[blk.label] = entry
        if is_rel: relative.add(blk.label)

        for inst in blk.body:                         # only Move / Mma carry Refs
            for ref in inst.srcs + inst.dsts:
                if ref.gen is not None:
                    by_ref[id(ref)] = (entry.get(ref.gen, 0) + ref.gdelta) % max(1, ref.gen.ring)
                elif ref.abs_gen is not None:
                    by_ref[id(ref)] = ref.abs_gen

        for be in back.leaving(blk.label):            # transfers apply on LEAVING
            for xf in be.xfers:
                by_xfer[(blk.label, xf.gen.id)] = (entry.get(xf.gen, 0) + xf.adv) % max(1, xf.ring)

    return Reaching(prog, by_ref, by_xfer, relative)
```

**Fixpoint — and why there is no iteration.** A general reaching-value analysis must iterate
because a loop header's input depends on its own output. Here it does not: `_resolve_phi_entry`
gives the header a *declared* entry map, independent of the back edge, so the dependency graph of
the `entries` map is **acyclic**. Reverse postorder then visits every block after all of its
non-back-edge predecessors, so a single sweep computes the exact answer. Termination is trivial:
one pass over V blocks.

Two consequences a maintainer must hold onto:

1. **The cut is what makes the analysis cheap, and it is also what makes `of()` a
   representative-trip fact.** You cannot remove one without the other. If a future consumer
   genuinely needs the trip-varying generation, the fix is *not* to iterate this analysis — the
   value has no fixpoint over ℤ_ring except the trivial "may be anything". The fix is to widen to a
   *set* of generations at the point of use, which is exactly what `MemTokenAssignment` already
   does for relative blocks (`gir/analyses/mem_tokens.py:185-188`, next paragraph).

2. **`_entry_of`'s use of `entries` is order-dependent** — a predecessor absent from `entries` is
   simply skipped. That is safe under RPO on a reducible CFG and unsafe otherwise. `walk_rpo`'s
   correctness therefore matters to *this* analysis specifically, and that dependency is why
   `walk_rpo` was fixed to route through `successor_labels`: its private successor switch handled
   only `Goto`/`CondGoto`, so a `CondChain` header or `Return` sink fell into the "unreachable,
   append in insertion order" tail and `gen_reaching` then visited blocks in the wrong order
   (`gir/nodes.py:344-351`).

**Complexity.** O(V + E) for the RPO walk and `BackEdges`, plus O(R) where R is the total number
of `Ref`s in the program — every `Ref` is touched exactly once. R is the dominant term: a bf16
kernel at `MIWaveTile[2,2]`, `DepthU 64` has on the order of a few hundred `Ref`s across all
blocks. Memory is O(R) for `by_ref`. Nothing here is ever a compile-time cost; the expensive
analyses in this package are the O(accesses²) pairwise ones (§9).

##### 6.2.8 The consumers, and the one that had to be taught the contract

| consumer | what it asks | how it handles relativity |
|---|---|---|
| `TokensPass` (`gir/passes/tokens.py:134`) | `reach.of(ref)` for the shared `Ref` of every LDS `Move`, to build the completion token `('lds', unit, (gen,), region…)` | takes it as-is; the token is a *logical* name and only the within-body distinction matters |
| `MemTokenAssignment` (`gir/analyses/mem_tokens.py:144, 185`) | the same generation, to name a *storage* buffer `(operand, region, generation)` and hand it a dense integer id | **widens to the whole ring** when the block is relative — see below |
| `LdsHazards` (`gir/analyses/lds_hazards.py:386, 388, 417, 421`) | the generations of a producer/consumer pair, to compute their trip distance | **keeps the pair, conservatively**, when either block is relative (`:386` — `_provably_disjoint` returns `False`, i.e. "cannot prove disjoint", so the cross-block edge is still appended at `:377`), and **refuses** a both-peel-pinned same-block pair in a relative frame (`:421`, recorded as an `Unresolved`); the comparison that survives the shift is the loop-carried branch (`:404-408`, `(a.gdelta - b.gdelta) % ring`), which never consults `is_relative` |

The widening in `MemTokenAssignment` is worth reproducing as a case study, because it is the one
place where reading `of()` as absolute reached hardware. A memory token is turned by the backend
into an LDS pseudo-register: a copy *defines* it, a read *uses* it, and the ordinary def-use chain
then forces the read to wait for the right producer. That is an **absolute buffer identity
compared across blocks** — precisely what `of()` does not give in a relative frame. Measured on
2026-08-19: `drain0`'s two predecessors genuinely disagree, so `_entry_of` flags it and returns
`RELATIVE_BASE`; on the degenerate path where the steady loop never runs, the resident buffer is
the prologue's, and the stamped token named the *other* generation. The read was ordered against a
copy that is not its producer and left unordered against the one that is. In a microscaled kernel
that produced `-nan` (a wrong-generation E8M0 scale poisons the multiply; wrong-generation data
often stays finite) in 23 of 540 cells, every one of them on that path
(`gir/analyses/mem_tokens.py:161-188`). The repair is not to make `of()` absolute — it cannot be —
but to answer the *may* question honestly: in a relative frame the access may touch any generation
of the ring, so it carries every id and the backend orders it against all of them. Conservative
where being optimistic loses an edge.

That is the template for any new consumer: **decide whether your question is relative or absolute,
and if it is absolute, check the flag and widen.**

##### 6.2.9 What the tests pin

- `test_gen_reaching_steady_plr1` (`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:215`) — on the canonical bf16 kernel
  with one level of read-ahead, the steady body must contain `Ref`s at both `gdelta = 0` (the head
  read) and `gdelta = 1` (the read-ahead), and `of()` must resolve every one of them. This is the
  non-vacuity guard: an analysis returning `None` everywhere would otherwise pass a weaker test.
- `test_gen_reaching_1lds_all_zero` (`:229`) — with a single LDS buffer (`ring = 1`) every
  resolved generation must be `0`. This pins the `mod max(1, ring)` arithmetic and the degenerate
  no-rotation case, where a generation stops identifying a chunk at all.
- `test_loop_copies_residue_timeline_spans_the_chain` (`:1130`) — with a two-block steady chain,
  the sequence of generations in `steady1` must be `steady`'s sequence advanced by exactly one
  ring step, and the back-edge `GenXfer.adv` must be 2. This is the statement that the chain sits
  on **one** residue timeline rather than each copy restarting it.
- `test_gen_entry_propagates_along_a_fallthrough_chain` (`:1158`) — the sharpest of the four. It
  rewrites the header's phi to `entry_val = 1`, bumps the version, and asserts that the first
  generation in `steady1` is `(1+1) % 2 = 0`. The point of the rewrite is stated in the docstring:
  defaulting a phi-less block's entry to 0 *looked* right only because the header's `entry_val`
  happens to be 0, and with a non-zero entry the chain would silently restart the timeline. The
  test manufactures the shape that distinguishes the two implementations.

There is **no direct unit test of `is_relative`, of `RELATIVE_BASE`, or of the transitivity fix**.
The behaviour is exercised only indirectly, through `MemTokenAssignment`'s widening and through
`LdsHazards`' refusal, both of which have their own tests (`test_gir.py:2900` and `:1839`
sections). Given that transitivity was a real defect and that its symptom was a wrong numeric
result rather than a crash, a direct fixture — a three-block chain
`prologue/steady → drain0 → drain1` asserting `is_relative` on **both** drains — is the single
most valuable test to add to this file.

##### 6.2.10 Extension notes

- **Adding a second independently-rotating ring** costs nothing: every map is keyed by `Gen`, and
  `by_xfer` by `(block, gen.id)`. This already happens (A-shared and B-shared are distinct `Gen`s).
- **Adding a `Ref` kind with a residence** requires touching exactly the transfer at `:129-133`.
  Note the `elif`: a `Ref` carrying both `gen` and `abs_gen` resolves as `gen` and the `abs_gen` is
  silently ignored. That combination is meaningless by construction (§3.2) but nothing rejects it;
  `G-SEMANTIC` does not cover it. A one-line assertion here would close it.
- **If the block count ever grows** (persistent loops), the RPO walk and the single sweep still
  hold; only `Dominators` needs the attention described in §6.1.3.
- **Do not add a `resolved_gen` field to `Ref`.** It is a per-block derived fact and a field would
  be read without its frame, which is the entire failure mode this section documents.

#### 6.3 `dep_defuse.py` (54 lines) — indexing the dependency edges inherited from layer 1

##### 6.3.1 Concept: what a `dep` is, and where it comes from

Layer 1 does not hand GIR a bare list of instructions; it hands it a *schedule with obligations*.
Each LoopIR instruction carries a set of **awaits** — statements of the form "before this
instruction runs, the following earlier movement must have completed". The lowering threads those
onto every GIR verb as `Move.deps` / `Mma.deps` (`gir/nodes.py:108`, `:133`), a tuple of triples:

```
(dep_name, counter, kind)
    dep_name : str   which movement is being awaited
    counter  : int   the completion counter value to wait for
    kind     : str   the HAZARD CLASS of the obligation
```

`kind` is drawn from a **closed set of four**, defined in layer 1 at
`Tensile/LoopModel/ir.py:500-502`:

```
RAW_KINDS = { "RAW-residency", "crossing-RAW" }        true dependences
WAR_KINDS = { "rotation-WAR",  "inplace-WAR"  }        anti-dependences
```

- **`RAW-residency`** — the consumer needs the producer's value; the data must be *resident*.
- **`crossing-RAW`** — the same, but the producer and consumer sit in different reduction chunks
  (the read crosses a chunk boundary into a buffer an earlier chunk's copy filled).
- **`rotation-WAR`** — the writer must wait for prior *readers*, because it is about to overwrite
  the ring slot they are reading.
- **`inplace-WAR`** — the same anti-dependence, for a resource with no rotation at all (ring 1),
  where the writer reuses the identical storage.

The RAW/WAR distinction is the one field that changes *issue order*: an anti-dependence means the
owning instruction must be issued **after** its prior readers, which is the opposite constraint
from a true dependence.

##### 6.3.2 The one upward import in the whole of `gir/`

`gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py:19` does `from ....LoopModel.ir import is_war`. This is the **only
import-time reach back up into layer 1 from `gir/`** (`gir/render.py:93` makes the one other upward
reference, a function-local `from ...LoopModel.ir import OBLIGATION_KINDS` inside the deps renderer,
which does not affect import-time closure); everything else in the package is closed over
`gir/` plus the standard library, which is what keeps the whole graph and analysis stack
importable and unit-testable with no compiled `rocisa` present. The import is narrow — one
predicate over one string — and deliberate: the hazard-kind vocabulary is layer 1's, and
duplicating the classification here would create a second table to keep in sync.

`is_war(kind)` (`Tensile/LoopModel/ir.py:505`) **raises** on a kind outside the closed set rather
than answering `False`. That is the important half. Eight call sites used to dispatch on
`kind.endswith("WAR")`, a suffix test standing in for a classification: a new anti-dependence whose
name does not happen to end in those three letters silently joins the true-dependence arm, and a
new true dependence that does end in them silently joins the anti-dependence arm. Neither shows up
as an error; both show up as a wrongly ordered schedule. The measured instance was that the suffix
test forced copy-last placement on `crossing-RAW` obligations that needed copy-*first*
(`Tensile/LoopModel/ir.py:484-499`). Because `DepDefuse.add` calls `is_war` unfiltered, **this
analysis is the point at which an unknown dependency kind anywhere in the program becomes a loud
`ValueError`** — a property that matters more than anything it returns (§6.3.5).

##### 6.3.3 `DepDefuse` (`gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py:24`) — the result object

Three members plus a constructor:

- **`__init__()` (`:25`)** — two empty dicts, `_raw` and `_war`, both keyed by `id(inst)` and
  valued with `[(dep_name, counter)]`. The same identity-keying caution as `Reaching` (§6.2.3)
  applies, with one difference: `DepDefuse` does **not** hold a reference to the `Program`, so
  nothing in this class prevents an instruction from being collected and its id reused. In
  practice the `AnalysisManager` holds the result only as long as the program version is current
  and the caller holds the program, so it has never bitten — but it is a strictly weaker guarantee
  than `Reaching`'s, and the one-line fix (store `prog`) costs nothing.

- **`add(inst)` (`:29`)** — partition one instruction's `deps` by hazard class:

  ```
  add(inst):
      raw, war = [], []
      for (dep, counter, kind) in getattr(inst, "deps", ()):
          (war if is_war(kind) else raw).append((dep, counter))
      self._raw[id(inst)] = raw
      self._war[id(inst)] = war
  ```

  `getattr(inst, "deps", ())` is defensive against a node type that does not declare the field;
  both `Move` and `Mma` do, so the default never fires today. Note the partition is **total and
  disjoint by construction** — every dep lands in exactly one list — which is what the test asserts
  (§6.3.6). The `kind` itself is *discarded*: a consumer can learn that an edge is an
  anti-dependence but not *which* anti-dependence, so `rotation-WAR` and `inplace-WAR` are
  indistinguishable downstream. That is a real narrowing and it is undocumented. If a future
  consumer needs to tell a ring rotation from an in-place reuse (they demand different placement
  when the ring depth is 1), the triple must be kept.

- **`raw(inst)` (`:36`)** and **`war(inst)` (`:39`)** — the two lookups, each returning `[]` for an
  instruction that was never `add`ed (a `Mark`, for instance). One line each.

##### 6.3.4 `DepDefuseAnalysis` (`gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py:43`)

- **`cache_key` (`:45`)** — a property returning the literal `"DepDefuse"`. One of only three
  analyses that override the default (§4.2), and like the other two it is a *no-op in effect*
  because the default is already the class name — except that the class is called
  `DepDefuseAnalysis` and the key is `DepDefuse`, so here the override actually does change the
  key. Its purpose is to pin the cache key to a name that survives a class rename.

- **`run(prog, am)` (`:48`)** — the whole analysis:

  ```
  run(prog, am):
      res = DepDefuse()
      for blk in prog.blocks.values():          # INSERTION order; order is irrelevant
          for inst in blk.body:
              if isinstance(inst, (Move, Mma)):
                  res.add(inst)
      return res
  ```

**Classification, stated plainly.** There is no lattice, no meet, no direction and no fixpoint.
This is a **materialisation**: it walks every instruction once, reads a field that is already
there, and files it in two dictionaries. It does not consult the CFG, does not call `am` for
anything, and would give the identical answer over a shuffled bag of instructions. The module
docstring is honest about this — *"This is PURE: it only reads `deps` already on the nodes; it
never mutates"* (`:14`) — and it is registered as an `Analysis` only so that it participates in
the manager's caching and version invalidation like everything else.

**Complexity.** O(number of `Move` + `Mma` nodes × deps per node). Both factors are small: a few
hundred instructions, at most a handful of deps each. Memory is two dicts of the same size.

##### 6.3.5 What it is actually for today — and the docstring defect

Grep the tree for `.raw(` and `.war(` and you find **exactly one caller, and it is a test**
(`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:401, 404`). The only production reference is
`gir/passes/tokens.py:124`:

```python
am.get(DepDefuseAnalysis(), prog)   # available for L3 WAR-forwarding; consistency
```

— which discards the result. So the queryable index has **zero production readers**, and what the
line buys is the second word in that comment: running the analysis forces `is_war` over every
dependency kind in the program, so an unrecognised kind raises during the token pass instead of
being silently misclassified somewhere later. It is a **validation gate wearing an index's
clothes**.

Two things follow, and a maintainer should decide between them rather than leaving the ambiguity:

1. If the index is wanted, wire it up. `TokensPass`'s own docstring already describes a use —
   *"DepDefuse is consulted so a read with no RAW LDS residency (a direct-to-register
   global→register read) gets no LDS token"* (`gir/passes/tokens.py:13-14`) — but the body does
   not do that; it decides the same question from the `Ref` spaces instead. The docstring
   describes an intention, not the code.
2. If only the validation is wanted, say so: rename the call site's comment to "validate the
   dependency-kind vocabulary", or better, give `DepDefuseAnalysis` an explicit
   `validate_only=True` path so the intent is in the type rather than in a comment.

**A second, smaller documentation defect in the same file.** The module docstring advertises three
query methods (`:10-12`):

```
reach.raw(inst)     -> [(dep_name, counter), …]
reach.war(inst)     -> [(dep_name, counter), …]
reach.counter(inst) -> the completion counter of the inst's producing hop
```

`DepDefuse` has no `counter` method. The third line describes an API that does not exist and never
has in this class. It should be deleted or implemented; leaving it invites a caller to write
`dd.counter(inst)` and get an `AttributeError` at codegen time. (The variable name `reach` in the
docstring is also borrowed from `gen_reaching`'s result and is confusing here — the object is a
`DepDefuse`, not a `Reaching`.)

##### 6.3.6 What the tests pin

One test, `test_dep_defuse_indexes_awaits` (`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:396`):

```python
dd = AnalysisManager().get(DepDefuseAnalysis(), prog)
steady = prog.block("steady")
assert [e for i in steady.body if isinstance(i, Move) for e in dd.raw(i)], "expected RAW edges"
for i in steady.body:
    if isinstance(i, Move):
        assert len(dd.raw(i)) + len(dd.war(i)) == len(i.deps)
```

The first assertion is the non-vacuity guard — an implementation that returned two empty dicts
would otherwise satisfy the second. The second is the real contract: **the partition is total and
lossless**, no edge dropped and none double-counted. That is precisely the property a suffix-test
classification could violate silently, so the test is aimed at the right thing. What it does *not*
check is that an edge lands in the *correct* half; a hypothetical `is_war` that answered `True` for
everything would pass both assertions. A stronger fixture would construct a `Move` with one known
`RAW-residency` and one known `rotation-WAR` dep and assert the split by name.

##### 6.3.7 Extension notes and the one structural decision to preserve

54 lines and no lattice, so there is little to weigh — but two of its properties are load-bearing
and one is a defect waiting for a second consumer.

**Preserve the upward import, and preserve its being the only one.** `dep_defuse.py:19` reaches up
into layer 1 for the hazard-kind classifier (`is_war`), and it is the single upward import in the
whole of `gir/` (§6.3.2). That is deliberate and it is the *right* direction of dependency: the
kind vocabulary is θ's, the classification rule was written once there, and re-implementing it
here as a string suffix test is exactly the defect that was removed. If you add a kind, add it in
layer 1 and let the classifier raise on the unknown — **do not** add a local fallback here. The
raise is the only thing that turns an unmodelled hazard kind into an error rather than a silently
mis-partitioned edge.

**It is an index, not an analysis, and the class name should keep saying so.**
`DepDefuseAnalysis` subclasses `Analysis` because that is how results get cached, not because it
computes a fixpoint; §6.0's table classifies it honestly and its own docstring says "it only reads
`deps` already on the nodes". If a future change gives it a transfer function — say, propagating a
dependence through a phi — it stops being an index and the docstring must stop saying it is one.
That sentence is not pedantry: §6.0 opens with the recorded incident where a module's docstring
claimed a dataflow it did not implement and emitted zero results under a shape it had not
anticipated.

**Add `self._prog = prog`.** `DepDefuse` keys its two dicts on `id(node)` and, unlike `Reaching`,
does **not** retain the `Program` — so nothing stops the keyed nodes being collected and their ids
recycled under a *different* object. It is safe today only because the `AnalysisManager`'s
version-keyed cache makes a stale result unreachable before that can matter. Making the two
consistent is one line and removes the need to reason about lifetimes at all (§6.6 observation 3).

**Extending it.** The natural extension is a *reverse* index — "which instructions depend on this
one" — which today every consumer builds inline by scanning. It is four lines here and belongs
here, keyed the same way. The rule to follow is the one that made this module worth having: return
a **query object**, not the raw dicts, so a consumer cannot key on `id(node)` itself and cannot
re-derive the partition rule. Two dicts escaping would put the classification back in three places,
which is where it started.

#### 6.4 `loop_shape.py` (213 lines) — the loop's shape, its trip count, and the covering check

##### 6.4.1 Concept: pre- versus post-test is not a declaration

Whether a loop is pre-tested (`while (p) { body }`) or post-tested (`do { body } while (p)`) is not
a property anyone writes down. It is **where the conditional branch sits**. Put the exit test on a
block that also does work and the work happens first — post-test. Put it on a block that only
tests and the work happens in the blocks it guards — pre-test. The *same predicate* means a
different trip count in the two shapes, off by exactly one.

Nothing in GIR derived that, and nothing checked the consequence, which is how a real off-by-one
survived. The lowering emits the steady region as **one** block that both *is* the body and
carries the exit test on its terminator:

```
Block(phase='steady', preds=('prologue','steady'),
      term=CondGoto(iter < T-M, 'steady', 'drain0'))
```

Read as a pre-tested loop, that runs the body for `iter = 0 … T-M-1`, covering chunks `0 … T-M-1`.
Read as what it actually is — post-tested — it runs for `iter = 0 … T-M` **inclusive**, `T-M+1`
times, covering chunks `0 … T-M`. Meanwhile the peel drain handles chunks `T-M … T-1`. So chunk
`T-M` is computed **twice**, at every trip count. The defect was never observed in output because
GIR's predicate is never emitted — the pre-existing kernel scaffold branches on its own compare and
GIR only labels the edge — but every analysis downstream reasons over the loop GIR *claims* to
describe (`gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:8-20`).

##### 6.4.2 The invariant, and why it needs no trip count

`T` — the total number of reduction chunks — is a **runtime symbol**. "How many times does this
run" is therefore not a number and cannot be asserted against one. What *is* checkable is a
**covering statement**, stated symbolically:

```
    steady  covers  [0, n_steady)         n_steady = trips × chunks-per-trip
    drain   covers  [T-M, T)              M drain steps, one chunk each
    together, exactly [0, T) — no gap, no overlap   ⟺   n_steady == T - M
```

Both sides are **linear in `T`**, so the comparison is exact integer arithmetic on `(coeff, const)`
pairs rather than a comparison of rendered strings. The off-by-one above fails it immediately:
`n_steady = T-M+1 ≠ T-M`, and the message names it as an OVERLAP of 1 chunk.

The check is wired in as the verifier's `G-TRIP` invariant (`gir/verify.py:331-334`), which is what
gives it teeth against the one class of change most likely to break it: a **structural pass** is
permitted to reshape the CFG (rotate the loop, adjust the trip count), and `G-TRIP` is the gate
that stops it from quietly moving the trip count while doing so.

##### 6.4.3 What the module states it does **not** cover

Two cases raise rather than guess (`gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:33-36`): a loop whose exit predicate
is not of the form "counter against a bound over the trip symbol", and a chunks-per-trip that the
back edge's generation transfer does not state. The stated reason is the right one — *an
unverifiable loop must not read as a verified one*. In practice the "raise" is partly a "skip"; see
§6.4.8, where three separate `continue` paths are enumerated honestly.

##### 6.4.4 `Linear` (`gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:54`) — the arithmetic

A frozen dataclass, `coeff * T + const`, where `T` is the runtime trip symbol.

- **`__add__(self, k)` (`:58`)** — returns `Linear(coeff, const + k)`. Note the asymmetry: `k` is
  an **int**, not another `Linear`; `Linear + Linear` raises `TypeError`, because `int.__add__`
  returns `NotImplemented` and the frozen dataclass defines no `__radd__`. **No call site anywhere
  in the package.** It is dead, and if kept it should gain a `Linear` overload.
- **`scaled(self, k)` (`:61`)** — returns `Linear(coeff * k, const * k)`. One call site, in
  `LoopShape.run` (`:176`), computing `covers = trips.scaled(per_trip)`.
- **`render(self, sym="T")` (`:64`)** — a human-readable form: `"3"` when the coefficient is zero,
  `"T"` / `"2*T"` when the constant is zero, `"T - 2"` / `"2*T + 1"` otherwise. Used only in the
  violation message (`:209`) and in tests (`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2407`).

Two `Linear`s compare with the dataclass's generated `__eq__`, which is exactly the "exact integer
arithmetic" the invariant needs — no string comparison, no symbolic simplifier.

**Why `Linear` and not the IR's own `Bound`/`Trips` nodes?** Because those describe *control-flow
tests*, are frozen into the terminator, and `Bound` cannot express a coefficient at all. `Linear`
is a throwaway arithmetic type local to this check. That is the right split, and it is also the
source of the division limitation in §6.4.8.

##### 6.4.5 `Loop` (`gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:72`) — the result record

A frozen dataclass, one per back edge, with eight fields:

```
header    : str      the block the back edge targets
latch     : str      the block whose terminator carries the back edge
tester    : str      the block whose terminator LEAVES the loop — NOT always the latch
position  : str      PRE | POST, derived (module constants at :48)
trips     : Linear   how many times the loop's work runs
per_trip  : int      chunks one trip consumes
covers    : Linear   chunks the loop covers = trips × per_trip
exit_to   : str      the block the exit edge targets
```

The `latch` / `tester` split is the distinction the whole analysis turns on and is the reason
there are two fields rather than one. `PRE = "pre-test"` and `POST = "post-test"` are plain
strings (`:48`) — deliberately readable, since they appear in the violation message.

The class is re-exported from `gir/analyses/__init__.py:32` under the alias **`LoopShapeInfo`**, to
keep the bare name `Loop` out of a namespace that already exports a great many node types. Nothing
in the tree imports the alias.

##### 6.4.6 The five helper functions

**`_does_work(blk)` (`:83`)** — `any(isinstance(i, (Move, Mma)) for i in blk.body)`. A block that
only tests does no work. `Mark`s explicitly do not count as work, which is correct: a Mark is a
semantic fact at a point, not a data movement, and a block containing only a phase-boundary Mark is
still a pure test block.

**`_loop_blocks(prog, header, latch)` (`:88`)** — the **natural loop**: the blocks reachable from
the header that can also reach the latch.

```
_loop_blocks(prog, header, latch):
    succ = successors(prog)
    reach(s) = { every block reachable from s by >= 1 edge }      # DFS, iterative
    fwd = reach(header) | {header}
    return { b in fwd : b == latch or latch in reach(b) }
```

- **`reach(start)` (`:93`)** — the nested closure: an explicit stack DFS returning the set of
  blocks reachable from `start` by **one or more** edges. `start` itself is included only if it is
  on a cycle, which is why the caller unions `{header}` back in at `:102`.
- **Complexity: O(V·(V+E)).** `reach` is O(V+E) and is called once for the header plus once per
  block in `fwd`. At V ≤ 12 this is free. **The concrete improvement, if V ever grows:** compute
  the *backward* reachability from the latch once, on the reversed graph, and intersect —
  `fwd ∩ bwd(latch)` is the same set in O(V+E) total instead of O(V·(V+E)). That is a ten-line
  change and it is the right one to make the day a persistent outer loop pushes the block count up.

**`_exit_tester(prog, blocks)` (`:106`)** — the block whose terminator leaves the loop.

```
_exit_tester(prog, blocks):
    for lab in sorted(blocks):                       # ALPHABETICAL — see below
        t = prog.blocks[lab].term
        tgts = (t.t_target, t.f_target)  if t is a CondGoto
             | (t.body, t.exit_target)   if t is a LoopBack
             | ()                        otherwise
        if tgts and any(target not in blocks for target in tgts):
            return lab
    return None
```

This is the function the docstring calls the distinction the analysis turns on (`:107-114`). In a
post-tested loop the latch carries the exit test, so `tester == latch` and the tester does work. In
a pre-tested loop the *header* carries it and the latch back-edges unconditionally, so
`tester != latch` and the tester does no work. An earlier version looked only at the latch, found
no test at all in the pre-tested shape, and silently reported *no loop* — which is worse than being
wrong, because a missing loop is also a missing coverage check.

Three sharp edges live in these ten lines and none is currently reachable, which is exactly why
they should be written down:

1. **`sorted(blocks)` is alphabetical, not CFG order.** If a loop has two exits — an early break
   plus the counted exit — the tester returned is whichever block label sorts first. There is no
   principled reason for that choice; it is an artefact of wanting determinism.
2. **`CondChain` is not in the terminator switch.** A loop whose exit is a multi-arm chain yields
   `tgts = ()`, so it is skipped, the function returns `None`, and `LoopShape.run` `continue`s —
   the loop **vanishes** from the result, and with it from `G-TRIP`. `EarlyExitPass` builds
   `CondChain`s only on the *prologue*, outside any loop, so this is inert today. It goes live the
   moment a loop acquires a multi-way exit. The fix is a one-line addition to the switch, and it
   should be made pre-emptively.
3. **`Goto` and `Return` are not in the switch either.** An unconditional jump out of a loop body
   (a `Return` mid-loop, say) is not an exit as far as this function is concerned.

**`_test_position(prog, tester)` (`:124`)** — `POST if _does_work(prog.blocks[tester]) else PRE`.
Purely structural: no phase name, no flag, nothing declared. One line, and the entire pre/post
derivation.

**`_trips_from_node(t)` (`:133`)** — the trip count, **read** off the terminator rather than
reconstructed:

```
_trips_from_node(t) -> Linear(1 if t.trips.var else 0, -t.trips.sub)
```

The docstring (`:134-140`) records what this replaced and why it matters. The previous version
reconstructed the count from the exit comparison plus the test position, which required assuming
that the counter starts at 0 and steps by +1. Neither assumption is stated anywhere, and **the back
end does not share them** — the pre-existing kernel scaffold initialises its loop counter to the
count and *decrements*, exiting when it drops to an end value. Same trips, opposite direction.
Reconstructing across that gap is where the off-by-one of §6.4.1 lived. The `LoopBack` terminator
now **states** the count (`gir/nodes.py:248-279`), so there is nothing to reconstruct, and the test
position no longer changes the answer at all — it has become purely an emission property, recorded
for information.

**But note what this function drops: `Trips.div`.** A `Trips` node means `(var - sub) // div`, and
`_trips_from_node` reads only `var` and `sub`. `Linear` has no division, so the divisor cannot be
represented, and the returned `trips` is therefore **`div` times too large** whenever `div > 1`.
This is not hidden — the pipeline sidesteps it by refusing to check such loops (§6.4.8) — but the
`Loop.trips` field is documented as "how many times the loop's work runs" and for a multi-block
body it is not. A consumer other than the coverage check would be misled. Renaming the field, or
carrying the divisor into `Linear` as a third component, are the two honest repairs.

##### 6.4.7 `LoopShape` (`:144`) and `LoopShape.run` (`:147`)

```
LoopShape.run(prog, am) -> [Loop]        # one per back edge, in CFG order
    for be in am.get(BackEdges(), prog):
        blocks = _loop_blocks(prog, be.header, be.src)
        tester = _exit_tester(prog, blocks)
        if tester is None:      continue     # an infinite loop has no exit test to read
        term = prog.blocks[tester].term
        if term is not a LoopBack: continue  # not a counted loop: no trip count to state
        position = _test_position(prog, tester)
        trips    = _trips_from_node(term)
        per_trip = term.trips.div            # chunks one trip consumes

        if be.xfers:                         # CROSS-CHECK, only where a second statement exists
            adv = max(xf.adv for xf in be.xfers)
            if per_trip != adv: raise ValueError("two statements of chunks-per-trip disagree")

        emit Loop(be.header, be.src, tester, position, trips, per_trip,
                  trips.scaled(per_trip), term.exit_target)
```

**Classification.** Not a dataflow analysis and it does not claim to be: a per-back-edge structural
derivation, with one transitive-closure sub-computation. No lattice, no meet, no iteration.
Direction is irrelevant. Complexity is **O(B · V · (V+E))** where B is the number of back edges
(1, or 2 with a tail loop), dominated by `_loop_blocks`.

**The cross-check at `:167-173` deserves its own paragraph**, because it is a careful piece of
engineering that reads like an accident. Chunks-per-trip is stated *twice* in a well-formed
program: once by the trip node's divisor, and once by the back edge's generation advance
(`GenXfer.adv`). Two statements of one fact is exactly the shape that produces silent divergence,
so they are compared — but **only when the second statement exists**. A direct-to-register kernel
stages nothing through LDS, so it has no generations, no transfers, and `adv` says nothing;
demanding agreement there would be comparing against a *default* rather than against a fact, and
would reject a perfectly good program. `max(...)` over the transfers rather than "all equal" is a
looser reading than it could be — two operands could in principle advance by different amounts —
but the lockstep condition that makes a fused movement one pointer already forbids that upstream
(§5, `refs.copy_unit`).

**Which terminator is read.** `term` comes from the **tester**, while `be.xfers` comes from the
**latch**. In the post-tested shape they are the same block. In the pre-tested shape the header
carries the `LoopBack` and the latch carries the transfers, and both are correct — the trip count
belongs to the test, the generation advance belongs to the back edge. The code gets this right
without commenting on it.

##### 6.4.8 `reduction_coverage_violations(prog, loops)` (`:180`) — the covering check

```
reduction_coverage_violations(prog, loops) -> [str]        # [] means clean
    M = prog.meta.get("M")
    if M is None:                                  return []      # skip 1
    drains = [labels whose phase startswith "drain"]
    if not drains:                                 return []      # skip 2
    required = Linear(1, -M)                       # steady must cover [0, T-M)
    for lp in loops:
        if not lp.exit_to.startswith("drain"):     continue       # skip 3: not the reduction loop
        if lp.per_trip != 1:                       continue       # skip 4: NOT EXPRESSIBLE
        if lp.covers != required:
            emit "loop {header} ({position}, {per_trip} chunk/trip) covers chunks
                  [0, {covers}) but the {M} drain steps cover [T-M, T), so the two
                  {OVERLAP|LEAVE A GAP} by {n} chunk(s) — they must together be exactly [0, T)"
```

**It returns rather than raises**, so the caller decides: the verifier turns the list into a
`GirVerifyError` prefixed `G-TRIP` (`gir/verify.py:331-334`), while a report-only harness or a test
can print it. That is the right split — a checker that can only abort is unusable from a diagnostic
tool.

**Scoping to the reduction loop** is done by `exit_to.startswith("drain")`: the reduction loop is
the one whose exit leads into the drain chain, because the drain is what completes its coverage. A
tail loop (the remainder of the reduction axis modulo the chunk size) exits elsewhere and is
correctly untouched — its coverage is a different statement that nothing checks today.

**The OVERLAP-versus-GAP wording** is chosen by `lp.covers.const > required.const` (`:210`) and the
magnitude by `abs(lp.covers.const - required.const)`. Note both look only at the **constant**: if
the coefficients differ (a `2*T` covering against a `T`) the message reports a chunk count derived
from the constants alone, which is meaningless. That case is unreachable only because of skip 4.

**Skip 4 is the module's one named hole, and it is a limit of the predicate form, not a choice.**
With a multi-block steady chain of `n` blocks sharing one back edge, one trip consumes `n` chunks
and the loop must run `(T - M) / n` times. The IR's `Bound` node is `var + const` with no division,
so that bound cannot be *written*, never mind checked — and `_trips_from_node` drops `Trips.div`
(§6.4.6), so `Loop.covers` comes out as `n·(T - M)`, over-covering by exactly the factor `n`. The
comment at `:198-205` is explicit that skipping *silently* is what would make this a hidden hole,
so the skip is named there and asserted in a test that pins the wrong answer deliberately. The
configuration is unreachable from the package's real entry point, which never requests a
multi-block body.

**Two further limits that are *not* named in the source and should be:**

- **A loop whose terminator is a `CondGoto` produces no `Loop` at all** (`:155-156`), so `G-TRIP`
  says nothing about it. Every hand-built CFG in the test suite that uses `CondGoto` — including
  the tail-loop and multi-exit-header fixtures — is therefore unchecked by the covering invariant.
  The lowering emits `LoopBack` on every steady loop, so production programs are covered; a future
  pass that reintroduces a `CondGoto` loop would silently lose the check.
- **`M is None` or no drain blocks returns `[]` (a *pass*), not "cannot check".** A program that
  lost its drain chain to a buggy structural pass reads as clean. Returning a distinguishable
  "not applicable" would let the verifier decide whether silence is acceptable.

##### 6.4.9 What the tests pin — including the deliberate control

The `LoopShape` section of the suite is `Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2354-2466`, and it is built around
a synthetic control program, which is the part worth copying elsewhere.

**`_pre_tested_loop_prog()` (`:2358`)** hand-builds a four-block CFG — `pre → head → body → head`,
`head → drain0` — in which the header carries the phis and a `LoopBack` and has an **empty body**,
while `body` holds the single work `Move` and the `GenXfer`. Its docstring states exactly why it
exists: *"Without it, an analysis that unconditionally answered 'post-test' would pass every
assertion we make about the real Program, since the real one IS post-tested — the bug being pinned
and the answer being checked would coincide."* That is the non-vacuity discipline this suite
applies throughout, made explicit.

**`test_loop_test_position_is_DERIVED_from_where_the_branch_sits` (`:2386`)** asserts three things:
the real kernel's steady loop reads as `POST`; the synthetic one reads as `PRE`; and **both report
`trips.render() == "T - 2"`**. The third is the point — equal trip counts reached from different
predicate bounds, which is only possible if the count is read from the node rather than
reconstructed from the comparison plus the position.

**`test_reduction_covering_invariant_holds_and_is_enforced_as_G_TRIP` (`:2410`)** runs
`reduction_coverage_violations` over the fully built program at three prefetch depths (peel depths
1, 2 and 3) and demands `[]` from each, then runs it over the synthetic pre-tested loop and demands
`[]` there too. The second half is the satisfiability guard: a check that is always-failing and a
check that is correct are indistinguishable from the first half alone. The docstring also records
that this test is a *second, independent* statement of the invariant, because `verify_gir` runs it
too and a hand-built `Program` need not go through `verify_gir`.

**`test_multi_copy_loop_coverage_is_not_yet_EXPRESSIBLE` (`:2434`)** pins the hole. For `n ∈ {2,3}`
it asserts `per_trip == n`, asserts `covers.coeff == n` — i.e. it asserts the **wrong** answer,
deliberately, so that the over-coverage is visible in the suite rather than being a `continue`
nobody reads — and asserts `reduction_coverage_violations(...) == []`, recording that `G-TRIP`
currently says nothing. It then re-runs the single-copy case and asserts `per_trip == 1` and a
clean result, so the exemption is demonstrably narrow rather than a blanket disable. This is the
right way to encode a known gap: as an executable statement of the current behaviour that will fail
loudly the day someone fixes it.

##### 6.4.10 The multi-body steady region and the dynamic trip count, restated together

These are the two facts this module exists to make first-class, and they interact.

**The multi-body steady region** is the shape where the steady loop's body is `n` fall-through
blocks — `steady`, `steady1`, …, `steady{n-1}` — sharing **one** back edge from the last to the
first. The reason to have it is that replicating the body puts copy *i* at chunk *i* on one residue
timeline, so each copy's buffer index is a compile-time residue rather than a rotation that must be
re-derived at runtime. The structural consequences are all pinned by `test_loop_copies_chain_shape`
(`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:1103`): only the **first** block carries the phis, only the **last**
carries the transfers and the loop terminator, the intermediate blocks end in plain `Goto`s, and
back-edge detection still reports exactly one loop. `LoopShape` handles this correctly at the
*shape* level — `header` is the first block, `latch` the last, `per_trip = n` — and incorrectly at
the *arithmetic* level, for the `Linear`-has-no-division reason above.

**The dynamic trip count** is the modelling decision that a loop states *how many times it runs*
rather than *what comparison ends it*. A comparison is one encoding of a count, and decoding it
requires three facts that live outside the node: where the counter starts, which way it steps, and
where the test sits. None of those is shared with the back end. Making the count the primitive
collapses all three into an emission choice made by the one place that knows which register is live
and what convention it already follows — and it is what lets `_trips_from_node` be a two-field
read. The `div` field is the part of the count that `Bound` could not express at all, which is why
`Trips` is a distinct node and not `Bound` renamed (`gir/nodes.py:259-263`).

The two meet in `Loop.covers = trips × per_trip`: the trip count says how many times, the
multi-body factor says how much per time, and the covering invariant compares their product against
`T - M`. Fix the division and the multi-body case becomes checkable with no other change.

##### 6.4.11 Extension notes for `loop_shape.py`

- **To close the multi-body hole**, give `Linear` a rational or a divisor field, or (simpler) have
  `_trips_from_node` return `Linear(1, -sub)` *paired with* the divisor and compute
  `covers = Linear(coeff, const)` directly from `(var - sub)` — since `covers = trips × div` and
  `trips = (T - sub) // div`, `covers` is just `T - sub` when the division is exact. That is a
  three-line change; the remaining work is stating and checking the *exactness* precondition, which
  the trip node's own documentation already flags as a separate obligation.
- **Add `CondChain` to `_exit_tester`'s terminator switch** before a loop acquires a multi-way
  exit. Today the loop silently disappears from the analysis; that failure mode is invisible.
- **Replace the O(V·(V+E)) `_loop_blocks`** with a forward-reach ∩ backward-reach intersection if
  the block count ever grows past a few dozen.
- **Do not make `reduction_coverage_violations` raise.** Two callers want two behaviours, and the
  return-a-list shape is what supports both.
- **`_exit_tester`'s `sorted()`** should become "first in CFG order" if a second exit ever exists,
  and the choice should be documented as a policy rather than left as an artefact of determinism.

#### 6.5 `reg_band.py` (59 lines) — validate the register rotation width, never decide it

##### 6.5.1 Concept: `W`, and why GIR is not allowed to choose it

A read from LDS lands in a register, and with read-ahead enabled the read for chunk *k+1* must not
clobber the register the multiply for chunk *k* is still reading. So registers rotate too, on
their own ring of width **`W`** — a value entirely separate from the LDS ring depth `S`. A
register residence is therefore `(group, slot)` with `slot ∈ [0, W)`, where `group` is a partition
index (an operand may have several independently rotating register bands; a microscaled fp8 A
operand has a low half that rotates over 2 slots and a high half that is in-place with `W = 1`).

`W` is a **layer-1 decision**. It is baked into the upstream slot expression as a modulus and
carried into GIR on each register `Ref.reg_ring`. The schedule model proves it is invariant under
reordering and fixes it when it searches for the LDS ring depth, so by the time GIR sees the
program the number is already settled. Deciding it here would create a second authority that can
disagree with the scheduler — and a disagreement between the two would not be a crash, it would be
