```
             for pl in solver.solve(on_conflict) ]
```

**`_flow.delta(a, b)` (`:226`)** — the frame conversion, four lines including the comment:
`adv_of.get(a, 1)` when `(a, b)` is a back edge, else `0`. Absolute chunks need no forward
re-framing; the back edge re-enters the same block one trip later, so the value leaving must be
`adv` further along to be comparable with the header's own trip-0 requirement. The `back_pairs`
parameter of `_flow` is **unused** — `delta` closes over the locally rebuilt `back_set` instead —
which is a dead argument worth deleting. The file also imports `successor_labels`, `BLOCK_ENTRY`
and `BLOCK_EXIT` without using any of them.

**`_flow.on_conflict(kind, detail)` (`:232`)** — raises `AssertionError` for both `"join"` and
`"critical-edge"`, with the same "Reported, not resolved" phrasing as its sibling in §7.3.5, naming
the movement, the blocks, and the two chunk values.

**The convention this placement fixed — the out-of-bounds load.** The docstring at `:203-212`
records it in full and it is the single strongest argument for solving over the whole program. The
previous walk emitted an advance only where a copy *demanded* a chunk different from the one in
hand, anchored just before that copy. The prologue's own copy demands the chunk the tile setup
already left the descriptor on — so it demanded nothing, and **no advance was ever emitted in the
prologue**. GIR's descriptor then ran one chunk behind the hand-written scaffold's convention for
the whole loop, while still inheriting the scaffold's stagger-wrap constant, so the wrap fired an
iteration early and the address landed *below* the tensor base: an out-of-bounds load. Under
AVAIL/ANTIC the prologue→steady edge carries chunk 0 → chunk 1, so the advance lands at the
prologue's exit right after its copy, and the statement "GIR places every advance, prefetch 0's
included" becomes true rather than aspirational.

Note what makes this an *emergent* fix rather than a patch: nothing in the code says "also emit one
in the prologue". The backward fixpoint discovers that the steady body's demand is anticipated at
the prologue's exit, and the exit-def rule places it there.

##### 7.4.5 Tests

The `gr_increment` section of `Tests/unit/test_gir.py` (from `:407`) and the `gr_increment dataflow`
section (from `:1398`) between them pin the count, the anchor, the payload and the scope.

* **`test_gr_increment_follows_the_copy_that_used_the_descriptor` (`:408`)** — every Mark anchors
  **after** a copy `Move`; the payload is exactly `{unit, chunks, to_chunk}` and nothing else (no
  stride, no bytes — the layer split, asserted); `chunks == 1`; and the prologue carries **M**
  advances per operand, not M−1: M−1 between its own peel fills plus the hand-off at its exit,
  exactly one of which has `region.before is BLOCK_EXIT`. The docstring labels the M−1 version as
  the superseded convention and names it as the out-of-bounds failure described above.
* **`test_gr_increment_advances_one_chunk_per_copy` (`:1413`)**, parameterized over 1, 2 and 3
  steady body blocks — the shape the old structural rule got catastrophically wrong. It asserts
  three separate things: every steady body block advances the address; **nothing outside the peel
  and the steady body does** (the drain's global reads are scaffold-owned, and an increment there
  would double-advance — a negative case the test notes had been dropped when the scope widened to
  the prologue); and the per-trip total equals the back edge's `adv`, which equals the number of
  body copies. Finally it re-walks each block asserting every advance has a preceding copy of its
  own movement to supersede.
* **`test_gr_increment_first_copy_has_no_advance` (`:1460`)** — the very first copy of each movement
  carries no increment before it, because the tile setup leaves the address on that chunk and
  advancing first would skip chunk 0 entirely. Its docstring records that the previous version of
  this test was **vacuous**: it walked the same sequence the implementation seeds `cur` from, so the
  inequality it checked was false by construction and the assertion could not fail for any
  implementation — it restated a line of the code. The current form re-derives the chunk each copy
  fetches from the emitted body.
* **`test_pipeline_applies_marks_and_verifies` (`:445`)** — across PLR1/PLR0/1-LDS configurations,
  the number of applied `swap` and `gr_increment` Marks in the finalized body equals the number of
  `PendingMark`s the two analyses returned, `prog.pending` is cleared, and `verify_gir` passes. This
  is the plan→apply conservation check for both analyses at once.
* The two `walk_violations(prog) == []` assertions inside the fp8 sweeps (`:4001`, `:4031`) and the
  full-order plan checks exercise `gr_increment` indirectly at every element width and split.

A gap worth recording: there is **no** direct unit test of `_reqs`'s `npeel // nreg` division. Its
correctness is covered only transitively, through split configurations that would raise (the
negative-advance case) or miscompare on hardware (the spurious-advance case). A three-line test
that builds a two-region movement with four peel copies and asserts the chunk sequence
`0,0,1,1` would make the property explicit and cheap to keep.

##### 7.4.6 Weaknesses and extension advice

* **`chunks` is always 1 in practice, and L3 refuses anything else.** GIR can express a multi-chunk
  advance and the back end cannot execute one. That is a deliberate expressivity gap and it is
  policed at the emitter (`gir_to_rocisa.py:433-437`), not here. If a future schedule genuinely
  needs a 2-chunk advance (a steady body consuming two chunks per trip with a single descriptor),
  the change is on the L3 side — a scaled increment — and nothing in this analysis moves.
* **The scope assertion is a test, not an invariant.** "No increment outside the peel and the steady
  body" is checked by `test_gr_increment_advances_one_chunk_per_copy`, not by the verifier. Since a
  drain increment would double-advance against the scaffold's own drain global reads, promoting it
  to a `G-*` check is a small, worthwhile hardening.
* **Three imports of private names** (`_unemitted_edges`, `_n_regions`, plus `_topo` duplicated).
  Promote to a shared module rather than copying, and never copy.
* **Dead argument and imports**, listed in §7.4.4.
* **A third global pointer** (prefetch-to-L2, provenance #216) is the most likely next extension.
  It is a new movement whose copies target a different destination space, so it needs its own
  `_copy_of` predicate and its own seed; it should be a sibling module reusing
  `ValuePlacementSolver`, not a mode flag threaded through this one. The thing to watch is that the
  new pointer's requirement is still an *absolute chunk on the same timeline*, so its `delta` can be
  copied verbatim — if it is not, that is a signal the new pointer needs a different frame and
  therefore a genuinely separate derivation.

#### 7.5 `gir/analyses/region_increment.py` (245 lines) — the storage-region walk

##### 7.5.1 Concept: a third displacement, and one author for it

A **storage region** (the first of the two meanings of "region" in §1.4) is one of the
storage-disjoint pieces an operand's LDS tile is split into. A split tile is loaded by one
`tensor_load_to_lds` **per region**, and the TDM descriptor has to move between them. That
displacement is distinct from both of the previous two:

| displacement | moves | scope |
|---|---|---|
| `swap` (copy hop) | the descriptor's **LDS write address** to the next generation | across trips |
| `gr_increment` | the descriptor's **global read address** to the next reduction chunk | across trips |
| `region_increment` | the descriptor **within one chunk's tile**, between the regions it is split across | inside one block |

**The defect that created this module.** The displacement used to have two owners.
`KernelWriterAssembly.globalReadDo` performed the walk *inside itself* — load region 0, advance,
load region 1 — and the chunk-increment primitive subtracted the advance back off so the per-chunk
round trip closed. GIR emits one copy `Move` per region and calls the loader once per `Move`, so
the two owners disagreed: `+2` region steps applied against `−1` removed left the descriptor a
region ahead every chunk, and one load read past the tile. Every kernel in a particular wave-tile
class miscompared (provenance #236). The fix is a policy, stated at the top of the file: **one
author per displacement.** The loader now loads exactly the region the descriptor is on, this
analysis says where the descriptor moves, and the chunk increment applies the plain stride with no
correction.

##### 7.5.2 Why a program-order scan and not a fixpoint

This is the one analysis in this section that is *not* built on `ValuePlacementSolver`, and the
docstring (`:18-28`) argues the case rather than assuming it. The reasoning is worth reproducing
because it is the correct way to decide the question for any future displacement:

*The chunk an address points at is a genuine dataflow fact*: it is carried across blocks and back
edges, joins have to agree, and there is no way to know it locally. *The region walk is not that.*
It opens and closes **within one chunk's copies**, which the emitter lays out consecutively in one
block, so its whole extent is visible in program order and there is nothing to propagate. Modelling
it as a fixpoint would be vocabulary, not analysis.

What makes that safe rather than merely convenient is that **the closure is checked**. The
verifier's `G-WALK` (`gir/verify.py:214`, delegating to `walk_violations`) requires the net
displacement per unit per block to be zero *and* every copy to load the region the walk has reached.
So a walk that escapes a block — which would mean the locality assumption is false — fails loudly
instead of silently leaving the descriptor displaced. The assumption is not merely documented; it
is a verified invariant, and if a future schedule ever spreads one chunk's region loads across two
blocks, the verifier will say so and *that* is the moment to reach for the solver.

##### 7.5.3 Reading the region off the coordinate

**`region_of(prog, ref)` (`:39`)** — the region coordinate tuple a shared `Ref` names, or `()` when
the tile is unsplit:

```
rms = prog.meta["region_modes"].get(ref.tile.operand) or ()
if not rms: return ()
coord = dict(ref.tile.coord or ())
return tuple(coord.get(rm) for rm in rms)          # None for an axis the coord does not pin
```

A region split **is a coordinate** — it lives in `Tile.coord` along the operand's region axes — and
that is exactly why GIR can answer "which region" where the hand-written scaffold cannot: the
scaffold has a `bothHalves` escape hatch because *its* split order and loop order differ, not
because the fact is unknowable. Note the deliberate `None` in the output tuple for an unpinned
axis; `_flat` turns that into a refusal rather than a guess.

**`_flat(region, prog, operand)` (`:52`)** — the region tuple as one integer, mixed-radix over the
operand's region axes with the innermost last:

```
idx = 0
for (mode, value) in zip(region_modes[operand], region):
    if value is None: return None                  # UNPINNED — refuse, do not guess
    idx = idx * max(1, mode_extents[mode]) + int(value)
return idx
```

The `None` return is a modelling gap declared in place (`:57-64`): a Φ-fused group may tile its
members on *different* region axes, and the fused instance's coordinate then names only one
member's axis, so the walk cannot be derived for that movement. The chosen response is layered:
this analysis **emits nothing** for such a movement, `walk_violations` **reports it as a violation**
(§7.5.5), and the emitter **refuses** if one ever reaches emission. Skipping here rather than
raising keeps the analysis total for shapes that are only ever built in tests, while leaving no
silent path to wrong code. That three-way split — skip, report, refuse — is a pattern worth copying
for any other partial derivation.

**`_n_regions(prog, unit)` (`:75`)** — how many storage regions a movement is *actually* split
into, read from `meta['unit_regions']` and defaulting to 1. The docstring names the trap: this must
**not** be derived from `region_modes` being non-empty. An operand can own a region *axis* while
being split into one region — the microscaling scale operands are the case: they carry their
parent's region axis (so the grid indexing works) while having a single storage region. Its copy is
a single movement carrying no region coordinate, so treating the axis as a walk asks it for a value
it correctly does not have. This function is also what `gr_increment._reqs` imports rather than
re-deriving (§7.4.3).

##### 7.5.4 `_split_copies` and the by-index pairing precondition

**`_split_copies(prog, blk)` (`:85`)** returns `[(node, unit, flat_region, region_tuple,
region_modes)]` for the region-split copy `Move`s of one block, in program order:

```
for node in blk.body:
    members, refs = copy_unit(node)                 # None for a non-copy
    skip if members is None or _n_regions(prog, members) <= 1     # unsplit: no walk at all
    reg = region_of(prog, refs[0]);   skip if empty
    flat = _flat(reg, prog, refs[0].tile.operand);  skip if None  # unpinned axis
    ---- PRECONDITION CHECK ----
    for each other member ref r in refs[1:]:
        other = _flat(region_of(prog, r), prog, r.tile.operand)
        if other is not None and other != flat:  RAISE ValueError
    ---- end check ----
    emit (node, members, flat, reg, region_modes[refs[0].tile.operand])
```

**The precondition, in full.** Everything after the first line of the body reads `refs[0]` — one
member of a possibly-fused movement — and derives the whole walk from it. That is justified by a
property of Φ fusion: **a fused group pairs its members by index.** The partition names an index
*j*, and region *j* of A moves with region *j* of B, even when the two operands are split along
*different* axes (A cut on its free axis, B on the reduction axis, say). One aliased descriptor
group advances both members with **one** step. So naming one member's axis is not a simplification
that loses the other member's displacement; it is the only form the back end can execute — its
region-step primitive walks **one axis per step**, and the emitter refuses a multi-axis step
outright (`gir_to_rocisa.py:205-216`) — and it is *sufficient* precisely because the indices agree.

**What the check rejects.** If any other member of the same fused movement resolves to a *different*
flat region index than `refs[0]` does, `_split_copies` raises a `ValueError` naming both members and
both indices (`:119-124`). It does **not** raise when the other member's index is `None`
(unpinned) — that case is already handled by the skip-report-refuse layering of §7.5.3, and raising
here would turn a declared modelling gap into a hard build failure for shapes that only exist in
tests.

**Why widening this check would be unsound, not merely conservative.** Suppose the check were
relaxed to "emit a step derived from `refs[0]` even when the members disagree". The emitted Mark
carries one `steps` scalar and one `axis_steps` vector, both derived from A's coordinate, and L3
turns them into **one** add on **one** descriptor register. Because the descriptor is *aliased* —
that is what a fused movement means — that single add is the only displacement either member will
ever receive. A member sitting at index *k* ≠ *j* therefore gets A's displacement applied to its own
base, and its `tensor_load` reads the wrong region of its own tile. There is no conservative
fallback available: the analysis cannot emit two steps (one register), cannot emit the larger step
(they are displacements on different axes with different strides), and cannot decline to step (the
copies of the *other* member then all read region 0). Every widening produces a load at a wrong
address, which is silent memory corruption of the accumulator, not a slowdown. That is the precise
sense in which the check is a **precondition** and not a heuristic: the code below it has no correct
behaviour when it fails, so the only sound responses are "reject" or "implement a genuinely
different lowering with one add per axis per member" — and the second requires a new L3 primitive.

**Why it is checked here at all, given that upstream enforces it.** The agreement is guaranteed by
the Solution-level validator, which rejects a fuse whose members have different region counts. It
used to be *only* assumed here, and the file's comment (`:110-114`) states the objection plainly:
an assumption that upstream can change is exactly how the `refs[0]` reads in this file came to look
like a dropped fact to every reader. A precondition read silently at four sites is worse than a
precondition checked once and cited three times.

**The test, and its non-vacuity half.**
`test_a_fused_movements_members_are_paired_by_index_and_that_is_CHECKED`
(`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:4789`) has two parts and both are necessary. The positive part builds the
shipping mixed-axis fuse across four loop orders through the full Solution→θ→GIR bridge, asserts
each program actually emits `region_increment` Marks (so the sweep is not vacuous), and asserts
every Mark's `axis_steps` names **at most one** axis — the property that makes it executable. The
negative part hand-builds two `Ref`s whose operands own *different* region axes and asserts they
resolve to different flat indices (1 and 0), with an explicit comment that the disagreeing shape
"must be constructible or the assertion is untestable". A check nobody can trigger is decoration;
the test proves this one can be.

##### 7.5.5 The scan, the closing step, and the per-axis vector

**`RegionIncrementRegions.run(prog, am)` (`:138`)** — the whole analysis, per block:

```
for each block:
    at, prev = {}, {}        # unit -> region it sits on / that unit's last copy node
    vec, axes = {}, {}       # unit -> its per-axis coord tuple / its axis names
    for (node, unit, reg, rtup, rms) in _split_copies(prog, blk):
        cur = at.get(unit, 0)                       # the setup leaves it on region 0
        if reg != cur:
            emit region_increment {unit, steps: reg-cur, from_region: cur, to_region: reg,
                                   axis_steps: _axis_delta(rms, vec[unit], rtup)}
                 in Region(block, after=prev[unit], before=node, policy=EARLIEST)
        at[unit], prev[unit], vec[unit] = reg, node, rtup
    # CLOSE THE WALK
    for unit, reg in sorted(at.items(), key=str):
        if reg != 0:
            emit region_increment {unit, steps: -reg, from_region: reg, to_region: 0,
                                   axis_steps: _axis_delta(axes[unit], vec[unit], zeros)}
                 in Region(block, after=prev[unit], before=BLOCK_EXIT, policy=EARLIEST)
```

Two details carry weight.

*The window is tight on both ends* (`:148-152`). `after` is this unit's **previous copy**, `before`
is **this** copy. The comment explains why this matters more here than for the other Marks:
`EARLIEST` with an open `after` would hoist every step to the block entry, which **nets to zero**
while leaving every copy reading the wrong region. A descriptor step is only meaningful *between*
the two loads it separates. This is also why `G-WALK` checks positions and not just the net
(§7.5.6).

*The closing step is emitted, not folded* (`:159-162`). The chunk stride the increment primitive
applies assumes the descriptor is back at the chunk base, so anything left displaced at the block
exit is walked back explicitly. Emitting it rather than folding it into the stride is the entire
point of the module: the subtraction used to live *inside* the increment, where nothing related it
to the advance it undid. `sorted(at.items(), key=str)` makes the closing order deterministic across
units (a `unit` is a tuple, so `key=str` is a stable total order without requiring comparability).

**`_axis_delta(rms, frm, to)` (`:176`)** — `{mode: delta}` for the non-zero axes of one step:

```
{mode: int(b) - int(a) for (mode, a, b) in zip(rms, frm, to) if int(b) != int(a)}
```

**Why the flat `steps` scalar is not enough once two region axes are live** (`:177-185`). `steps` is
the difference of two mixed-radix indices, so a back end could only turn it into bytes by
multiplying *one* stride — right while a single axis moves, wrong the moment two do. In a 2×2
region grid the flat step `2 → 1` is actually "free axis −1, reduction axis +1", whose byte
displacement is `−D_free + D_red`, not `−1 × D`. The per-axis form is the one a descriptor can
actually execute, and it degenerates to the old scalar exactly when one axis is live — which is
every shape shipped so far. Both fields are emitted; L3 reads `axis_steps` to *decide whether it can
proceed* and `steps` to decide how many single-region walks to issue (`gir_to_rocisa.py:495-530`).

`test_an_operand_on_TWO_region_axes_WALKS_with_a_per_axis_step`
(`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:3656`) sweeps seven two-axis split configurations and asserts three things:
`walk_violations` is empty; every emitted region step carries a non-empty `axis_steps`; and — the
sharp part — that the flat scalar is the **mixed-radix combination** of the per-axis deltas, not
their sum. Its comment gives the counterexample that forces the distinction: `{K_split:+1,
K_split2:−1}` sums to zero and is nevertheless a real step (flat 1 → 2 over radices [2,2]).

##### 7.5.6 `walk_violations` — the checker

**`walk_violations(prog)` (`:188`)** returns `[]` or a list of human-readable strings. It is called
by `verify_gir`'s `G-WALK` check (`gir/verify.py:214-225`) and directly by several tests. It
replays the walk in **program order** over the finalized body, accumulating `steps` from
`region_increment` Marks and comparing against each split copy's own region as it is reached:

```
for each block:
    at = {}                                  # unit -> running region position
    for node in body, in order:
        if node is a region_increment Mark:  at[unit] += steps
        elif node is a split copy Move:
            flat = _flat(region_of(refs[0]), ...)
            if the region is named but UNPINNED (flat is None):  report a violation
            if flat is None (unsplit): skip
            if at[unit] != flat:  report "loads region X but the descriptor is on Y"
    for each unit with a non-zero residue: report "the walk must close"
```

**Two properties, and the second alone is not enough.** The docstring (`:189-202`) records that the
first version of this checker verified only the *net* displacement, and that measuring it cost a
bug: the net is zero even when every step has been hoisted to the block entry ahead of all the
copies — net-clean and uniformly wrong. Property (1), "every split copy loads the region the
descriptor is on", is the one that actually matters; property (2), "the walk closes", is what makes
the *next* chunk's stride correct. The original hardware bug was (2) failing; the placement bug this
checker later found was (1).

**"Cannot tell" is not "fine".** The unpinned-axis branch (`:218-230`) used to `continue` on the
same rule `_split_copies` skips by, so a movement whose walk was **dropped entirely** reported
clean — the verifier agreeing with the defect it exists to catch. It now emits a violation naming
the operand, the region tuple and the operand's region modes, and stating that the shape is
unsupported rather than clean. This is the general lesson the file states in one line and that is
worth carrying to every checker in this package: *a checker must never round "cannot tell" down to
"fine".*

`test_G_WALK_FIRES_when_the_walk_is_dropped_duplicated_or_HOISTED`
(`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:3167`) is the corresponding three-way mutation test: from a clean split
program it (a) removes one step, (b) duplicates one, and (c) moves every step to the block entry,
and requires `verify_gir` to raise with `G-WALK` in all three cases. Case (c) is the one that
motivated the checker's present form.

##### 7.5.7 The rest of the tests

* `test_the_descriptor_STEPS_between_consecutive_regions_of_one_tile` (`:3099`) — in both the
  prologue and the steady body, no two consecutive copies of one movement fill the same region, and
  every adjacent pair is separated by exactly the step between their regions. It uses a local
  `_walk` helper (`:3082`) that re-derives the sequence from `region_of`/`_flat`/`_n_regions`
  rather than from the analysis's output.
* `test_the_walk_CLOSES_so_the_chunk_stride_stays_plain` (`:3127`) — net zero per unit per block,
  over *every* block including the drain.
* `test_an_UNSPLIT_movement_emits_no_walk_at_all` (`:3142`) — the whole mechanism sits behind
  `unit_regions > 1`, so a non-split kernel is untouched. This is what makes the byte-neutrality
  sweeps of the split work meaningful rather than tautological.
* `test_each_region_is_loaded_ONCE_with_its_OWN_token` (`:3151`) — adjacent property, but it pins
  the same coordinate reading: each of a movement's regions is loaded exactly once per chunk and no
  two share a memory token.
* The `_walked(name)` helper (`:3071`) deliberately uses `build_gir` rather than `lower_to_gir`,
  because the walk is placed by a *pass*: reading it off the unlowered form would find nothing, and
  `G-WALK` correctly rejects that form (copies at region 1 with no step to get there).
* The fp8 sweeps (`:4001`, `:4031`) assert `walk_violations(prog) == []` at both split axes and
  every element width, checking that the split is a coordinate fact and the element width is an
  address fact and the two are independent.

##### 7.5.8 Complexity, weaknesses and extension advice

**Complexity.** `run` is a single pass over every block body, with `_split_copies` doing O(members)
work per copy and `_flat` doing O(region axes) — so O(instructions) overall, with constants of 1–2.
`walk_violations` is a second pass of the same shape. Both are negligible: a steady body has tens of
nodes and at most two split movements with at most four regions each. There is nothing here worth
optimizing, and the natural micro-optimization (caching `region_modes[operand]` lookups) would save
microseconds while making the two passes diverge.

**Sharp edges and honest gaps.**

* **The unpinned-axis gap is real and open.** A Φ-fused group whose members are tiled on different
  region axes cannot have its walk derived, because the fused instance's coordinate names only one
  member's axis. The three-layer response (skip / report / refuse) means it cannot produce wrong
  code, but it also means such a configuration simply cannot be built. Closing it requires the
  fused copy's coordinate to carry *every* member's region axis, which is a change in the lowering
  and in θ, not here.
* **`_split_copies` returns a 5-tuple.** `(node, unit, flat, region_tuple, region_modes)` is one
  field past comfortable, and `run` unpacks it positionally at `:143`. A small frozen dataclass
  (`SplitCopy`) would cost nothing and would make the `rtup`/`rms`/`vec`/`axes` bookkeeping inside
  `run` legible; that bookkeeping is currently four parallel dicts keyed by unit, which is the one
  genuinely hard-to-read stretch in these four modules.
* **The closing step's `axis_steps` is computed against `vec.get(unit, ())`**, i.e. the last copy's
  coordinate tuple, and `axes.get(unit, ())` for the mode names (`:168-170`). If a unit's copies
  somehow disagreed on their region-axis *arity*, the `zip` in `_axis_delta` would silently truncate.
  It cannot happen today (arity is a per-operand fact from `meta`), but the truncation is silent and
  an explicit length assertion would be cheap.
* **`region_of` returns `()` for an unsplit tile and a tuple containing `None` for an unpinned
  axis** — two different "no answer" values distinguished only by convention. `_flat` handles both,
  but every caller must remember which is which. The tests hit this: `_walk` in the test file has to
  write `_flat(reg, ...) if reg else None`.
* **The one-axis-per-step restriction is an L3 property**, not a GIR one. GIR expresses a grid step
  perfectly well; the emitter refuses it. If a future descriptor gains a two-axis add, nothing in
  this module changes — only the refusal at the emitter is lifted. That is the right place for the
  restriction to live, and it should stay there.

**If you extend this to a displacement that is *not* block-local**, re-read §7.5.2 first. The
decision to scan rather than solve rests entirely on the claim that one chunk's region loads are
consecutive within one block, and that claim is *checked* by `G-WALK`. The moment `G-WALK` starts
failing on a legitimate schedule, the answer is not to weaken the check — it is to move this
analysis onto `ValuePlacementSolver` with the flat region index as the value, `edge_delta = 0`, and
`modulus = n_regions` (the walk is cyclic and closes, so the ring domain is the right one). All the
machinery already exists; only the access enumerator would be reused from here.

#### 7.6 Cross-cutting notes for the four modules

**Dead code and unused parameters, in one place.** Every item here was verified by grep, and none of
it affects behaviour:

| location | item |
|---|---|
| `gir/analyses/swap_regions.py:63` | `CondGoto`, `Goto` imported, never used |
| `gir/analyses/swap_regions.py:65` | `BLOCK_ENTRY`, `BLOCK_EXIT` imported, never used |
| `gir/analyses/swap_regions.py:178` | `_topo` — reachable only through the dead local at `:244` |
| `gir/analyses/swap_regions.py:236-244` | `fwd_preds` / `fwd_succs` / `order` — computed, never read |
| `gir/analyses/swap_regions.py:150` | `_unemitted_edges`'s `headers` parameter, accepted and unused |
| `gir/analyses/gr_increment.py:54` | `successor_labels` imported, never used |
| `gir/analyses/gr_increment.py:56` | `BLOCK_ENTRY`, `BLOCK_EXIT` imported, never used |
| `gir/analyses/gr_increment.py:196` | `_flow`'s `back_pairs` parameter — `delta` closes over a locally rebuilt `back_set` |
| `gir/analyses/gr_increment.py:255` vs `swap_regions.py:178` | two near-identical `_topo` implementations; the second is dead, the first is live |

The safe cleanup, in order: delete the four unused imports; delete `swap_regions._topo` and its
three dead locals; delete `_unemitted_edges`'s `headers` and update both call sites; delete
`_flow`'s `back_pairs`; then move `gr_increment._topo` into `cfg.py` beside `successors`. Nothing
in that list changes a single emitted instruction, and each step is independently testable against
the existing suite.

**The private-import coupling.** `gr_increment.py` imports `_unemitted_edges` from `swap_regions.py`
and `_n_regions` from `region_increment.py`. Both are deliberate — the alternative is a second
derivation that drifts — but importing an underscore-prefixed name across modules is a signal the
name belongs somewhere shared. A future cleanup should promote `_unemitted_edges` (it is a property
of the CFG, so `cfg.py`) and `_n_regions` (it is a reading of `prog.meta`, so alongside the other
meta readers). Do not solve it by copying.

**Determinism.** All four modules produce output in a deterministic order without relying on set
iteration: `_units` uses first-seen order over an ordered dict, `solve` sorts block labels, and the
region walk's closing loop sorts by `str(unit)`. The one place a `set` is returned is
`_unemitted_edges`, and its only use is membership testing. This matters because the emitted
assembly is diffed byte-for-byte against baselines in the validation workflow; a non-deterministic
Mark order would make that diff useless.

**Where compile-time cost sits, across the four.** Six solver runs per kernel over a 4–12 block CFG,
plus a handful of O(instructions) body scans. The measured cost is not visible next to LoopIR
lowering or rocisa emission. If profiling ever says otherwise, the first thing to attack is the
repeated body scanning (§7.3.7), not the fixpoints.

#### 7.7 `gir/analyses/gl2_prefetch.py` (~110 lines) — the L2 warm-up, #216

The fifth region analysis, and the odd one out in every dimension: it runs no fixpoint, reads no
other analysis (`am` is accepted and ignored), consults `Program.params` rather than `Program.meta`,
and produces a Mark that names nothing.

**What GL2 is.** `PrefetchGL2` (0/1/2, gated on the `HasGlobalPrefetch` asm cap) warms L2 for a
chunk `PrefetchGlobalRead + PrefetchGL2` ahead while the real global→shared copy runs at
`PrefetchGlobalRead`. It carries its own state end to end — its own address VGPRs
(`states.<op>.startVgprGL2PrefetchAddr`, `gl2nl` per operand) and its own increment SGPRs. It never
touches the TDM descriptor and never names a region coordinate.

**Three consequences, each contradicting the obvious guess.**

1. *It is not placed relative to the copy.* `gr_increment` is `EARLIEST` because the descriptor it
   writes feeds a `tensor_load` in the same trip. GL2 feeds **nothing** in this trip, so it has no
   producer to sit beside and `region.after` is block entry.
2. *It is not per region.* Under `TDMSplit` the copy becomes one instance per region and
   `region_increment` follows it. `Components/GL2Prefetch.py` contains no reference to `TDMSplit` or
   `split` at all — GL2 advances by a whole `DepthU` once per chunk regardless — so this analysis
   emits **one Mark per steady block at every split factor**. That is the same rate as
   `gr_increment`, because the scaffold's own placement is one per `_loopBody` call and `_loopBody`
   runs once per loop copy (`KernelWriter.py` ~6288). Keying it per region would issue N prefetches
   of one address range and burn N × `gl2nl` memory-pipe slots for nothing.
3. *It is not one instruction.* `issueLoad`/`incrementAddr` both loop `for i in range(gl2nl)` per
   operand, and the operand set includes `MXSA`/`MXSB` and sparse `Metadata`. The Mark stands for
   that whole block — measured at 5 `global_prefetch_b8` per mark on the mxf8 TileSpan shape — which
   is why *where* it lands is a real cost question rather than noise.

**Ownership.** `SIA.noSchedGlobalRead` returns early under `UseLoopModel`, which used to mean GL2 was
*dropped*, and `Solution.py` rejected `PrefetchGL2` for exactly that reason. That early return is now
what **makes room** for GIR to own it: the rejection is lifted and the pair is emitted at the Mark.
The rule the rejection list encodes is unchanged — whatever `noSchedGlobalRead` schedules must be
either GIR's or rejected — and one item moved columns. `DirectToLds` and the sparse metadata read are
still in the rejected column. What stays scaffold-owned is the **prologue** fill (`KernelWriter`'s
`counterL <= PGR` / `Skip_GL2` block), which sits outside the main loop and outside GIR's dataflow;
the **drain** gets no Mark at all, because the `counterL <= PGR+GL2` clamp exists precisely to stop
prefetching there.

**Measured, on `loopmodel_mxf8_gfx1250.yaml`'s TileSpan x TDMSplit block (2026-08-24, CPU-only codegen).** 34/34
kernels generate; 15 are ULM1 × GL2. In-loop `global_prefetch_b8` count: **75 with the Mark, 0 with
the analysis disabled** — so GIR is the sole source of the in-loop GL2 under ULM, and the emission is
attributable rather than assumed. The 17 non-GL2 kernels are **byte-identical** with the analysis
fully disabled, which is the inertness claim at codegen level. `f8` regression: 112/112, 112/112,
88/88.

**One trap this cost an hour to.** The branch first tagged its emission with `_tag` (a floating
`addComment0`), and under `ScheduleIterAlg=4` StinkyTofu reorders the body, so the comment no longer
marks what it was written above and never appeared in the `.s` at all. Fifteen kernels emitted the
block and no assembly said GIR had put it there; the only way to attribute it was to rebuild with the
analysis disabled and diff. `_append_tag` (§9) is the instruction-attached form that survives
reordering — its own docstring says so — and every other act already used it.

---

### 8. `gir/analyses/` III — LDS buffer ids, rotation frames, and hazards

Three modules, `lds_buffers.py` + `frame_map.py` + `frame_hazards.py`, and one subject: **which two
LDS accesses can touch the same bytes, and how far apart do they run.** The layering is strict and
one-directional, because the previous shape — one module that numbered storage *and* did dataflow —
is what let a storage question and a generation question answer each other in a loop.

```
LdsBufferIds   storage identity      (operand, region, ring)      depends on NOTHING
      |
FrameMap       rotation coordinate   which ring each Gen stands at, per block
      |
FrameHazards   ordered pairs         RAW / WAR / WAW, per frame
```

#### 8.1 The ownership boundary, stated first

GIR owns exactly two things about synchronisation:

1. the **memory token** — a name for a piece of LDS storage, attached to every access that touches
   it and to every ordering point that stands between accesses; and
2. the **copy order** — the sequence in which the movements are emitted, which is what an
   order-driven scheduler reads as the specification.

GIR does **not** own synchronisation *placement in instructions*. It never emits an `s_barrier`,
never computes a wait count, never chooses `dscnt`/`tensorcnt` values. The Mark kind is `fence`,
and its realization — a wait plus a barrier — is chosen by the rocisa adapter. A maintainer
reaching for "emit a barrier here" in this layer has crossed the boundary: add the *fact* (a token,
or a `fence` Mark with the right token set) and let layer 3 pick the instruction.

#### 8.2 What a memory token actually is

A memory token is **not a label**. It is an **LDS pseudo-register**. StinkyTofu turns the token set
carried on an instruction into operands of a synthetic register class: a producer is a def, a
consumer is a use, and a barrier is **both**. Two consequences follow and neither is optional:

* a barrier that names no token is a **full drain** — legal, conservative, and equivalent to naming
  every token. `memoryToken=None` lowers to a plain `SBarrier`;
* the wait a barrier emits is `countFrom(src) - 1`, the number of entries younger than the
  dependence it names. **Naming more storage can only make the wait smaller**, so a fence that
  names a buffer it does not order costs latency with no ordering in exchange.

#### 8.3 `lds_buffers.py` — the ONE numbering

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Buffer:
    operand: str      # A, B, MXSA, ...
    region:  tuple    # one value per region axis; () when the tile is not split
    ring:    int      # which of the operand's rotating buffers, in [0, depth)
```

Every id is a byte range. Under an S-deep rotation an operand owns S of them; *which generation*
occupies one is `FrameMap`'s question, layered on top. The module depends on no other analysis —
every input is tile metadata already on the `Ref` — and it is the one numbering the frames, the
hazards and the tokens all speak in.

`Geometry.regions_of(ref, is_write)` returns, per region axis, the **set** of values the access may
touch. A coord pins the axis, or the access touches every region; a *read* of an agent-relative
operand pins nothing either, its region being a fact about the wave rather than the coord.
`ids_for(ref)` is the may-set over the whole ring; `at(ref, ring)` narrows it to one rotation
position.

#### 8.4 `frame_map.py` — the rotation coordinate

A `Frame` is an immutable phase vector, one entry per Gen ring, absent entries reading 0. The
dataflow is forward over **sets** of phase vectors with union as the meet — not a collapse onto a
representative — and `_classes` folds frames that differ by a *uniform* rotation of every ring,
since those are the same picture one trip on.

`entrances(block)` yields one frame per **distinct entrance picture**. A back edge is not an
entrance — it is this block one rotation on — and neither are two forward edges differing by a
uniform rotation.

`cut(block)` is the single frame a block's *stamps* are resolved in. **This is the authoritative
frame for anything that reaches the emitted contract**, because `tokens_for(ref)` resolves through
it and that is what lands in `Move.token_ids`. Anything that needs a block's frame must use `cut`;
see §9.4 for what happened when a second derivation appeared.

#### 8.5 `frame_hazards.py` — the ordered pairs

```python
RAW = "RAW"        # write -> read   (residency)
WAR = "WAR"        # read  -> write  (rotation anti-dep)
WAW = "WAW"        # write -> write  (rotation output-dep)
```

`SharedTouch` is one endpoint — `(block, pos, inst, ref, is_write, operand, regions)`. `Hazard` is
an ordered pair plus `ring`, `gap`, `cross_agent`, `cross_block`; `gap == 0` means one execution of
the pair, `gap >= 1` a later instance of the consumer. `FrameHazardSet` stores each edge **once**
and keeps `(producer frame, consumer frame, edge index)` per instance, so one edge can be live in
several frames and `instances()` hands back the same object each time.

`needing_fence()` returns the cross-wave edges and is **the only place the fence/no-fence decision
is made**. A same-wave edge is discharged by program order plus the completion counter.

##### 8.5.1 The pairing rule — a killing reaching-defs, and what a read does NOT kill

`_walk` runs one `(block, frame)` in program order:

```python
older = ((() if reads.get(s) else writes.get(s, ())) if not touch.is_write
         else set(reads.get(s, ())) or set(writes.get(s, ())))
```

Read both arms, because each encodes a rule that removes a barrier the emitted code does not need:

* **A read pairs with the last write only if nothing has read it yet.** Visibility is monotone: the
  fence that made a write visible to the first reader made it visible to every later one. Without
  this, a write pairs with *every* reader, and the second half of a read group split across the back
  edge opens its own barrier at the top of the loop for a write that is already visible.
* **A write pairs with the readers since the last write, and with that write only if there are
  none.** Nothing refills an LDS buffer it has not consumed, so a read almost always sits between
  two writes and the RAW into it plus the WAR out of it already order them. The surviving WAW is the
  genuinely-unread overwrite.

A write still kills: `writes[s], reads[s] = {(frame, id(touch))}, set()`. The entry, not the
instruction, is what is paired — the same instruction arriving over the back edge is a *later*
instance however identical the object is.

---

### 9. `gir/analyses/` IV — fences and dependence tokens

Two modules, `fence_regions.py` (where the ordering points go) and `dep_tokens.py` (what they
name), plus the two checks in `verify.py` that re-derive both from the final body.

#### 9.1 A fence sits at one of its hazard's OWN two ends

`_admissible_slots(hazard, n_slots, block)` is the whole placement law. A fence discharges an edge
only at one of the edge's own ends, so a block that is neither offers nothing — an intermediate
block lies on some path, and the producer can re-reach the consumer around it via the back edge.

```python
if hazard.same_trip and hazard.in_program_order:
    return frozenset(s for s in range(n_slots) if a < s <= b)
return frozenset(s for s in range(n_slots) if s > a or s <= b)      # the WRAP: two halves
```

A wrap has two disjoint halves — the end of the producing trip and the top of the consuming one —
so `_windows` returns one `Region` per contiguous run and the naming layer spends that freedom.

#### 9.2 Two tiers: RAW stamps the barrier, WAR rides it

`_cover` places in two passes, and the tier key is the hazard kind, not the cost:

```python
for stamps in (True, False):
    tier = {i for i in remaining if (hazards[i].kind == RAW) is stamps}
```

* **Tier 1, RAW.** Only a RAW buys a wait — the consumer must observe the producer's *data*, which
  is what a memory token is for. Its slot is placed as **late** as its window allows, because every
  slot it gives up is a load that has to have landed while the loads issued after it stay in flight.
* **Tier 2, WAR and WAW.** These need a barrier between their ends but **no name on it**. They
  *ride* a tier-1 barrier whenever one is legal for them — StinkyTofu makes every barrier a waitcnt
  point, so riding one orders them for free. Naming a WAR's buffer would wait on the load issued
  just after the fence, which is exactly how the wait gets pinned to 0.

#### 9.3 `merge` — one barrier per slot, not one per buffer

The cover is computed **per buffer** — `(operand, region, ring)` — so a fence names only the storage
it orders; grouping an operand's two regions onto one fence makes it name both, and then every load
defs one of its names and the wait can never leave anything in flight. But a *separate cover per
buffer* also opened a *separate barrier* per buffer, even where one slot discharged them all.

`_one_barrier(covers, n_slots, block)` merges cover sets whose `_admissible_slots` intersections
still intersect; `_cover_slot` puts the merged barrier at the latest slot discharging every edge.
The cover stays per buffer; what merges is the **barrier**, of which a block needs one per slot.

`FenceRegions(merge=True)` is the switch and folds into `cache_key` so the settings cache
separately. It is meaningful **only for tier 1**: a tier-2 edge already rides a RAW barrier rather
than opening its own.

#### 9.4 `dep_tokens.py` — the name comes from the FENCED BLOCK's frame

```python
def naming(self, edges, block):
    """The tokens a fence in `block` must name: what THAT block's own stamps call the storage."""
```

For each RAW edge, the token is `tokens_for(end.ref)` for the end that lives in `block`. This is the
**same function** that produces `Move.token_ids`, so the barrier and the accesses it orders always
speak one frame's names.

> **The rule, and why it is spelled out.** A fence's name and a Move's stamp are one fact. The stamp
> resolves at `fm.cut(block)`. Any second derivation of "which frame names this block" will agree in
> the steady block and **invert in a drain block**, which legitimately runs at both parities — the
> fence names A#0/B#0 while the reads it exists for are stamped A#1/B#1, zero overlap, and to
> StinkyTofu a barrier that defs 0 and 2 orders nothing against a `ds_read` that uses 1. Resolve
> through `tokens_for` at the fenced block, never in parallel.

`choose(prog, options, edges, repeating, preds)` then pins the window to a concrete point, scored by
`_in_flight` — the loads still outstanding at that point, which is the wait the barrier would emit.
It walks back over **real predecessor paths**, since the load a loop-top fence waits on was issued
on the previous trip, and takes the smallest count any path gives.

#### 9.5 The two checks, and the property they must not be derived from

`verify._check_token_reuse` (G-TOKEN-REUSE) and `tool/fence_token_check.unseparated_edges` both
re-derive separation from the fences actually present in the final body:

```python
pins = set(dep.tokens_for(h.consumer.ref)) if h.kind == RAW else set()
```

**The bar is the consumer's stamp** — what the backend carries — not what the fence claims. A
WAR/WAW needs a barrier between its ends and is checked with `separating()` alone. Deriving `pins`
from the same function that *writes* the fence makes both checks true by construction: they then ask
"does the fence name what the fence names?", return clean on a misnamed fence, and the fault they
exist to catch becomes invisible. **When a check cannot fail, it is derived from the thing it is
checking.**

`_check_frame_coverage` (G-TOKEN-FRAME) asks a *different* question — do the two ends share a stamp,
so StinkyTofu orders them — and `tokens_for` is authoritative for it. It skips `h.gap` instances:
only one execution of a pair is at stake, since two instances are separated by the back edge and the
scheduler that could reorder them works inside a basic block.

### 10. `gir/analyses/` V — the short path and uniform placement

Two analyses, at opposite ends of the size scale. `short_path.py` is 566 lines and the largest
single module in `gir/analyses/`; it answers one question with a full two-space reaching-definitions
simulation. `uniform_placement.py` is 159 lines and answers one question with two reachability sets.
They are in the same section because they are the two *whole-program structural* analyses — neither
places a `Mark`, neither returns a plan, and both are consumed by a decision about the **shape** of
the program rather than about the contents of a block.

#### 10.1 The problem `short_path.py` exists to solve: one kernel, two structures

A software-pipelined reduction loop has a **peel depth** `M`: the prologue issues `M` chunks' worth
of global→shared copies before the loop starts, and a matching `M`-step drain finishes the compute
for those chunks after the loop ends. `T`, the runtime number of reduction chunks, is not known at
compile time. When `T` is not large enough to fill and drain the pipeline, the steady loop must not
run at all — there is a second, **degenerate** execution path, and every pipelined kernel has one.

The two layers this package sits between describe that second path with **different structure**.

```
scaffold (TensileLite, hand-written):
        prologue ──► Cond ──► steady loop ──► drain
                       └──────────(skip)────────┘        prologue and drain are SHARED by both
                                                          paths; a small T merely skips the loop

LoopIR (layer 1, produced by Tensile/LoopModel/):
        Cond { prologue ──► steady loop ──► drain }   else   { short0 ──► short1 ──► … }
                                                          two DISJOINT arms; the else arm is a
                                                          complete unpipelined emission of the
                                                          same schedule
```

`loopir_to_gir` lowers the LoopIR shape faithfully: it emits `M` real blocks named `short0` …
`short{M-1}`, and the prologue's terminator is a `CondGoto` whose false edge enters `short0`
(`loopir_to_gir.py:702`). **Folding** means deleting those blocks and retargeting that false edge
into the head of the drain chain, so the degenerate case is served by the prologue's copies followed
by the drain's computes and no extra code is emitted at all.

The lowering used to fold **unconditionally**, discarding the else arm on the stated claim that "the
scaffold reconstructs it from prologue + drain". Nobody had checked the claim. This analysis exists
because it is false for a substantial fraction of the configuration space, and — this is the part
that matters — it is *true* for the shapes that actually ship, so a checker that got it wrong in
either direction would be believed.

#### 10.2 Why the fold can fail: it is a reordering

Both shapes contain the same *work*. What differs is the **order**. The short arm interleaves:

```
copy chunk 0, compute chunk 0, copy chunk 1, compute chunk 1, …
```

while the folded path separates:

```
copy chunk 0, copy chunk 1, …  |  compute chunk 0, compute chunk 1, …
```

Separating makes **every peeled chunk's shared buffer live at once**. The shared buffers rotate over
a ring of depth `S`. With `S < M`, the copy for chunk `k` lands on the same ring slot as the copy for
chunk `k - S`, and on the separated order that slot has not yet been read. The earlier chunk's read
then reads the *later* chunk's data.

That is not a hazard a fence can repair. A fence orders two accesses that are already to the right
addresses; here the def-use edge itself is broken — the consumer is wired to a different producer.
No barrier, wait-count or scheduling change recovers it. The only remedies are "do not fold" or
"deepen the ring", and the ring depth is a schedule decision made a layer up.

So the fold is a **legality question about a reordering**, and the right tool for it is the tool
compilers use for reordering legality: compare the def-use relation before and after.

#### 10.3 The abstraction: two location spaces, and values rather than producers

The analysis simulates both instruction sequences and compares, **for every consumer, which
producer's value reaches it**. That is textbook reaching definitions, run twice and diffed. Two
things have to be pinned down before it means anything: what a *location* is, and what a *value* is.

**Locations.** Data is handed over in exactly two places in this IR, so there are two location
spaces:

```
shared    ('shared',   operand, generation)
register  ('register', operand, group, slot, free-tile-coord)
```

A shared location is written by a **copy** (global→shared `Move`) and read by a **read**
(shared→register `Move`). A register location is written by a read and consumed by an `Mma`.

The register location names **four** things, and the fourth is the one that took a defect to
discover. `group` and `slot` name the *register rotation*: the schedule rotates a read's destination
over a ring of width `W` so that a read issued ahead of its consumer does not clobber the value the
current `Mma` is still using. But the rotation is only one axis. The *free-tile coordinate* — `M`'s
inner coordinate for the A operand, `N`'s for B — selects a physically different VGPR that the model
leaves to allocation. Omitting it merged `A(k1, m0)` with `A(k1, m1)`: they share a rotation slot, so
every read of one appeared to clobber the other, and the analysis reported breaks everywhere
(provenance: #227).

**Values.** This is the decisive design choice of the whole module, so it gets its own subsection.

#### 10.4 The decisive rule: compare the VALUE delivered, not the producer's identity

The obvious formulation is: for each consumer, is the *same instruction* its producer on both paths?
That formulation is wrong here, and wrong in a way that produces confident false SPLITs.

The two arms are **deliberately different schedules**. The short arm is the *unpipelined* emission of
the same schedule: because it never enters the steady loop, there is no next chunk to read ahead
into, so its read-ahead displacement is reset to zero (`dr = 0`), while the drain keeps the
schedule's own read-ahead distance `dr(θ)`. Consequently the two arms are not instruction-isomorphic
and "the same instruction" is not a well-defined question. At `dr > 0` the drain's read at coordinate
`(k0, m0)` in step 0 is prefetching that coordinate *from the next chunk*, while the arm's read at
the same coordinate is fetching the *current* one. Comparing producers reports that as a difference.
It is a real difference in *which instruction runs*, and a meaningless one — what the consuming
`Mma` depends on is the *data* it receives, and the data is the same.

So each producer carries a **value**, and it is values that are compared (`short_path.py:341-347`):

| producer | value tuple | why |
|---|---|---|
| copy | `('copy', operands, coord, occurrence)` | The k-th copy of a given operand-and-coordinate fetches reduction chunk k, on **both** arms. The occurrence index therefore *is* the chunk index — a path-independent name for the data. |
| read | `('read', operands, coord, <value of the copy that filled its source buffer>)` | **Transitive**, and that is load-bearing (see below). Two reads moving the same data out of the same buffer into the same register are the *same value* wherever they sit. |
| `Mma` | `None` | An `Mma` defines nothing this analysis tracks; the accumulator is not a rotating resource here. |

The read value chains to the producing copy rather than naming the source *generation*. Naming the
generation is an identity for the chunk **only while the ring is at least as deep as the peel**. At
`S = 1` every generation is 0, so a generation-keyed value called two reads of *different chunks*
equal and returned a false FOLD — on precisely the configuration that most needs the ring-depth
answer. Chaining to the producer says *which data*, at any ring depth. `Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2147`
is the fixture that pins this.

The pay-off of the value formulation is visible in the opposite direction too. The prologue's
read-ahead fill has no peel-step index at all — it lives in a block that is not a drain step — so a
producer-identity comparison classified it as "not the arm's read" and recorded a break. Under the
value formulation it *delivers exactly the value the arm's own first read does*, so it matches. The
shipping default configuration reported 24 breaks under producer identity, every one an artefact.

#### 10.5 The consumer key: correspondence is structural, comparison is by value

Before two consumers' inputs can be compared, the consumer in one arm must be paired with *its*
counterpart in the other. That pairing is **structural**, and it is a different key from the value:

```
consumer key = (kind, step, operands, coord, groups)
```

`kind` is `'read'` or `'mma'`; `step` is the index of the block within its chain (drain step `i` on
the folded path, short step `i` in the arm — the fold identifies the two); `operands` and `coord` are
the instruction's own destination identity.

Three deliberate choices in that key:

* **The position within the step is not part of it.** Position was meaningful while the two arms
  were the same schedule; the read-ahead reset made them differ on purpose, so keying on position
  would declare every corresponded pair distinct.
* **`groups` is part of it** (`_groups`, `short_path.py:121`). A *split read* — one where the
  read's register destinations fall into more than one width class, so the emitter issues one
  instruction per class — puts two instructions at the *same* `(operand, coord)`, distinguished only
  by which register groups they fill. The microscaling-fp8 shape is the real case: its `lo` half
  rotates over a 2-deep register ring while its `hi` half is written in place. Without `groups` in
  the key the correspondence is ambiguous, and `_trace` **raises** rather than pairing the wrong two
  (`short_path.py:333-335`). That raise is how the omission was found.
* **The key is checked unique.** A key must name one instruction per arm. Duplicate ⇒ raise.

A copy never gets a consumer key (`short_path.py:330`: `key = None if k == 'copy' or step is None`).
Copies have no tracked uses — their source is global space, which the analysis does not model — so
there is nothing to compare at one. An instruction in a block with no step index (the prologue) gets
no key either. Both are counted as **extras**.

**An extra is not a defect and is never penalized.** It is an instruction with no counterpart key:
the prologue's read-ahead fill, and the drain's forward prefetch for the *next* output tile. Its
*value* still participates in the walk exactly like any other producer — which is the mechanism by
which the prologue fill supplies the value the arm's first read produces. `FoldVerdict.extras`
carries the count purely as an observability number.

#### 10.6 `_trace` — one forward walk of one arm

`_trace(prog, labels, entry, step_of, free_modes)` (`short_path.py:291`) is the simulator. It is a
single straight-line walk over an ordered list of block labels; there is **no fixpoint and no
CFG traversal**, because each arm is by construction a straight chain (prologue → drain0 → drain1 →
… , or short0 → short1 → …). Returns `(reach, keys, extras)`.

```
_trace(prog, labels, entry, step_of, free_modes):
    last  = {}          # location -> the VALUE currently resident there
    reach = {}          # consumer key -> {location: value that reaches it}
    keys  = set()       # every consumer key this arm defines
    copy_seen = {}      # (operands, coord) -> how many copies so far  ==  chunk index
    extras = 0

    for lab in labels:                       # in chain order
        blk  = prog.blocks[lab]
        step = step_of(lab)                  # None for the prologue
        base = _frame_base(blk)              # see 10.7 — the block's chunk frame
        for inst in blk.body:
            skip Mark nodes
            k = _kind(inst)                  # 'copy' | 'read' | 'mma' | None
            skip if k is None
            ops, crd   = _operands(inst), _coord(inst)
            defs, uses = _defs_uses(inst, entry, free_modes, base)

            key = None if (k == 'copy' or step is None) else (k, step, ops, crd, _groups(inst))
            if key is not None:
                raise if key already in keys          # correspondence must be 1:1
                keys.add(key)
                if uses:  reach[key] = { u: last.get(u, ENTRY) for u in uses }
            else:
                extras += 1

            if   k == 'copy':  value = ('copy', ops, crd, copy_seen[(ops,crd)]++)
            elif k == 'read':  src   = the one 'shared' entry of `uses`, if any
                               value = ('read', ops, crd, last.get(src, ENTRY) if src else None)
            else:              value = None            # an Mma produces nothing tracked

            for d in defs:  last[d] = value
    return reach, keys, extras
```

`last` is **not** reset per block: the whole arm is one timeline, which is exactly what makes the
prologue's definitions visible to the drain's uses. `ENTRY = ('<entry>',)` (`short_path.py:255`) is
the sentinel meaning "this arm never wrote this location".

The cost is one pass over the instructions of both arms, `O(I)` with a dictionary update per def and
per use: `I` is the total instruction count of prologue + drain + short, measured at 66 for the
plain bf16 default and 902 for the largest microscaling fixture.

#### 10.7 The frame problem: resolving a drain generation on the folded path

This is the subtlest part of the module and the source of a whole family of artefactual SPLIT
verdicts (provenance: #230). It is worth stating carefully, because the same class of error recurs
elsewhere in this package.

A `Ref` in GIR names its shared residence in one of two ways. A block whose accesses have a
compile-time-known chunk index — the prologue, and the short arm — carries `abs_gen`, a concrete
integer. A block inside or after the steady loop cannot: its buffer depends on how many trips ran,
which is runtime data. Such a `Ref` carries a loop-carried `Gen` (the one SSA value class in GIR)
plus an integer `gdelta` offset, and the concrete generation is computed as

```
generation = (entry_value_of(gen) + base + gdelta) mod ring
```

**`_entry_gens(prog)` (`short_path.py:132`)** supplies the `entry_value_of` term. It walks every
block's phi list and returns `{gen.id: phi.entry_val}`. This is where the folded path's semantics
enter the resolution, and it is a consequence rather than a convention: on the folded path the
steady loop takes **zero** trips (that is what a small `T` means), so every loop-carried generation
still holds its phi's entry value, and a drain `Ref` resolves against that value directly. On a real
execution with trips, it would not.

**`_generation(ref, entry, base=0)` (`short_path.py:171`)** applies the formula. It returns
`int(ref.abs_gen)` when the ref pins an absolute generation, the modular expression above when it
carries a `Gen`, and `None` when the ref names no shared residence at all (a register-only ref).
`max(1, ref.gen.ring)` guards against a zero ring.

**`_frame_base(blk)` (`short_path.py:146`)** supplies `base`, and it is the correction. The question
it answers is: *the chunk position that this block's `gdelta = 0` is stated against, on the folded
path.*

A drain `Ref`'s `gdelta` is **not** relative to the loop's exit. It is relative to the long path's
chunk position `T`: drain step `i` works on chunk `T - M + i`, so its own chunk is spelled
`gdelta = i - M`. Resolving that against the phi entry with `base = 0` gives

```
resolved  = (0 + i - M) mod ring
should be = (0 + i)     mod ring      ⟺   M ≡ 0 (mod ring)
```

so the base-0 resolution silently assumes the peel depth is a whole number of ring revolutions. At
ring 2 that is true for `M = 2` and false for `M = 1` and `M = 3` — which is exactly the
fold / split / split pattern that was observed and mis-attributed to a ring-depth collision. At
`M = 1` the drain's own-chunk read resolved to generation 1, which *nothing on the folded path had
written*, and the analysis reported an `UNWRITTEN` break against a generation that does not exist.
**The break was in the resolution, not in the schedule.**

The fold identifies drain step `i` with short step `i`, i.e. with chunk `i`. Under the fold,
therefore, the drain's `T` *is* `M`, and the base is `M`. The implementation derives that from the
block's own two frame fields rather than reading a program-wide `M`:

```python
def _frame_base(blk):
    if blk.gen_rel is None:
        return 0                       # absolute-generation block: prologue, short arm
    return blk.chunk_base - 1 - int(blk.gen_rel)
```

`gen_rel` is the reduction-chunk position the block's `gdelta` values were computed against;
`chunk_base` is the block's own position on the global chunk timeline. Deriving from those two is
not stylistic: `chunk_base` is a **per-path** fact stored per block, and reading a program-wide `M`
here would be the same frame confusion one level up. A block with no loop-relative frame contributes
no offset, which is why the prologue and the short arm both get 0.

There is a unit test for the identity itself, not just for its consequence:
`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2599` asserts `chunk_base - 1 - gen_rel == M` for *every* drain block at
`M = 1, 2, 3`, and `_frame_base(prologue) == 0`. And there is a negative control,
`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2617`, which monkey-patches `_frame_base` back to a constant 0 and asserts
that (a) the `M = 1` configuration stops folding, and (b) the break it produces has the *frame*
signature — a read whose value chains back to `ENTRY` — rather than the ring-depth signature, where
the read chains to a real copy. Keeping the negative control is what stops a future "fix" that
simply makes everything fold.

#### 10.8 The location helpers

Six small functions turn an IR node into the keys the walk uses. They are small, but each one
encodes a decision, and three of them were the site of a defect.

**`_kind(inst)` (`short_path.py:101`)** — classifies an instruction as `'copy'`, `'read'`, `'mma'`
or `None`, **from the destination space, never from a name**. An `Mma` is `'mma'`; a `Move` whose
destinations include a shared tile is a `'copy'`; any other `Move` is a `'read'`. Everything else
(a `Mark`, in practice) is `None` and is skipped. Reading the hop off the spaces rather than off a
flag is the same rule the node set itself follows.

**`_operands(inst)` (`short_path.py:110`)** — the operand tuple an instruction names *on its
destination*: for an `Mma`, the tuple of its sources' operands; for a `Move`, the tuple of its
destinations'. A Φ-fused copy — one cooperative load instruction serving several op-classes through
an aliased descriptor — therefore names several operands here, and that is intended: the fused
movement is one identity, and naming it by its first member would make the other members invisible.

**`_coord(inst)` (`short_path.py:117`)** — `inst.coord` for an `Mma`, `inst.dsts[0].tile.coord` for
a `Move`. A one-liner.

**`_groups(inst)` (`short_path.py:121`)** — the register groups an instruction touches, as a tuple,
taken from the sources of an `Mma` and the destinations of a `Move`, filtered to register-space
refs. Part of the consumer key, for the split-read reason given above.

**`_free_coord(free_modes, operand, coord)` (`short_path.py:186`)** — projects a coordinate onto the
operand's own **free-tile modes**, in the canonical order those modes are declared in, and returns
the result as a tuple of `(mode, value)` pairs.

Two properties make it non-trivial.

*It is read per operand from `Program.meta['free_modes']`, not derived by subtracting the reduction
modes from the coordinate.* The historical reason was that an `Mma` source `Ref` used to carry the
whole `(K, M, N)` coordinate, so the B operand's ref mentioned `M_inner` even though B is broadcast
over it; keying on that would have split B's register per `m`, inventing differences instead of
merging them. **That is now fixed at source** — the lowering projects each `Mma` source onto its own
operand's presence when it builds the ref (`loopir_to_gir.py:462` records the fix) — so this function
no longer has to repair an over-wide ref.

*It still cannot trust the coordinate's own order, and that is why the per-operand lookup remains.*
The two spellings this must equate do not both come from an `Mma`. When one instruction moves several
logical tiles at once — a wide `ds_load` whose *quantum* spans two tiles along an axis — that axis is
**absent** from the read's coordinate upstream, and `refs.covered_coords` re-inserts it by
*appending*. The consuming `Mma`'s coordinate carries the same axis in its declared position. Since
keys are compared for equality, `(M_inner, M_split)` and `(M_split, M_inner)` would be different
keys and every wide read's second tile would look unfed. Imposing `free_modes`'s order canonicalises
both spellings. The function now does exactly one job (canonicalisation) where it used to do two.

**`_defs_uses(inst, entry, free_modes, base=0)` (`short_path.py:221`)** — the whole location model in
thirty lines. Returns `(defs, uses)` as lists of location keys.

```
_defs_uses(inst, entry, free_modes, base):
    if inst is an Mma:
        uses = [ ('register', op, group, slot, free_coord)  for each register source ]
        defs = []                                  # an Mma defines nothing tracked
        return

    for each shared SOURCE ref:
        g = _generation(ref, entry, base);  if g is not None: uses += ('shared', op, g)
    for each DESTINATION ref:
        if shared:    g = _generation(...);  defs += ('shared', op, g)
        if register:  for c in refs.covered_coords(ref):        # ONE def, MANY locations
                          defs += ('register', op, group, slot, _free_coord(..., c))
```

The `covered_coords` expansion (`short_path.py:249`) is the counterpart of the quantum subtraction
described above: a quantum-wide read is a **single definition that fills every coordinate of its
footprint**, so it must be registered at each of them. `covered_coords` returns `(coord,)` for every
ordinary read, so this is a no-op except on the wide ones. Skipping it is not subtle in its effect —
at the microscaled-fp8 shape the analysis reported sixteen consumers reading a location the arm never
writes, and concluded the arm could not stand alone.

Note the deliberate asymmetry: the `Mma` branch returns early with empty `defs`, so the accumulator
never enters the location space at all. The accumulator is not rotated and is not a resource whose
producer can change under the reordering, so tracking it would add locations and no information.

#### 10.9 The pairing ladder: `pairing_cause` and `_folded_producer`

Once both walks are done, each corresponded consumer is examined location by location: the folded
path supplied one value, the arm supplied another. Two functions turn that into a verdict input.

**`_folded_producer(f_map, loc, s_src)` (`short_path.py:517`)** — *"what value does this consumer
receive at this location on the folded path?"*

The consumer is the same instruction on both sides, so it reads the same *number* of locations in
the same *roles* — but the location **keys** differ between the two chunk frames, because the two
arms peel different chunk indices and therefore name different generations. So:

```
_folded_producer(f_map, loc, s_src):
    if loc in f_map:                      return f_map[loc]        # frames happen to coincide
    same = [ v for k,v in f_map.items() if k[0]==loc[0] and k[1]==loc[1] ]   # same space+operand
    if len(same) == 1:                    return same[0]           # unambiguous role match
    if len(same) == 0:                    return ('<absent>',)
    raise ValueError(...)                                          # ambiguous: refuse to guess
```

The fallback is sound only because no consumer today reads two locations of the same space *and*
operand: a read sources one buffer, and an `Mma` takes one register per operand. If one ever appears
the ambiguity must be resolved by carrying the **role** on the use, not by guessing which of the two
to pick — hence the raise rather than a heuristic.

**Sharp edge:** the `s_src` parameter is accepted and **never referenced in the body**. It is dead.
It is presumably a remnant of an earlier version that tried to match by value; leaving it in place
suggests the matching is value-aware when it is purely positional. Deleting it is a safe two-line
change, and a future maintainer who wants role-aware matching should add the role to the location
key rather than re-purposing this parameter.

**`pairing_cause(f_src, s_src)` (`short_path.py:260`)** — classifies one corresponded consumer's
producer pair, returning `None` when the two frames agree and one of three cause strings otherwise.
The *order of the rungs is load-bearing*:

```python
def pairing_cause(f_src, s_src):
    if f_src == s_src and s_src not in _UNSERVED:  return None          # genuine agreement
    if s_src in _UNSERVED and f_src in _UNSERVED:  return UNWRITTEN     # neither frame serves it
    if s_src in _UNSERVED:                         return ARM_UNWRITTEN # the arm's own defect
    if f_src in _UNSERVED:                         return UNWRITTEN     # frames do not meet
    return OVERWRITTEN                                                  # ring too shallow
```

with `_UNSERVED = (ENTRY, ('<absent>',), None)` (`short_path.py:257`) — the three spellings of "no
producer reached here".

**The first rung is the trap, and it was a real defect.** The obvious ladder starts
`if f_src == s_src: return None`. At `f_src == s_src == ENTRY` that says "both sides agree that
nothing wrote this" and records no break at all — so `fold_breaks` comes out empty and the verdict
message reports the folded path SOUND on the exact input that proves it is not. The guard
`and s_src not in _UNSERVED` is what closes it.

**The second rung is the mirror trap.** Both-unserved must be blamed on the *folded* path, because
`ARM_UNWRITTEN` is deliberately filtered out of `fold_breaks` downstream — it asserts "the arm is
broken but folding rescues it", and here folding rescues nothing. Classifying both-unserved as
`ARM_UNWRITTEN` would drop it straight back out of the decision.

The three causes (`short_path.py:89-95`) have different root causes and different owners, which is
why they are not collapsed into one:

| cause | meaning | who fixes it |
|---|---|---|
| `UNWRITTEN` | the folded path reads a location nothing on it wrote — the two frames do not meet | the frame derivation, or the peel structure |
| `OVERWRITTEN` | a different producer got there first — the ring is too shallow for the separated order to keep every peeled chunk live | nobody: this is the genuine SPLIT, and deepening the ring is a schedule decision one layer up |
| `ARM_UNWRITTEN` | the *short arm* reads something it never wrote; the folded path is not at fault | the arm's construction in the schedule emitter |

Collapsing `UNWRITTEN` and `OVERWRITTEN` is exactly what let the summary "the fold is legal iff
ring ≥ peel depth" look like the whole story while a frame bug was producing the same verdicts for a
different reason.

`pairing_cause` lives at module scope with a single caller. That is deliberate: the ladder's order
is the content, and a second inline copy would drift. This package has a documented recurring
failure shape — one rule written twice, agreeing on every ordinary input and diverging on the
degenerate one — and the read-ahead traversal, the read's tree level and the fence cover have each
been an instance of it.

`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2639` tests the ladder directly, rung by rung, rather than through a whole
program. The test's own docstring records why: *no configuration in the standing matrix reaches the
both-unserved rung*, and two attempts to construct one failed — which is precisely why the defect
went unnoticed for as long as it did. Unit-testing the classification is the only way that rung is
covered at all.

#### 10.10 The verdict objects

**`Break` (`short_path.py:358`)** — a frozen dataclass recording one consumer whose value changed:

```
consumer   the consumer key (kind, step, operands, coord, groups)
location   the location key whose producer differs
folded     the value the FOLDED path supplies there
short      the value the SHORT ARM supplies there
cause      UNWRITTEN | OVERWRITTEN | ARM_UNWRITTEN   (default OVERWRITTEN)
```

Breaks are **per (consumer, location)** and are not deduplicated by location. That matters when
reading a count: at the microscaling-fp8 fixture the analysis reports 32 breaks over **4 distinct
locations** and 32 distinct consumers — thirty-two `Mma`s each consuming one of four A-registers. A
maintainer who reads "32 breaks" as "32 distinct broken buffers" will look in the wrong place. The
distinct-location count is the diagnostic number, and it is not currently reported; adding it to the
`SPLIT` reason string would be a cheap improvement.

**`FoldVerdict` (`short_path.py:370`)** — the frozen result object, with nine fields:

| field | contents |
|---|---|
| `verdict` | one of `FOLD` / `SPLIT` / `UNSOUND` / `NA` / `VACUOUS` (`short_path.py:85`; the literals are the lower-case strings `"fold"`, `"split"`, `"unsound"`, `"n/a"`, `"vacuous"`) |
| `reason` | a human-readable sentence, embedded in the pass's record and in the debug dump |
| `breaks` | the `Break` tuple from check F2 |
| `missing` | short-arm consumer keys absent from the folded path — check F1 |
| `unbound` | short-arm consumers with no def inside the arm — check F0 |
| `extras` | count of folded-path instructions with no counterpart key |
| `obligations` | preconditions the *consumer* of this verdict must satisfy |
| `folded_blocks` | the label tuple the folded walk used: `(prologue, drain0, drain1, …)` |
| `short_blocks` | the label tuple the arm walk used, in chunk order |

`folded_blocks` and `short_blocks` are not decoration: the mutating pass derives what it deletes and
what it rewires from **these lists**, so the mutation cannot disagree with what was proven.

**`FoldVerdict.foldable` (`short_path.py:383`)** — a property, `verdict in (FOLD, VACUOUS)`: *may the
short blocks be deleted?* `VACUOUS` counts because an unreachable arm is pure code growth. It is
currently **unreferenced** — the mutating pass switches on `verdict` directly — so it is an
unexercised convenience. Either use it in the pass or delete it; leaving a second spelling of the
delete-condition around is how the two drift apart.

**`FoldVerdict.causes()` (`short_path.py:388`)** — a histogram `{cause: count}` over `breaks`. Its
only call site is inside the module itself, at `short_path.py:505`, where the `SPLIT` reason string
is composed. That call site is worth naming as a wart: it constructs a **throwaway second
`FoldVerdict`** (`FoldVerdict(SPLIT, breaks=fold_breaks).causes()`) purely to histogram a list it
already has. A free function over a break list, or a `causes()` that takes the list as an argument,
would say the same thing without fabricating an object whose other eight fields are lies.

**The five verdicts and what each means to the caller** (the mutating pass, `passes/fold_short_path.py`,
covered in the passes section):

| verdict | condition | pass action |
|---|---|---|
| `FOLD` | every def-use pairing survives the reordering | delete the arm, retarget the false edge into the drain head |
| `VACUOUS` | no legal trip count reaches the arm | delete the arm (see 10.12 — this no longer fires) |
