the thing most likely to drift* — a new case in `_regions_of`, a fuse key changing spelling.
Sharing an id where the storage is disjoint is **lost parallelism, not a miscompile**, so the
message calls it a precision failure and names both keys.

Note the asymmetry: V1 only inspects pairs that `LdsHazards` already produced an edge for. Two
disjoint accesses with no hazard edge between them are never compared. That is fine for the
precision question (no edge, no false ordering) but it means V1's coverage is exactly
`LdsHazards`'s edge set, not the full pairwise product.

**V3 — FENCE COVER (`:292-300`).** Every `Mark(kind='fence')` in every block must carry a non-empty
`at['tokens']`. A fence whose token set misses one end of the hazard it stands between is emitted,
looks right in a dump, and **orders nothing**. The comment names the shape it was written for: a
split operand where the fence covered region 0's buffers and silently omitted region 1's, so the
reader waited on the half that was already there.

The check is deliberately weak — it asserts *non-emptiness*, not *sufficiency*. A fence carrying
one token id when it needed three passes. Making it sufficient means re-deriving the cover
(`FenceRegions`' job) inside the verifier, which would be a second authority for the same fact;
the current compromise is that `FenceRegions` computes the set and `G-TOKEN` only checks it did not
come out empty. If you want a real cover check, the right shape is a *cross-check* in the sense of
§12.2.11: an independent re-derivation compared for equality, not a re-implementation trusted
alone.

**Negative controls** (`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:3026`, parameterised): clearing one `Move`'s
`token_ids` must produce the message "the emitter reads the STAMP", and emptying one fence's
`at['tokens']` must produce "carries no token ids". Both run against a fused cross-agent fixture
so the Φ path is actually exercised. There is **no** negative control for V1 or for the
`tokens.unresolved` branch of V2 — those two are the least defended sub-properties in the file.

##### 12.1.8 The post-pipeline `G-WAW` check, and why it is not here

Worth naming because a reader will look for it: there is a thirteenth invariant,
`_check_rotation_waw` (`gir/passes/pipeline.py:74`), and it deliberately does **not** live in
`verify.py`. It asserts that every rotating buffer that is written is also read, and that no write
covers an axis no read covers — the two degenerate cases in which a write-after-write between
generations `t` and `t+S` is *not* implied by the write-after-read the ledger already files.

The reason for the separate home is stated at `gir/passes/pipeline.py:100-104`: the invariant is a
property of the **final** program, and `verify_gir` is also called mid-pipeline and directly on
un-piped `lower_to_gir` output, where a rotating buffer legitimately has writes and no reads yet.
Putting it in `verify_gir` failed 448 of 948 tests for that reason alone. `run_pipeline`'s tail is
the one place that sees the finished program.

That is a precedent a future maintainer should follow rather than fight: **an invariant that only
holds of the finished program belongs at the pipeline tail, not in the well-formedness gate.** The
cost is that a hand-built `Program` never gets it. The alternative — a `stage` parameter on
`verify_gir` selecting which invariants apply — was not taken, and would be worth taking if a
second such invariant appears.

##### 12.1.9 `G-EMIT` — an unemitted block is a stated decision, and its losses are counted

**`_check_emit(prog)` (`gir/verify.py:303`)** guards the `model_only` flag on `Block` (§3.6). A
model-only block is one GIR reasons over that **no back end emits**. That is not a contradiction:
the kept short-trip arm is real control flow in the *model* — it participates in dataflow, joins,
and generation resolution — while the emitter, which requests blocks by *phase name* and never asks
for `short{i}`, produces no instructions for it.

The danger is precise: because the emitter selects by name, an unemitted block is
**indistinguishable from a forgotten one**, and any `Mark` an analysis places in it is silently
discarded. This is not hypothetical — `FenceRegions` really does place `fence` Marks into the kept
arm, and they really do vanish. `G-EMIT` does **not** forbid the drop. It forbids the drop being
*invisible*.

```
counted  = short_loop['model_only']['marks_dropped']      (0 if the record is absent)
actual   = number of Marks with kind != 'phase_boundary'
           sitting in blocks flagged model_only
declared = set of labels flagged model_only

if declared and short_loop has no 'model_only' record:  raise   # flag with no reason
if actual != counted:                                   raise   # drop not accounted for
```

`phase_boundary` Marks are excluded because they are labels, not state changes: losing one costs
nothing. Every other kind — `fence`, `swap`, `gr_increment`, `region_increment`, `gsu_guard` — is a
state change whose loss must be on the record.

**The counting loop is written oddly** and a reader should not be misled by it:

```python
counted = 0
for rec in (prog.meta.get("short_loop") or {}).get("model_only", {}),:
    counted += rec.get("marks_dropped", 0) if rec else 0
```

The trailing comma at `gir/verify.py:305` makes that a one-element tuple, so the loop body runs
exactly once. It is `counted = rec.get('marks_dropped', 0) if rec else 0` written as a loop. The
loop form presumably anticipated several records; there is only ever one. Simplify it.

**The record is owned by exactly one mechanism**, and that is a coupling worth naming: the only
place `G-EMIT` looks for a reason is `meta['short_loop']['model_only']`. A future pass that flags a
block `model_only` for a reason unrelated to the short arm has nowhere to record it and will fail
the first sub-check no matter how carefully it documents itself. If a second producer of
`model_only` blocks ever appears, the record must be lifted to a top-level `meta` key
(`meta['model_only'] = [{blocks, reason, marks_dropped, kinds_dropped}, ...]`) and this check
generalised to sum over the list. That is a ten-line change and it should be made *before* the
second producer, not after.

**Who writes the record.** `RecordUnemittedPass` (`gir/passes/record_unemitted.py`), the last pass
in the pipeline. It refuses to invent a reason: flagging a block `model_only` without a recorded
verdict makes it raise `ValueError("no pass recorded why")`
(`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2555-2561` pins that).

**Measured behaviour.** The parameterised test at `Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2513-2532` records the
actual drop counts across four fixtures: a single-agent kernel's kept arm carries **0** Marks, and
the cross-agent fused and unfused multi-agent fixtures carry **6** each, all of kind `fence`. The
test's own comment makes the right point: the number is not what is being asserted; that it is
*recorded rather than vanishing* is.

**Negative controls,** both present and both good: appending one extra `fence` Mark to a
model-only block *after* the count was taken must raise with `G-EMIT`
(`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2535`), and flagging any block `model_only` with no record must raise with
"model_only but nothing records WHY" (`:2548`).

**False-negative surface.** `actual != counted` is a *count*, not a *set*. Removing one dropped
fence and adding one dropped swap keeps the count equal and passes. The record does carry
`kinds_dropped` (a tuple of kinds) and the test asserts on it, but `_check_emit` never reads it.
Comparing the kind multiset instead of the integer is a two-line strengthening with no downside.

##### 12.1.10 `G-UNIFORM` — a proc-scoped rendezvous is on every participating agent's path

**`_check_uniform_placement(prog, am)` (`gir/verify.py:321`)** is a delegation to the
`UniformPlacement` analysis (`gir/analyses/uniform_placement.py:121`), raising if it returns any
violations and quoting up to six of them.

**The concept, in full.** An **agent** is an independently-scheduled execution stream — in practice
a wave. A `fence` Mark whose `scope` is proc-wide (`block` or `cluster`, the closed tuple
`PROC_SCOPES` at `gir/analyses/uniform_placement.py:68`) is realized as a rendezvous: a workgroup
barrier that every wave of the workgroup must arrive at. The safety argument that justifies the
fence set — "every cross-agent hazard is covered by some selector" — is a *coverage* argument. It
says each obligation **carries** a selector. It says nothing about the selector lying on a path
every participating agent actually runs.

And a rendezvous some agents skip **does not race — it HANGS**. That failure mode is invisible to
the coverage argument by construction, which is why this is a separate invariant rather than a
consequence of the fence analysis.

**The test.** A rendezvous is uniformly placed iff no execution can bring one agent of the scope to
it and not another. GIR can express agent divergence in exactly two ways:

- **(R) block role.** `Block.role != 'all'` means only some agents run the block.
- **(P) an agent-discriminating guard.** A terminator predicate whose truth differs per agent.

So the condition is: on **every** entry→fence path, every block admits all agents of the scope and
every guard is agent-uniform. "On some entry→fence path" is the intersection of forward
reachability from the entry and backward reachability to the fence's block — a pure CFG test with
no dominator tree and no hazard counting.

**The agent set is taken from `scope`, not from the hazards.** A workgroup barrier rendezvouses
*every* wave of the workgroup, not merely the waves that touch the buffers the cover selected. So
the quantifier is over the *realization's* set, a superset of the obligation's participants. That
is what makes the check sound, and it is why no `agents` field was added to the Mark: `scope`
already is the agent set.

**A `model_only` block is deliberately not a violation here.** Nothing emits it, so no agent
reaches the selector and none can be split from another. That the covered hazard then goes unfenced
on that path is a *safety* question, and it is exactly what `G-EMIT` records.

**How much of this is live today — the honest answer, and it is the single most important
vacuity note in `verify.py`.** Both rules are currently **structurally inert**:

- (R) is inert because `Block.role` is `'all'` everywhere; wave specialization is unimplemented.
- (P) is inert **by vocabulary**: `Pred` is defined as a structured symbolic predicate over
  trip-count symbols with no hardware in it, and `Bound` can hold only a trip symbol plus a
  constant. GIR **cannot spell** an agent-discriminating guard.

That is not the same as the schedule satisfying the premise. It means the tree-structural test is
looking for a shape the tree has no node for. The declared escape hatch is
`prog.meta['agent_varying_symbols']`: the first `Pred` that tests something per-agent must name its
symbol there, and the check fires from that moment.

**And the part it structurally cannot see.** The agent-discriminating branches that *do* exist in
the emitted kernel — `s_bitcmp1_b32 s[sgprWaveIdx],0` followed by
`s_cbranch_scc1 label_SkipStaggerA`, emitted by the TensileLite scaffold's stagger logic — are
**scaffold-owned and have no GIR node at all**. `G-UNIFORM` is therefore sound only relative to
GIR's own tree. The real deadlock surface is closed at a second, independent layer:
`Tensile/Lowering/uniform_emission.py` runs the same question over the emitted instruction stream,
where those arms are visible. Both are wanted, and the division is: **this one guards the decoder,
the emission one guards the back end.**

A future maintainer must not read "G-UNIFORM passes" as "no hang is possible". Read it as "the
decoder did not sink a rendezvous into a branch *it* created".

**Tests.** `Tests/unit/test_uniform_placement.py` has seven analysis-level cases — a uniformly
placed fence accepted (`:46`), a role-restricted block (`:52`), a role-restricted *ancestor*
(`:60`), an agent-varying guard (`:67`), the non-vacuity control that a *trip-count* guard on the
identical shape is **not** a violation (`:78`), a multi-exit-header arm inspected too (`:86`), and
a non-proc scope ignored (`:101`) — plus `test_G_UNIFORM_is_wired_into_verify_gir` (`:109`), whose
docstring names the defect it guards: "the analysis is only worth having if the verifier runs it —
the defect being fixed is precisely that `scope` reached nothing but a comment string". That is the
wiring test every delegated check should have and only this one does.

##### 12.1.11 `G-TRIP` — the steady loop and the drain cover the reduction exactly once

**`_check_trip(prog, am)` (`gir/verify.py:331`)** delegates to `reduction_coverage_violations`
(`gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:180`), passing the `LoopShape` analysis result.

**The invariant.** Let `T` be the runtime trip symbol — the total number of reduction chunks, never
a compile-time number — and `M` the peel depth. The steady loop must cover chunks `[0, T-M)` and
the `M` drain steps cover `[T-M, T)`; together, exactly `[0, T)`. Every chunk computed once,
none twice, none missed.

The check is **symbolic in `T`**, which is what makes it possible at all: `LoopShape` derives a
`Linear(coeff, const)` expression for what the loop covers, and the requirement is the literal
`Linear(1, -M)`. Equality of two linear forms, no trip count needed.

```
M = meta['M'];  if M is None: return []
drains = blocks whose phase starts with 'drain';  if none: return []
required = Linear(1, -M)
for lp in loops:
    if not lp.exit_to.startswith('drain'): continue     # not the loop the drain completes
    if lp.per_trip != 1: continue                       # see below — a NAMED hole
    if lp.covers != required:
        report OVERLAP (covers.const > required.const) or GAP, with the chunk count
```

**Why this exists.** Its absence is how a one-chunk overlap at *every* `T` went unnoticed: chunk
`T-M` was in both the loop's range and the drain's, so it was computed twice, at every problem
size. The loop's *shape* had never been related to the drain's *coverage* by anything. It is also
the invariant against which a structural pass is checked — a pass that rewires the CFG cannot
quietly move the trip count without failing here.

**The trip count is read, not reconstructed.** `LoopBack` states the count directly (§3.5), so
`LoopShape` reads it. Deriving it from a comparison instead needs three facts that live outside the
node — where the counter starts, which way it steps, where the test sits — and two off-by-ones came
from exactly that reconstruction.

**A named, deliberate hole: `per_trip != 1`.** With a multi-block steady chain (`loop_copies = n`,
`n` blocks sharing one back edge) one trip consumes `n` chunks, so the loop must run `(T-M)/n`
times. `Bound` is `var + const` — **there is no division** — so that bound cannot be *written*,
never mind checked. The chain therefore over-covers by a factor of `n` and `G-TRIP` says nothing.
The comment at `gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:198-205` is explicit that skipping silently is what
would make this a hidden hole, so it is named there and *asserted* in
`test_multi_copy_loop_coverage_is_not_yet_EXPRESSIBLE` (`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2434`), which pins
`covers.coeff == n` and pins that `reduction_coverage_violations` returns `[]` anyway. This is the
right way to carry a limitation: the test fails if the hole is ever *closed* without updating it,
and the reader of the suite sees the gap instead of a `continue` nobody reads. The hole is
unreachable from `build_gir`, which never passes `loop_copies > 1`.

**Other false negatives.** `M is None` and "no drain blocks" both return `[]` — same
metadata-dependence as `G-CFG`(3). The scoping `lp.exit_to.startswith('drain')` means a loop whose
exit target is named anything else is not checked, which is correct for the tail loop and a hole
for a mis-phased one.

**Second, independent statement.** `test_reduction_covering_invariant_holds_and_is_enforced_as_G_TRIP`
(`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:2410`) re-asserts the property directly over `PrefetchGlobalRead ∈ {1,2,3}`
rather than through `verify_gir`, and its docstring gives the reason: the verifier could be
bypassed; `build_gir` runs it, but a hand-built Program need not. It also runs a synthetic
*pre-tested* loop over the same predicate and asserts it covers exactly `[0, T-M)` — a satisfiable
witness, so the check is not simply always-failing. Having a positive witness alongside the
negative controls is the cheapest anti-vacuity measure there is.

##### 12.1.12 `G-GEN-SSA`, `G-NOITER`, `G-SEMANTIC`, `G-OPERANDS` — the four node-level checks

**`_check_gen_ssa(prog)` (`gir/verify.py:110`)** — SSA discipline over the one SSA value class,
`Gen` (a loop-carried buffer generation, §3.2).

```
defs = {}                                   # gen.id -> number of phi defs
for blk, for phi in blk.phis:  defs[phi.gen.id] += 1
uses = { ref.gen.id for every Ref of every Move/Mma that carries a gen }

for gid, n in defs:
    if n > 1:            raise   "has n phi defs (must be exactly one)"
    if gid not in uses:  raise   "defined but never used (dropped consumer)"
for gid in uses:
    if gid not in defs:  raise   "used but has no phi def"
```

Three properties: single definition, no dead definition, no undefined use. The **no dead
definition** clause is the strict one and it is the point of the check: a `Gen` that is defined and
never used means a consumer was dropped somewhere in the lowering, and a dropped consumer is
otherwise silent. The error message adds the corollary the design relies on — a scaffold-owned
span (a piece of the kernel GIR reasons about but does not own, such as the drain descriptor swap)
must **not** mint a `Gen` def, precisely so it does not show up here as a false positive.

Two divergences between the docstring and the code, both worth knowing:

- The module docstring (`:12`) says "exactly one def (a phi **or a GenXfer**)". The code counts
  **only phis**. A `Gen` transferred across a back edge by a `GenXfer` with no matching phi
  therefore fails as "used but has no phi def". In practice every `Gen` has a phi, so the stricter
  reading is the live one; the docstring is one revision behind.
- Uses are collected from `_refs_of`, i.e. from `Move`/`Mma` operands only. `Mark` payloads
  (`swap`'s `gen_from`/`gen_to`) are **not** uses. Those payloads are plain integers, so this is
  consistent — but it means a `swap` is not enough to keep a `Gen` alive, which is the correct
  semantics and an easy thing to get wrong when adding a Mark kind.

**`_check_noiter(prog)` (`gir/verify.py:135`)**, with its nested predicate **`bad(coord)`
(`:136`)** — `any(mode == 'iter' for mode, value in coord)`. Raises if any `Ref`'s
`tile.coord`, or any `Mma`'s own `coord`, mentions the reduction-loop induction variable, spelled
`'iter'`.

The rationale is structural rather than stylistic: the cross-trip relation lives in the `Gen` phi.
A coordinate that *also* carried the trip index would give the IR two ways to say the same thing,
and they diverge — one is updated by a pass, the other is not. `'iter'` is a **string literal**
here, which is the check's only weakness: the mode name is a convention, and a lowering that spelled
it `'k_iter'` would pass. `loopir_to_gir` used to hardcode the name in several places and was
cleaned up to carry it; the verifier was not updated to read it from `meta`.

**`_PHYSICAL_ATTRS` (`gir/verify.py:146`)** — the tuple
`('vgpr', 'addr', 'byte_off', 'reg_off', 'vector_width', 'color')`.

**`_check_semantic(prog)` (`gir/verify.py:149`)** — for every body instruction, `hasattr(inst, a)`
for each of those six names; raise on a hit. GIR nodes structurally have no physical field, so this
guards against *accidental attachment*: `Move`, `Mma` and `Mark` are non-frozen dataclasses, so
`inst.vgpr = 7` in some pass would succeed silently and the IR would then carry a back-end decision
it must not.

**Its false-negative surface is large and specific.** The check inspects **the instruction only** —
not its `Ref`s, not their `Tile`s. And a `Ref` is *exactly* where a physical field would most
plausibly be attached, because a `Ref` is the thing that would own an address or a register colour.
`Ref` and `Tile` are frozen dataclasses, so a *dynamic* attachment is impossible; but a *declared
field* named `addr` added to `Ref` would sail straight through. Extending the loop over
`_refs_of(inst)` and each `ref.tile` is three lines and closes it. Do that.

The second surface: the list is a **denylist of six names**. Anything called `lds_offset`,
`sgpr`, `wait_cnt` or `swizzle` is unconstrained. A frozen node set with an explicit allowlist of
fields would be the real enforcement; the denylist is a smoke detector, not a wall.

**`_check_operands(prog)` (`gir/verify.py:381`)** — every register-resident `Mma` source must be
produced by some `Move`:

```
produced = { (dst.tile.operand, dst.tile.space) for every Move dst }
for every Mma src s:
    if s.tile.space == 'register' and (s.tile.operand, s.tile.space) not in produced:
        raise  "dangling operand"
```

This is what stops a microscaling kernel's `MXSA`/`MXSB`, or a sparse kernel's `meta`, from being
consumed by a WMMA with no read ever having fetched them — an open operand set (§3.3) means there
is no fixed list to check against, so the check has to be derived from what the program contains.

**But it is coarse to the point of near-vacuity, and the reader should know exactly how coarse.**
The key is `(operand, space)`, not the coordinate. So it proves "operand `A` is read *somewhere* in
the program into *a* register" and nothing more. It cannot detect: a source at a coordinate no read
fills; a source in the wrong block; a source read after its consumer. All three of those are real
defect shapes, and all three are caught by `check_register_dataflow` in the *other* file — which is
the honest way to describe `G-OPERANDS`: it is a cheap presence check whose real job is done
elsewhere. The historical defect where an `Mma` source `Ref` carried the *whole* `(K,M,N)` coord so
that a broadcast operand named a location no read writes (repaired by projecting each source onto
the operand's own presence at construction) is precisely a bug `G-OPERANDS` could not see and
`G-NOITER` could not see either, because "only `'iter'` is forbidden" was the only constraint on a
coordinate.

##### 12.1.13 `G-MARK` — the payload schema, plus the one value-dependent rule

**`_check_marks(prog)` (`gir/verify.py:398`)**:

```
for every Mark in every block:
    if kind not in MARK_KINDS:                       raise "unknown Mark kind"
    missing = [k for k in _MARK_SCHEMA[kind] if k not in (at or {})]
    if missing:                                      raise "missing fields"
    if kind == 'swap':
        key = 'operand' if at.get('hop') == 'read' else 'unit'
        if key not in at:                            raise "must name its pointer with '<key>'"
```

The closed-kind check makes `MARK_KINDS` (`gir/nodes.py:157`) an actual type rather than a
convention: a typo'd kind is rejected at the gate instead of being silently ignored by every
consumer's `if kind == ...` chain.

The `swap` rule is the value-dependent one §12.1.2 explained. Note the *default* branch: anything
whose `hop` is not the literal `'read'` is treated as a copy hop and required to carry `unit`. So a
`swap` with a misspelled or missing `hop` is checked as a copy swap — which is a reasonable
default, but it does mean `hop` itself has no value-domain check even though `_MARK_SCHEMA`
requires its presence. Adding `hop in ('read','copy')` is one line.

**False-negative surface.** No value domains anywhere (§12.1.2), no forbidden extra keys, and no
per-kind *count* or *placement* rule — a `region_increment` in the tail block, a `fence` with
`edges = 0`, a `gr_increment` naming a unit that does not exist: all pass. The check is a
presence-of-keys check and should be read as exactly that.

##### 12.1.14 `verify_gir` — the driver, and why the order is what it is

**`verify_gir(prog, expect_steady_loops="one")` (`gir/verify.py:422`)** constructs a fresh
`AnalysisManager`, runs all twelve checks, and returns `True`. It raises on the **first** violation.

```python
am = AnalysisManager()
_check_term(prog)                                   # G-TERM
_check_cfg(prog, am, expect_steady_loops)           # G-CFG
_check_walk(prog)                                   # G-WALK
_check_tokens(prog, am)                             # G-TOKEN
_check_emit(prog)                                   # G-EMIT
_check_uniform_placement(prog, am)                  # G-UNIFORM
_check_trip(prog, am)                               # G-TRIP
_check_gen_ssa(prog)                                # G-GEN-SSA
_check_noiter(prog)                                 # G-NOITER
_check_semantic(prog)                               # G-SEMANTIC
_check_operands(prog)                               # G-OPERANDS
_check_marks(prog)                                  # G-MARK
return True
```

The order is **not** the docstring's order, and it is not arbitrary either, though the source does
not say so. `_check_term` runs first because every later check that touches the CFG —
`_check_cfg`'s back-edge query, `_check_uniform_placement`'s reachability, `_check_trip`'s loop
enumeration — reads `preds`/`succs`, and a dangling target there produces a confusing secondary
failure. After that the ordering is roughly "structural before local": the whole-program shape
checks come first, the per-node checks last, so the first message a developer sees describes the
largest thing that is wrong.

**The fresh `AnalysisManager` is a real cost decision.** `verify_gir` does not accept one from the
caller, so the five analyses it needs — `BackEdges`, `MemTokenAssignment`, `LdsHazards`,
`UniformPlacement`, `LoopShape` — are recomputed on every call even when the caller
(`run_pipeline`) has just finished with a warm manager holding several of them. That is a
deliberate simplification (the verifier cannot then be poisoned by a stale cached result) and it is
also the obvious optimisation: give it an optional `am=None` parameter defaulting to a new manager.
Note that `run_pipeline` calls `am.invalidate()` after every pass anyway, so today the warm manager
would have little in it; the two changes belong together.

**`expect_steady_loops`** is the only knob, threaded to `_check_cfg` and meaning `'one'` (default,
single-tile scope) or `'ge1'` (persistent / grid-stride scope, where an outer time loop is a
legitimate second header). No caller passes `'ge1'` today.

**Returning `True`** rather than `None` is what lets the tests read `assert verify_gir(prog)`, which
they do at 26 call sites across the unit tests (`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:147`, `:1055`, `:1188`,
`:1245`, …).

##### 12.1.15 Cost, and how it scales

Every check is a linear or near-linear scan over a very small program. The concrete `n` values,
which is what decides whether any of this is worth optimising:

| quantity | typical | worst seen |
|---|---:|---:|
| blocks `V` | 4–8 | ~12 (`prologue + steady + 3 drain + 3 short + tail`) |
| body nodes per block | 20–80 | a few hundred at large `DepthU × MIWaveTile` |
| `Gen` ids | 2–4 | 8 (split × two operands) |
| Marks per program | 5–30 | ~60 |

Per check: `G-TERM`, `G-GEN-SSA`, `G-NOITER`, `G-SEMANTIC`, `G-OPERANDS`, `G-MARK`, `G-EMIT` and
`G-WALK` are all `O(nodes)` with tiny constants. `G-CFG` is `O(V+E)` plus one `BackEdges` (a
dominator computation, `O(V·E)` in the naive iterative form, negligible at `V ≤ 12`). `G-TRIP` is
`O(loops)`. The two that actually cost something are `G-TOKEN`, which pulls in `LdsHazards` — an
`O(accesses²)`-flavoured pairwise analysis, the single most expensive thing the verifier triggers —
and `G-UNIFORM`, which does a forward and a backward reachability per proc-scoped fence,
`O(fences · (V+E))`.

In absolute terms `verify_gir` is far below the noise floor of a kernel build (which shells out to
a compiler), and it runs once per kernel from `run_pipeline`. **Do not optimise it.** If profiling
ever says otherwise, the fix is the shared `AnalysisManager` above, not a rewrite: `LdsHazards`
would then be computed once for `FenceRegions`, `TokensPass` and `G-TOKEN` together instead of
three times.

##### 12.1.16 Extending `verify.py` — concrete advice

1. **Adding a `G-*` check.** Write `_check_xxx(prog)` (add `am` only if you need an analysis), add
   one line to `verify_gir`, add a paragraph to the module docstring's invariant list, and — this
   is the non-negotiable part — add a **negative control**: a fixture that breaks the property and
   asserts `pytest.raises(GirVerifyError, match="G-XXX")`. **Six of the twelve have one** —
   `G-TERM` (three: missing terminator, dangling arm target, and the positive `Return` control),
   `G-CFG` (the mis-phased second loop), `G-WALK` (drop / duplicate / hoist), `G-TOKEN` (unnamed
   access, token-less fence), `G-EMIT` (undeclared flag, post-count Mark) and `G-UNIFORM` (the
   wiring test). `G-TRIP` has an independent restatement and a pinned-hole test instead of a raise
   control. **The five with nothing at all — `G-GEN-SSA`, `G-NOITER`, `G-SEMANTIC`, `G-OPERANDS`,
   `G-MARK` — are, with `G-GEN-SSA` excepted, exactly the checks whose false-negative surfaces are
   described above as largest.** That correlation is not a coincidence: a check nobody has tried to
   break is a check nobody has thought hard about.
2. **Before writing a *new* check, ask whether the property holds only of the finished program.**
   If so it belongs at `run_pipeline`'s tail beside `_check_rotation_waw`, not here (§12.1.8).
3. **Prefer delegation to an analysis over logic in the verifier.** `G-WALK`, `G-UNIFORM` and
   `G-TRIP` are four lines each because the property lives in a pure, separately-testable analysis
   returning a list of strings, and the verifier only decides whether a non-empty list is fatal.
   That shape lets a report-only harness print what the verifier would raise on. Follow it.
4. **The three highest-value strengthenings, in order:** (a) value domains in `_MARK_SCHEMA` —
   `scope ∈ PROC_SCOPES`, `hop ∈ {read, copy}`, `steps` an int — which closes a hole that currently
   runs from `G-MARK` into `G-UNIFORM`; (b) extend `_check_semantic` over `Ref`s and `Tile`s;
   (c) drop the `if blk.succs:` / `if declared:` guards in `_check_term` by making the fields
   mandatory.
5. **Make `phase` structured.** Half of `G-CFG`'s false negatives are string-prefix matching on a
   free-form label. A `(kind, index)` pair with `kind` an enum removes them all and simplifies
   `render.py` and the emitter's fork selection at the same time.
6. **Give `GirVerifyError` fields.** `invariant`, `block`, `detail`. The tests would then assert on
   `e.invariant == "G-WALK"` instead of substring-matching prose, and messages could be reworded
   without breaking the suite.

#### 12.2 `gir/verify_dataflow.py` — five semantic checks over the emit plan

##### 12.2.1 Concept: an oracle for "does this schedule compute the right GEMM?"

`verify_gir` proves the IR is well-formed. This file proves it is **correct**: that every WMMA
reads the data its own coordinate names, that every value a read fetches is consumed before it is
overwritten, and that the reads of one steady trip cover the operand exactly once. It does all of
this with **no rocisa, no assembler and no GPU** — pure Python over a list of dictionaries.

**Why it exists, concretely.** Over three days in August 2026 a family of defects in the
tile-splitting work was found the expensive way: run kernels on hardware, bisect a pass/fail
matrix, one build cycle per bisection step. A numeric miscompare tells you "wrong"; it never tells
you *which read*. Every one of those defects turned out to be a one-line violation of an invariant
this file now states. The file's own docstring enumerates four, and they map one-to-one onto the
checks:

| defect | what actually happened | which check catches it |
|---|---|---|
| the region term | reads of a 2-region operand all came out `region = 0`, so region 1 was never read and region 0 was read twice | **region coverage** |
| the register rate | the split axis was excluded from the register-rotation rate, so the rotation width `W` collapsed to 1 and both regions loaded into **one** vgpr generation — the second read clobbering the first before its WMMA consumed it | **overwrite-before-use** |
| asymmetric split | the *unsplit* operand's reads carried `region ∈ {0,1}` with the reduction index pinned to 0, so it fetched the same unroll half twice under two different region labels | **region coverage** (a region the operand does not have) *and* **source coverage** (a missing reduction index) |
| the read-ahead peel | the prologue primed one substep where the steady body consumes two, so the first trip's `wmma u=1` read a generation nothing had written | **use-before-def** at the loop header |

##### 12.2.2 The model: what a register is, and what it holds

The whole file rests on one modelling decision. A register is named **exactly as the leaf emitter
names it**:

```
    (operand, group, reg_buf, tile_flat)
```

which the emitter renders as `Valu{operand}_X{reg_buf}_I0 + wtRegStride * tile_flat`. And that
register **holds a source coordinate**:

```
    (tile_flat, k_flat)
```

— the operand's flat free-tile index and its **absolute** reduction index. Both are mixed-radix
projections the schedule already computes and `emit_plan` already attaches to every read act
(`gir/emit_plan.py:143` and `:164` compute `tile_flat` and `k_flat`).

A `wmma(idx0, idx1, u)` act **demands** `(idx0, u)` from its first matmul input's register and
`(idx1, u)` from its second. `emit_plan._plan_mma` computes `idx0`/`idx1`/`u` with the *same*
projection function used for the read's `tile_flat`/`k_flat` (`gir/emit_plan.py:204-206`), which is
what makes the two directly comparable and is the reason those two fields exist on the read act at
all.

So the entire semantic check reduces to one question: **does the register the WMMA names hold the
coordinate the WMMA asks for?**

**What this deliberately does not model.** It does not check **addresses**. Whether region `r`
really sits at `r * splitBoundary` in LDS is arithmetic owned by `Lowering/lds_geometry.py` and
pinned by its own tests. These checks prove the plan names a *coherent set of coordinates*; the
geometry then places them. The one exception is `check_address_keys` (§12.2.8), which crosses that
line on purpose and has to be handed the missing geometry fact by its caller.

##### 12.2.3 The four helpers

**`_wmma_inputs(prog)` (`gir/verify_dataflow.py:47`)** — returns `(in0, in1)`, the operand names of
the two matmul inputs, read from `prog.meta['mma_inputs']` and padded with `None` when the list is
short. **There is no `'A'`/`'B'` literal anywhere in this file**, and that is a hard rule the
package enforces on itself: operand names are *data*. A kernel whose inputs are not literally named
`A` and `B` — and microscaling kernels add `MXSA`/`MXSB` as further register sources — must work
unchanged. `_plan_mma` learned the same lesson the hard way: it used to string-compare
`tile.operand == "A"` and silently produced `(None, None)` for any other naming
(`gir/emit_plan.py:211-214`).

**`_reg_name(at)` (`gir/verify_dataflow.py:53`)** — the four-tuple key above, built from a read act's
or a WMMA act's `at` dict:

```python
return (at["tc"], at.get("group"), at["reg_buf"], at.get("tile_flat", at["tile"]))
```

`at['tc']` is the op-class ("tensor char" in TensileLite vocabulary; here just the operand name).
The `at.get("tile_flat", at["tile"])` fallback matters: **`tile_flat`, not `tile`**. The register
file is *not* region-displaced. A split operand's LDS storage is displaced by region, but the wave
still holds one vgpr group per *free tile*, numbered across the whole tile — so the flat index is
the register and the within-region index is only the address. Using `tile` here would make two
regions' reads collide in the model while they do not collide in hardware, producing a flood of
false OVERWRITE-BEFORE-USE reports. The fallback to `at["tile"]` covers an act that predates the
split work and carries no `tile_flat`.

**`_expected(prog, at, which)` (`gir/verify_dataflow.py:61`)** — given a WMMA act and `which ∈
{0,1}`, returns the triple `(operand, tile_index, reduction_index)` that input demands:
`(in0, at['idx0'], at['u'])` or `(in1, at['idx1'], at['u'])`. Three lines, and the only place the
"first input takes `idx0`, second takes `idx1`, both take `u`" convention is written down on the
checking side.

**`_RegFile` (`gir/verify_dataflow.py:68`)** — the abstract register file: one dict,
`slots: {name -> (tile_flat, k_flat, used)}`, where `used` is the boolean "has a WMMA consumed this
value yet". That third component is what turns a plain value-tracking walk into an
*overwrite-before-use* detector.

- **`_RegFile.__init__(self, initial=None)` (`:71`)** — `self.slots = dict(initial or {})`. The
  `initial` parameter is **never passed** by any caller; `check_register_dataflow` always starts
  from an empty file.
- **`_RegFile.snapshot(self)` (`:74`)** — returns a copy of `slots` with every `used` forced to
  `True`. **This method is dead code.** A repository-wide grep finds the definition and nothing
  else. It was written for a walk strategy that no longer exists: the intended use was clearly
  "enter the loop's second pass with every register marked consumed, so only genuinely
  loop-carried refills are reported", and the current implementation instead just walks the loop
  twice and *labels* the second pass's violations (§12.2.5), which is strictly more informative.
  `snapshot` and the `initial` parameter should be deleted together; leaving a plausible-looking
  unused method beside a subtle walk is an invitation for someone to "fix" the walk by calling it.

##### 12.2.4 `_walk` — the abstract interpreter

**`_walk(prog, phase, regs, viol, acts=None)` (`gir/verify_dataflow.py:78`)** walks one block's
plan in program order, mutating `regs` and appending to `viol`. It is the transfer function for the
whole file and it is 38 lines. `acts` overrides the plan (so a test can hand in a *mutated* plan
without reverting the source that fixed the defect); otherwise it calls
`plan_block(prog, phase)`.

```
for i, act in enumerate(acts):
    at = act.at

    if act.kind == "read":
        name = _reg_name(at)
        src  = (at['tile_flat'], at['k_flat'])          # what this read fetches
        prev = regs.slots.get(name)
        if prev exists and prev.used is False and prev.source != src:
            VIOLATION  OVERWRITE-BEFORE-USE
        regs.slots[name] = (src.tile, src.k, used=False)

    elif act.kind == "wmma":
        for which in (0, 1):
            op, idx, u = _expected(prog, at, which)
            if op is None: continue                     # a one-input kernel: nothing to check
            buf = at['bufA'] if which == 0 else at['bufB']
            cand = [n for n in regs.slots
                    if n.operand == op and n.reg_buf == buf and n.tile_flat == idx]
            if not cand:
                VIOLATION  USE-BEFORE-DEF
                continue
            for n in cand:
                held_t, held_k, _ = regs.slots[n]
                if (held_t, held_k) != (idx, u):
                    VIOLATION  WRONG SOURCE
                regs.slots[n] = (held_t, held_k, used=True)
```

Three faults, and the distinctions between them are the file's whole value:

- **OVERWRITE-BEFORE-USE** — a register is refilled with a *different* source while still holding
  an unconsumed one. The `prev[0], prev[1] != src` guard is important: refilling a register with
  the *same* source is redundant but harmless, and reporting it would be noise. The message says
  "the rotation width cannot hold both generations", which is the actual diagnosis — the schedule
  asked for more live values than `W` slots.
- **USE-BEFORE-DEF** — no register of this operand, in this buffer, at this tile index has been
  filled at all. This is the peel/prologue fault: the pipeline was not primed.
- **WRONG SOURCE** — a register *exists* and is *live*, but holds a different `(tile, k)` than the
  instruction needs. This is the region/projection fault family: the read fetched a coherent value
  into a register that a different coordinate's WMMA then consumed.

**Candidate selection is by `(operand, reg_buf, tile_flat)` — the `group` component of the register
name is not compared.** `_reg_name` includes `group` (the register-partition index) in the key, so
two groups get distinct slots, but the WMMA's `cand` filter ignores it. In practice that is
harmless because multi-group operands are refused upstream: `_plan_mma` raises `NotImplementedError`
if one operand spans two register groups (`gir/emit_plan.py:250-256`), so `group` is constant
per operand today. If multi-group ever lands, this filter must gain the group component or it will
match a register from the wrong partition. Note it down.

**The `for n in cand` loop marks *every* matching slot used**, and reports WRONG SOURCE once per
mismatching slot. With `group` constant there is exactly one candidate, so this is a one-iteration
loop; with several it would produce one message per group, which is probably what you want.

**Vacuity note.** If `prog.meta['mma_inputs']` is missing or empty, `_wmma_inputs` returns
`(None, None)`, `_expected` returns `op = None`, and the WMMA branch `continue`s on **both**
inputs — so the entire WMMA half of the walk becomes a no-op while reads still update the file, and
`check_register_dataflow` returns `[]`. That is the file's most dangerous vacuity mode: a metadata
key silently disables the check. Nothing asserts `mma_inputs` is present. **Add that assertion.**
It is one line, and it converts "returns clean" into "raises, because we cannot tell".

##### 12.2.5 `check_register_dataflow` — the pipelined shape, walked as hardware runs it

**`check_register_dataflow(prog, entry="prologue", loop="steady", plans=None) -> list`
(`gir/verify_dataflow.py:119`)**.

```
viol, regs = [], _RegFile()
get = (a lambda returning None) if plans is None else plans.get
if entry in prog.blocks:  _walk(prog, entry, regs, viol, get(entry))
if loop not in prog.blocks: return viol
_walk(prog, loop, regs, viol, get(loop))          # first trip
n = len(viol)
_walk(prog, loop, regs, viol, get(loop))          # second trip, SAME register file
for j in range(n, len(viol)):
    viol[j] = "[loop-carried] " + viol[j]
return viol
```

**Why the loop is walked twice, and why that is the crux of the whole file.** A software-pipelined
loop has two distinct obligations:

1. The **peel** must prime whatever the first trip reads before reading it. The first pass over the
   loop body exposes any failure here, because the register file entering it contains exactly what
   the prologue put there.
2. The loop must **sustain itself**: whatever the *next* trip reads before writing, this trip must
   have left behind. A single pass cannot see this at all — by the end of one pass the file
   contains everything that pass's own reads produced, so any use-before-def in the loop-carried
   direction has already been accidentally satisfied.

Walking the same block twice against one register file is the minimal simulation that exposes both.
It is not an approximation of a fixpoint; for this shape it *is* the fixpoint, because the register
file's content stabilises after one full trip (the loop writes the same slot set each time).

**The `[loop-carried]` labelling** (`:140-141`) exists so a reader is not hunting for the fault in a
straight-line reading of the block. A violation reported only on the second pass is by construction
a cross-trip one; saying so in the message is free and turns a confusing report into a diagnosis.

**The `plans` parameter** is how a test injects a deliberately-broken plan. `plans` is
`{phase: [EmitAction]}`, normally produced by `plan_program(prog)`. `_mutated`
(`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:3595`) takes a real program, rebuilds one phase's act list with a function
applied to each read act's `at` dict, and hands the result in. That is the pattern for writing a
negative control **without reverting the source that fixed the defect**, and it is why this file has
four genuine negative controls where `verify.py` has nine covering twelve checks:

- forcing every read's `region` to 0 reproduces the region-term defect (`:3607`);
- relabelling one operand's reads with a region it does not have reproduces the asymmetric-split
  defect (`:3619`);
- forcing every read's `reg_buf` to 0 reproduces the register-rate collapse and must produce
  **OVERWRITE-BEFORE-USE** (`:3629`);
- deleting the *last* read from the prologue's act list reproduces the peel defect and must produce
  **USE-BEFORE-DEF** (`:3639`), with a guard first (`assert len(reads) >= 2`) so the probe is not
  silently testing a peel that primes nothing.

That last guard is a **non-vacuity assertion on the fixture itself**, and it is the habit that
makes negative controls trustworthy. Copy it.

**False-negative surface.**

- Only two blocks are walked: `entry` and `loop`, by *name*, defaulting to `'prologue'` and
  `'steady'`. **The drain is never checked**, and neither is a second steady block of a multi-block
  chain (`steady1`, …), nor the short arm. A register fault confined to the drain is invisible.
  Extending to the drain needs a decision about the drain's own frame (each drain step is a
  different chunk position) and is genuinely more work than it looks.
- If `'prologue'` is absent — the one-hop kernel — the loop is walked with an empty file, so the
  first pass reports USE-BEFORE-DEF for every read-ahead value. In practice a one-hop kernel has no
  LDS reads at all, so there is nothing to report; but the degeneracy is unguarded.
- Two passes catch a distance-1 loop-carried dependency. A schedule that read a value *two* trips
  ahead would need three passes. Nothing in the model prevents such a schedule; nothing checks it.

##### 12.2.6 `check_region_coverage` — and the agent-relative exemption

**`check_region_coverage(prog, phase="steady", acts=None) -> list`
(`gir/verify_dataflow.py:145`)**.

```
have = prog.meta['operand_regions']            # {op-class -> region count}, theta's own number
seen = {}                                      # {op-class -> set of regions its reads name}
for act in plan:
    if act.kind == 'read':
        seen[act.at['tc']].add(act.at.get('region', 0))

agent_rel = set(prog.meta['region_agent_relative'])

for op, regions in sorted(seen.items()):
    want = set(range(max(1, have.get(op, 1))))
    if regions != want and op in agent_rel and regions and not (regions - want):
        continue                               # UNDER-coverage, agent-relative: correct
    if regions != want:
        report, distinguishing:
            (regions - want) non-empty  ->  "a region the operand does not have"
            otherwise                   ->  "a region nothing reads"
```

**What it proves in the ordinary case.** The regions an operand's reads *name* are exactly the
regions the operand *has*. Under-coverage means a region is filled by a copy and never consumed —
the data was loaded and thrown away, and some other region was read twice in its place.
Over-coverage means a read names a region that does not exist, which on the address side is a
displacement into somebody else's bytes.

**The agent-relative exemption, and why the asymmetry is the correct one.**

The vocabulary first. A storage region is normally a property of the **coordinate**: the read
instruction's own `Tile.coord` carries a value along the operand's region axes, and that value
selects the region. But for some operands it is a property of the **agent**. The local-read address
assignment offsets each wave by a per-wave stride, so at a four-wave shape wave `w` sits *entirely*
inside region `w` and its reads name region `w` alone. The static instruction is the same for every
wave; which region it touches depends on which wave executes it. `prog.meta['region_agent_relative']`
is the set of op-classes for which this holds, and it is set on the **read hop only**.

Now the argument. `check_region_coverage` reads **one agent's plan** — the emit plan is the
instruction stream a single wave executes. The question "does every region the copy fills get named
by some read?" is the right question *only while the region is a property of the coordinate*. When
it is a property of the agent, the correct statement is:

> the union **over agents** covers every region; a single agent's plan never does.

Demanding coordinate coverage from one agent's plan therefore reports a **correct** schedule as
under-coverage. That is not a tolerable false positive: this file's whole purpose is to be the
first thing that fails, so a systematic false positive on a legal configuration would either be
suppressed by hand or would train people to ignore the checker. Under-coverage must be exempt.

**Over-coverage is not exempt, and the asymmetry is forced.** Naming a region the operand does not
have is a *displacement into other bytes* — the read address gains a `region * splitBoundary` term
for a region that does not exist, and lands in memory belonging to something else. No distribution
of work over agents can make that correct. The agent story explains why *fewer* regions appear in
one agent's plan than the operand has; it offers no mechanism whatsoever by which *more* appear.
Formally: the agent distribution is a partition of the region set among agents, so each agent's
region set is a **subset** of the operand's. A subset can be proper (that is under-coverage, and
expected); it cannot contain a non-member.

That is exactly what the guard encodes. Read the three conjuncts at
`gir/verify_dataflow.py:176` in order:

```python
if regions != want and op in agent_rel and regions and not (regions - want):
    continue
```

- `op in agent_rel` — the exemption applies only to operands declared agent-relative.
- `regions` non-empty — an operand whose reads name **no** region at all is still a fault. "This
  agent reads none of it" is not a distribution, it is a missing read.
- `not (regions - want)` — **the subset condition**. Nothing outside `want` may appear. This single
  clause is what makes the exemption one-directional, and it is the whole derivation above,
  compiled.

**This is the same fact applied twice, on two different sides,** and that is why it is trustworthy
rather than ad hoc. `mem_tokens.py:152` already draws the identical distinction on the **ordering**
side, with the opposite consequence: an agent-relative read is **widened to carry every region's
token**, because the producers of the regions this static instruction does not *name* may still be
the producers of the region it *touches* on some other wave, and leaving them unordered is a race.
So the same premise gives "widen the token set" for ordering and "narrow the coverage demand" for
coverage. Two consequences, one fact. When a third consumer of the agent-relative flag appears, the
right move is to check it against both of these before inventing a third reading — and be warned
that this has *already* had to be taught to three separate checkers independently.

**Historical note worth carrying.** A message from this very check was once cited as *proof* that
the model needed a new narrowing construct on the read hop — the argument being "the checker says
the reads do not cover the regions, therefore the read must be able to name a narrower set". The
conclusion stood for a day. It was wrong: the checker was asking a *coordinate* question about an
*agent* fact. What made it survive a day was that no dump printed any region facts, so nobody could
see the mismatch. Both halves were fixed — this exemption, and the region/agent block in the
renderer (§14). The lesson is general and belongs in any future checker: **a violation message is
evidence about the checker's premises as much as about the program.**

**Negative controls, all three directions** (`test_region_coverage_agent_relative_is_covered_by_the_agents`,
`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:4631`). The test builds a two-line stub `Program` and a one-act plan naming
only region 0 for an operand with 2 regions, and asserts:

1. **not** agent-relative → under-coverage **is** reported ("a region nothing reads"). This is the
   *non-vacuity guard*: the exemption below is only meaningful because the same input faults
   without it.
2. agent-relative → clean.
3. agent-relative, reads naming regions `{0,1,2}` on a 2-region operand → **still** reported ("does
   not have").

Three assertions, and each one fails if the guard's corresponding conjunct is deleted. That is what
a controlled exemption looks like.

**False-negative surface.**

- `have = meta['operand_regions']` defaults to `1` for any operand not listed, so `want = {0}`. An
  operand whose region count is *missing* from the metadata is checked against the trivial
  expectation and passes. The metadata is θ's; nothing cross-checks it here.
- Only the `'steady'` block by default. A prologue that fills the wrong regions is not covered.
- The check is over **regions named**, not over *how many times each is named*. Reading region 0
  twice and region 1 once passes region coverage entirely — it is `check_source_coverage` that
  catches the duplicate, which is why the two must be run together and why `check_plan` runs both.
- Coverage is aggregated over the whole block, so a read naming region 1 for the *wrong tile* still
  contributes to coverage.

##### 12.2.7 `check_source_coverage` — one trip reads each source coordinate exactly once

**`check_source_coverage(prog, phase="steady", acts=None) -> list`
(`gir/verify_dataflow.py:187`)**.

```
in0, in1 = _wmma_inputs(prog)

want = {}                                   # operand -> set of (tile, k) its WMMA demand
for act where kind == 'wmma':
    for (which, op) in ((0, in0), (1, in1)):
        want[op].add((act.at['idx0' if which==0 else 'idx1'], act.at['u']))

got = {}                                    # operand -> LIST of (tile_flat, k_flat) its reads fetch
for act where kind == 'read':
    got[act.at['tc']].append((tile_flat, k_flat))

for op in want:
    dups    = coordinates appearing MORE THAN ONCE in got[op]
    missing = want[op] - set(got[op])
    extra   = set(got[op]) - want[op]
    report each non-empty set with its own message
```

**The conservation law.** A reorder, a split or a peel **moves** work; it never adds or loses any.
So over one steady trip the multiset of source coordinates the reads fetch must equal, exactly, the
set the WMMA consume. Three failure directions, each named separately:

- **DUPLICATE** — two reads fetch the same source. One of them is redundant, and it is usually the
  signature that a *coordinate was projected away*: two distinct positions collapsed onto one index
  because a projection dropped an axis.
- **MISSING** — part of the tile never reaches a register.
- **EXTRA** — a read fetches something no WMMA consumes.

**The expected set is derived from the block's own WMMA, not from extents.** That is the crucial
design choice: it needs no extent bookkeeping of its own and therefore cannot drift from the
schedule. It also means it is a **relative** check — it proves the reads and the WMMA of *this
block* agree with each other, not that either agrees with the mathematical GEMM. If a whole axis
were dropped from both the reads and the WMMA, both sides shrink together and the check passes.
That is the check's principal false-negative surface and it is intrinsic to the design; the
absolute statement lives in the parity tests that compare GIR's per-stage op counts against the
upstream tree's (`test_gir_op_parity_with_loopir`, `Tests/unit/test_gir.py:158`).

**`dups` uses `seq.count(c)` inside a comprehension over `seq`** (`gir/verify_dataflow.py:215`),
which is `O(n²)` in the number of reads per operand per block. With `n` in the tens-to-low-hundreds
that is a few thousand comparisons and invisible; at a hypothetical large unroll it would be the
first thing to bite. `collections.Counter` is the one-line fix if it ever matters.

**Secondary surfaces.** An operand that appears in `got` but not in `want` (reads with no WMMA at
all — a scale operand consumed by no instruction) is **never examined**, because the outer loop is
`for op in sorted(want)`. And the whole check is per block, defaulting to `'steady'`, so prologue
and drain reads are outside it.

##### 12.2.8 `check_address_keys` — the one check that crosses into geometry

**`check_address_keys(prog, packed, phase="steady", acts=None, force_within=False) -> list`
(`gir/verify_dataflow.py:230`)**. It is **not** part of `check_plan` and has no production caller;
it is invoked only from the test suite.

**The problem it solves.** `check_source_coverage` proves the reads name distinct *source*
coordinates. That is **not** the same as distinct *addresses*. The read leaf builds an address from
**two coupled choices**:

```
region term :  region * splitBoundary      if the regions are PACKED, else 0 (nothing)
coordinate  :  the WITHIN-REGION one       if PACKED, else the FLAT one
```

and the two must move **together**. Take the region term away (because the split is contiguous)
while keeping the within-region coordinate, and there is nowhere left for the region to live: every
region `r > 0` lands on region 0's bytes — with the plan still perfect by every other check in this
file. Measured on a real configuration where the split cuts the *outer* axis of the LDS image (so
the regions are contiguous, not separately packed): **every** region-1 read repeated its region-0
address, across 1056 of 1056 cells.

**Why `packed` is a callable parameter and not derived.** Whether an operand's regions form
separately packed LDS blocks is a property of the **LDS layout** — it depends on which axis the
split cuts and on whether the LDS tile is unroll-major — and the schedule does not model addresses
and must not learn to. So the caller supplies `packed: operand -> bool`. That keeps the layering
intact: this file checks coordinate coherence, and the one geometry fact it cannot do without is
injected.

```
keys = {}
for read act:
    op     = at['tc']
    p      = bool(packed(op))
    within = p or force_within
    key = ( at['region'] if p else 0,
            at['tile']   if within else at['tile_flat'],
            at['k']      if within else at['k_flat'] )
    src = (at['tile_flat'], at['k_flat'])
    if keys.setdefault((op, key), src) != src:
        report "reads sources X and Y at the SAME address key K -- one reads the other's bytes"
```

The key is the *address decomposition*; the value is the *source*. Two different sources arriving
at one key means one read is fetching the other's bytes. The message also prints whether the
operand is PACKED or CONTIGUOUS and which components the address is built from, which is what makes
the report actionable rather than merely alarming.

**`force_within` is the anti-vacuity device, and it deserves imitation.** It decouples the pair —
within-region coordinate with **no** region term — which is exactly the pre-fix leaf. It exists so
a test can demonstrate that the check *catches the defect*, rather than merely *agreeing with the
fixed code*. The negative control (`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:3940`) asserts three things in
sequence, and all three matter:

1. `packed=False, force_within=True` (the pre-fix leaf) → violations containing "SAME address key";
2. `packed=False` (correct contiguous scheme) → clean;
3. `packed=True` (correct packed scheme) → **also** clean.

The third assertion is the one that proves the point: the packed decomposition is injective on its
own, so a check that only modelled the two *correct* schemes could never have seen the defect. The
defect is the **decoupling**, and only a check parameterised over the decoupling can find it.

The positive sweep (`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:3921`) runs both layouts against both split axes — four
cells — so each half of the `(axis, layout)` diagonal is exercised on each axis.

**Its principal weakness: it is not wired into anything.** `check_plan` does not call it, and
`KernelWriter` therefore does not either. The reason is the `packed` parameter — nobody has plumbed
`lds_geometry.region_split_is_packed` through to the semantic gate. That is a small piece of work
(`packed = lambda op: region_split_is_packed(...)` at the `KernelWriter` call site) and it would
close the one defect class this file knows about and does not check in production. **Do it.**

**Other surfaces.** `at['region']` defaults to 0 when absent, so an unsplit operand collapses to
`(0, flat_tile, flat_k)` and the check degenerates into "no two reads fetch different sources at
the same flat coordinate" — true but vacuous. And like the others it is one block, default
`'steady'`.

##### 12.2.9 `check_plan` — the aggregate, and its production wiring

**`check_plan(prog, plans=None) -> list` (`gir/verify_dataflow.py:277`)** — three of the five
checks, concatenated:

```python
steady = None if plans is None else plans.get("steady")
out  = check_region_coverage(prog, acts=steady)
out += check_source_coverage(prog, acts=steady)
out += check_register_dataflow(prog, plans=plans)
return out
```

`check_address_keys` is **not** included (§12.2.8: it needs a geometry callable nobody supplies).
`check_register_dataflow` receives the whole `plans` dict because it walks two blocks; the other
two receive only the steady act list.

The docstring's claim is exact and worth quoting because it states the file's precise scope:
"empty means the plan computes the GEMM its θ describes — **up to the address geometry**, which
`lds_geometry` owns."

**The production wiring, and the story behind it.** `check_plan` is called once per kernel from
`KernelWriter._loopModelGirProgram` (`KernelWriter.py:3777`), immediately after `build_gir` and
before the Program is cached:

```python
viol = check_plan(prog)                                  # KernelWriter.py:3803
if viol:
    raise ValueError("UseLoopModel: the GIR plan fails its own semantic check ...")
```

Three deliberate properties of that call site, all argued in the comment at `KernelWriter.py:3789-3801`:

1. **It raises, loudly.** It is not a rejection in the solution-validation layer. The code-generation
   path under test must be able to emit every solution the reference path emits, so a
   path-specific reject is a *parity failure*, not a safety measure — and it is **silent**: the
   solution stops appearing in the results, the reference twin still generates and passes, and the
   matrix reads green with the arm under test quietly absent. Failing the build names the defect
   instead.
2. **The contract is "this must never fire."** If it does, the plan is wrong and the plan gets
   fixed; the configuration is never gated off.
3. **It is cheap** — pure Python over the plan, no rocisa — which is what makes a per-kernel gate
   affordable at all.

**How it got there is the single most instructive fact about this file.** For a period,
`check_plan` existed, was correct, had four negative controls, and was called **only from the unit
tests**. It was therefore a test-only oracle whose coverage was whatever the sweeps happened to
include — and no sweep covered the degenerate case of a single substep per trip. A sweep of 648
configurations later found the separation to be perfect: **216 of 216** configurations at one
substep were flagged USE-BEFORE-DEF, and **0 of 432** elsewhere, independent of every other
parameter. Those 216 accounted for all sixteen numeric failures of that shape observed on hardware.
A build-time answer that surfaced only after a GPU run, because nobody had called the function.

The lesson generalises past this file: **an oracle that is not on the build path is a test, not a
gate**, and its coverage is bounded by the imagination of whoever wrote the sweep.

##### 12.2.10 The live-in coverage question, and its current status

The property a reader will look for and should understand precisely: *every value the steady block
uses before defining — its upward-exposed uses, its **live-in** set — must be covered by a
definition the prologue performs.* This is textbook liveness; in a normal compiler it would be a
backward `LIVE-IN` fixpoint over the CFG, meeting at the loop header against the prologue's
`DEF` set.

**GIR does not compute that fixpoint, and it does not need to for the register file**, because
`check_register_dataflow` already decides the same question *operationally*: it walks the prologue
into an abstract register file, then walks the loop body, and any read of a slot the prologue did
not fill is reported as USE-BEFORE-DEF. For a straight-line prologue and a single-block loop —
which is the shape every kernel currently has — walking is exactly as strong as the fixpoint, and
strictly more informative, because it names the *instruction* rather than the *slot*.

**Status.** The invariant exists, fires correctly, and is now wired into the build path
(§12.2.9). The historical gap was never the invariant; it was the wiring, plus the one schedule
shape it exposed. Two deliverables were identified and the second has landed:

1. **Fix the peel** so the prologue primes the first generation in the degenerate one-substep case,
   where the steady body is emitted in a read-for-the-next-trip shape that needs a primed register.
2. **Wire `check_plan` into the build path** so a plan failing its own semantic check cannot be
   emitted — done, `KernelWriter.py:3803`.

The ordering mattered: wiring before fixing would have turned sixteen wrong-numbers cells into
sixteen build failures and stopped the matrix from running at all.

**What is genuinely still missing**, and should be stated plainly rather than implied:

- **The LDS side has no live-in check.** `check_register_dataflow` models the *register file*
  only. Whether the shared buffer a steady read consumes was filled by a prologue copy is asked
  nowhere in this file. It is partially covered from the other direction — `LdsHazards` finds the
  producer/consumer edges and `_check_rotation_waw` (§12.1.8) proves no rotating buffer is written
  and never read — but "read and never written" has no checker at all.
- **The drain is unmodelled** (§12.2.5). Its live-ins are whatever the last steady trip left, and
  nothing verifies that.
- **The block set is hardcoded by name** (`'prologue'`, `'steady'`). A multi-block steady chain or
  a kept short arm is skipped silently.

Anyone implementing the real fixpoint should note it buys correctness only in shapes GIR cannot
currently build (multi-block loop bodies, several prologue paths joining at the header). The
cheaper and higher-value work is extending the *walk* to the drain and to the LDS space.

##### 12.2.11 The cross-check pattern — two independent derivations forced to agree

Both files rely, in three separate places, on the same structural idea, and it is worth naming
because it is the most effective defect-finding pattern in the package.

**The pattern.** When one fact is needed by two parties, do not compute it once and share it.
Compute it **twice, by genuinely different routes**, and assert the two agree. The value is not
redundancy — it is that a bug in either derivation must also be a bug in the *other*, in the *same
direction*, to escape. Self-consistency is no defence.

**Instance 1 — `_check_tokens`' V2b (`gir/verify.py:272-278`).** The analysis derives the token set
from the Program; a pass stamps `Move.token_ids`; the check compares them. A pass that truncated
the stamp cannot hide, because the analysis does not read the stamp. This found a real bug on the
day it was written.

**Instance 2 — the pointer def-use oracle (`_simulate_pointer`, `Tests/unit/test_gir.py:1284`).**
A test-side simulator walks the finalized program as hardware would and recomputes the required
generation *from first principles* — `(true_chunk + carry) % ring`, where `carry` is the
frame-free offset and `true_chunk` is the block's actual position in an execution of a given number
of trips — treating a `swap` Mark as the only thing that moves the pointer. It shares **no code**
with the analysis that placed those swaps. Its docstring states the payoff exactly: a bug in the
placement analysis "cannot hide here by being self-consistent — which is exactly how the previous
placement rules passed their own unit tests while emitting a double swap".

**Instance 3 — `check_source_coverage` itself (§12.2.7).** The expected coordinate set is derived
from the *WMMA* acts and the observed set from the *read* acts. Those are produced by two different
functions in `emit_plan` (`_plan_mma` and `_plan_move`) from two different node types, projecting
two different coordinate sources. They agree only if the schedule is coherent.

**Why it is worth repeating.** Every dominant defect in this subsystem has had the same shape: *two
places compute one fact, they agree on the common case, and they diverge on the degenerate one.*
The region walk (loader vs. incrementer, `+2` against `−1`). The register rotation width (the
scheduler's count vs. the register-name table's). The token set (analysis vs. stamp). In each case
one side was authoritative and the other was a convenient re-derivation, and nothing compared them.
A cross-check turns that class of bug from "found on hardware after a bisect" into "found at build
time with both values printed".

**Concrete advice for adding one.** (a) The second derivation must not import the first — if it
calls the same helper, it is a re-run, not a check. (b) It must be *simpler* and *slower* than the
production one; the production path may be an incremental fixpoint, the oracle should be a
brute-force simulation. (c) It must have a non-vacuity guard: assert the fixture actually exhibits
the phenomenon (`assert len(reads) >= 2`, `assert prog.meta.get("region_agent_relative")`) so a
degenerate fixture cannot make the comparison trivially true. (d) Report both values in the
message. A cross-check that says "mismatch" without printing the two derivations has thrown away
most of its value.

##### 12.2.12 The standing sweep, cost, and how to extend `verify_dataflow.py`

**The standing sweep.** `test_the_whole_order_x_split_x_prefetch_matrix_has_a_CLEAN_emit_plan`
(`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:3579`) runs `check_plan` over the cross product produced by
`_sweep_params` (`:3567`): **6** loop orders × **7** split configurations × **2** global-prefetch
depths × **2** local-prefetch depths = **168** configurations, asserting `[]` for every one and
collecting the failures into one message rather than stopping at the first. Its docstring states
its role: "this is the test that should FAIL FIRST from now on". A numeric miscompare says "wrong";
this says "operand B never reads region 1" or "wmma u=1 reads a register nothing filled", and that
is the whole difference between a bisect and a fix.

Two further sweeps exercise `check_plan` through the *product* layer rather than by constructing
the schedule directly — the 8-bit-element parity test (`Tests/unit/test_gir.py:3994-4000`) and the
split-independence test (`:4023-4030`), both of which route a real Solution dict through the
parameter bridge first. That distinction matters: a bridge that drops a key is invisible below the
product layer, and several defects have been exactly that.

**Cost.** `plan_block` is `O(body)` with small constants; `_walk` is `O(acts)` with a dict lookup
per act plus, on the WMMA branch, a **linear scan over `regs.slots`** to find candidates
(`gir/verify_dataflow.py:99-100`). That makes `check_register_dataflow` `O(acts × slots)`. With
`acts` in the low hundreds and `slots` in the low tens per block, times three walks, it is a few
tens of thousands of operations per kernel — well under a millisecond, and negligible beside the
compiler invocation that follows.

If it ever does matter, the fix is obvious and local: **index `regs.slots` by
`(operand, reg_buf, tile_flat)`** — exactly the tuple the candidate filter tests — instead of
scanning. That turns the WMMA branch into a dict lookup and makes the walk `O(acts)`. The reason
it was not done is that `_reg_name` also carries `group`, so the natural key and the natural filter
differ by one component; resolving that (either compare `group` in the filter, or drop it from the
name) is the prerequisite, and it is the same decision multi-group support will force anyway
(§12.2.4).

**Extension advice, concrete.**

1. **Add the missing metadata assertions.** `mma_inputs` missing silently disables the WMMA half of
   `_walk` (§12.2.4); `operand_regions` missing silently reduces region coverage to the trivial
   expectation (§12.2.6). Both should raise. This is the single highest-value change in the file
   and it is about four lines.
2. **Wire `check_address_keys` into `check_plan`** by plumbing the packed predicate from the LDS
   geometry module at the `KernelWriter` call site (§12.2.8). It is the one known defect class the
   production gate does not cover.
3. **Extend the walk beyond `prologue`/`steady`.** Take the block names from the CFG rather than
   from defaults: walk every prologue-phase block in order, then the steady chain in order, twice,
   then the drain chain once. The hard part is the drain's frame, not the walking.
4. **Model the LDS space the way the register file is modelled.** A second abstract file keyed by
   `(unit, region, generation)`, filled by copy acts and drained by read acts, would give
   read-before-fill and fill-before-drain for shared memory with the same machinery — and would
   close the "read and never written" hole noted in §12.2.10.
5. **Delete `_RegFile.snapshot` and the `initial` parameter** (§12.2.3). Dead code beside subtle
   logic is a hazard, not a spare part.
6. **Preserve the three habits that make this file trustworthy** when adding a check: derive the
   expectation from a *different* source than the observation; give every check a negative control
   built by mutating a real plan (`_mutated`, `Tests/unit/test_gir.py:3595`) rather than by
   reverting source; and put a non-vacuity assertion on the fixture itself.

##### 12.2.13 Summary: what each check proves, and what makes it vacuous

| check | proves | vacuous when |
|---|---|---|
| `G-TERM` | `preds`/`succs` agree with terminators; every target exists | `preds`/`succs` are empty (both sub-checks are skipped); a new terminator type falls through `_term_targets`' default |
| `G-CFG` | the pipeline block counts match `meta['M']` and the fold verdict; one reduction loop | `meta['M']` or `meta['short_loop']` absent; zero loop headers; a mis-phased block |
| `G-WALK` | every split copy is on the region the descriptor reached, and the walk closes per block | no split copies in the block; `unit_regions` wrongly says 1 |
| `G-TOKEN` | every shared access named; the stamp equals the analysis; disjoint storage unshared; fences carry ids | before `TokensPass` (stamp half off); V1 only sees pairs `LdsHazards` produced; V3 checks non-emptiness, not sufficiency |
| `G-EMIT` | every `model_only` block has a recorded reason and its discarded Marks are counted | counts compared as an integer, so kind-for-kind swaps pass |
| `G-UNIFORM` | no proc-scoped fence sits behind a role restriction or agent-varying guard | **structurally inert today**: `role` is `'all'` everywhere and `Pred` cannot spell an agent test; scaffold-owned wave branches are invisible |
| `G-TRIP` | steady coverage + drain coverage = `[0, T)` exactly | `meta['M']` absent; no drain blocks; `per_trip != 1` (named, asserted hole) |
| `G-GEN-SSA` | one phi def per `Gen`, no dead def, no undefined use | Marks are not uses, so a Gen kept alive only by a Mark reports as dead (correctly, but be aware) |
| `G-NOITER` | no coordinate carries the trip index | the mode name `'iter'` is a hardcoded literal |
| `G-SEMANTIC` | no physical attribute on a body instruction | **`Ref`s and `Tile`s are not inspected**; only six attribute names are denied |
| `G-OPERANDS` | every register `Mma` source has *some* producing `Move` | keyed by `(operand, space)` only — coordinate, block and order are all unchecked |
| `G-MARK` | kind is in the closed set; required keys present; a swap names the right pointer key | no value domains anywhere; extra keys unconstrained; `hop` itself unvalidated |
| `check_region_coverage` | reads name exactly the operand's regions | `operand_regions` missing; agent-relative operands exempt from *under*-coverage by design; steady block only |
| `check_source_coverage` | reads and WMMA of the block agree coordinate-for-coordinate | relative, not absolute — dropping an axis from *both* sides passes; operands with reads but no WMMA are skipped |
| `check_register_dataflow` | no use-before-def, overwrite-before-use or wrong-source over `prologue → steady → steady` | `mma_inputs` missing disables the WMMA half entirely; drain and extra steady blocks unwalked; distance-2 loop carries unmodelled |
| `check_address_keys` | the region term and the coordinate choice move together | **not called in production**; unsplit operands degenerate to a tautology |
| `check_plan` | the three checks above, as one list | excludes `check_address_keys`; steady block only |

---

### 13. `gir/emit_plan.py` and `gir/quantum.py` — the emission plan and the movement quantum

These two modules are the last pure-Python stage of the lowering stack: everything above them is a
graph, everything below them imports `rocisa`. `emit_plan.py` (313 lines, 10 definitions) turns a
finalized GIR block into a flat ordered list of *acts* — one per instruction layer 3 must emit, with
every index already a concrete integer. `quantum.py` (248 lines, 8 definitions) then decides, for
the read acts, **which of them actually issue an instruction and into which register**, under a
tile-merge supplied from outside the model.

The pair is deliberately separated from `gir_to_rocisa.py` so that the correctness-critical
arithmetic — which tile, which reduction substep, which storage region, which register generation —
is unit-testable in a plain `pytest` with no compiled extension present. `emit_plan.py` imports only
three GIR-internal modules (`Lowering/gir/emit_plan.py:41-43`); `quantum.py` imports **nothing at
all** except `dataclasses` (`Lowering/gir/quantum.py:51-53`) and receives the merge as a callable.

#### 13.1 What an emit plan is, and why it is a flat list

**The problem.** A finalized GIR block body is a list of `Move`, `Mma` and `Mark` nodes whose
operands are `Ref`s over `Tile`s whose coordinates are `(mode, value)` pairs — `K_inner=1`,
`M_split=0`, `M_inner=1`. A leaf emitter, by contrast, wants numbers: *tile 3, substep 1, register
buffer 0*. Somebody has to collapse a coordinate over an arbitrary set of named modes into the small
integers the emitters index by, and that collapse depends on the loop order (which mode is the
fastest-varying), on each operand's own presence (which modes it is *indexed by* at all, as opposed
to broadcast over), and on the mode extents.

**The abstraction.** An **act** — `EmitAction(kind, at)` (`Lowering/gir/emit_plan.py:46`) — is one
entry in that flat list: a `kind` string and an `at` dict of already-resolved values. There is no
node reference in an act and no way back to the IR; the act *is* the interface. `plan_block`
(`:296`) produces the list for one block in body order, `plan_program` (`:311`) does it for every
block.

The eight act kinds, their producers and their payload keys:
