you which of the three things went wrong.

The two-line head `gir_text` prepends is not produced by this module:

```
# GIR dump (observability; the finalized layer-2 program handed to L3)
# counts = {'prologue': {...}, 'steady': {...}, ...}
```

so a real `OutputLoopIR` dump begins with `gir_counts` output before `render_gir`'s first line. The
unit tests call `render_gir` directly and therefore do not see it.

**A note on section markers in the output — and a reading hazard.** Two of the renderer's fixed
strings embed markers of the form "§" plus a number: `# Φ fuse groups: … (… — "§2.8 move 9")` and
`# "§2.2" absorbed axes …`. **Those two tokens are quoted *output text*, not references into this
report.** They are leftover pointers into a design note outside the code, they carry no
information for a reader of this report, and each concept is explained in full below, in place.
The hazard is specific and worth naming because the two numbering spaces collide: this report also
*has* a §2.2 (the module inventory), so the string `§2.2` means one thing when it appears in a
rendered dump quoted here and another thing everywhere else. Wherever a quoted marker appears in
the prose of §14 it is written in quotation marks for exactly that reason; inside the verbatim dump
excerpts (§14.15 and the fragments above) it is reproduced as-is, because those blocks are the
renderer's literal output. Deleting the markers from the two format strings is a safe one-line
cleanup that nobody has made, and it would retire the collision as well as the dangling pointer.

#### 14.2 The grammar of a dump

`render_gir` (`gir/render.py:304-345`) is a straight-line string accumulator. There is no traversal
logic and no recursion; it appends to a list `L` and joins with newlines at `:345`. The shape is
fixed:

```
render_gir(prog):
    L  = [ one Program header line ]                       # :305-306
    L += _theta_facts_lines(prog)                          # :307   0..7 comment lines
    L += _short_loop_lines(prog)                           # :308   0..5 comment lines
    for blk in prog.blocks.values():                       # :309   INSERTION ORDER, not RPO
        L += [ one blank line + block header + ':' ]       # :310-332
        L += [ '  phi:  …'  for each blk.phis ]            # :333-334
        L += [ '  Mark…' | '  copy…' | '  read…' | '  mma…' for each blk.body ]   # :335-341
        L += [ '  xfer: …' for each blk.xfers ]            # :342-343
        L += [ '  ' + _term_line(blk.term) ]               # :344
    return "\n".join(L)
```

Four things about that skeleton are worth fixing in your head before reading any dump.

**Block order is insertion order, not control flow.** `prog.blocks` is an insertion-ordered dict
(`gir/nodes.py:469`, documented at `:462`), and the loop at `:309` walks it as-is. `Program.walk_rpo`
(`gir/nodes.py:487`) exists and does compute reverse-post-order, but the renderer does not use it. In
practice the lowering inserts `prologue`, `steady`, `drain0…drainM-1`, then `short0…shortM-1`, so a
kept short arm — which is reached *from* `prologue`, before `steady` — prints **last**, after the
drain chain it does not participate in. Read the `preds`/`succs` fields on each header, not the page
order, to reconstruct the graph. Switching the loop to `walk_rpo()` would be a two-character change
and would make the dump read in execution order; the reason not to is that insertion order is stable
across analysis changes and RPO is not (a retargeted edge reorders the whole listing, so a
`diff` of two dumps would show spurious movement). That tradeoff is worth re-deciding if you find
yourself hand-tracing paths often.

**Only three node kinds print inside a body.** The `if/elif/elif` at `:336-341` handles `Mark`,
`Move` and `Mma`. Anything else in `blk.body` is **silently dropped** — no `else`, no marker. Today
the body only ever holds those three (the lowering constructs nothing else and `G-SEMANTIC`
would reject a foreign node), so the omission is currently unobservable; but if you add a fourth node
class, the first symptom will be a dump that is missing instructions with no indication that anything
was skipped. Adding `else: L.append(f"  ?? {inst!r}")` costs one line and removes that whole failure
mode. This is the single most valuable change a future maintainer could make to this file.

**Indentation is the only structure.** Everything inside a block is indented two spaces; block
headers and the leading comment blocks are flush left. Comment lines begin with `#`. There is no
nesting deeper than that — GIR is a flat CFG, so the dump is flat too.

**Blank lines separate blocks.** The `\n` at the start of `head` (`:310`) puts an empty line before
every block header, including the first, so there is always a blank line between the comment preamble
and `Block prologue`.

The complete line vocabulary, with the function that builds each:

| line | built by | line |
|---|---|---:|
| `Program(entry=…, M=…, S=…, order=…)` | `render_gir` inline | `:305` |
| `# Φ fuse groups: …` | `_theta_facts_lines` | `:255` |
| `#   <op>: N storage regions on <axes> — …` | `_theta_facts_lines` | `:278` |
| `#   movement A+B: N regions …` | `_theta_facts_lines` | `:281` |
| `# agent-distributed operands: …` | `_theta_facts_lines` | `:286` |
| `# §2.2 absorbed axes …` | `_theta_facts_lines` | `:291` |
| `# mode extents: … reduction=… mma inputs=…` | `_theta_facts_lines` | `:296` |
| `# per-region completion (π): ON …` | `_theta_facts_lines` | `:300` |
| `# short-loop (T <= M) arm: …` | `_short_loop_lines` | `:186` |
| `#   FOLDED …` / `#   KEPT …` / `#   verdict=…` | `_short_loop_lines` | `:195/197/199` |
| `#   OBLIGATION ON THE SCAFFOLD…` | `_short_loop_lines` | `:214/219` |
| `#   The prologue block sits OUTSIDE …` | `_short_loop_lines` | `:229` |
| `Block <phase> …:` | `render_gir` inline | `:310-332` |
| `  phi:  genN = φ(entry:v, back) ring=S` | `render_gir` inline | `:334` |
| `  Mark  <kind> <at-dict>` | `render_gir` inline | `:337` |
| `  copy  <srcs> -> <dsts> …` | `_move_line` | `:128` |
| `  read  <srcs> -> <dsts> …` | `_move_line` | `:128` |
| `  mma   <dst> += <srcs>   # <block> …` | `_mma_line` | `:134` |
| `  xfer: genN' = (v + adv) % ring` | `render_gir` inline | `:343` |
| `  term: …` | `_term_line` | `:152-167` |

That is the whole language. The rest of §14 goes line by line.

#### 14.3 The `Program` header line

```
Program(entry=prologue, M=1, S=A=[g0:2, shared:2] | B=[g0:2, shared:2] | MXSA=[…] | MXSB=[…],
        order=['K_inner', 'M_split', 'M_inner', 'N_split', 'N_inner'])
```

(wrapped here; it is one physical line). Built at `gir/render.py:305-306` from four facts, three of
which are `Program.meta` lookups with no default handling — a missing key prints `None`, which is
correct behaviour for a debug view and would be wrong for anything else.

- **`entry`** — `Program.entry`, the label of the block control enters at. Always `prologue` on the
  shipping lowering, but it is read, not assumed.
- **`M`** — the peel depth: how many reduction chunks the prologue issues before the steady loop, and
  therefore how many drain steps follow it. `M=1` above; the `PGR3/PLR0` example in §14.5 has `M=3`
  and correspondingly three `drain{i}` blocks.
- **`S`** — the rotating-buffer depths, printed as the `repr()` of whatever object layer 1 put in
  `meta['S']`. On the current decoder that is a per-operand map whose `__str__` reads
  `A=[g0:2, shared:2] | B=[…]`: operand `A` has a register group `g0` of rotation width 2 and an LDS
  ring of depth 2. `shared:1` means in-place LDS (no swap will ever be emitted for that operand, and
  §14.12's `Mark swap` lines will be absent for it — a unit test asserts exactly that asymmetry).
- **`order`** — `meta['inner_order']`, the loop-order word: the inner modes from outermost to
  innermost. **This is the radix order every coordinate in the dump is written in**, and it is the
  first thing to check when a body looks reordered: `['K_inner','M_split','M_inner','N_split',
  'N_inner']` is a `KMN` kernel with both tile axes split.

#### 14.4 `_theta_facts_lines` — the premises the blocks are derived from

**`_theta_facts_lines(prog) -> list[str]`** (`gir/render.py:234-301`). Input: the `Program`. Output:
zero to seven comment lines, all flush-left, all beginning `# `. Reads only `prog.meta`; touches no
block. Called once, from `render_gir:307`, before any block prints.

**The problem it solves.** A GIR block listing prints coordinates and operands. It does *not* print
whether a given coordinate names a **storage region**, whether that region is chosen by the
**agent** (the wave) rather than by the coordinate, which operands share **one fused movement**, or
how many regions a movement has. Those are facts of the schedule object the program was built from,
they live in `Program.meta`, and each of them changes how the body below must be read. A dump that
omits its premises makes a wrong premise unfalsifiable.

That is not a hypothetical. A comment in `LoopModel/translate.py` — the one this renderer's own
docstring points at, near the region/agent binding — carried the conclusion "the read's region needs
a narrowing selector", justified by a region-coverage checker's message. The checker was asking
a *coordinate* question about an *agent* fact — it wanted to know which region a coordinate names,
when the answer was "whichever region the wave running the instruction lives in". The wrong premise
survived a full day of investigation because nothing in any dump said the operand was agent-relative.
The same failure at a different site is on record a second time (#176). Printing the premises is the
fix.

**The emission rule.** Each block below prints only when it has something to say — with one
deliberate exception, the mode-extent line, which every kernel with an inner mode gets. It is the
radix table the rest of the dump's coordinates are read in, and there is no kernel for which that is
uninteresting. (The docstring at `:248-250` states this exception explicitly; an earlier version
claimed "printed only when non-trivial" across the board, which the code contradicted.)

**Algorithm.**

```
_theta_facts_lines(prog):
    m, out = prog.meta, []

    # 1. Φ fuse groups — only groups of size > 1
    fuse = m['fuse_groups'] or ()
    if any(len(g) > 1 for g in fuse):
        out += "# Φ fuse groups: " + join('+'.join(g) for g in fuse if len(g) > 1)

    # 2/3. storage regions, per operand and per movement — only counts > 1
    regions = {op: n for op, n in m['operand_regions'] if int(n or 1) > 1}
    if regions:
        rmodes    = m['region_modes'] or {}
        agent_rel = set(m['region_agent_relative'] or ())
        for op in sorted(regions):
            axes = '/'.join(rmodes[op]) or '(no axis)'
            who  = <the per-hop sentence>  if op in agent_rel else 'coordinate-relative on every hop'
            out += f"#   {op}: {regions[op]} storage regions on {axes} — {who}"
        units = {u: n for u, n in m['unit_regions'] if int(n or 1) > 1}
        for u in sorted(units, key=str):
            out += f"#   movement {'+'.join(u)}: {units[u]} regions (the walk is per MOVEMENT…)"

    # 4. agent-distributed operands — only the truthy ones
    dist = [op for op, v in sorted(m['agent_distributed']) if v]
    if dist: out += "# agent-distributed operands: " + ', '.join(dist)

    # 5. absorbed axes — only operands with a non-empty tuple
    qa = {op: axes for op, axes in m['quantum_axes'] if axes}
    if qa: out += "# §2.2 absorbed axes (removed from presence, re-inserted as `spans`): …"

    # 6. mode extents — UNCONDITIONAL when any inner mode exists
    ext = m['mode_extents'] or {}
    if ext: out += "# mode extents: k=v,…   reduction=…   mma inputs=…"

    # 7. per-region completion — only when ON
    if m['per_region_completion']: out += "# per-region completion (π): ON — …"
    return out
```

Every dict lookup is `m.get(key) or {}`, so a `Program` built by hand in a test with an empty `meta`
produces zero lines rather than a `KeyError`. That defensiveness is load-bearing: several unit tests
construct three-block `Program`s directly (`test_gir.py:1197-1205` for instance) and render them.

**Line 1 — `# Φ fuse groups: A+B, MXSA+MXSB   (one cooperative movement, one completion — §2.8 move 9)`**
(`gir/render.py:253-256`). A *fuse group* is a set of op-classes whose `global → shared` copies were
merged into **one cooperative instruction with one completion event**: one aliased descriptor serves
both, and piece *j* of A moves with piece *j* of B. The consequence for reading the body is direct —
a `copy` line whose sources are `A.global{…}+B.global{…}` is **one** instruction, not two printed
together, and it produces **one** completion token that both operands' reads await. Only groups of
size > 1 print, so an unfused kernel omits the line entirely. The trailing parenthetical's section
marker points at an external design note and can be ignored; the sentence before it is the whole
content.

**Line 2 — `#   A: 2 storage regions on M_split — <who>`** (`gir/render.py:258-278`). An operand's
LDS tile can be *split* into storage-disjoint pieces; each piece is a **storage region**, and the
axes that enumerate them are its `region_modes`. `2 storage regions on M_split` says A's tile is cut
in half along the `M_split` axis, so `A.shared{M_split0}` and `A.shared{M_split1}` are different
memory, not two coordinates of one buffer. When an operand has region modes but only one region
(the MX scale operands are the standing case), the count is 1 and the line is suppressed by the
`> 1` filter at `:258` — deliberately, because "one region on an axis that could enumerate several"
is a fact about the axis, not about storage.

**The `<who>` clause, and the retraction it encodes.** This is the most carefully worded string in
the file, because its first version was wrong in two ways at once. It read:

> AGENT-relative: wave *w* reads region *w*, so ONE agent's reads name ONE region

Both halves were false, and the dump printed directly beneath it refuted the second: A's read lines
named **both** `M_split0` and `M_split1`. What `meta['region_agent_relative']` actually records
(set at `LoopModel/translate.py:585-591`) is that the *read hop's address* is chosen by the agent —
two waves execute the same read instruction against different regions. `mem_tokens.py:152-160` then
**widens** such a read to name *every* region's memory token, precisely because the instruction may
touch any of them. And the flag is set on the **read hop only**, never on the copy hop, so an
unqualified per-operand "agent-relative" over-claims for the copy: a copy writes the one region its
descriptor names, whoever runs it. Measured at the time of the fix: 8 of 8 agent-relative operands
have *disagreeing* hops, and the geometry dump in layer 1 (`LoopModel/render.py:426`
`render_geometry`) calls those same operands ASYMMETRIC. Two dumps of one schedule contradicting each
other is worse than either omitting the fact.

The current text (`gir/render.py:275-277`) is therefore:

```
region is the AGENT's on the read hop (address agent-chosen) and the COORDINATE's on the
copy hop — see render_geometry for the per-hop split
```

or, when the operand is not in the agent-relative set, `coordinate-relative on every hop`.

The regression fixture is
`test_gir.py:4670` `test_the_dump_shows_the_theta_facts_the_blocks_are_derived_from`, and it is
unusually well built: it asserts the *presence* of `"AGENT's on the read hop"` **and the absence** of
the retracted sentence (`test_gir.py:4694-4696`), then adds a non-vacuity control — an unsplit
single-wave kernel must **not** grow a `storage regions` line (`:4727-4730`), so the positive
assertions cannot be satisfied by boilerplate. Copy that pattern when you add a fact to this dump.

**Line 3 — `#   movement A+B: 2 regions (the walk is per MOVEMENT, not per operand — #236)`**
(`gir/render.py:279-282`). `meta['unit_regions']` is keyed by **completion unit** — a fuse group's
member tuple, or a one-element tuple for an unfused op-class — and says how many region instances
that *movement* actually emits. This is a genuinely different number from the per-operand count on
line 2, and the distinction is why it gets its own line: a coarse copy that moves both halves as one
instruction cannot offer its readers a per-region completion, so a read must not key its wait on a
region the copy never distinguished. Only counts > 1 print. Sorted by `str(u)` at `:280` because the
keys are tuples and are not otherwise orderable against each other.

**Line 4 — `# agent-distributed operands: A, B, MXSA, MXSB   (their cross-agent obligations are
block-scoped, #276)`** (`gir/render.py:284-287`). `meta['agent_distributed']` marks operands whose
data is partitioned across agents rather than replicated. The parenthetical is the consequence you
need when reading fence Marks: for such an operand, a cross-agent ordering obligation is discharged
at **block** scope rather than per access, so you will see one `Mark fence` with `'scope': 'block'`
covering many accesses instead of a fence per pair.

**Line 5 — `# §2.2 absorbed axes (removed from presence, re-inserted as `spans`): MXSA:(('M_split',
2),); MXSB:(('N_split', 2),)`** (`gir/render.py:289-292`). This is the header for the `<spans …>`
suffix documented in §14.8. The concept: when one `ds_load` instruction fills several logical tiles,
the axis it runs along is **removed** from the read hop's coordinate set upstream, so the read's
definition names a single location while every consumer names all of them. The line lists, per
op-class, which axes were removed and at what extent. Without it, a reader diffing a read against its
consumers sees a use of a location no def writes. Only operands with a non-empty tuple print, and the
tuple is rendered by plain `f"{k}:{v}"` — i.e. Python `repr` of the tuple, which is why the trailing
comma of a one-element tuple appears. It is ugly and it is unambiguous; a prettier
`MXSA:M_splitx2` spelling would match the `<spans>` suffix's own format and is worth doing.

**Line 6 — `# mode extents: K_inner=2, M_inner=2, M_split=2, N_inner=2, N_split=2   reduction=K_inner
mma inputs=A,B`** (`gir/render.py:294-298`). Three facts on one line, and the only line printed
unconditionally (given any inner mode):

- **mode extents** — the radix table. `M_split=2` means the coordinate `M_split` takes values 0 and 1,
  so `M_split1` is the last one. Sorted by name, *not* by `ord`; the `order=[…]` field of the
  `Program` header carries the ordering, this carries the sizes. (Layer 1's own dump had the mirror
  bug — reduction modes printed alphabetically directly under an `ord`-ordered levels line — and was
  fixed to print in `ord` order. Doing the same here would be consistent, though the two lines are
  far enough apart that the confusion has not been observed.)
- **`reduction=K_inner`** — which of those modes is the reduction (K) axis. Everything else is a free
  axis. This is what tells you that a `read A.shared{K_inner1,M_inner0}` is the *second* K sub-step of
  the chunk rather than a second tile.
- **`mma inputs=A,B`** — which op-classes are the multiply inputs, as distinct from the scale operands
  that also appear as `mma` sources. On the MX kernel the `mma` line has four sources but only two of
  them are here.

**Line 7 — `# per-region completion (π): ON — each region completes separately (#168)`**
(`gir/render.py:299-300`). A toggle. When ON, each storage region of a split movement gets its own
completion token, so a read of region 0 can proceed without waiting for region 1's copy. When OFF
(the default, and the case where the line is absent) the whole movement is one completion. If you are
staring at `tok=('lds', ('A','B'), (0,))` and wondering why the region tuple has one entry rather than
being absent, this line is the switch that decides it.

#### 14.5 `_short_loop_lines` — the degenerate-trip arm, and two claims that were once asserted

**`_short_loop_lines(prog) -> list[str]`** (`gir/render.py:170-231`). Input: the `Program`. Output:
zero lines when `meta['short_loop']` is absent, otherwise three to five comment lines. Reads
`prog.meta['short_loop']` and — this is the point of §14.5 — reads the entry block's terminator off
the CFG. Called from `render_gir:308`, immediately after the θ facts.

**The problem.** A software-pipelined loop with peel depth `M` needs `T > M` chunks for the steady
loop to be entered at all. When the runtime trip count `T` is at most `M`, the whole pipeline is
degenerate and a separate code path handles it. Layer 1 emits that as a two-armed conditional whose
`then` is `[prologue, steady, drain]` and whose `else` is the short arm. GIR does **not** keep that
shape: it hoists the prologue *out* of the guard (the prologue's copies are needed on both paths) and
then either **folds** the short arm into the drain chain or **keeps** it as its own `short{i}` blocks.

So a reader diffing the GIR against layer 1 sees an `else` arm that has vanished and a guard whose
meaning has changed, with nothing in the block listing saying either was intentional. These lines are
that statement. They are also, historically, where the dump lied twice.

**The record.** `meta['short_loop']` is written by the lowering and updated by `FoldShortPathPass`
(§7.3). The fields the renderer reads:

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `steps` | how many chunk steps the arm has — equal to `M` |
| `guards` | a tuple of `Pred \| None`, one per step; `None` = the step is unconditional |
| `verdict` | `'folded'`, `'kept'`, or (before the pass runs) `'unfolded'` |
| `fold` | the raw `FoldVerdict` verdict string, printed only on the fallback branch |
| `reason` | the analysis's prose explanation of the verdict |
| `obligations` | a tuple of prose preconditions the *consumer* must satisfy |
| `model_only` | (read by the verifier, not by the renderer) which blocks nothing emits |

**Algorithm.**

```
_short_loop_lines(prog):
    sl = prog.meta['short_loop'];  if not sl: return []
    guards = ', '.join(g.render() if g else 'unguarded' for g in sl['guards'])
    out = [f"# short-loop (T <= M) arm: {sl['steps']} chunk steps, guards [{guards}]"]

    verdict = sl['verdict']
    if   verdict == 'folded': out += "#   FOLDED into the drain chain (#183): {reason}"
    elif verdict == 'kept'  : out += "#   KEPT as its own `short{i}` blocks (#183 SPLIT): {reason}"
    else                    : out += "#   verdict={verdict!r} fold={fold!r}: {reason}"

    folded = (verdict == 'folded')
    for ob in sl['obligations']:
        out += "#   OBLIGATION ON THE SCAFFOLD" + ("" if folded else <a disclaimer>) + ": " + ob
    if not folded:
        out += "#   OBLIGATION ON THE SCAFFOLD (this program): route the kept arm's guard chain …"

    f_target = prog.blocks[prog.entry].term.f_target        # READ OFF THE CFG, not assumed
    out += "#   The prologue block sits OUTSIDE the peel-validity guard; the guard's false edge "
           "targets %s." % (f_target or "(no CondGoto on the entry block)")
    return out
```

**Header line.** `# short-loop (T <= M) arm: 3 chunk steps, guards [unguarded, T > 1, T > 2]`. Note
`T <= M`, not `T < M`: the entry guard the lowering emits is a **strict** `T > M`, so its false arm is
`T <= M`. The file said `T < M` in four places until it was corrected; the off-by-one matters because
`T == M` is exactly the trip count at which the steady loop runs zero times and the whole question
becomes live. The `guards` list renders each step's `Pred` through `Pred.render()`
(`gir/nodes.py:224`) and prints the literal word `unguarded` for a `None` — step 0 is always
unconditional (if you are on this path at all you have at least one chunk), and step *t* > 0 is
guarded by `T > t`.

**Verdict line, and the stale conclusion it replaced.** This used to be a hardcoded sentence:
"NOT lowered to GIR blocks". That stopped being true when the arm was given real `short{i}` blocks
and a fold pass. A dump that states a stale conclusion is worse than one that states nothing: this
one was read twice as evidence that the short path is entirely scaffold-owned, sending two
investigations of a `T <= M` miscompare away from the folded drain chain that actually runs it. The
line now **prints the verdict** rather than asserting one, and carries the analysis's own `reason`
string so you can see *why*:

```
#   FOLDED into the drain chain (#183): every def-use pairing survives the reordering
#     (24 corresponded instructions, 11 extra on the folded path)
```
```
#   KEPT as its own `short{i}` blocks (#183 SPLIT): 16 def-use pairing(s) change and 0
#     instruction(s) are absent under the folded order ([('overwritten', 16)]) — emit the short
#     arm as its own path
```

The third branch (`:198-200`) prints `verdict=… fold=… reason=…` verbatim and exists for the states
that are neither: `'unfolded'` (the pass has not run — you are rendering a `lower_to_gir` result
rather than a `build_gir` one, which the tests do routinely) and any future verdict string. It
degrades to showing you the raw fields instead of guessing, which is the right default for a debug
view.

**The obligation line, and why it is qualified.** An *obligation* is a precondition the fold analysis
cannot discharge and hands to whoever consumes the program. These are the part a reader debugging the
short path most needs, because they are exactly what the GIR does *not* guarantee.

The sharp edge: `short_path.py:470-473` builds **one constant obligation tuple, before the verdict is
decided**, and hands the same tuple to every outcome — FOLD, SPLIT, VACUOUS and UNSOUND alike. Its
text is about the *folded* drain chain ("the folded drain chain must be enterable at step M-T, not
only at step 0"). Printing it bare on a KEPT program hands the reader an obligation that program does
not have. So the renderer qualifies it (`gir/render.py:212-217`):

```
#   OBLIGATION ON THE SCAFFOLD (stated for the FOLDED path; this program is kept, so read it as
#     background, not as this program's obligation): the folded drain chain must be enterable at
#     step M-T, not only at step 0 — the short arm's `T > t` guards have no counterpart on a
#     single-entry chain (G3/#148; TensileLite's NoGlobalLoadLoop_k selection supplies this today)
```

and then states the kept arm's *real* obligation directly (`:218-220`), because it is in no tuple and
so cannot be printed from the record:

```
#   OBLIGATION ON THE SCAFFOLD (this program): route the kept arm's guard chain — G5/#150
#     (fold_short_path.py:33)
```

That is a hardcoded sentence with a source pointer, which is a compromise, and the source says so:
fixing the analysis to emit per-verdict obligations is its own task, and until it is done the dump
must not present a folded-path obligation as if it applied. **If you do that work, delete
`gir/render.py:212-220` and let the loop print the tuple unqualified.** That is the intended end
state; the qualification exists only because the analysis currently cannot express it.

**The false-edge line, and reading the CFG instead of asserting it** (`gir/render.py:222-230`). This
is the second claim that was once wrong. It used to read, unconditionally:

> The prologue block sits OUTSIDE the peel-validity guard; the guard's false edge targets the drain
> chain.

That holds on FOLD and on VACUOUS, where `fold_short_path` retargets the edge. It does **not** hold on
SPLIT: the pass returns early, the arm survives, and the edge still points at `short0`. So on exactly
the arm where a reader is most likely to be debugging, the sentence contradicted the block listing
four lines below it. The fix is the general principle worth taking away from this whole subsection:

> **A structural claim that the dump can simply LOOK UP must be looked up.**

The current code is three lines:

```python
entry = prog.blocks.get(prog.entry)
f_target = getattr(getattr(entry, "term", None), "f_target", None)
out.append("#   The prologue block sits OUTSIDE the peel-validity guard; the guard's false edge "
           "targets %s." % (f_target if f_target else "(no CondGoto on the entry block)"))
```

Two residual sharp edges in those three lines, both worth knowing:

1. **It still misses the shipping default.** The `getattr(..., "f_target", None)` chain means any
   terminator without an `f_target` attribute prints the fallback text. That is correct for
   `Goto`/`LoopBack`/`Return`, but it is also what a `CondChain` gets — and `EarlyExitPass` (§11.5)
   turns the two-way peel guard into a `CondChain` whenever the drain chain has more than one step,
   in which case the equivalent target is `term.default`, not `f_target`. Measured on the shipping
   bf16 default (`PrefetchGlobalRead=2, PrefetchLocalRead=1`, `M=2`, verdict FOLD): the entry
   terminator is
   `CondChain('T == 1' [toPGR1] -> drain1, 'T > 2' -> steady, else drain0)` and the line prints

   ```
   #   The prologue block sits OUTSIDE the peel-validity guard; the guard's false edge targets
   #     (no CondGoto on the entry block).
   ```

   even though the guard is right there and its equivalent false edge is `drain0`. The FOLD example
   below reads correctly only because that kernel has `M = 1`, which leaves a plain `CondGoto`. The
   fold's own test already knows the disjunction and reads
   `term.default if isinstance(term, CondChain) else term.f_target` (`test_gir.py:2189`).
   **Copying those two lines into the renderer is the single most concrete outstanding defect in this
   file** — it is a one-line fix that restores the line on the majority configuration.
2. The first half of the sentence — "the prologue block sits OUTSIDE the peel-validity guard" — is
   still an assertion, not a lookup. It is true of every program the current lowering builds (the
   prologue is the entry block, so it necessarily precedes its own terminator), so it is safe today;
   but it is the same *shape* of claim as the one that was wrong, and if the entry block ever stops
   being the prologue it becomes false silently.

**The two real dumps.** Same bf16 kernel, two prefetch depths. FOLD (`M=1`, ring depth 2 ≥ 1):

```
# short-loop (T <= M) arm: 1 chunk steps, guards [unguarded]
#   FOLDED into the drain chain (#183): every def-use pairing survives the reordering
#     (24 corresponded instructions, 11 extra on the folded path)
#   OBLIGATION ON THE SCAFFOLD: the folded drain chain must be enterable at step M-T, …
#   The prologue block sits OUTSIDE the peel-validity guard; the guard's false edge targets drain0.
```

KEPT (`PrefetchGlobalRead=3, PrefetchLocalRead=0` ⇒ `M=3` over a 2-deep ring):

```
# short-loop (T <= M) arm: 3 chunk steps, guards [unguarded, T > 1, T > 2]
#   KEPT as its own `short{i}` blocks (#183 SPLIT): 16 def-use pairing(s) change and 0
#     instruction(s) are absent under the folded order ([('overwritten', 16)]) — emit the short
#     arm as its own path
#   OBLIGATION ON THE SCAFFOLD (stated for the FOLDED path; this program is kept, …): …
#   OBLIGATION ON THE SCAFFOLD (this program): route the kept arm's guard chain — G5/#150 …
#   The prologue block sits OUTSIDE the peel-validity guard; the guard's false edge targets short0.
```

Everything that distinguishes the two arms is visible in five lines, and the last line agrees with
the block listing rather than contradicting it. That is the whole point of the rewrite.

#### 14.6 The block header

Built inline in `render_gir` (`gir/render.py:310-332`) — there is no helper, which is the one place
this file departs from its "one function per line kind" shape and is a reasonable candidate for
extraction if the header grows again.

```
Block steady  loop=True  gen_rel=0  chunk_base=0  path_chunk_base={}  preds=('prologue', 'steady')
                                                                      succs=('steady', 'drain0'):
```
(one physical line). Fields, in emission order:

- **`Block <phase>`** (`:310`) — `Block.phase`, which is also `Block.label` (`gir/nodes.py:430-432`
  makes `label` a property returning `phase`; the two are the same string and the renderer uses
  `phase`). This is the key the emitter requests blocks by, so it is the name to grep for in
  `KernelWriter`.
- **`loop=True`** (`:311-312`) — printed only when `Block.loop` is set, i.e. this block is a loop
  header. Exactly one block carries it on the shipping shapes.
- **`gen_rel=<int>`** (`:322-325`) — the *frame* the block's generation deltas are expressed in.
  `None` (and therefore absent) means the block's generations are **absolute**; an integer means they
  sit on an arbitrary base and only differences are meaningful. `steady` prints `gen_rel=0`;
  `drain0` in the `M=3` example prints `gen_rel=-3`, `drain1` `-2`, `drain2` `-1`. **This is the field
  that makes `gen@N` tags comparable or not across blocks**: two blocks' concrete generation numbers
  come from different origins unless their `gen_rel` agrees. The value is genuinely trip-parity
  dependent at a join — the drain head's predecessors disagree — which is why it is declared rather
  than fabricated.
- **`chunk_base=<int>`** (`:322-325`) — the block's position on the *global reduction-chunk timeline*.
  The prologue handles chunk 0; with `M=3` the steady loop starts at chunk 0 and `drain0/1/2` sit at
  chunks 1/2/3.
- **`path_chunk_base=<dict>`** (`:322-325`) — the per-incoming-edge override, `{pred_label: base}`.
  A block reached by two paths can sit at two different positions on that timeline and one integer
  cannot say so: on the folded shape, `drain0` runs one chunk past the last steady trip when reached
  from `steady` (`chunk_base=1`) but handles chunk 0 when reached from the folded `prologue` edge —
  hence `path_chunk_base={'prologue': 0}` in the mxf8 dump below. Empty (`{}`) means `chunk_base`
  holds on every path.

  **Sharp edge:** the guard at `:324` is `if _v is not None`, and an empty dict is not `None`, so
  `path_chunk_base={}` prints on **every** block that has no override — which is most of them. It is
  pure noise. Changing the guard to `if _v` would suppress it, at the cost of also suppressing
  `chunk_base=0` and `gen_rel=0`, both of which are meaningful zeros. The right fix is a per-field
  predicate, not a shared one.
- **`MODEL-ONLY (no backend emits this block; its ops are still counted below)`** (`:326-327`) —
  printed when `Block.model_only` is set. **This is the most important flag in the header.** A
  model-only block is one GIR reasons over and that *no backend emits*: the kept short arm is the
  standing case, because that runtime branch is owned by the surrounding TensileLite scaffold and the
  arm exists here only so the analyses can see it. Rendered identically to an emitted block — as it
  was until the flag was added — it makes the dump's op counts disagree with the `.s` file for a
  reason the dump never states. The parenthetical is the operative half: `gir_counts` **does** count
  these ops (§14.14), so if you are reconciling the dump against an assembly listing you must subtract
  them yourself. The verifier's `G-EMIT` check (`gir/verify.py:303-319`) independently requires that
  any `model_only` block be accompanied by a recorded reason in `meta['short_loop']['model_only']`,
  so an unexplained one is a hard error rather than a quiet dump artefact.
- **`preds=(…)` / `succs=(…)`** (`:328-331`) — printed only when non-empty, as Python tuples of
  labels. Because block order on the page is insertion order and not control flow (§14.2), these two
  fields *are* the graph. Note they are the block's **declared** edge sets, which `G-TERM`
  cross-checks against the terminator's actual targets; if they ever disagree, the verifier fires
  before you get to read the dump.

#### 14.7 `phi` and `xfer` lines — the SSA of the rotating buffers

```
  phi:  gen0 = φ(entry:0, back) ring=2
  ...
  xfer: gen0' = (v + 1) % 2
```

Both are inline one-liners (`gir/render.py:333-334` and `:342-343`) over `Block.phis` and
`Block.xfers`.

GIR has exactly one SSA value class, `Gen` (`gir/nodes.py:57`): *which buffer of a rotating ring an
access touches*. A `Gen` is **defined** by a `GenPhi` at a loop header and **advanced** across the
back edge by a `GenXfer`. The two lines are those nodes verbatim:

- `phi: gen<id> = φ(entry:<v>, back) ring=<S>` — `GenPhi.gen.id` is the generation's SSA identity,
  `entry_val` is the concrete generation on the loop-entry edge (an int, almost always 0), and
  `ring` is the ring depth `S` from `Gen.ring`. The literal string `back` is a placeholder: the
  back-edge incoming value is *not* stored on the phi — it is implied by the matching `GenXfer` — so
  there is nothing to print there. That is a real modelling choice (the transfer is a function of the
  generation, so storing it twice would let the two disagree), but the rendering makes it look like
  an omission. Printing the matching xfer's expression there instead of the bare word `back` would
  make each phi self-contained.
- `xfer: gen<id>' = (v + <adv>) % <ring>` — `GenXfer.adv` is how many generations one trip advances
  (1 on every shipping shape; a multi-block steady body could advance by more), and `ring` is the
  modulus. Keyed per `Gen`, so a kernel with four independently-rotating buffer sets prints four
  xfers, as the mxf8 dump does.

Four phis and four xfers in the mxf8 example (`gen0`…`gen3`) correspond to A-shared, B-shared,
MXSA-shared and MXSB-shared. Which id is which is **not** printed — you recover it from the `gen#N`
tags on the body's reads, e.g. `A.shared[gen#0[v]]` fixes `gen0` as A's. Stamping the operand onto
the phi line would remove that indirection and is a cheap improvement.

#### 14.8 Rendering one `Ref` — `_ref_str`, `_coord_str`, `_gen_str`, `_covers_str`

A `Ref` is a *use* of a `Tile` inside an instruction (`gir/nodes.py:70`), and it is the widest node in
the IR: ten fields in four independent groups (what fragment; shared residence loop-carried; shared
residence absolute; register residence; movement footprint; sizes). Rendering it is where the dump
either earns its keep or hides the thing you are hunting.

**`_ref_str(ref) -> str`** (`gir/render.py:67-79`) is the composer. Grammar:

```
<operand>.<space>{<coord>}[<tag>]<spans <covers>>
     │       │       │       │            └── _covers_str, omitted when empty
     │       │       │       └── _gen_str,   omitted when empty
     │       │       └── _coord_str,        omitted when empty
     │       └── Tile.space: 'global' | 'shared' | 'register'
     └── Tile.operand: 'A' | 'B' | 'acc' | 'MXSA' | …  (an OPEN set — never a literal in the code)
```

Real examples, all from one dump:

```
A.global{M_split0}
A.shared{K_inner0,M_inner0}[gen@0]
A.shared{K_inner1,M_inner0}[gen#0[v]]
A.register{K_inner0,M_inner0}[reg(g0,s0/W2)]
MXSA.shared{K_inner0,M_inner0}[gen#2[v]]<spans M_splitx2>
MXSA.shared{K_inner0,M_inner0}[gen#2[v+-1]]
```

**`_coord_str(coord) -> str`** (`gir/render.py:21-22`) — the one genuinely trivial helper. Input is
`Tile.coord`, a tuple of `(mode, value|None)` pairs; output is `mode` immediately concatenated with
`value`, comma-joined, **skipping any pair whose value is `None`**:

```python
",".join(f"{ax}{v}" for ax, v in coord if v is not None)
```

So `(('K_inner',0), ('M_inner',1))` renders `K_inner0,M_inner1`. Two consequences. First, an axis
present in the coordinate but *unpinned* (value `None`) is **invisible** — indistinguishable from an
axis that is not in the coordinate at all. That distinction matters (an unpinned axis means "any
value", an absent one means "this operand is broadcast over it"), and today only the θ-facts block
lets you tell them apart. Second, `M_split0` reads as one token; the axis name and the index are not
separated, so an axis name ending in a digit would be ambiguous. No shipping mode name does, but
nothing enforces it.

A coordinate never contains the reduction-loop induction variable `'iter'` — that is the `G-NOITER`
invariant (`gir/verify.py:135`), and the cross-trip relation lives in the `Gen` phi instead. If you
ever see `iter0` in a coordinate, the verifier has been bypassed.

**`_gen_str(ref) -> str`** (`gir/render.py:25-52`) — the buffer tag, and the most-revised function in
the file. It answers "which storage does this reference land in", and there are **three independent
answers, all of which can be simultaneously present**:

| rendering | source field(s) | question answered |
|---|---|---|
| `gen#<id>[v]` / `gen#<id>[v+<δ>]` | `Ref.gen` (a `Gen`), `Ref.gdelta` | *which phi feeds this*, offset by a read-ahead delta |
| `gen@<n>` | `Ref.abs_gen` (an int) | *which concrete buffer this reference lands on* |
| `reg(g<group>,s<slot>/W<ring>)` | `Ref.group`, `Ref.slot`, `Ref.reg_ring` | *which register partition, rotation slot and rotation width* |

```
_gen_str(ref):
    parts = []
    if ref.gen      is not None: parts += f"gen#{ref.gen.id}[v{'+%d'%gdelta if gdelta else ''}]"
    if ref.abs_gen  is not None: parts += f"gen@{ref.abs_gen}"
    if ref.group    is not None: parts += f"reg(g{group},s{slot}" + (f"/W{ring})" if ring else ")")
    return " ".join(parts)
```

Three deliberate decisions are encoded there, and each one is a fixed defect:

1. **The two generation forms are spelled apart.** They used to render as `gen0[v]` and `gen=0` —
   one character between an SSA *identity* and a concrete *integer*, in the same dump. They answer
   different questions and a reader scanning for one silently accepts the other. Now the sigils
   differ: `#` for identity, `@` for value. The split is also the peel/steady distinction made
   visible: a prologue fill or a short-arm access knows exactly which buffer it touches (its chunk
   index is a compile-time constant) and carries `abs_gen`; a steady or drain access does not (its
   buffer depends on trip parity) and carries a `Gen` plus a delta.
2. **The slot is not an alternative to them.** A `Ref` can carry a generation *and* a register
   residence — a shared→register read has both, a shared source generation and a register
   destination. The code was once an `if/elif/elif` with early returns, which showed only the first,
   so **a shared read's destination register was invisible whenever its source generation was
   pinned**. All present parts are now emitted, space-joined.
3. **`W` is printed beside the slot.** `reg_ring` is the register rotation modulus. A slot without
   its modulus does not say how deep the ring is: `s1` of a 2-deep and of a 4-deep ring are
   indistinguishable, and `W` is exactly the schedule fact GIR consumes (it is read off the upstream
   slot expression's modulus, never decided here) and that `RegBandAnalysis` (§6.5) validates. The
   `if ring else` at `:51` means `W` is omitted when `reg_ring` is `None`/0, so `reg(g0,s0)` means
   "the width was not supplied", not "width 1".

**Two cosmetic defects in `_gen_str`, both live.**

- The delta is formatted as `f"+{ref.gdelta}"`, unconditionally prefixing `+`. A **negative** delta —
  which every drain read has, since drain blocks reach *back* into earlier generations — therefore
  renders `gen#0[v+-1]`. That string appears throughout every drain block of every dump in this
  report. It is unambiguous and it is ugly; `f"{ref.gdelta:+d}"` gives `v-1` and is a one-token fix.
- `ref.gen` and `ref.abs_gen` are read through `getattr(..., None)` while `ref.group` is read
  directly (`:43`, `:46`, `:48`). All three are declared dataclass fields with defaults, so the
  `getattr` guards are dead defensiveness left over from a period when `Ref` was less settled. Not
  harmful; inconsistent, and they would mask a genuine typo in a field rename.

**A cross-line spelling inconsistency worth knowing when you grep.** `_gen_str` prints `gen#0`, but
the phi line prints `gen0` (`gir/render.py:334`) and the xfer line prints `gen0'`
(`gir/render.py:343`). The `#` was introduced in `_gen_str` only. So **`grep 'gen#0'` finds every
*use* of generation 0 and misses its defining phi and its transfer, while `grep 'gen0'` finds the phi
and the xfer and misses every use** — no single literal finds all three; you need `grep -E 'gen#?0'`.
Adding the `#` to the two inline format strings would make the three consistent; nothing reads them,
so it is safe.

**`_covers_str(ref) -> str`** (`gir/render.py:55-64`) — the `<spans …>` suffix.

Concept, from first principles. When one hardware instruction moves several logical tiles at once — a
wide `ds_load` that fills two tiles' worth of registers in one issue — the axis it runs along is
**removed from the read hop's coordinate set upstream**, so that the paired coordinates form a single
presence point (one step, one generation, one completion). That subtraction is what makes the merge
expressible at all: `ord` orders modes, and no reordering can get *inside* a single presence point,
so the pair is inseparable by construction.

The cost of the subtraction is that the definition names one location while every consumer names all
of them. `Ref.covers` is the second half: `((axis, extent), ...)` recording exactly which axes were
removed and how wide the span is, so `refs.covered_coords` (§5) can re-insert the individual
locations for the analyses that track locations. The alternative — emitting one `Ref` per covered
coordinate — was tried and rejected, because it files *N* residencies against a single completion
event, so one wait looks like it discharges only one of them.

Rendering is one line:

```python
"+".join(f"{ax}x{ext}" for ax, ext in (ref.covers or ()))
```

giving `M_splitx2` for a load spanning both values of `M_split`, and `M_splitx2+K_innerx2` for a
two-axis span. `_ref_str:76-78` wraps it as `<spans M_splitx2>` and omits the whole suffix when
`covers` is empty (the ordinary one-location reference, and the overwhelming majority).

**Why it is printed at all.** A dump showing only `coord` shows a read that appears **not to write
what the wmma reads**. That is the exact appearance that sent one investigation looking for a missing
read — "16 consumers read a location the arm never writes" — when the read was there and merely
wide. Printing the span is what makes the subtraction legible.

**When you will and will not see it.** `covers` is populated from the movement quantum
(`loopir_to_gir.py:421-425`), and the quantum is supplied *from outside* layer 1 — it is a
consequence of the LDS address layout and the emitter's folding behaviour, neither of which the
schedule object can see. A caller with no target facts gets an empty quantum and therefore the narrow,
one-tile-per-instruction form. **That includes every unit test** — but NOT the
`OutputLoopIR` dump, which builds no program at all: `Run.py:255` hands `gir_text` the writer's own
cached Program (`loopModelGirProgramCached()`), whose θ was built with `_loopModelTarget`'s
`ReadQuantum` map. So in practice `<spans …>` appears whenever the caller's target resolves a fold —
which the writer does, and therefore the dump does too. Concretely, feeding a two-tile scale load in by hand produces:

```
# §2.2 absorbed axes (removed from presence, re-inserted as `spans`):
#   MXSA:(('M_split', 2),); MXSB:(('N_split', 2),)
  read  MXSA.shared{K_inner0,M_inner0}[gen#2[v]] -> MXSA.register{K_inner0,M_inner0}[reg(g0,s0/W2)]
        <spans M_splitx2>  bufs=8 tok=('lds', 'MXSA', (0,))  deps[…]
```

and the same kernel without the map produces neither line. **That is a real gap in the shipping
debug artifact**: the configuration where the span matters most is the one the dump cannot show,
because the dump does not have the writer's resolved fold. Threading the writer's `ReadQuantum` into
`gir_text`'s program build — or, better, having the writer hand `gir_text` the *same* program it
emitted from, quantum included — would close it. It is listed again in §14.16.

#### 14.9 The instruction lines

**`_move_line(mv) -> str`** (`gir/render.py:124-128`). One `Move` — the only data-movement verb in
GIR, one hop down the memory hierarchy.

```python
kind = "copy" if any(d.tile.space == "shared" for d in mv.dsts) else "read"
srcs = "+".join(_ref_str(r) for r in mv.srcs)
dsts = "+".join(_ref_str(r) for r in mv.dsts)
return f"{kind:5s} {srcs} -> {dsts}{_token_str(mv)}{_dep_str(mv)}"
```

- **The `copy`/`read` label is derived from the destination space alone.** A `Move` with a shared
  destination is a `copy` (global → LDS); anything else is a `read`. That is right for the two hops
  that dominate, but it is a lie for a direct-to-register global load (a one-hop operand,
  `global → register`, no LDS at all): it prints as `read`, identically to an LDS read, and the only
  way to tell them apart is to notice `A.global` rather than `A.shared` on the source side. The
  information is on the line; the five-character label is not. `f"{'copy' if shared_dst else ('gread'
  if global_src else 'read'):5s}"` would fix it. (`gir_counts` classifies the same way and inherits
  the same conflation — §14.14.)
- **`+` joins the members of a fused movement.** `A.global{M_split0}+B.global{N_split0} ->
  A.shared{M_split0}[gen@0]+B.shared{N_split0}[gen@0]` is **one** cooperative instruction serving both
  operands, with one completion. The `+` is the same separator `_covers_str` uses for span axes and
  that the θ-facts block uses for fuse-group members, which is consistent but does mean `+` carries
  three meanings in one dump.
- The width `{kind:5s}` is what aligns `copy `/`read ` with `mma  ` so the four-character
  instruction column lines up.

**`_mma_line(mm) -> str`** (`gir/render.py:131-134`). One `Mma` — the compute verb.

```python
srcs = ",".join(_ref_str(r) for r in mm.srcs)
dst  = _ref_str(mm.dsts[0]) if mm.dsts else "acc"
return f"mma   {dst} += {srcs}   # {mm.block}{_dep_str(mm)}"
```

`Mma` has an **open operand set**: operand identity is read off `Ref.tile.operand`, there is no
`a`/`b`/`role` vocabulary, and `srcs` is `(A,B)` on a plain kernel, `(A,B,MXSA,MXSB)` on a
microscaling one, `(A,B,meta)` on a sparse one. The line therefore reads every source rather than
templating two. (It once hardcoded `C[...] += A*B` and read none of them; on the four-source MX
kernel that printed the same text for every instruction.) `mm.block` after the `#` is the hardware
WMMA block-group tag — `A(k)*B(k)` on the shipping decoder — and is a free-form string, not a
structured field. The `if mm.dsts else "acc"` fallback covers a hand-built node with no accumulator;
the lowering always supplies one.

Note that a source `Ref` names **the operand's own coordinate**, not the wmma's grid position:
`mma acc.register{K_inner0,M_inner0,N_inner0} += A.register{K_inner0,M_inner0}, B.register{K_inner0,
N_inner0}, …`. A broadcast operand's Ref used to carry the full `(K,M,N)` coordinate, so `A`'s use
named a location no read ever wrote; projecting each source onto the operand's own presence at
construction fixed it, and the visible payoff is in this line — the `N` wmma of one `m` row now print
one and the same `A` Ref, which makes the broadcast a legible identity rather than four look-alike
uses.

#### 14.10 `_token_str` — the buffer set and the completion class, spelled apart

**`_token_str(mv) -> str`** (`gir/render.py:101-121`). Input: a `Move`. Output: `""` or a
two-space-prefixed string like `  bufs=0,2 tok=('lds', ('A', 'B'), (0,))`.

Two different questions, both answered on this line, and keeping them apart is the whole point.

**`bufs=` — `Move.token_ids`, the dense LDS *storage* ids.** A memory token is an LDS pseudo-register:
`MemTokenAssignment` (§8.1) numbers the distinct LDS buffers a program touches, and stamps every
`Move`'s shared reference with the set of ids it may reach. **A token id IS the alias relation the
backend orders on** — the downstream scheduler takes the id as a def on the producer and a use on the
consumer, so two movements sharing an id must be ordered and two with disjoint ids need not be. It is
a **tuple**, not a scalar, because an access that does not pin its region axis may touch several
buffers and must name every one of them, or the halves it does not name go un-ordered. That is why a
drain read in the example below carries `bufs=0,1,2,3` (it may be reached in either trip parity, over
both regions) while a steady read of a pinned generation carries `bufs=0,2`.

**`tok=` — `Move.token`, the semantic *completion class*.** Stamped by `TokensPass` (§11.8): the
`('lds', unit, region)` triple naming *what completed* — which logical buffer this copy filled or this
read drained. The `unit` is the movement's member tuple (`('A','B')` for a fused pair, `'MXSA'` for a
lone op-class), and `region` is the region tuple when per-region completion is on.

```python
ids, tok = mv.token_ids, mv.token
bits = []
if ids: bits.append("bufs=" + ",".join(str(i) for i in ids))
if tok is not None: bits.append(f"tok={tok}")
return ("  " + " ".join(bits)) if bits else ""
```

**Why both, and why it was once neither.** With the ids unprinted, a token-assignment bug and a
placement bug produce the *same dump* — which is how one investigation into the exact footprint a
token should name stayed open as long as it did. And the first version that printed them used an
`elif` under a single `tok=` prefix. Two consequences: the semantic token became **unreachable** on
any pipeline-built program (measured: zero `Move`s lack `token_ids` after `TokensPass`, so the
`elif` never fired), and had it ever fired, the reader could not have told which of the two
quantities was on screen. `if`/`if` with distinct prefixes fixes both. The regression fixture asserts
that **both** substrings occur (`test_gir.py:4720-4723`), with the reason spelled out in the assertion
message.

Reading them together is what makes a fused copy legible:

```
copy  A.global{M_split0}+B.global{N_split0} -> A.shared{M_split0}[gen@0]+B.shared{N_split0}[gen@0]
      bufs=0,4 tok=('lds', ('A', 'B'), (0,))
```

One instruction; **two** storage buffers (A's region-0 buffer id 0, B's id 4); **one** completion
(`('A','B')`). If those two facts ever collapse into one number, a Φ-fused copy becomes
indistinguishable from two independent ones, which is exactly the confusion that duplicated waits.

#### 14.11 `_dep_str` — the ledger obligations, with their hazard kind

**`_dep_str(inst) -> str`** (`gir/render.py:82-98`). Input: a `Move` *or* an `Mma` (both carry
`deps`). Output: `""` or `  deps[kind:name@counter, …]`.

`Move.deps` / `Mma.deps` are the dependence edges inherited from layer 1's ledger, as
`(dep, counter, kind)` triples. `dep` is the dependence's name (e.g. `A+B:shared:copy`), `counter` is
the hardware completion counter class it is discharged against (e.g. `C_copy`, `C_read`), and `kind`
is its hazard class.

```python
from ...LoopModel.ir import OBLIGATION_KINDS
parts = []
for dep, counter, kind in inst.deps:
    mark = "" if kind in OBLIGATION_KINDS else " !UNKNOWN-KIND"
    parts.append(f"{kind}:{dep}@{counter}{mark}")
return "  deps[" + ", ".join(parts) + "]"
```

**Why the kind is on the line.** `kind` is the one field that decides *issue order*: a
write-after-read obligation means the writer must be placed **after** its prior readers, a
read-after-write means the reader must be placed after its writer. Until it was printed, the dump
showed neither the edge nor its class, so **a schedule that ordered a copy wrongly looked identical to
one that ordered it correctly.**

**The kinds are a closed set**, defined at `LoopModel/ir.py:500-502`:

| kind | class | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `RAW-residency` | RAW | a consumer needs the value to have arrived in the residence it reads from |
| `crossing-RAW` | RAW | a read in a later chunk depends on a copy issued in an earlier one |
| `rotation-WAR` | WAR | a copy about to overwrite a ring buffer must wait for the *previous* trip's readers |
| `inplace-WAR` | WAR | the same, on a depth-1 (in-place) ring where there is no other buffer to move to |

`OBLIGATION_KINDS` is the union `RAW_KINDS | WAR_KINDS`, and `is_war(kind)` (`LoopModel/ir.py:505`)
is **total** over it — it raises on anything else rather than defaulting, precisely so a new kind
cannot be silently classified as a true dependency. The renderer mirrors that discipline: an
unrecognised kind gets ` !UNKNOWN-KIND` appended **loudly** rather than being abbreviated away. That
suffix should never appear in a dump; if it does, someone added a kind in layer 1 without registering
it, and both this line and `is_war` are about to disagree with reality.

**Cost note.** The import of `OBLIGATION_KINDS` sits *inside* the function (`gir/render.py:93`), so it
runs once per instruction with `deps`. Python caches module imports, so the cost is a `sys.modules`
dict lookup per call — negligible against the string building around it, but it is **not** the only
place in `gir/` that imports from `LoopModel`: `gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py:19` does the same import
at MODULE scope (§15.2.2), and `gir/__init__.py` reaches it through `.analyses`, so importing the
`gir` package already loads `LoopModel.ir`. Deferring this one is therefore local hygiene, not what
keeps the package importable standalone; hoisting it would add no import-time dependency that
`dep_defuse.py:19` has not already created.

The regression fixture asserts both that `deps[` appears and that a real kind name is in the text
(`test_gir.py:4716-4719`), with the message stating why: without the class, a correctly and an
incorrectly ordered body render identically.

#### 14.12 `Mark` lines

Rendered inline, not by a helper (`gir/render.py:336-337`):

```python
if isinstance(inst, Mark):
    L.append(f"  Mark  {inst.kind} {inst.at}")
```

`Mark.kind` is one of a **closed set of six** (`gir/nodes.py:157-158`), and `Mark.at` is a
kind-specific payload dict printed as its Python `repr`. There is no per-kind formatting: what you see
is the dict, keys in insertion order. That is crude and it is also the right choice — the payload
schemas are enforced by the verifier's `G-MARK` check against a table (`gir/verify.py:75-95`), so
adding a key to a payload automatically shows up in the dump with no renderer change. A hand-written
per-kind formatter would be a second schema to keep in sync.

The five kinds you will actually see, with a real line for each:

```
Mark  phase_boundary {'phase': 'prologue'}
Mark  fence {'buffers': ('A','B','MXSA','MXSB'), 'tokens': (0,2,4,6,8,10), 'scope': 'block',
             'kinds': ('WAR',), 'edges': 12}
Mark  swap {'hop': 'copy', 'gen_from': 0, 'gen_to': 1, 'unit': ('A','B'), 'steps': 1}
Mark  swap {'hop': 'read', 'gen_from': 0, 'gen_to': 1, 'operand': 'B', 'steps': 1}
Mark  gr_increment {'unit': ('A','B'), 'chunks': 1, 'to_chunk': 2}
Mark  region_increment {'unit': ('A','B'), 'steps': 1, 'from_region': 0, 'to_region': 1,
                        'axis_steps': {'M_split': 1}}
```

- **`phase_boundary`** — inserted by the lowering at each block head; its `phase` is the block's own
  name, so it is redundant with the header. It exists because the emitter keys off it.
- **`fence`** — a proc-scoped ordering point. `buffers` names the operands covered, `tokens` the
  storage ids it fences, `kinds` which hazard classes it discharges, `edges` how many hazard edges
  this one fence covers (12 and 78 in the examples — the fence placement is a *set cover*, not one
  fence per obligation, and `edges` is the payoff figure). Note there is **no `barrier` Mark kind**:
  GIR carries the ordering obligation and the back end decides whether it becomes an `s_barrier`, a
  wait count, or nothing.
- **`swap`** — a buffer-pointer flip. `hop` is `'copy'` or `'read'`, and **the identifying key differs
  by hop**: a read swap names an op-class under `operand`, a copy swap names the whole fused movement
  under `unit`. That asymmetry is the model (a fused copy has one pointer, shared by the group; a read
  has one per op-class), and it is why the verifier special-cases this row. When you are counting
  swaps in a dump, `grep "Mark  swap"` and then split on `'hop'` — a unit test does exactly that to
  assert that a depth-1 ring contributes no swap while a depth-2 one does
  (`test_loopmodel.py:1697-1707`).
- **`gr_increment`** — the global-read address advance. `unit` is the movement, `chunks` how many
  reduction chunks it steps, `to_chunk` the chunk it lands on.
- **`region_increment`** — the load descriptor stepping between storage regions. Note the paired
  `steps: 1` / `steps: -1` Marks around the two-region copies in the mxf8 dump: the descriptor walks
  forward across the regions and then **rewinds**, because the next chunk starts at region 0 again.

The sixth kind, `gsu_guard`, is reserved and not produced today; you will not see it.

#### 14.13 `_pred_str` and `_term_line` — the terminator

**`_pred_str(p) -> str`** (`gir/render.py:137-149`). One line of code:

```python
return f"{p.render()!r}" + (f" [{p.label}]" if p.label else "")
```

`Pred` is a **structured** predicate — `lhs op rhs` where `rhs` is a `Bound` (`var + const`, or a bare
constant) — and `Pred.render()` (`gir/nodes.py:224`) formats it as `'T > 2'`, `'T == 1'`,
`'c <= 1'`. The `!r` wraps it in quotes so a predicate is visually a unit inside a longer terminator
line. `Pred.label` is the **scaffold hint**, attached downstream by `ScaffoldMapPass` (§11.6), and it
is the whole reason a consumer can route an arm to the right region of the surrounding TensileLite
scaffold — a dump that omitted it would make every terminator look label-free and unroutable, which
is indistinguishable from the pass not having run.

**Read the label as a route, not as an identification.** This is the third claim the file once got
wrong. The docstring used to gloss `toPGR1` as "the peel-validity entry guard", which reads as though
a `toPGR1` label *identifies* that one guard. It does not. `ScaffoldMapPass` stamps `toPGR1` on
**every** bare non-back-edge `CondGoto` (`gir/passes/scaffold_map.py:106-119`: any `CondGoto` whose
block is not a back-edge source gets the `peel_validity` role, and that role's label is `toPGR1`), and
on a `CondChain` it stamps `toPGR1` on the arm targeting the deepest drain step
(`scaffold_map.py:40-45`, `:79-86`). The measurable consequence, in the `M=3` KEPT dump:

```
term: CondGoto('T > 3' [toPGR1] -> steady, else short0)      # the peel-validity guard
term: CondGoto('T > 1' [toPGR1] -> short1, else end)         # short arm, step 1 validity
term: CondGoto('T > 2' [toPGR1] -> short2, else end)         # short arm, step 2 validity
```

Three distinct predicates, one repeated label. **The label says where the arm goes, not which arm it
is; the predicate beside it is what distinguishes them.** The other labels you will see are
`LoopEndL` on the steady `LoopBack`, `NoGlobalLoadLoop_k` on a drain-targeting `CondChain` arm, and
`TailLoopBegin` on a tail region's back edge.

**`_term_line(term) -> str`** (`gir/render.py:152-167`) — a five-way `isinstance` dispatch with a
fall-through. GIR **describes** control flow rather than implementing it, and the five node types
reflect that:

| terminator | rendering | note |
|---|---|---|
| `Goto` | `term: Goto(drain1)` | unconditional |
| `LoopBack` | `term: LoopBack(trips=T - 2 -> steady, exit drain0) [LoopEndL]` | states a **trip count**, not a comparison |
| `CondGoto` | `term: CondGoto('T > 3' [toPGR1] -> steady, else short0)` | two-way |
| `Return` | `term: Return` | a sink with no successors |
| `CondChain` | `term: CondChain('T == 1' [toPGR1] -> drain1, 'T > 2' -> steady, else drain0)` | **ordered** arms; first satisfied wins |
| anything else, incl. `None` | `term: <none>` | see below |

`LoopBack.trips` is a `Trips` node (`gir/nodes.py:247`) rendering as `(var - sub) // div`, printed via
`Trips.render()`. `div > 1` — a multi-block steady body consuming several chunks per trip — prints as
`(T - 2) // 2`. The reason a loop states a count and not a comparison is that a comparison needs three
facts to decode that live outside the node (where the counter starts, which way it steps, where the
test sits), and the backend's convention is the opposite of the natural one; holding the comparison
made every reader re-derive the count from assumptions, and two off-by-ones came from exactly that.

**The `term: <none>` fall-through (`:167`) is a trap.** It is reached both for a block whose `term` is
`None` — a genuine defect that `G-TERM` rejects — and for a terminator class the renderer does not
know about. The two are indistinguishable in the output. Since `verify_gir` will reject the first
case anyway, the honest rendering for the second is `term: <unknown {type(term).__name__}>`. One line.

#### 14.14 `gir_counts` — the machine-readable projection

**`gir_counts(prog) -> dict`** (`gir/render.py:348-370`). The only function in this module whose
output is consumed by code. Returns

```python
{ block_label: {'read': int, 'copy': int, 'mma': int, 'model_only': bool}, … }
```

keyed by `Block.phase`, one entry per block, including blocks with an empty body (they come out all
zeros).

```
gir_counts(prog):
    out = {}
    for blk in prog.blocks.values():
        c = {'read':0, 'copy':0, 'mma':0, 'model_only': bool(blk.model_only)}
        for inst in blk.body:
            if   isinstance(inst, Move): c['copy' if any(d.tile.space=='shared' for d in inst.dsts)
                                            else 'read'] += 1
            elif isinstance(inst, Mma):  c['mma'] += 1
        out[blk.phase] = c
    return out
```

`Mark`s are not counted — deliberately: the parity this feeds is about *data operations*, and the
Marks are the analyses' own output, not something layer 1 emitted. The copy/read classification is
character-for-character the same test `_move_line` uses (`:363` vs `:125`), so the dump's labels and
the counts can never disagree — and both inherit the same conflation of a direct-to-register global
load with an LDS read (§14.9).

**What it is for.** The **op-parity assertion**: GIR must hold exactly the read / copy / mma operations
that layer 1's unrolled view emits, per pipeline stage. `test_gir.py:159-184`
(`test_gir_op_parity_with_loopir`) walks the LoopIR tree itself with an independent unroller
(`test_gir.py:75`, `_loopir_stage_counts`) and compares stage by stage: prologue against prologue,
steady against steady, and the sum of every `drain*` block against the drain stage. It runs at two
prefetch depths. A second test (`test_gir.py:186-201`) pins the steady counts at
`{read: 8, copy: 2, mma: 8}` across all six loop orders, which is the statement that GIR is
loop-order-general — only the program *order* differs, never the op *set*.

**The `model_only` flag, and the counting decision it documents.** A model-only block's ops are
**counted**. That is the deliberate answer to a real tension:

- A consumer comparing against **layer 1** wants every op GIR holds, including the kept short arm's —
  they are ops the model carries, and omitting them would make the parity check fail for a reason
  that has nothing to do with a defect.
- A consumer comparing against the **emitted assembly** wants them subtracted, because no backend
  emits that block.

Folding them in *silently* made the totals disagree with the `.s` for a reason nothing in the output
stated. The resolution is that the count stays and **the flag rides along**, so the second consumer
can do the subtraction itself. Reporting the number without the flag is the part that was wrong.

Two tests enforce the flag's presence rather than its value, which is the right shape:
`test_gir.py:180-184` asserts that **every** block's counts carry a `model_only` key, with the
message "an op that reaches no `.s` file is indistinguishable here from one that does";
`test_gir.py:195-197` asserts `gc['steady']['model_only'] is False`, i.e. that the flag is not
vacuously true everywhere. `test_gir.py:163-166` shows the intended consumer pattern — project the
three op counts out with `_ops = lambda c: {k: c[k] for k in ('read','copy','mma')}` before comparing,
so the flag does not break dict equality.

**The remaining wart.** The flag is per block, and `gir_text` prints the whole dict, so the
`# counts = …` header of a real dump *does* let you see which blocks are model-only. But there is no
aggregate, and no "emitted total". A caller wanting "how many mma instructions will this kernel
actually issue" must filter and sum by hand. Adding a `gir_counts(prog, emitted_only=False)` keyword
— or simply a second helper that returns the two totals — is a five-line change and would remove the
one manual step this API still requires.

**Complexity.** `O(total instructions)`, one pass, no allocation beyond the result dict. On the
shipping shapes a `Program` has 3–8 blocks and 20–60 body nodes each, so this is microseconds and
runs unconditionally in `gir_text`. `render_gir` is the same order — one `str` per node, joined once
at the end — with the string building dominating. Neither is anywhere near a compile-time concern;
`render_gir` is called at most once per kernel and only when `OutputLoopIR` is on, and `gir_counts` is
called once per kernel on that same path plus once per parity test. There is no reason to optimise
either, and no cache would pay for itself.

#### 14.15 One real dump, end to end

The kernel: MX-scaled fp8, `KMN` loop order, both tile axes split into two storage regions, four
op-classes (`A`, `B`, and the two scale tensors `MXSA`/`MXSB`), peel depth 1, LDS ring depth 2. This
is the hardest shape the pipeline currently handles and it exercises almost every line kind.

**The preamble.**

```
Program(entry=prologue, M=1, S=A=[g0:2, shared:2] | B=[g0:2, shared:2] | MXSA=[g0:2, shared:2]
        | MXSB=[g0:2, shared:2], order=['K_inner','M_split','M_inner','N_split','N_inner'])
# Φ fuse groups: A+B, MXSA+MXSB   (one cooperative movement, one completion — §2.8 move 9)
#   A: 2 storage regions on M_split — region is the AGENT's on the read hop (address agent-chosen)
#      and the COORDINATE's on the copy hop — see render_geometry for the per-hop split
#   B: 2 storage regions on N_split — …same…
#   movement A+B: 2 regions (the walk is per MOVEMENT, not per operand — #236)
# agent-distributed operands: A, B, MXSA, MXSB   (their cross-agent obligations are block-scoped)
# mode extents: K_inner=2, M_inner=2, M_split=2, N_inner=2, N_split=2   reduction=K_inner
                mma inputs=A,B
# short-loop (T <= M) arm: 1 chunk steps, guards [unguarded]
#   FOLDED into the drain chain (#183): every def-use pairing survives the reordering
#     (24 corresponded instructions, 11 extra on the folded path)
#   OBLIGATION ON THE SCAFFOLD: the folded drain chain must be enterable at step M-T, …
#   The prologue block sits OUTSIDE the peel-validity guard; the guard's false edge targets drain0.
```

Everything you need to read the body is in those twelve lines:

- `M=1` ⇒ one drain block. `shared:2` ⇒ each operand's LDS ring is double-buffered, so you should
  see `Mark swap` for every one of them, and generation tags alternating between two values.
- `order=[K_inner, M_split, M_inner, N_split, N_inner]` ⇒ `K_inner` is outermost of the inner modes,
  `N_inner` innermost. Together with `reduction=K_inner` and `mode extents` (all 2), the whole
  coordinate space is 2×2×2×2×2.
- **Two fuse groups.** A copy line whose sources are `A.global{…}+B.global{…}` is one instruction; so
  is `MXSA.global+MXSB.global`. Expect two copy *events* per chunk-fill, not four — and in fact three
  copy lines, because the `A+B` movement has two regions and walks them.
- **A and B are region-split; the scales are not.** `A: 2 storage regions on M_split` and no line for
  `MXSA`/`MXSB`. So `A.shared{M_split0}` and `A.shared{M_split1}` are different memory, and
  `MXSA.shared{…}` has no region coordinate at all.
- **The regions are the agent's on the read hop.** A's *reads* below carry **no** `M_split` coordinate
  — the wave selects its own region — while A's *copies* do. If you see an `M_split` in a read
  coordinate on this kernel, that is the defect the retraction was written for.
- **`FOLDED`** ⇒ no `short{i}` blocks exist, the guard's false edge lands in `drain0`, and `drain0`
  has two predecessors.

**The prologue.**

```
Block prologue  chunk_base=0  path_chunk_base={}  succs=('steady','drain0'):
  Mark  fence {'buffers': ('A','B','MXSA','MXSB'), 'tokens': (0,2,4,6,8,10), 'scope':'block',
               'kinds': ('WAR',), 'edges': 12}
  Mark  phase_boundary {'phase': 'prologue'}
  copy  MXSA.global+MXSB.global -> MXSA.shared[gen@0]+MXSB.shared[gen@0]
        bufs=8,10 tok=('lds', ('MXSA','MXSB'), (0,))  deps[crossing-RAW:MXSA+MXSB:shared:copy@C_copy]
  Mark  gr_increment {'unit': ('MXSA','MXSB'), 'chunks': 1, 'to_chunk': 1}
  Mark  swap {'hop':'copy', 'gen_from':0, 'gen_to':1, 'unit': ('MXSA','MXSB'), 'steps':1}
  copy  A.global{M_split0}+B.global{N_split0} -> A.shared{M_split0}[gen@0]+B.shared{N_split0}[gen@0]
        bufs=0,4 tok=('lds', ('A','B'), (0,))  deps[crossing-RAW:A+B:shared:copy@C_copy]
  Mark  region_increment {'unit':('A','B'), 'steps':1, 'from_region':0, 'to_region':1,
                          'axis_steps': {'M_split': 1}}
  copy  A.global{M_split1}+B.global{N_split1} -> A.shared{M_split1}[gen@0]+B.shared{N_split1}[gen@0]
        bufs=2,6 tok=('lds', ('A','B'), (0,))  deps[crossing-RAW:A+B:shared:copy@C_copy]
  Mark  fence {… 'kinds': ('RAW',), 'edges': 12}
  Mark  region_increment {'unit':('A','B'), 'steps':-1, 'from_region':1, 'to_region':0,
                          'axis_steps': {'M_split': -1}}
  Mark  gr_increment {'unit':('A','B'), 'chunks':1, 'to_chunk':1}
  Mark  swap {'hop':'copy', 'gen_from':0, 'gen_to':1, 'unit':('A','B'), 'steps':1}
  read  A.shared{K_inner0,M_inner0}[gen@0] -> A.register{K_inner0,M_inner0}[reg(g0,s0/W2)]
        bufs=0,2 tok=('lds',('A','B'),(0,))  deps[RAW-residency:A+B@global:iter@C_copy]
  read  A.shared{K_inner0,M_inner1}[gen@0] -> A.register{K_inner0,M_inner1}[reg(g0,s0/W2)]  …
  read  B.shared{K_inner0,N_inner0}[gen@0] -> …
  read  B.shared{K_inner0,N_inner1}[gen@0] -> …
  read  MXSA.shared{K_inner0,M_inner0}[gen@0] -> …  bufs=8   tok=('lds',('MXSA','MXSB'),(0,))
  read  MXSA.shared{K_inner0,M_inner1}[gen@0] -> …
  read  MXSB.shared{K_inner0,N_inner0}[gen@0] -> …
  read  MXSB.shared{K_inner0,N_inner1}[gen@0] -> …
  term: CondGoto('T > 1' [toPGR1] -> steady, else drain0)
```

Read it as follows.

1. **No `gen_rel` on the header** ⇒ the prologue's generations are **absolute**, which is why every
   tag here is `gen@0` and not `gen#N[v]`. The prologue knows exactly which buffer it fills: chunk 0
   goes to generation 0.
2. **Three copies, two movements.** `MXSA+MXSB` moves once (the scales are unsplit); `A+B` moves twice,
   once per storage region, with a `region_increment` between them stepping the descriptor along
   `M_split`. The **rewind** `steps: -1` after the second copy is what returns the descriptor to region
   0 for the next chunk. If you are debugging a split kernel that reads garbage on its second chunk,
   a missing rewind is the first thing this dump would show.
3. **The `bufs=` ids are the map of LDS.** Twelve ids exist (0…11): 2 regions × 2 ring generations for
   each of A (0,1,2,3) and B (4,5,6,7), and 2 ring generations for each of MXSA (8,9) and MXSB
   (10,11). The prologue's copies write the even ones — generation 0 — and its reads read them back.
4. **A read names `bufs=0,2`, not `bufs=0`.** A's read carries no `M_split` coordinate (the region is
   the agent's), so the access may reach *either* region and must be ordered against both producers.
   That widening is `mem_tokens.py:152-160`, and this line is where you see it happen. Compare
   `MXSA`'s read: `bufs=8` alone, because MXSA is unsplit.
5. **Two fences, different kinds.** The first is `kinds: ('WAR',)` and sits *before* the copies: it
   separates this chunk's writes from whatever read the buffers previously (on a loop back-edge, the
   prior trip). The second is `kinds: ('RAW',)` and sits *after* the copies and before the reads: the
   reads must see the copies' data. `edges: 12` on each says one fence discharges twelve hazard edges
   — the placement is a set cover, not one fence per obligation.
6. **The terminator is `'T > 1'`, strictly greater than `M`.** Its false arm is `T <= 1`, and (verdict
   FOLDED) it targets `drain0`, matching the preamble's last line.

**The steady block** (abridged; 16 reads, 3 copies, 8 mma).

```
Block steady  loop=True  gen_rel=0  chunk_base=0  path_chunk_base={}  preds=('prologue','steady')
              succs=('steady','drain0'):
  phi:  gen0 = φ(entry:0, back) ring=2
  phi:  gen1 = φ(entry:0, back) ring=2
  phi:  gen2 = φ(entry:0, back) ring=2
  phi:  gen3 = φ(entry:0, back) ring=2
  Mark  fence {…'tokens': (0..11), 'kinds': ('RAW','WAR','WAW'), 'edges': 78}
  Mark  phase_boundary {'phase': 'steady'}
  copy  MXSA.global+MXSB.global -> MXSA.shared[gen#2[v+1]]+MXSB.shared[gen#3[v+1]]
        bufs=9,11 tok=('lds',('MXSA','MXSB'),(1,))
        deps[rotation-WAR:MXSA:shared:lastread@C_read, crossing-RAW:MXSA+MXSB:shared:copy@C_copy,
             rotation-WAR:MXSB:shared:lastread@C_read]
  …  gr_increment / swap(copy) / the two A+B region copies / fence(RAW) / rewind / swap(copy) …
  read  A.shared{K_inner1,M_inner0}[gen#0[v]] -> A.register{K_inner1,M_inner0}[reg(g0,s1/W2)]
        bufs=0,2 tok=('lds',('A','B'),(0,))
        deps[rotation-WAR:A:g0:lastread@C_read, RAW-residency:A+B@global:iter@C_copy]
  …
  mma   acc.register{K_inner0,M_inner0,N_inner0} += A.register{K_inner0,M_inner0}[reg(g0,s0/W2)],
        B.register{K_inner0,N_inner0}[reg(g0,s0/W2)], MXSA.register{…}, MXSB.register{…}
        # A(k)*B(k)  deps[RAW-residency:A@shared@C_read, …×4]
  …
  Mark  swap {'hop':'read','gen_from':0,'gen_to':1,'operand':'B','steps':1}
  Mark  swap {'hop':'read','gen_from':0,'gen_to':1,'operand':'A','steps':1}
  …
  read  A.shared{K_inner0,M_inner0}[gen#0[v+1]] -> A.register{K_inner0,M_inner0}[reg(g0,s0/W2)]
        bufs=1,3 tok=('lds',('A','B'),(1,))
  …
  xfer: gen0' = (v + 1) % 2      (and gen1'…gen3')
  term: LoopBack(trips=T - 1 -> steady, exit drain0) [LoopEndL]
```

The three facts that make this block legible, none of which are in the instruction text alone:

1. **`gen_rel=0`** ⇒ the deltas are relative to *this trip's* frame. `[gen#0[v]]` is the buffer the
   loop entered with; `[gen#0[v+1]]` is the *other* one. So the software pipeline is visible directly:
   the copies write `v+1` while the reads of the first half of the body read `v`, and then — after the
   four `Mark swap {'hop':'read'}` — the reads switch to `v+1` as well, because those are the
   read-ahead loads for the *next* trip.
2. **The four `phi` lines are the four rings**, and the four `xfer` lines advance each by 1 mod 2. A
   ring of depth 2 advancing by 1 each trip is plain double buffering; the dump states it rather than
   requiring you to infer it from the tags.
3. **The dep kinds tell you the placement constraints.** The steady copy carries a `rotation-WAR`
   against `lastread` — it is about to overwrite the buffer the *previous* trip read from, so it must
   be issued after those reads — plus a `crossing-RAW`, because a read in the next chunk will consume
   it. The `mma` carries four `RAW-residency` edges, one per source. Those are exactly the edges the
   fence Mark's `edges: 78` is covering.

Also note the `read` swap Marks are per **op-class** (`'operand': 'B'`) while the `copy` swap Marks
are per **movement** (`'unit': ('A','B')`) — the asymmetry described in §14.12, visible in one block.

**The drain block.**

```
Block drain0  gen_rel=-1  chunk_base=1  path_chunk_base={'prologue': 0}  preds=('prologue','steady')
              succs=('end',):
  Mark  fence {… 'kinds': ('RAW',), 'edges': 24}
  Mark  phase_boundary {'phase': 'drain0'}
