*whether the reader owes that displacement* differs, and that is `packed`, not this
(`tdm_split.py:163-164`; the same statement appears at `KernelWriterAssembly.py:19136-19139`).
`test_tdm_split.py:56-67` asserts `du_g.ldsStepBytes == mt_g.ldsStepBytes == 3072` for exactly this
reason: "getting this backwards would put region 1 at half a row instead of half a tile". Second,
it is post-pad, so callers add it *after* their own `_pad`, never before — an obligation restated
at `lds_geometry.py:267-269` and honoured at `leaves.py:730` (`_pad(raw) + regionOff`).

**`packed: bool = False`** — `split_packs_lds(axis, unrollMajor)`, §17.5.

**`dim1SpanPerRegion: int = 0`** — the per-region extent along **descriptor dim1**, in elements, or
`0` when the split did not cut dim1: `(extent // factor) if splitDim == 1 else 0`
(`tdm_split.py:175`). The multi-wave path needs it because there the descriptor's dim1 is
re-derived per region from the live `Group1` register: `_tdmSplitDim1ForRegion`
(`KernelWriterAssembly.py:20196`, called from `:20266`) computes region 1's dim1 as
`H0 - dim1SpanPerRegion`, clamped at zero. Returning `0` when the split took dim0 makes
`H1 == H0` fall out with no branch. It replaced a hardcoded `MacroTile // 2`, which was wrong on
both counts once the axis and the factor became parameters (`tdm_split.py:133-137`,
`test_tdm_split.py:142-152`).

**`isSplit`** (`tdm_split.py:140-142`) — the property `factor > 1`. A one-line readability helper;
its value is that call sites read `geo.isSplit` rather than re-deriving the threshold.

**`_pad(off, blockSize, padBytes)`** (`tdm_split.py:104`) — the block-padding expansion, three
lines: `off += (off // blockSize) * padBytes` when both are non-zero. It is a private duplicate of
the same expansion the read leaf applies (`leaves.py:503-507`) and the scaffold applies inline. It
is duplicated rather than shared because sharing it would require `tdm_split` to import something
or `leaves` to be importable, and the expression is three tokens. That is an accepted, documented
duplication — but it is a duplication, and if the padding scheme ever changes (a different bank
conflict rule, a non-uniform pad) there are at least three sites to change and no test that pins
them together.

**`derive(factor, axis, *, tlu, mt, du, bpe, ldsBlockSizePerPad=0, ldsPadBytes=0)`**
(`tdm_split.py:145`) is the constructor and the only supported way to build a `TdmSplitGeometry`.
All the shape arguments are keyword-only, which is deliberate: `mt` and `du` are two ints of the
same type whose confusion is precisely the historical defect above, and positional passing would
make that confusion a silent one.

```
derive(factor, axis, tlu, mt, du, bpe, blockSize, padBytes):
    if factor <= 1 or axis is None:
        return TdmSplitGeometry()                       # the INERT geometry
    unrollMajor = not tlu
    freeDim     = 0 if tlu else 1
    splitDim    = freeDim if axis == AXIS_MT else 1 - freeDim
    extent      = mt if axis == AXIS_MT else du
    tileBytes   = round(mt * du * bpe)
    return TdmSplitGeometry(
        factor, axis, splitDim,
        strideAxis        = 'free' if axis == AXIS_MT else 'reduction',
        globalConstBytes  = round(extent * bpe) // factor,
        ldsStepBytes      = _pad(tileBytes // factor, blockSize, padBytes),
        packed            = split_packs_lds(axis, unrollMajor),
        dim1SpanPerRegion = extent // factor if splitDim == 1 else 0)
```

The early return at `tdm_split.py:153-154` is the emission-neutrality guarantee, and it is
enforced at the point of derivation rather than at each consumer: an unsplit operand gets
`globalConstBytes == ldsStepBytes == 0` and `packed == False`, so every consumer's expression
collapses to what it computed before this module existed.
`test_tdm_split.py:81-88` sweeps that over both layouts and all three axis values.

**Who calls it.** Exactly one place: `KernelWriterAssembly.tdmSplitGeometry`
(`KernelWriterAssembly.py:19115-19131`), which reads `split_of`, `tP["tlu"]`,
`kernel["MacroTile{idx}"]`, `kernel["DepthU"]`, `tP["bpeGR"]` and the two padding parameters, and
returns the geometry. Three writer methods then consume it — `tdmSplitLdsBoundary`
(`:19144,19160`), `tdmSplitGlobalInc` (`:19176-19180`), and the descriptor setup at `:19314-19316`
and `:19475-19477` — plus the two `dim1SpanPerRegion` readers at `:11411-11412` and `:20208-20209`.
It is re-derived on every call rather than cached; see §17.14 for why that is fine.

**One sharp edge in the caller, not in `derive`.** `tdmSplitLdsBoundary`
(`KernelWriterAssembly.py:19144-19160`) does *not* always return `geo.ldsStepBytes`: under
`LDSSegmentInterleave == 1` it substitutes a segment-layout stride that this module knows nothing
about. So `TdmSplitGeometry.ldsStepBytes` is the region step **except** on the segment-interleave
path, and any reasoning that treats it as universal is wrong there. The override is flagged in the
writer's docstring but not in this module's, and `lds_geometry.region_bytes` takes the boundary
from the *writer* (`leaves.py:551-560` threads `splitBoundaryBytes` down from
`writer.tdmSplitLdsBoundary`) precisely so that the read side follows the override automatically
rather than recomputing `ldsStepBytes` itself.

**Test coverage of `derive`**, all against emitted assembly (`test_tdm_split.py:5-11` names the
kernels):

| test | line | what it pins |
|---|---|---|
| NT MT split reproduces the descriptor | `:37-45` | `splitDim 0`, `strideAxis 'free'`, `globalConstBytes 32` (emitted `s_mov_b32 s[sgprtdmAGlobalSplitIncs], 32`), `ldsStepBytes 3072` (emitted `…tdmALdsSplitIncs, 3072`), `packed True` |
| TN MT split | `:48-53` | `splitDim 1`, `packed False` — the shape that was already correct |
| DU split moves the axis, not the partition | `:56-67` | `ldsStepBytes` equal on both axes; `globalConstBytes` 64 vs 32 |
| MT/DU constants diverge off the coincidence shape | `:70-78` | `mt=128,du=32` → 128 vs 32 |
| factor 1 is inert | `:81-88` | 6 (layout × axis) cells |
| the regions tile the tile exactly once | `:91-97` | `ldsStepBytes * factor == mt*du*bpe` for factors 2 and 4, both axes |

That last one is the property that makes the region walk's "close back to zero" meaningful: `n`
steps of `ldsStepBytes` return the pointer to its start with no gap and no overlap.

#### 17.7 `wave_region_span` — how many regions **one wave** reaches

`wave_region_span(kernel, tc)` (`tdm_split.py:179`) answers a question that looks like the split
factor and is not (provenance: #245).

**The distinction.** `nsplit` is a property of the **macro tile**: how many pieces it is cut into,
how many `tensor_load`s the copy issues. The copy side genuinely needs that number — it really does
write every region. The **read** side needs something else: how many of those regions *this wave's
own tiles* actually land in. A wave does not own a contiguous slab of the macro tile. Its tiles are
handed out `VectorWidth` at a time in adjacent rows, and then the next group starts a whole
`MIWaveGroupShape` rows later, which is how the intervening rows get handed to the other waves. So
the map from a wave's tile index to a free-axis position is piecewise, and dividing the index by
"tiles per region" is only the same as dividing the position by "rows per region" when the vector
groups happen to line up with the region cut.

**The two derivations**, both already present in `lds_geometry`:

```
    row(t)    = (t // VW) * (MI * MIBlock * MIWaveGroup * VW) + (t % VW)
    region(t) = row(t) // (MacroTile // nsplit)               # by POSITION
    vs.
    region(t) = t // (MIWaveTile // nsplit)                   # by INDEX
```

They coincide at `MIWaveGroup [1,1]`, where the groups land exactly on the region boundaries — which
is why the discrepancy went unnoticed. At `MIWaveGroup [2,2]` the group jump is a **whole region**,
so a wave's two tiles sit adjacent at rows 0 and 1 and are **both in region 0**, while the index
form splits them across regions and hands the second one region 1's memory token. A wrong region
here is not a wrong address alone: `MemTokenAssignment` uses the region to name the storage
(§8.1) and `FenceRegions` then orders the read against the wrong producer, with nothing downstream
able to notice — GIR carries the region as a coordinate, so a mis-derived region is simply believed.

**The algorithm** (`tdm_split.py:205-235`):

```
wave_region_span(kernel, tc):                      # tc is "A" or "B"
    mt, _ = TDM_SPLIT_AXIS[int(kernel['TDMSplit'+tc] or 0)]
    if mt <= 1: return 1                           # unsplit, or a DU split
    t01   = 0 if tc == 'A' else 1
    mi    = kernel['MatrixInstruction']
    miDim = mi[t01]; miBlk = mi[3+t01] if len(mi) > 4 else 1
    wg    = (kernel['MIWaveGroup'] or mi[7:9])[t01]
    wt    = (kernel['MIWaveTile']  or mi[5:7])[t01]
    vw    = kernel['VectorWidth'+tc] or 0
    if vw <= 0:                                    # AUTO, not yet derived
        regPer = kernel.ProblemType['MacDataType'+tc].numRegisters()   if available
        if regPer is None: return mt               # cannot tell -> the SPLIT FACTOR
        vw = max(1, 4 // regPer)
        while vw > 1 and wt % vw: vw //= 2
    macroTile    = wt * wg * miDim * max(1, miBlk)
    rowsPerRegion= max(1, macroTile // mt)
    groupShape   = miDim * max(1, miBlk) * wg * vw
    rows = { ((t // vw) * groupShape + (t % vw)) // rowsPerRegion  for t in range(max(1, wt)) }
    return max(1, min(mt, len(rows)))
```

It builds the **set** of distinct regions the wave's `MIWaveTile` tiles land in, and returns its
cardinality clamped to `[1, nsplit]`. That is the honest computation: not a formula that assumes
uniformity, but an enumeration over `MIWaveTile` tiles — a loop of length 1 to 8 in practice.

Four implementation choices are recorded in the source and each is a decision a future editor could
plausibly reverse:

1. **It reads `TDMSplit{tc}` directly rather than through `split_of`** (`tdm_split.py:203-205`).
   The reason is that it is only ever asked about `A` and `B`, where `split_of`'s MXS/Metadata
   guard is vacuous, and routing through it would require a `ProblemType["Sparse"]` key that a
   hand-built θ dict has no reason to carry. This is a real coupling: if `split_of` ever gains a
   term that *does* apply to A/B, this function will not see it.

2. **A DU split returns 1.** The early `if mt <= 1: return 1` covers both "unsplit" and "cut the
   reduction axis", because a reduction-axis cut leaves every tile present in every region — the
   regions differ in *k*, not in *which tile*. So the span question is only meaningful for an MT
   split.

3. **The `VectorWidth` auto path** (`tdm_split.py:216-230`). `VectorWidth{A,B}` may still be the
   `-1`/`0` auto sentinel when this is called from the θ bridge, before `Solution.py` resolves it.
   Rather than guess, the function *replays the rule that decides it*: the largest power of two
   that divides `MIWaveTile` and fits in one register of elements (`4 // bytesPerElement`, via
   `DataType.numRegisters()`). And when the dict carries neither the pinned width nor a dtype to
   derive it from, it returns **the split factor** — the previous reading — so that an incomplete
   dict (a hand-built θ fixture) behaves exactly as it did before this function existed rather than
   receiving a guessed span. That is the right default: the split factor is the *conservative*
   answer, since a span below the factor is what unlocks the sharper schedule.

4. **`min(mt, …)`** clamps a span that somehow exceeds the region count, and `max(1, …)` floors it.
   Both are defensive; neither should fire.

**Consumers.** `LoopModel/bridge.py:129-130` puts both operands' spans into θ as
`"TDMSplitWaveRegions"`, and `SolutionStructs/Solution.py:1065-1075` uses it as the divisor in the
`VectorWidth`-fits-a-region gate — replacing a `% nsplit` test that rejected shapes the model
handles correctly (`MIWaveTile` 1 and 7). Note the belt-and-braces at `Solution.py:1069-1072`: the
call is wrapped in `try/except` and falls back to `_span = _n`, the old stricter predicate, if
anything raises. That is a gate, so failing closed is right.

**The tests, and the one that is really about methodology.**

* `test_tdm_split.py:284-299` pins the pass/fail matrix directly: `MIWaveGroup[2,2] MIWaveTile 2`
  → span 1 (both of a wave's tiles are in region 0), the two `MIWaveGroup[1,1]` shapes → span 2,
  and unsplit → 1. The kernel-dict fixture is `_wrs_kernel` (`test_tdm_split.py:269-281`), which
  builds only the keys `wave_region_span` reads and includes a two-line `_DT` stub with a
  `numRegisters()` method — that stub is what exercises the auto-`VectorWidth` path.
* `test_tdm_split.py:302-316` cross-checks the span against an **independent oracle**,
  `region_derivation_check.check_tiles`, asserting the biconditional
  `wave_region_span(k, tc) < nsplit  ⟺  the oracle reports a mislabelled tile`. Two derivations of
  one fact must agree, and a span below the factor is *exactly* the condition under which the
  index-derived region disagrees with the position-derived one.
* `test_tdm_split.py:367-409` is the one to read before touching any of this. It records that
  `lds_geometry.tiles_per_region`'s `max(1, …)` is **not a repair but a floor that is only sound
  because `Solution.py` guarantees divisibility**: at `MIWaveTile 1` with a 2-way MT split it
  returns 1, claiming one tile per region when the truth is half a tile, and every downstream
  `t % tiles_per_region` then computes against a fabricated divisor. Removing that gate emitted
  those kernels and the client took a **segmentation fault** (800 result rows before, 686 after).
  And the differential oracle **could not see it**, because `check_tiles` applies the same
  `max(1, per)`: at one tile both derivations collapse to 0 and it reports agreement. The lesson
  the test states in full at `:382-386` — *a differential oracle must be shown able to report a
  difference at the input in question before its agreement means anything* — is the most
  transferable thing in this section.
* `test_tdm_split.py:319-364` is about a *gate* rather than this function, but it lives here
  because the gate's predicate is `split_of`'s region **count**, not raw parameter equality. Since
  the knob fixes the factor at 2, `(TDMSplitA, TDMSplitB) = (1, 2)` and `(2, 1)` are both
  two-region pairs differing only in axis, and a mixed-axis pair is admissible because the
  multi-wave descriptor init is a runtime wave-parity branch in which each side derives its own
  geometry. Narrowing the predicate recovered 24 f8 and 40 mxf8 solutions with every
  previously-emitted kernel byte-identical.

#### 17.8 `lds_geometry` constants: `BPR` and `LANE_INTERLEAVE`

**`BPR = 4`** (`lds_geometry.py:21`) — bytes per register. A VGPR on this target is 4 bytes; the
constant exists so that "how many registers does this many elements occupy" is spelled
`elems * bpe / BPR` rather than `/ 4`.

**`LANE_INTERLEAVE = 2`** (`lds_geometry.py:30`) is the interesting one. It is *how many lanes share
one range of K positions*, and therefore how far apart, in chunk-widths, a single lane's
consecutive local-read chunks sit along the unroll axis.

It is a **constant taken from the scaffold rather than re-derived**, and the reasoning is worth
reproducing. The scaffold spells it as a bare `* 2` in
`Components/LocalRead.py:calcGfx1250LdsOffset` — "the WMMA V3 LDS layout uses a ×2 factor on the
unroll stride". It is *also* equal to `WavefrontSize // matrixInstTO` (32 // 16) for every shape the
GIR read path accepts. Two readings, one value. Rather than pick the derived form and risk it
diverging from the scaffold on a shape where the two disagree, the module keeps the scaffold's
constant and lets `read_fragments`'s K-extent check (below) *pin* it against `MatrixInstK` on every
single kernel. If a shape ever arrives where the two readings differ, that check fails loudly with
the numbers, which is exactly the behaviour you want from a constant you did not derive
(`lds_geometry.py:23-29`).

**"Two readings, one value" — measured, not asserted.** The claim is worth checking rather than
believing, so here is the arithmetic over the shape set the GIR read path actually accepts.
`matrixInstTO` is `min(MatrixInstM, MatrixInstN)` (`leaves.py:517`), and `WavefrontSize` is 32
because gfx1250 is Wave32:

| accepted shape (from the three ULM matrices) | `MatrixInstM×N×K` | `matrixInstTO` | `WavefrontSize // TO` | `LANE_INTERLEAVE` |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| bf16 (`loopmodel_bf16_gfx1250.yaml`) | 16 × 16 × 32 | 16 | **2** | 2 |
| fp8 (`loopmodel_f8_gfx1250.yaml`) | 16 × 16 × 64 | 16 | **2** | 2 |
| fp8, the deeper `MI_K` | 16 × 16 × 128 | 16 | **2** | 2 |
| MX-scaled fp8 (`loopmodel_mxf8_gfx1250.yaml`, both `MXBlock`s and every MT) | 16 × 16 × 128 | 16 | **2** | 2 |

The two readings agree on every row, and they agree *for a structural reason rather than by luck*:
the read path **rejects** every non-square matrix instruction outright
(`leaves.py:519-527`, `NotImplementedError` when `MatrixInstM != MatrixInstN`, because a non-square
instruction puts several instruction tiles inside one wave tile and the fragment table below has no
term for the extra `matrixInstTO * ti` displacement). With M = N forced, `matrixInstTO` is just
`MatrixInstM`, and every WMMA shape in the three ULM matrices has `MatrixInstM = 16` — only `K`
varies (32 at bf16, 64 and 128 at fp8, 128 at MX). So `32 // 16 = 2` is not a coincidence repeated
four times; it is a consequence of a gate one file away, and `K` — the only thing that moves — does
not enter the derived form at all.

**What the alternative would actually cost.** Deriving `LANE_INTERLEAVE` as
`WavefrontSize // matrixInstTO` would produce the identical constant on all four rows — so the
change buys **zero** behaviour today and costs three things:

1. `lds_geometry.py` currently takes a *duck-typed context*, not a kernel dict, precisely so it
   stays pure arithmetic that unit-tests without rocisa (§17.1). `WavefrontSize` and
   `MatrixInstM/N` are kernel keys, so the derived form either widens that interface or threads two
   more scalars through every call site.
2. The derived form would **track the scaffold's `WavefrontSize`, not the LDS layout**. Those are
   the same number today; if a future target is Wave64 with the same 16×16 WMMA, the derived form
   silently answers 4 while the layout's `×2` factor in `Components/LocalRead.py` is unchanged —
   the two readings would diverge, and the derived one would be the *wrong* one.
3. It would delete the invariant that currently pins the constant. `read_fragments` checks
   `nOuter · nInner · vwTrLoad · LANE_INTERLEAVE == matrixInstK` on **every kernel**
   (`lds_geometry.py:84-88`) and raises with all six numbers if it fails. A derived constant makes
   that check partly self-referential.

So the trade is: keep a hardcode that is checked on every kernel by an independent equation, or
take a derivation that is checked by nothing and is wrong first on the one axis (wavefront size)
most likely to change. That is a good pattern to copy — **when you must hardcode a value that
another component also computes, hardcode it *and* add a cheap invariant that would fail if the
other component's value changed** — and it is worth restating what makes it work here rather than
in general: the invariant (`… == matrixInstK`) is an equation in *different* quantities, not a
restatement of the constant. An invariant that recomputed the constant the same way would catch
nothing.

#### 17.9 `read_fragments` — which `ds_read`s one local-read act decomposes into

**The problem.** GIR emits **one read act** per (tile, reduction-substep) pair. The hardware does
not. A lane's `MIInputPerThread` elements for one substep are neither one contiguous run nor one
instruction, and *two* nestings produce them:

* **inner (`v`)** — one `lrvw`-element chunk (`LocalReadVectorWidth`) takes `lrvw / vwTrLoad`
  instructions, where `vwTrLoad` is how many elements **one** `ds_read` moves: `blockWidth`
  registers of `bpeDS`-byte elements, i.e. `blockWidth * BPR / bpeDS`. For bf16, `b128` /
  `b128_tr_b16` at `blockWidth 4` moves 8 elements against `lrvw` 8, so the loop is degenerate. For
  fp8's transpose read, `b64_tr_b8` at `blockWidth 2` moves 8 elements against `lrvw` 16, so it runs
  twice.
* **outer (`i`)** — there are `inputPerThUnroll / lrvw` such chunks, and they are **not adjacent**.
  The other lanes covering this K range each take one chunk before this lane's next one, so
  consecutive chunks are `LANE_INTERLEAVE` chunk-widths apart.

**The signature and the return shape.**

```python
read_fragments(blockWidth, bpeDS, lrvw, inputPerThUnroll, matrixInstK) -> tuple
```

returns `((unrollElems, regOff), …)` — one pair per emitted `ds_read`, both relative to the act's
own base: the first a displacement along the **unroll axis in elements**, the second a **register**
offset. The caller multiplies `unrollElems` by its own `UnrollStride` and `bpeDS` and adds the
result to the act's base byte address (`leaves.py:728-729`), and adds `regOff` to the act's base
register (`leaves.py:734-736`).

**The algorithm** (`lds_geometry.py:75-91`):

```
vwTrLoad = blockWidth * BPR / bpeDS            # elements ONE ds_read moves
nInner   = lrvw // vwTrLoad
nOuter   = inputPerThUnroll // lrvw
regSpan  = inputPerThUnroll * bpeDS // BPR     # registers this tile occupies

CHECK 1 (registers): nInner and nOuter non-zero, and
                     nOuter * nInner * blockWidth == regSpan
CHECK 2 (K extent):  nOuter * nInner * vwTrLoad * LANE_INTERLEAVE == matrixInstK

return ( ((v + i*nInner*LANE_INTERLEAVE) * vwTrLoad,      # unroll elements
          blockWidth * (v + nInner*i))                    # register offset
         for i in range(nOuter) for v in range(nInner) )
```

Read the element expression carefully: the *inner* index `v` advances by one `vwTrLoad`, while the
*outer* index `i` advances by `nInner * LANE_INTERLEAVE` of them. The register expression has no
interleave term at all — registers are dense, `blockWidth` apart, in emission order. That asymmetry
is the whole content of the function: **the LDS side is interleaved, the register side is not.**

**One expression for both read paths and both dtypes.** The scaffold states this same decomposition
**four** times — a `bpeDS`-per-branch walk under `enableLDSTr`, plus `calcGfx1250LdsOffset` for the
general unroll-major path — each with the numbers baked in (`numUnrolledIncrements = 32`,
`vwTrLoad = 8`, `2 * (innerIdx + 2 * outerIdx)`). Every one of those literals is a *value* of this
formula at a particular shape, and the GIR read leaf needs all four cases from one place
(`lds_geometry.py:50-54`).

**The two checks, and why *both* are necessary.** Either alone waves through a wrong table
(`lds_geometry.py:66-74`):

* **REGISTERS.** The fragments must exactly fill the per-tile register span
  `inputPerThUnroll * bpeDS / BPR` — no gap (a register the WMMA then reads *unwritten*) and no
  overlap (a fragment clobbering its predecessor). `test_tdm_split.py:249-256` supplies two shapes
  that fail it: `lrvw 6` against a per-read width of 8 (the chunk cannot be tiled at all), and
  `blockWidth 3` (`b96`) against `lrvw 8`, where the fragments cover 6 of the tile's 8 registers so
  two would go unwritten.
* **K EXTENT.** This lane's fragments, times the lanes it interleaves with, must cover the
  substep's whole `MatrixInstK`. This is the check that fails if `LANE_INTERLEAVE` is wrong for a
  shape, and it fails *with the numbers*. `test_tdm_split.py:257` supplies a shape where the
  registers tile perfectly but the K extent is half of what it should be — "the case a
  register-only check would wave through while every read lands in the wrong K position".

On failure it raises `NotImplementedError` with the full arithmetic in the message
(`lds_geometry.py:80-88`). It **raises rather than returning a plausible table**, and the test that
pins this states the reason (`test_tdm_split.py:260-261`): the caller emits from it, so a wrong
table is silently wrong numerics with nothing in the assembly that names the fault. The read leaf
catches and re-raises with the operand character prefixed (`leaves.py:541-543`), which turns a
mis-shaped kernel into a generation-time failure rather than a numerically wrong kernel.

**The measured table.** `test_tdm_split.py:208-230` is four rows, every number read off emitted
assembly:

| shape | `blockWidth, bpeDS, lrvw, ipt, MIk` | fragments |
|---|---|---|
| bf16 LDS-transpose (`ds_load_tr16_b128`) | `4, 2, 8, 16, 32` | `(0,0), (16,4)` |
| bf16 general (`ds_load_b128`) | `4, 2, 8, 16, 32` | `(0,0), (16,4)` |
| fp8 LDS-transpose (`ds_load_b64_tr_b8`) | `2, 1, 16, 32, 64` | `(0,0), (8,2), (32,4), (40,6)` |
| fp8 general (`ds_load_b128`) | `4, 1, 16, 64, 128` | `(0,0), (32,4), (64,8), (96,12)` |

The first two rows being *identical* is the point of including both: the read path changes the
strides the caller multiplies by, not the decomposition. The third row is the only one where the
inner loop is live (`nInner == 2`), producing the `8` and `40` offsets that no two-level-free
formula generates.

The fourth row is **the discriminating one**, and it is why this function exists at all. Before it,
the leaf emitted a fixed two-fragment table. That was correct for every bf16 shape because bf16
always has `nInner == 1` and `inputPerThUnroll / lrvw == LANE_INTERLEAVE`, so
`i * LANE_INTERLEAVE * vwTrLoad` *coincides* with `inputPerThUnroll` — a numerical coincidence that
made the wrong spelling look general (`lds_geometry.py:61-64`). It breaks the moment
`inputPerThUnroll / lrvw != LANE_INTERLEAVE`, which is exactly fp8 at `MatrixInstK 128`: four
chunks spaced 32, not 64. Two of them would have been emitted at the wrong K positions.

The independently-stated invariants are re-checked from the outside by
`test_tdm_split.py:233-246`, which asserts over three shapes that the register offsets are exactly
`range(0, ipt*bpeDS//BPR, blockWidth)`, that `len(frags) * elemsPerRead * LANE_INTERLEAVE == miK`,
and that no two fragments name the same element offset.

**Measurements behind it** (`lds_geometry.py:56-60`), both from the passing bf16 matrix:

```
NT LDSTr MT32x32 DU128 : per act 0 and 1536 bytes; substeps 3072 apart.
                         UnrollStride 48 elements (MT 32 + pad 16) x bpe 2
                         -> 16 and 32 elements, and 32 == MatrixInstK.
TN general MT32x32 DU64: per act 0 and 32 bytes; substeps 64 apart at UnrollStride 1.
```

**Called from** exactly one place: `LeafEmitters.buildLdsReadContext`
(`leaves.py:538-543`), which stores the result on the read context as `fragments`. The context's
default is the degenerate one-read act `((0, 0),)` (`leaves.py:110`) so that a hand-built context in
a test still emits something coherent; every context the builder returns overrides it. The emit
loop is then dtype-independent — one `ds_read` per fragment, the same code for bf16's two and fp8's
four (`leaves.py:726-736`).

**A boundary that is enforced elsewhere.** `read_fragments` assumes one wave tile per matrix
instruction. A non-square `MatrixInstruction` puts several instruction tiles inside one wave tile,
with a per-tile displacement the fragment table has no term for; rather than extend the formula
untested, `buildLdsReadContext` rejects that case outright with a `NotImplementedError`
(`leaves.py:520-528`). If you ever need non-square instructions, that is where the extra nesting
level has to be added — and it belongs *here*, as a third loop, not in the leaf.

#### 17.10 `region_row_elems` — the per-region row extent, and the one-formula rule

```python
region_row_elems(extent, ldsPad, unrollMajor, nsplit, axis=AXIS_MT) -> int
```
(`lds_geometry.py:110`) returns the **length of one row, in elements, along the LDS image's inner
axis** — of one *region* when the split packs regions separately, of the whole tile otherwise:

```
    packed = region_split_is_packed(unrollMajor, nsplit, axis)
    return (extent // max(1, nsplit) if packed else extent) + ldsPad
```

**The derivation.** §17.5 established that a packed split repacks the image as
`[region][outer][inner/n]`. The row is the inner run, so in a packed region it is `inner/n` long;
the row pad is added after, once, because each region is padded like any other array. When the
split does not pack, the image is unchanged and the row is the full extent. Two lines of code, but
the *value* is the distance between consecutive positions along the outer axis, which is the
multiplier on the outer coordinate in every address on both sides of the read.

**`extent` is supplied by the caller, and that is the whole content of the design.** Which axis is
inner depends on the layout, so the function cannot know whether to divide `MacroTile` or `DepthU`
— it divides whatever it is given:

* tile-major `[unroll][free]`: `extent = MacroTile{tc}` — `leaves.py:508` and
  `LraTileAssignment.py:70` on the `not unrollMajor` branch. The scaffold's local-read walk has **no**
  tile-major caller: `LocalRead.py:759` still spells `UnrollStride` as a raw `MacroTile{tc} + LdsPad`
  (see the scope limitation below).
* unroll-major `[free][unroll]`: `extent = _DepthU{tc}` — `leaves.py:551-552`,
  `LocalRead.py:761-762` (as `tileStride`), `LraTileAssignment.py:70` on the `unrollMajor` branch.

The function was once named `mt` end to end, which was right only while every caller was
tile-major. `test_gir.py:3323-3333` pins the four-cell table that this parameterisation buys, and
records the measurement behind the unroll-major half: on TN with `TDMSplitA/B = 2` the descriptor
was already correct (`tile0 = 32`, `LdsSplitIncs = 2176`) while every read still stepped a free tile
by a whole `DepthU`, walking out of the region on every tile after the first.

**The one-formula rule — and the historical defect it exists to prevent.** This value is needed in
*two* places that must agree:

1. the **per-read immediate offsets**, computed in the read leaf (`leaves.py:508,551`) and in the
   scaffold's local-read walk (`LocalRead.py:762`);
2. the **per-lane base register**, where `LraTileAssignment` multiplies the lane's outer coordinate
   by the row (`LraTileAssignment.py:868`, via `_rowElemsForRegion` at `:40-71`).

Those were two independent spellings of `extent + ldsPad`. Shortening only the first is what
happened: measured on `Cijk_Ailk_Bjlk MT32x32x64` (2026-08-17), the base register emitted
`kOffset *= 32` against immediates already built for 16, so **the two halves of one address sat in
different frames** and every lane with a non-zero outer component read the wrong row
(`lds_geometry.py:126-130`, `test_gir.py:3303-3311`, `LraTileAssignment.py:59-64`).

`_rowElemsForRegion` (`Components/LraTileAssignment.py:40`) is the adapter that lets the scaffold's
base register participate: it reads `split_of`, reads `UnrollMajorLDS{tc}`, picks the extent by
layout, and calls `region_row_elems`. It is a 30-line docstring around a four-line body, and the
docstring is the interesting part — it names the same defect from the other side.

**The scope limitation you must know about.** `Components/LocalRead.py:745-756` records that the
scaffold applies the shortening on **the unroll-major row only**. The other packed diagonal — an MT
split on a tile-major operand — would want the same treatment on `UnrollStride` and deliberately
does not get it there, because that case reaches the function through the `enableLDSTr` reads whose
inner coordinate is assembled from `vCols`/`eIdx` terms the scaffold code cannot cleanly separate
from the outer one, and it was not in the matrix that measured the DU half. The GIR path handles
both diagonals, because there the region is a fact carried on the IR rather than something
recovered by division. So: **the scaffold read path and the GIR read path have different coverage of
the packed diagonal**, and that asymmetry is deliberate and recorded rather than accidental.

#### 17.11 `fold_inner_offset` — a packed split makes the address PIECEWISE

```python
fold_inner_offset(innerElems, extent, unrollMajor, nsplit, axis=AXIS_MT) -> (region, innerInRow)
```
(`lds_geometry.py:135`) is `region_row_elems`'s counterpart: that one shortens the row, this one
says which row-block a coordinate past the end of the shortened row belongs to.

```
    if not packed:  return (0, innerElems)          # unsplit callers unaffected
    span = extent // nsplit
    return (innerElems // span, innerElems % span)
```

**Why a division is unavoidable.** The unsplit image is one linear map `f*extent + u`. The packed
split image is

```
    region * splitBoundary  +  ( f * (extent/n)  +  u mod (extent/n) )
```

and there is **no linear expression for the second form**, because the region jump is a *padded byte
boundary*, not an element stride: `splitBoundary` is `_pad(tileBytes/n)`, which is not
`(extent/n) * something` in general. So any emitter that builds the inner coordinate by
accumulating — `rIdx * step + localReadOffset`, as the scaffold does — has to divide somewhere. Doing
it here keeps the scaffold read path and the GIR read path (which gets the same answer from the
IR's region coordinate instead of by dividing) from disagreeing about where the boundary is
(`lds_geometry.py:141-147`).

Passing the **full** extent, not the per-region span, is what makes `region == 0,
innerInRow == innerElems` fall out for every unpacked caller (`lds_geometry.py:149-150`).

**The caller obligation, and where it is enforced.** This function divides a **starting** offset. It
cannot notice that a read spanning `w` elements *straddles* the boundary, and it cannot see the
per-lane component that the base register adds at run time. Both gaps are closed by a
`Solution.py` rejection rather than by code here: `Solution.py:5117-5120` rejects a DU split unless
`(DepthU // n) % MatrixInstK == 0`. The reasoning at `Solution.py:5102-5113` is worth restating —
if the per-region span is a whole number of `MatrixInstK` slabs, then every lane's contribution to
one WMMA's K slab lies inside the region that slab belongs to and the lane term never carries
across a boundary; if it is not, some lanes silently read the next region's bytes with no verifier
able to see it. That rejection is **not** scoped to the GIR path, because the packed layout is
created by the *descriptor*, which both code paths share.

**Consumers.** `Components/LocalRead.py:1683-1688`, on the unroll-major branch, folds
`rIdx * numElementPerRead * UnrollStride * 2 + tP["localReadOffset"]` — note that it folds the
**total**, not either term alone; folding either alone would put consecutive iterations of the same
read in different regions (`LocalRead.py:1670-1681`). It returns `(byteOffset, region *
splitBoundaryBytes)` as a pair so the caller can add the region jump *after* the block pad.

**Tests.** `test_gir.py:3337-3345` walks the four values `u ∈ {0, 16, 32, 48}` at `extent 64,
n 2` and demands `(0,0), (0,16), (1,0), (1,16)` — `u` there being the scaffold's real
`rIdx * numElementPerRead * 2 + localReadOffset` on the measured TN kernel.
`test_gir.py:3348-3354` asserts the *inert* half: every non-diagonal cell returns the coordinate
untouched, "or the shortening and the fold would double-count each other on the layouts where
regions are a contiguous continuation".

`test_gir.py:3357-3383` is the best single artefact in the whole section: it composes the entire
read-side arithmetic for one real kernel and pins the resulting byte offsets.

```
MT=32, DU=64, BPE=2, NSPLIT=2, LdsBlockSizePerPad=256, LdsPad=8 elements
pad(b)   = b + (b // 256) * 16
boundary = pad(MT*DU*BPE // NSPLIT)            == 2176  ( == tdmALdsSplitIncs )
row      = region_row_elems(DU, 0, True, 2, AXIS_DU)   == 32

addr(vIdx, rIdx, lro):
    region, uInRow = fold_inner_offset(rIdx*8*2 + lro, DU, True, 2, AXIS_DU)
    return pad((vIdx * 16 * row + uInRow) * BPE) + region * boundary

-> [0, 32, 1088, 1120,  2176, 2208, 3264, 3296]
   and  max(first four) < boundary <= min(last four)      # the regions are disjoint
```

Three terms are pinned there at once: the free-tile stride is the **shortened** row (32, not 64),
the unroll coordinate **folds** so `lro = 32` becomes region 1 at in-row 0, and the region jump is
added **after** the block pad because the boundary is itself already padded. What the scaffold
emitted before the fix was `0, 32, 2176, 2208 | 64, 96, 2240, 2272` — byte-identical to the
*unsplit* kernel, i.e. it had not reacted to the split at all, while the descriptor was already
writing two blocks 2176 apart.

#### 17.12 `addr_coord_on_split_axis` — one rule, and the two halves are not interchangeable

```python
addr_coord_on_split_axis(within, flat, ctx) -> int
```
(`lds_geometry.py:163`) picks **which coordinate the address uses along the axis the split cut**:
the within-region one when the regions are separately packed, the flat one when they are a
contiguous continuation. The body is one conditional
(`lds_geometry.py:187-188`), reading `ctx.unrollMajor`, `ctx.nsplit`, and
`getattr(ctx, "splitAxis", AXIS_MT)`.

**Why it cannot be either one unconditionally.** The region term and the coordinate are **two halves
of one address**, and they must be derived from the same predicate:

* **PACKED** — region `r` is its own padded block, so the address is
  `r * splitBoundary + (within-region coordinate)`. `region_bytes` supplies the first term and this
  function must supply the second. Using the flat coordinate here would double-count the region.
* **CONTIGUOUS** — the split's loads reproduce exactly the image one unsplit load produces, so
  `region_bytes` is **0** and there is *nowhere else* for the region to go. The coordinate must
  therefore be the flat one, or region `r>0` addresses region 0's bytes.

**The measurement (2026-08-18).** On NT (tile-major) with `TDMSplitA/B = 2`, a DU split cuts the
image's **outer** axis and is therefore contiguous — and every `r1` read repeated its `r0`
address:

```
    unsplit   k=0 -> 0, 1536      k=1 -> 3072, 4608
    split     r0  -> 0, 1536      r1  -> 0, 1536
```

because `k` had been folded to the within-region value while `region_bytes` correctly returned 0.
Half the reduction was read twice and half never — **1056 of 1056 cells** on that arm
(`lds_geometry.py:181-186`).

**The asymmetry that hid it.** The *tile* axis already obeyed this rule in both directions:
`tile_row` returns the flat vector-group index on the unroll-major path and `t % tiles_per_region`
on the packed one, and `region_bytes` is 0 in the former. The *reduction* axis had only the packed
half implemented, which is invisible for as long as the only reachable packed diagonal is the DU
one (`lds_geometry.py:176-179`). Adding the DU half on the other layout is what exposed it. This is
an instance of the general shape called out in §17.15: two coordinate axes obeying one rule, with
the rule implemented completely on one and half-implemented on the other.

**How the caller supplies both values.** The GIR read leaf takes `kIdx` (within-region, read off
the IR's region-relative reduction coordinate) and `kFlat` (the absolute reduction index) and calls
`addr_coord_on_split_axis(kIdx, kIdx if kFlat is None else kFlat, ctx)` (`leaves.py:716`). Unsplit
and MT-split reads have `kFlat == kIdx`, so the selection is inert for them —
`test_tdm_split.py:189-197` sweeps that over both layouts and all three axis values, which is why
the rule could be added without re-measuring the green cells.
`test_tdm_split.py:155-186` is the four-cell diagonal read from the address side, and it asserts
the *consistency* of the pair explicitly: `(region_bytes(ctx, 1) != 0) is packed`.

There is a related checker one layer up: `gir/verify_dataflow.check_address_keys`
(`gir/verify_dataflow.py:230`) exists to catch a plan in which the two halves have been decoupled.
It takes `packed` as a **callable** `operand -> bool` supplied by the caller
(`gir/verify_dataflow.py:243-244,260`) rather than deriving it, precisely because whether a region
is a packed block is a property of the LDS layout that this module owns.

#### 17.13 `tile_row`, `tiles_per_region`, `region_bytes` — the tile axis

These three compose into the tile-axis half of the address, and they are best read together.

**`tiles_per_region(ctx)`** (`lds_geometry.py:231`) — how many of this operand's wave tiles live in
one region:

```
    if ctx.splitAxis != AXIS_MT:  return max(1, ctx.miWaveTileAxis)      # a DU split divides no tiles
    return max(1, ctx.miWaveTileAxis // max(1, ctx.nsplit))
```

**Only an MT split divides the tiles.** The wave tiles are laid along the operand's free axis, so
cutting that axis hands each region `MIWaveTile / nsplit` of them. Cutting the reduction axis
leaves every tile present in every region — the regions differ in *k*, not in *which tile* — so the
count is the full `MIWaveTile` and `tile_row`'s `t % tiles_per_region` correctly degenerates to `t`.

The `max(1, …)` is **a floor, not a repair**, and it is sound only because `Solution.py` rejects
shapes where `MIWaveTile` does not divide by the wave's region span (`Solution.py:1065-1075`). At
`MIWaveTile 1` with a 2-way split it returns 1 while the truth is half a tile, and everything
downstream then divides by a fabricated divisor. Removing that gate produced a client
**segmentation fault**; the full account, and the reason the differential oracle could not see it,
is in `test_tdm_split.py:367-409` and summarised in §17.7. If you touch the floor, that test's
first assertion (`tiles_per_region(ctx(1, 2)) == 1`) is designed to fail and force a re-measure.

**`tile_row(ctx, t)`** (`lds_geometry.py:191`) — the LDS **row index** of this operand's wave-tile
`t`:

```
    if not ctx.unrollMajor:                      # transpose / tile-major path
        return t % tiles_per_region(ctx)
    vw    = max(1, ctx.vectorWidth)
    group = ctx.MIWaveGroupShape[ctx.tile01] if ctx.MIWaveGroupShape else vw
    return (t // vw) * group + (t % vw)
```

Two different answers for the two layouts, and each needs its own justification.

*Unroll-major: the vector-group formula.* **The distribution is by vector group.** A wave takes
`VectorWidth` **adjacent** tiles — adjacent rows — and then the next group of tiles starts a whole
`MIWaveGroupShape[tile01]` rows later; that jump is what hands the intervening rows to the other
waves. So `row(t) = (t // VW) * groupShape + (t % VW)`. The old expression was `tileStrideElems *
t`, which is exactly the **second term alone**. It agreed with the hardware only while every tile
sat in one vector group (`MIWaveTile <= VW`) — and every test pinned `MIWaveTile == VectorWidth ==
2`, so the missing jump never showed.

Measured 2026-08-17 on `MT32x32 KMN PGR2/PLR0 unsplit`, operand A's `ds_load` offsets
(`lds_geometry.py:205-210`):

```
    scaffold (passes) : 0, 32, 64, 96,  2176, 2208, 2240, 2272
    ours     (failed) : 0, 32, 64, 96,   128,  160,  192,  224
```

`row(1)` at `VW=1` is `1*16 + 0 = 16` rows → raw `16*64*2 = 2048` → padded → 2176, which is the
scaffold's number; the old form gave one row, 128. At `VW=2` it gives `0*32 + 1 = 1` row = 128,
unchanged — which is precisely why the defect survived every test. `test_gir.py:3273-3292` pins both
columns and applies the same `_pad` the leaf does.

*Unroll-major returns a **raw row index**.* The caller multiplies by the row stride and applies
`_pad`, so the block padding is added once, at the end, exactly as before (`leaves.py:717`,
`lds_geometry.py:212-213`).

*The vector-group jump is scoped to the unroll-major path*, and the scoping is not cosmetic. On the
transpose path `tileStrideElems` is already `MIWaveGroupShape[tile01]` — a per-**tile** stride, not a
row stride (`leaves.py:555-556`) — so the group jump is baked into the multiplier and applying it
again would double-count. `test_gir.py:3527-3537` pins that: on the transpose path with
`vectorWidth 2, MIWaveGroupShape [32,32]`, unsplit, the indices pass through as `[0,1,2,3]`.

*Tile-major takes the index modulo the region.* A tile-major region is a self-contained packed block
whose tiles are numbered from zero, so tile `t` reads at in-region index `t % tiles_per_region`, and
the block itself is reached by `region_bytes`. Splitting the displacement into those two independent
terms — the region picks the block, the index picks the tile inside it — is what keeps them from
interfering. `test_gir.py:3540-3558` pins three cases; the interesting one is `MIWaveTile 2,
nsplit 2 → [0, 0]`, where tile 1 is the only tile of region 1, so its in-region index is 0 and its
*whole* displacement is the 3072-byte block base rather than the 32-byte in-row step the global
index would have given.

**`region_bytes(ctx, region)`** (`lds_geometry.py:245`) — the byte displacement from the operand's
LDS base to the start of region `r`:

```
    if not region_split_is_packed(ctx.unrollMajor, ctx.nsplit, ctx.splitAxis)
       or not ctx.splitBoundaryBytes:
        return 0
    return region * ctx.splitBoundaryBytes
```

This is **non-zero exactly on the packed diagonal**, and the docstring at `lds_geometry.py:248-266`
is the single clearest statement of the whole rule — the two layouts spelled out with their
measurements, ending in the summary that on whichever diagonal packs, "the region IS a base
displacement, the row stride shrinks to the region's row length, and the inner coordinate is
in-region".

`splitBoundaryBytes` is the writer's own `tdmSplitLdsBoundary` — the same quantity the copy side
walks by — threaded down through the read context (`leaves.py:551-560`) rather than recomputed, so
the read and the write cannot disagree about where region `r` lives. It is **already padded**, so
callers add it after `_pad`, not before (`leaves.py:730`).

`test_gir.py:3240-3260` pins the layout asymmetry (`[0, 0]` unroll-major, `[0, 3072]` tile-major)
with both measurements in the docstring; `test_gir.py:3263-3270` pins emission neutrality at
`nsplit == 1` on both layouts.

**The composed address.** Putting §17.10–§17.13 together, the GIR read leaf's per-`ds_read` byte
offset is (`leaves.py:716-730`):

```
    kAddr    = addr_coord_on_split_axis(kIdx, kFlat, ctx)            # §17.12
    tileBase = tileStrideElems * tile_row(ctx, tileIdx) * bpeDS      # §17.13, §17.10
    base     = tileBase + kAddr * substepStrideBytes
    regionOff= region_bytes(ctx, region)                             # §17.13
    for (unrollElems, fragReg) in ctx.fragments:                     # §17.9
        raw    = base + unrollElems * UnrollStride * bpeDS
        offset = _pad(raw) + regionOff                               # pad BEFORE the region jump
```

Five of the eight functions in `lds_geometry` appear in those six lines, and `region_row_elems`
supplies both `tileStrideElems` and `UnrollStride` one layer up. That is the reason the module is
worth keeping whole: the address is a *sum of terms each of which is a diagonal-dependent choice*,
and having every term derive its choice from one predicate is what keeps the halves in the same
frame.

#### 17.14 The root cause worth remembering: it was the address, not the schedule

When operand-splitting was first turned on under the GIR path, it failed broadly — hundreds of
kernels across several parameter blocks, on both layouts, at several loop orders. The failure had
every superficial characteristic of a *synchronisation* bug: results were wrong in a way that
depended on the pipeline depth, changed with the prefetch settings, and looked different on
one-wave and four-wave configurations. The obvious suspects were all in the layers above this one —
the LDS memory tokens that name which storage a read observes, the completion waits derived from
those tokens, the barrier placement, and the ordering of the copy and read hops within a block.

**Every one of those was correct.** The whole class traced to a single missing term in the LDS tile
stride: `tile_row` was computing `tileStrideElems * t` where the hardware distribution is
`(t // VW) * MIWaveGroupShape + (t % VW)` — the vector-group jump described in §17.13. Reads landed
in the wrong rows; the wrong rows sometimes belonged to another region; the wrong region then made
the *correct* token machinery order the read against a producer that was not its producer. The
symptom presented one layer above the defect.

Three things made it hard to see, and all three are reusable diagnostics:

1. **The wrong expression is a special case of the right one.** At `MIWaveTile == VectorWidth`, the
   group term is zero and the two forms agree exactly. Every fixture pinned `MIWaveTile ==
   VectorWidth == 2`. A formula that is right on the whole test matrix and wrong in general is
   invisible to the test matrix by construction.
2. **The failure was numeric, not structural.** Nothing in the emitted assembly names a row index.
   A `ds_read offset:128` is as well-formed as a `ds_read offset:2176`; only a differential against
   a known-good emitter, or a lane-level interpreter, can tell them apart.
3. **The address is a sum of independently-chosen terms.** With four terms each selected by a
   diagonal predicate, a single wrong term produces an address that is *plausible* — right
   magnitude, right alignment, right region count — and there is no local invariant that catches it.

**The general lesson, stated as an ordering.** When a GEMM kernel with a split, a rotation or a
repacked layout produces wrong numbers, check in this order:

```
    1. the ADDRESS ARITHMETIC     (this section)  — is every term in the same frame?
    2. the REGION / TOKEN LABELS  (§8.1)          — does the label match the address?
    3. the ORDERING               (§8.13, and the
                                   hazard/placement analyses) — waits, barriers, hop order
```

and not the reverse. Ordering machinery is generic, exercised by every kernel, and covered by
dataflow checks that run on every build; address arithmetic is per-shape, exercised only by the
shapes in the matrix, and the *only* thing that checks it is a numeric comparison against hardware.
The prior probability is strongly on the arithmetic.

The concrete way to check item 1 without a GPU is the one the tests use: compose the whole address
in Python from these functions for the specific kernel, and compare the resulting list of byte
offsets against the offsets in the emitted `.s` file. `test_gir.py:3357-3383` is a worked template
for exactly that. Two independent instruments support the same workflow —
`Lowering/asm_lane_eval.py`'s `LaneEval`, a per-lane symbolic interpreter over emitted assembly, and
`Lowering/lds_region_check.py`, which answers "does one `ds_load` straddle two storage regions?" —
and both are cheap to run.

**And the corollary about oracles.** Two of the derivations in this section are cross-checked by an
independent one (`region_derivation_check.check_tiles`, which recomputes the region from the
tile *position* and compares it against the region derived from the tile *index*). That oracle is
genuinely useful — it is what pinned the wave-span defect. But it shares `tiles_per_region`'s
`max(1, …)` floor, so at `MIWaveTile 1` both of its derivations collapse to zero and it reports
agreement it is *incapable* of withholding. A differential oracle must be shown able to report a
difference at the input in question before its agreement is evidence
(`test_tdm_split.py:382-386`). If you add an oracle here, add with it a test that makes the oracle
*fail*.

#### 17.15 Complexity, compile-time cost, and where the cost actually is

Every function in both modules is **O(1) in the size of the kernel** except two:

| function | complexity | practical `n` |
|---|---|---|
| `read_fragments` | `O(nOuter * nInner)` | 2 or 4 fragments; never more than 8 |
| `wave_region_span` | `O(MIWaveTile)` set build | 1–8 |
| everything else | O(1), a handful of integer ops | — |

Total compile-time cost is negligible and there is nothing here worth optimising. `derive` is
re-invoked on every call to `KernelWriterAssembly.tdmSplitGeometry` — several times per kernel, from
five call sites — and constructs a frozen dataclass each time. At roughly a dozen integer operations
per call, against a kernel generation that emits thousands of instruction objects through a
compiled extension, that is unmeasurable. **Do not add a cache**; it would introduce a staleness
question (the geometry depends on `kernel` and `tP`, both mutable dicts) in exchange for nothing.

The one place where a real cost *could* appear is if `wave_region_span` were called inside a loop
over shapes during solution enumeration. It is not: `Solution.py:1065-1075` calls it twice per
candidate solution, inside a gate that already does far more work. If a future caller does put it in
an inner sweep, memoising on the tuple `(TDMSplit, MatrixInstruction, MIWaveGroup, MIWaveTile,
VectorWidth, dtype)` is trivial and safe, because the function reads nothing else.

#### 17.16 Weaknesses, sharp edges, and dead code — the honest list

1. **Duck typing with silent defaults.** `tile_row`, `tiles_per_region`, `region_bytes` and
   `addr_coord_on_split_axis` all take an untyped `ctx` and read attributes off it. Three of them
   use `getattr(ctx, "splitAxis", AXIS_MT)` (`lds_geometry.py:188,240,270`) and
   `region_split_is_packed` / `region_row_elems` / `fold_inner_offset` default `axis=AXIS_MT`
   (`lds_geometry.py:94,110,136`). Every one of those defaults *silently selects a diagonal cell*.
   A caller that forgets to thread `splitAxis` gets the MT answer, which is right on one layout and
   wrong on the other, with no error. **Concrete fix:** make `splitAxis` a required argument and a
   required context field, and let the two existing context dataclasses
   (`leaves.LdsReadTileContext:63`, `region_derivation_check.TileCtx:45`) supply it explicitly. The
   defaults bought backward compatibility during a migration that is now finished.

2. **Two names for one bit.** `tlu` and `unrollMajor` are negations, and only `derive`
   (`tdm_split.py:156`) converts. `derive` takes `tlu`; every function in `lds_geometry` takes
   `unrollMajor`. Passing the wrong polarity is a one-character mistake that type-checks and
   selects the opposite diagonal cell. A future cleanup should pick one and convert at the module
   boundary.

3. **`split_factors` does not apply `split_of`'s exclusions.** §17.4. Two readings of one parameter
   ten lines apart, differing in whether sparse/MXS operands are filtered. Today it is harmless;
   it is exactly the shape of defect the module was created to eliminate.

4. **`_pad` is duplicated three ways.** `tdm_split._pad` (`:104`), the read leaf's local `_pad`
   (`leaves.py:503-507`), and the scaffold's inline expansion. Nothing pins them together. If the
   padding scheme changes, all three change, and only a hardware run will notice if one does not.

5. **`TdmSplitGeometry.packed` has no non-test reader.** `Solution.py:5054` records this: the field
   is derived on every `derive` call and consumed by nobody in shipping code — the read side asks
   `region_split_is_packed` directly instead. It is not dead in the sense of being wrong (it is the
   same function), but it is a second route to one answer, and a future edit that changes one and
   not the other creates the exact divergence class this section is about. Either delete the field
   or make the read side read it.

6. **`ldsStepBytes` is overridden on the segment-interleave path.** §17.6. The geometry's own field
   is not the region step on `LDSSegmentInterleave == 1`, and nothing in `tdm_split.py` says so.

7. **The scaffold read path covers only one packed diagonal.** §17.10 — deliberate, measured,
   recorded at `Components/LocalRead.py:745-756`, but a real coverage asymmetry between the two
   emitters that anyone extending the split matrix must know.

8. **The `AXIS_DU` re-export at `lds_geometry.py:18` has no production consumer.** It is imported
   for re-export with a `# noqa: F401` and used only by tests (`test_gir.py:3331,3344,3351,3369`).
   Harmless, and arguably right — a reader of `lds_geometry` should be able to name both axes
   without knowing they live in `tdm_split` — but it is worth knowing that the two constants have
   two import paths.

9. **`wave_region_span` reads `TDMSplit{tc}` directly rather than through `split_of`.** §17.7,
   point 1. A justified shortcut with a stated reason, and a coupling that will not survive a
   change to `split_of`'s guard.

10. **`region_derivation_check` shares the floor it is meant to audit.** §17.14, final paragraph.

#### 17.17 Extending this code: concrete advice

**Adding a new split factor (beyond 2).** Change `TDM_SPLIT_AXIS` (`tdm_split.py:32`) to map new
parameter values, and nothing else in these two modules — every formula is already written in terms
of `factor`/`nsplit` rather than a literal 2, and `test_tdm_split.py:91-97` already exercises factor
4. The work is entirely upstream (`Solution.py` gates, the θ four-list) and downstream (the
descriptor walk's region loop, the number of `tensor_load`s). Do add a factor-3 case to the tiling
test to catch a non-power-of-two divisibility assumption; the current tests use 2 and 4 only.

**Adding a split on a third axis.** The diagonal in `split_packs_lds` is written as a two-way XNOR
(`tdm_split.py:101`) and would need to become a lookup of "is this axis the image's inner one".
That is the *right* generalisation: define a function `inner_axis(layout) -> axis` and write
`split_packs_lds` as `axis == inner_axis(layout)`. It is a strictly clearer statement of the rule
that this section spent §17.5 deriving, and it is a two-line change today.

**Adding a new dtype or read instruction.** `read_fragments` is already general over
`(blockWidth, bpeDS, lrvw, inputPerThUnroll, MatrixInstK)`. Add a row to
`test_tdm_split.py:208-226` with numbers read off the emitted assembly *before* changing anything;
if the existing formula reproduces them, you are done. If it raises, read which of the two checks
fired — "registers" means the instruction width does not tile the tile, "MatrixInstK" means the lane
interleave is wrong for the shape and `LANE_INTERLEAVE` needs to stop being a constant.

**Making `LANE_INTERLEAVE` shape-dependent.** The derived form is `WavefrontSize // matrixInstTO`.
If a shape ever needs it, thread those two values into `read_fragments` and keep the K-extent check
— which is the thing that will tell you whether the derived form is right.

**Anything that tempts you to import.** Do not. If you need a `Solution` field, pass it in. If the
argument list gets long, add a frozen dataclass *in the caller's module* and duck-type it here, the
way `LdsReadTileContext` and `TileCtx` already do. The unit tests for this arithmetic are the only
tests in the package that can pin an address without a GPU, and they exist only because these two
files import nothing.

---

### 18. The standalone checkers and the independent simulator

Four modules in `Tensile/Lowering/` are not on the LoopIR → GIR → rocisa path at all. They do not
produce instructions, they do not mutate the IR, and three of the four are never called by shipped
code. They exist to *disprove* claims the main path makes about itself:

| module | L | the claim it attacks |
|---|---:|---|
| `uniform_emission.py` | 245 | "every GIR fence is reached by every wave of its scope" |
| `region_derivation_check.py` | 103 | "the storage region a wave tile is *named* by is the storage region it *sits* in" |
| `asm_lane_eval.py` | 380 | (no claim of its own — it is the instrument the next row uses) |
| `lds_region_check.py` | 315 | "one `ds_load` touches exactly one storage region" |

#### 18.0 Why a separate checker layer exists at all

The GIR pipeline already carries twelve well-formedness invariants (the `G-*` gate in
`gir/verify.py`) and five semantic checks over the emit plan (`gir/verify_dataflow.py`). Those are
*internal* checks: they read the same data structures the passes wrote, in the same vocabulary. An
internal check is excellent at catching an inconsistency between two parts of the model and
completely blind to the model being uniformly wrong. Two failure shapes recur in this codebase and
neither is reachable from inside GIR:

1. **The fact has no node.** GIR's control-flow graph contains the software-pipeline stages and the
   trip-count guards, and nothing else. The wave-parity branches that the assembly scaffold emits
   around the Tensor-Data-Mover setup — `s_bitcmp1_b32 s[sgprWaveIdx], 0` followed by
   `s_cbranch_scc1 label_SkipStaggerA`, so that even waves run one arm and odd waves skip it — are
   *scaffold-owned*. They have no GIR node, so a GIR analysis asking "can an agent skip this fence?"
   walks a graph in which the skip does not exist and truthfully answers *no*. The answer is sound
   with respect to GIR and useless with respect to the machine.
2. **The fact is not in the instruction.** Whether the 32 lanes of a single `ds_load` all land in
   the same storage region is a property of the *per-lane address*. The instruction text carries a
   wave-uniform `offset:` immediate and one base VGPR; the lane spread lives in that VGPR, built at
   kernel init from `vgprSerial`. Reading the assembly as text cannot see it, and reading GIR
   cannot see it either, because GIR carries the region a read *names*, as a coordinate — a read
   that spans two regions is simply mis-described, and no amount of dataflow over a description
   finds an error in the description.

Both shapes have the same cure: **ask the question in a place, and in a language, that the model
does not control.** `uniform_emission` re-asks the uniformity question over the emitted rocisa
stream, where the scaffold's arms are ordinary items in a list. `lds_region_check` re-asks the
region question over the *executed* address, by interpreting the emitted setup code one lane at a
time. `region_derivation_check` re-asks the region question a third way — from compile-time shape
only — so that two derivations of one fact can be compared without a kernel at all.

#### 18.0.1 The methodological point: agreement between independent implementations

`asm_lane_eval.LaneEval` deserves a paragraph before any of its code, because the reason it exists
is a claim about what counts as evidence, and that claim shaped three other modules.

The address a lane reads from LDS is produced by `Components/LraTileAssignment.py`. That component
does not *compute* the address; it *emits the arithmetic* that computes it. So there are two
obvious ways to check the address:

* **(a) Re-derive it in Python.** Write a function that reproduces `LraTileAssignment`'s rules and
  compare its output against what the region model expects.
* **(b) Interpret the emitted instructions.**

Route (a) was tried and rejected, and the rejection is recorded verbatim at
`Lowering/asm_lane_eval.py:13-19`. A Python re-derivation of an emitter's rules is a
**transcription**. A checker built on a transcription tests the transcription: it agrees with the
kernel exactly when both are right, *and* exactly when both are wrong in the same way — which is
precisely the failure this tool is built to rule out. If the transcription is written by reading
the emitter (and there is no other way to write it), then the two share every misunderstanding
their author had.

Route (b) has no such freedom. The interpreter consumes the instruction stream the assembler will
consume. If the kernel's address arithmetic is wrong, the interpreter faithfully reproduces the
wrong address, and the region check sees the wrong region. The interpreter can only be wrong about
*instruction semantics*, which is a much smaller and much more independently checkable surface than
"the whole tile-assignment scheme" — and, critically, it is a surface where the interpreter's
author and the emitter's author had to agree with a third party (the ISA) rather than with each
other.

The general rule, which recurs in `region_derivation_check` and in the tests of both:

> A model is verified when a **second, independently derived** implementation agrees with it. Two
> spellings of one derivation agreeing with each other is not evidence.

The corollary is equally load-bearing and is easier to forget: **a differential oracle must first
be shown capable of disagreeing at the input in question.** `Tests/unit/test_tdm_split.py:367`
exists solely to record a case where that step was skipped — see §18.2.4.

#### 18.0.2 Failure policy at a glance

The four modules differ sharply in when they run and what a finding costs. This table is the
summary; each subsection justifies its row.

| module | runs | on a finding | blast radius |
|---|---|---|---|
| `uniform_emission.check_uniform_placement` | **in production**, once per `UseLoopModel` kernel, from `KernelWriter.py:11501` | raises `UniformEmissionError` (a `RuntimeError` subclass) | **fatal for one kernel** on the benchmark path; fatal for the whole run on the library-build path — see §18.1.5 |
| `region_derivation_check.check_tiles` | never in production; unit tests (`test_tdm_split.py:302`, `:367`) and offline sweeps | returns a `[Finding]` list | **advisory** — pure data, no exception |
| `lds_region_check.check` | never; **no in-tree caller** — an offline diagnostic invoked by hand on a `.s` file | returns `(accesses, violations, notes)`; raises only when the interpreter refuses | **advisory**, but the refusal path is a hard `RuntimeError` |
| `asm_lane_eval.LaneEval` | only via `lds_region_check` | raises `UnsupportedInstruction` on any opcode or operand it cannot model | fatal to the enclosing check, deliberately |

Two of the four therefore have no automated pressure keeping them honest. That is a genuine
weakness and it is named again in §18.6.

---

#### 18.1 `uniform_emission.py` — the hang detector

##### 18.1.1 The defect it exists to prevent

A GIR *fence* with `scope='block'` is realized as a workgroup barrier. A workgroup barrier is a
**rendezvous**: it completes when every wave of the workgroup has arrived. If the barrier is
emitted at a program point that only *some* waves execute, the arriving waves wait for waves that
will never come. On this hardware the outcome is one of two things, and both are unacceptable:

* the arrivers wait forever — a **hang**, which from the outside looks like a wedged GPU with no
  stack, no message and no failing assertion; or
* the hardware releases them at some later barrier, in which case every synchronization in the
  kernel has silently shifted by one — a **race** that reproduces only under a particular schedule.

Neither is debuggable after the fact. This is why the check fails rather than warns; see §18.1.5.

##### 18.1.2 Why the question has to be asked twice

The same question is asked at two layers, by two modules, and neither subsumes the other:

* **Layer 1, over GIR.** `gir/analyses/uniform_placement.py:121` walks the GIR CFG and reports a
  violation when a proc-scoped fence lies in, or downstream of, a block whose `role` restricts it to
  some agents, or behind a terminator predicate whose symbol the program declared agent-varying
  (`prog.meta['agent_varying_symbols']`). It is wired into the verifier as `G-UNIFORM`.
* **Layer 2, over the emitted rocisa module.** `uniform_emission.check_uniform_placement`
  (`uniform_emission.py:214`).

Layer 1 is **structurally inert today**, and the source says so at
`gir/analyses/uniform_placement.py:38-46`: `Block.role` is `'all'` in every block the lowering
produces, because wave specialization is unimplemented; and GIR's predicate vocabulary (`Pred` over
a trip symbol plus a constant) *cannot spell* an agent-discriminating guard. So layer 1 searches
its tree for a shape the tree has no node for. That is not the same as the schedule being safe — it
means the instrument cannot register the reading.

Layer 2 is where the arms actually are. `KernelWriterAssembly._applyStaggerTDM` and the
wave-separated Tensor-Data-Mover initialization / global-offset / increment emitters open exactly
the shape shown in §18.0: a scalar bit test on the wave index, a conditional branch over a body,
and a join label. Those instructions are in the emitted module. A text-level scan can see them.

So: layer 1 guards the *decoder* (it will fire the day a schedule genuinely places a fence under an
agent-varying guard it can spell), and layer 2 guards the *backend* (it fires the day our fence
lands inside a scaffold arm). Both are wanted. All *shipped* safety against this hazard is layer 2.

##### 18.1.3 What counts as "agent-discriminating"

The module defines an **agent-discriminating arm** as a half-open span of the flattened item list,
opened by a forward conditional branch whose condition depends on an agent identity and closed by
the first later occurrence of that branch's target label. Three rules decide the condition
(`uniform_emission.py:129`):

1. **The branch tests `EXEC`** (`s_cbranch_execz` / `execnz`, recognized by `"Exec"` appearing in
   the rocisa class name). `EXEC` is the per-lane execution mask, so this is lane-discriminating by
   construction. This is the only *structural* rule of the three.
2. **The branch's condition came from a vector compare** (`v_cmp*` writing VCC). A vector compare is
   per-lane in form.
3. **The condition's producer reads an agent-identity register.** `AGENT_ID_REGS`
   (`uniform_emission.py:85`) is the regex `\bsgprWaveIdx\b|\bvgprSerial\b|\bsgprWaveId\b` —
   the wave index within the workgroup, and the flat thread id.

Rule 3 is a **sniffer** over instruction text and it is the check's soundness limit: an agent id
laundered through a temporary more than `_LOOKBACK` instructions before the branch is not
recognized. `_LOOKBACK` is 12 (`uniform_emission.py:94`), against emitters that place the producer
one or two instructions before the branch — it is slack, not a tuned parameter.

##### 18.1.4 The algorithm, and every definition in the file

The whole module is five functions, one exception class and three module-level constants. It walks
the **flattened** rocisa module — `rootModule.flatitems()`, a linear list of instruction and label
objects — and never touches the tree.

**`_text(item)`** — `uniform_emission.py:97`. Returns `str(item)` with everything from the first
`//` stripped and trailing whitespace removed, or `""` if `str()` raises. The stripping matters:
the emitters attach explanatory comments that mention register names (`// check wave parity`), and
matching `AGENT_ID_REGS` against a comment would classify on prose rather than on operands.

**`_is_label(item)`** — `uniform_emission.py:106`. `type(item).__name__ == "Label"`. Trivial, but
note it is a *name* comparison, for the same reason as the next function.

**`_branch_target(item)`** — `uniform_emission.py:110`. Returns the label name a conditional branch
jumps to, or `None` if `item` is not a conditional branch. The test is on the rocisa **class name**
(`startswith("SCBranch")` or `startswith("SCLongBranch")`), then `getattr(item, "labelName", None)`.

Matching on the class name rather than importing every branch type is deliberate: the set of branch
classes grows (`SCBranchExecZ`, `SCBranchSCC1`, …), and a missing import would make this function
silently return `None` for a real branch — i.e. make the check *skip a region*. A safety check may
have false positives; it may not have silent false negatives caused by its own import list.

There is one soundness limit recorded at the matching site rather than as a footnote: the
**long-form** branches do not survive to this point. `SCLongBranchScc0` and its siblings dissolve
inside `flatitems()`; what arrives is their expansion, whose actual transfer of control is an
`s_setpc_b64`, and this function does not model an indirect jump. An arm opened by a long branch is
therefore invisible here. None is emitted on the `UseLoopModel` path today. The `SCLongBranch`
prefix in the test is thus vestigial-but-harmless — it would match a long-branch object if one ever
did survive flattening.

**`_condition_kind(items, i)`** — `uniform_emission.py:129`. Implements the three rules of §18.1.3.
Returns a human-readable reason string, or `None` when the branch is agent-uniform as far as this
check can tell.

```
_condition_kind(items, i):
    if "Exec" in class_name(items[i]):
        return "branch on EXEC (lane-discriminating)"
    for j in i-1 down to max(0, i-12):              # _LOOKBACK = 12
        t = _text(items[j])
        if t is blank: continue
        if t matches _SETS_COND:                    # the FIRST producer wins
            if t matches _VECTOR_CMP:  return "branch on VCC from a vector compare: ..."
            if AGENT_ID_REGS in t:     return "condition reads an agent id: ..."
            return None                             # a uniform scalar compare
    return None                                     # no producer found in the window
```

`_SETS_COND` (`:88`) is the set of SCC/VCC producers: `s_bitcmp0/1_b32/b64`, `s_cmp_*`, `s_cmpk_*`,
`s_and_b32/b64`, `s_andn2_b32/b64`, `s_or_b32/b64`, `s_test_*`, `v_cmp*`. `_VECTOR_CMP` (`:90`) is
just `v_cmp*`. The scan stops at the *first* producer found, which is the correct reading of the
hardware: the branch consumes the most recent write of the condition register.

The `return None` in the middle branch is the important one — it is what keeps the check quiet on
`s_cmp_eq_u32 s[sgprGSU], 1` (a split-K guard) and on loop trip-count compares. Every wave of a
workgroup evaluates those identically. Without that branch the check would fire on nearly every
fence in the main loop; `Tests/unit/test_uniform_placement.py:160` pins exactly this.

**`agent_discriminating_regions(items)`** — `uniform_emission.py:148`. Returns
`[(start, end, target, reason)]`: the half-open spans of the item list that only some agents
execute.

```
agent_discriminating_regions(items):
    label_at = {}                              # first index of each label, by name
    for i, it in enumerate(items):
        if _is_label(it): label_at.setdefault(it.getLabelName(), i)

    out = []
    for i, it in enumerate(items):
        tgt = _branch_target(it)
        if tgt is None: continue
        why = _condition_kind(items, i)
        if why is None: continue
        end = label_at.get(tgt) or label_at.get("label_" + tgt)
        if end is None or end <= i: continue    # unresolved, or a BACKWARD branch
        out.append((i, end, tgt, why))
    return out
```

Two details carry weight.

*The name fixup.* A branch's `labelName` attribute holds the bare name (`SkipStaggerA`); a `Label`
object's `getLabelName()` returns it with the emitter's `label_` prefix. The lookup tries both.
Forgetting this would make every span unresolvable and the check vacuous — a check that never fires
because it can never resolve an endpoint looks exactly like a check that passes.

*`end <= i` drops backward branches.* A loop back-edge is not a skip: every agent that runs the
body runs all of it. Treating a back-edge as opening a region would place every steady-body fence
"inside an arm" and make the check fire on every kernel.
`Tests/unit/test_uniform_placement.py:176` is the fixture for this, and it asserts the *empty* list
— one of the few tests in the suite that pins a negative.

**`check_uniform_placement(rootModule, ownedBarriers, kernelName="")`** — `uniform_emission.py:214`.
The entry point, and the only one a caller uses.

```
check_uniform_placement(rootModule, ownedBarriers, kernelName):
    items   = list(rootModule.flatitems())
    regions = agent_discriminating_regions(items)
    owned   = { id(b) for b in ownedBarriers or () }
    at      = { id(it): first index of it   for it in items if id(it) in owned }

    _STATS['kernels'] += 1;  _STATS['regions'] += len(regions);  _STATS['owned'] += len(at)

    findings = [ message(pos, s, e, tgt, why)
                 for (bid, pos) in at.items()
                 for (s, e, tgt, why) in regions
                 if s < pos < e ]
    _STATS['inside'] += len(findings)
    if findings: raise UniformEmissionError(...)          # message quotes the first 4
    return findings                                       # == [] on success
```

`ownedBarriers` is matched by **object identity**, not by any attribute. That is forced: a GIR fence
is realized as the same `SBarrier` class the scaffold emits, and rocisa's nodes are compiled
objects that reject an added Python attribute, so there is no place to write a marker. Identity is
the only honest signal that a barrier is ours. It is also the currency the sibling machinery already
uses — `KernelWriter._stripBarriers(rootModule, keep=self.states.girOwnedBarriers)` at
`KernelWriter.py:11486` removes every scaffold barrier and keeps exactly the GIR-owned ones by the
same test. The list itself is created at `KernelWriter.py:7907` and appended to at the single point
that creates a fence, `gir_to_rocisa._register_fence` (`gir_to_rocisa.py:307`), which walks the
freshly built code tree and records every `SBarrier` in it.

Scoping the judgment to owned barriers is a deliberate policy, not an optimization: *a scaffold
barrier inside a scaffold arm is the scaffold's business*, and may well be intentional.
`Tests/unit/test_uniform_placement.py:191` pins that by calling the check with an empty owned list
over a module that does contain a barrier inside an arm, and asserting no finding.

**`UniformEmissionError`** — `uniform_emission.py:174`. The exception, and the whole failure
policy; see §18.1.5.

**`_STATS` and the report hook** — `uniform_emission.py:74-79`. A four-key module-level dict
(`kernels`, `regions`, `owned`, `inside`). With `TENSILE_UNIFORM_EMISSION_REPORT=1` in the
environment, an `atexit` hook prints the totals; otherwise the cost is three integer increments per
kernel. The reason this exists is stated in the source and is worth repeating as a general
principle: **a check that never fires must be able to show that it ran over real structure.** Zero
findings and zero regions look identical in a build log, and only one of them is good news.

One sharp edge in that instrumentation: `_STATS['owned'] += len(at)`, and `at` counts only the
owned barriers that were **found in the module**. A barrier in `ownedBarriers` that is not in this
module — stripped earlier, or emitted into the epilogue, which is appended after this call site —
is silently not counted, and the discrepancy between `len(ownedBarriers)` and `len(at)` is never
reported. If you are ever debugging "the check says it saw fewer fences than I emitted", that is
the line to look at.

##### 18.1.5 Failure policy: why fatal, and why exactly one kernel

`UniformEmissionError` derives from `RuntimeError`, and the choice of base class *is* the policy.
`KernelWriterAssembly.getSourceFileString` wraps kernel generation in
`except RuntimeError as e: printWarning(...); code = ""; errcode = -2`
(`KernelWriterAssembly.py:227-230`). So raising a `RuntimeError` subclass costs one kernel, named
in a warning, and the enclosing sweep continues. A bare `Exception` escapes that handler, propagates
out of the joblib worker and kills the whole build — measured on a deliberate fault injection as
`RC=1` with 63 kernels unbuilt.

*Why fail rather than warn.* The defect is a hang or a schedule-shifted race (§18.1.1). A warning in
a twenty-thousand-line build log is how several months of defects in this area survived.

*Why one kernel is the right blast radius.* A finding is **our** placement bug. It is not an invalid
configuration — the schedule model accepts these kernels — and it is not a gap in the non-GIR
