#### 19.7 A short checklist for a change to this package

1. **Re-run the pure suite first.** `cd Tensile/Tests/unit && PYTHONPATH=<root> python3 -m pytest
   --noconftest -p no:cacheprovider test_gir.py test_value_placement.py test_tdm_split.py` — 660
   assertions, under a minute, no build.
2. **Did you add a raise?** Then it needs a test that *triggers* it. The suite's own rule: a check
   that has never been seen to fire is not a check.
3. **Did you add a degradation?** Then it needs to be in the §19.2.8 table, or it needs to become a
   raise.
4. **Did you touch the CFG?** Then your pass is a `StructuralPass`, it owes `preds`/`succs`,
   `verify_gir`, and `prog.bump()`, and it must run inside `ScaffoldShapePass` before everything
   else.
5. **Did you add a `meta` key?** Then something must consume it. Every one of the seventeen keys the
   lowering writes is read by at least one analysis or by the emit plan; an unread key is a fact
   nobody is acting on, which is worse than an absent one because it reads like coverage.
6. **Did you widen a capability in `leaves.py`?** Then confirm it is a *widening* and not a new
   path — check whether the register packing, the stride, or the per-load register count changes.
   The refusal messages say which.
7. **Did you change what a Mark means?** Then update `_MARK_SCHEMA` (`gir/verify.py:75`), the
   `_plan_mark` payload (`gir/emit_plan.py:274`) and the `emit_block` dispatch arm
   (`gir_to_rocisa.py:110`) together. All three read the same `at` dict and none of them validates
   the others.
8. **Hand back for the hardware run.** Nothing in this package can tell you the emitted assembly is
   correct; §19.3.6 lists exactly what the suite cannot see.

---

#### 19.8 Symbol index: can it fail, and what does it do?

The catalogue above is organised by *failure*, so the definitions that cannot fail did not need an
entry there. This closing index covers them, so that every named thing in the package is accounted
for in this section. Entries are one line unless the symbol has a sharp edge worth naming. Symbols
already discussed above are not repeated.

**`gir/nodes.py`.** `Tile.coord_map()` (`:49`) and `Tile.shape_map()` (`:52`) are `dict(...)` over
the two tuple fields, so a consumer can index a coordinate or a size by mode name instead of
scanning; they exist because the fields are *tuples* (frozen and hashable, which a `Tile` must be to
be a dict key) and a tuple is the wrong shape for lookup. `Program.add_block(blk)` (`:477`) inserts
by label into the insertion-ordered block dict and returns the block, so a lowering can write
`b = prog.add_block(Block(...))` and keep the handle. Neither validates: `add_block` silently
replaces an existing label. Nothing does that today, and `G-CFG`'s phase counts would catch the
usual accident (two prologues), but a duplicate `steady1` would not be noticed.

**`gir/refs.py`.** `first_shared_ref(refs)` (`:32`) returns the single shared-space `Ref` or `None`.
It is for the **read** hop only, where the source is one op-class's shared tile and a second shared
source would be a *different movement*, not a member of this one — using it on a copy is the exact
bug `copy_unit` exists to prevent, so the two are deliberately separate functions rather than one
with a flag. `read_operand(inst)` (`:95`) returns the operand of a `shared → register` `Move`, or
`None`; it requires **both** a shared source and at least one register destination, which is what
excludes a copy (shared in `dsts`) and a direct-to-register global read (no shared at all).

**`gir/analyses/cfg.py`.** `BackEdgeSet.__iter__` (`:73`) yields the `BackEdge` records.
`BackEdgeSet.entering(label)` (`:87`) filters on `be.header` — the edges that *re-enter* the loop at
`label`. `BackEdgeSet.is_back_edge(src, target)` (`:91`) is the membership predicate. These three are
trivial, but the *fourth* member of the family, `leaving(label)` (`:76`), is where a real defect
lived and it explains why the naming is so careful: `leaving` filters on `be.src`, and the method it
replaced was called `headed_by`, which meant the exact **opposite** for the one case where source and
header differ — a multi-block loop body, where the back edge leaves the *last* copy while the header
is the first. The address-advance analysis asked `headed_by(header)`, got nothing, and silently
emitted **no increments at all**.

**`gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py`.** `DepDefuse` (`:24`) is the result object: two `id(inst)`-keyed maps
(`__init__` `:25`), `add(inst)` (`:29`) splits an instruction's `deps` triples into the two lists by
asking layer 1's `is_war(kind)` predicate — this is the one upward import in the whole `gir/`
subpackage (`gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py:19`) — and `raw(inst)` (`:36`) / `war(inst)` (`:39`) are the
accessors, each returning `[]` for an instruction never added. `DepDefuseAnalysis` (`:43`) walks
every `Move` and `Mma` in every block and indexes them; its `cache_key` (`:45`) pins the name
`"DepDefuse"`. `TokensPass` demands it (`gir/passes/tokens.py:124`) purely to force the consistency
walk; nothing currently *reads* the indexed edges, which are there for a layer-3 write-after-read
forwarding path.

**`gir/analyses/fence_regions.py`.** `_already_fenced(hazard, block, fenced, doms, reachable, succ)`
(`:107`) asks whether a fence placed in an **earlier** block already stands between a cross-block
hazard's two ends on every path. Without it the cover is per-block and blind across blocks — the
last steady copy feeds reads in two consecutive drain steps, so the second asks for a fence of its
own even though the first's already separates them. The condition is deliberately narrow, and
getting it narrow took two attempts: reachability alone wrongly accepts the prologue (which precedes
the producer), dominance alone wrongly accepts it too, and the candidate must also be a **different
block from the producer's**, because a loop block is reachable from itself along its own back edge
and so satisfies "reachable from the producer" for free while saying nothing about whether the fence
sits *after* it. That last clause went unnoticed while the first drain block had two predecessors;
once the degenerate arm was lowered to its own blocks the steady block began dominating the drain,
and a steady-entry fence started masking the real steady→drain requirement.
`_touched(blk, tokens)` (`:183`) lists `[(body_index, {token ids})]` for the block, in program order.
`_tokens_across(blk, slot, touched, reachable, tokens, covered)` (`:196`) computes what a fence at
`slot` must **name**, and it is one of the load-bearing definitions in the package: plain liveness
over the CFG,

```
live_across(point) = { b : b touched on some path INTO the point }
                   ∩ { b : b touched on some path OUT of the point }
```

with both halves spanning **blocks**, unioned with the endpoints of the edges the cover selected. It
must be liveness and not "the edges that placed it" because a barrier's entire ordering power is its
token set — the scheduler gives it each token as both a def and a use, so a buffer the barrier does
not name is not chained through it at all and its accesses may migrate across. A fence at slot 0 of
a drain block has nothing before it *in its own body*, yet every buffer the steady loop filled
reaches it; a within-block test would name none of them and emit a fence that orders nothing. A
block on a cycle is in its own reachable set, so a loop body's fences name everything the body
touches — which falls out of the definition rather than being a special case, and is not
conservatism: the back edge genuinely makes an access "before" the point in one trip an access
"after" it in the previous. The union-over-covered-edges form it replaced had been propped up by an
over-approximation elsewhere; fixing that widening correctly shrank one steady fence's token set from
three ids to one and took a multi-wave split configuration from 42 to 62 failures **without moving
any fence** — only the names on them changed.

**`gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py`.** `Reaching.is_relative(block_label)` (`:41`) reports whether that
block's entry generations could **not** be merged from its predecessors and were assigned an
arbitrary base; a consumer needing an *absolute* buffer identity must check it and widen.
`_resolve_phi_entry(blk)` (`:51`) returns `{Gen: entry_val}` from a header's phis — and its docstring
carries a correction worth keeping: a header phi contributes the declared entry value on the entry
edge and the transferred value on the loop edge, and those are **not** the same (ring 2, advance 1:
trip 0 enters at generation 0, trip 1 at generation 1), so keying on the declared value fixes a
*representative trip*, not an invariant. That is sound for the consumers that exist, because the LDS
memory token is a **logical** buffer name whose only requirement is the relative this-buffer-versus-
that-buffer distinction within one body. An earlier version of the docstring asserted the equality,
which is false and invited reading the resolved value as an absolute generation.
`_entry_of(blk, entries, relative=())` (`:69`) is the real merge: a header's entry is declared;
otherwise every known predecessor that **agrees** on a generation contributes it, and a generation
the predecessors disagree on — or that no predecessor supplies — gets `RELATIVE_BASE = 0` (`:66`)
with the block flagged relative. The disagreement is genuine, not a modelling slip: the first drain
block's two predecessors are the last steady copy and the prologue, and the generation the steady
loop leaves is trip-parity-dependent, so no compile-time constant is the merged value. What this
used to do was return `{}` — silently base 0 — documented as "there is nothing to merge", which
reads as a fact rather than a placeholder; a consumer then could not tell a merged generation from a
fabricated one, and one did read it as absolute. **Relativity is transitive** and was not: a block
inheriting from a relative predecessor inherits the arbitrary base with it. The old "exactly one
known predecessor → inherit" special case is gone, because one predecessor trivially agrees with
itself and the merge already covers it.

**`gir/analyses/gr_increment.py`.** `GrIncrementRegions` (`:104`) is the analysis class; its `run`
(`:122`) enumerates the movements (`_units`, `:155`) and calls `_flow` (`:196`) per movement.
`_reqs(prog, lab, unit)` (`:166`) is the per-block requirement list `[(inst, absolute_chunk)]`, and
it holds one of the sharpest corrections in the package: **a copy is not a chunk**. A region-split
movement delivers one reduction chunk with `nregions` load instructions, so the prologue's positional
index counts *loads* while the chunk derivation needs *chunks* — off by exactly that factor. At
two-deep prefetch with a two-way split, one operand's four prologue copies were read as chunks
0,1,2,3 instead of 0,0,1,1: the address ran to chunk 3 while the steady frame demanded 2, and the
solver closed the gap with a `−1` advance the emitter cannot express, so kernel generation raised.
At one-deep prefetch the same error is one *spurious* advance with no negative — no raise, just a
descriptor a chunk ahead, which is why those kernels built and miscompared instead. Dividing by
`nregions` is exact because the regions of one chunk are issued consecutively and in order, and that
is not an assumption: it is what the region-walk analysis emits and what `G-WALK` checks in program
order, so a violation is a verifier error rather than a silently wrong chunk here. `_topo(prog,
fwd_succs, fwd_preds)` (`:255`) is a Kahn topological order with back edges cut, appending any block
left unordered so it is still visited deterministically.

**`gir/analyses/swap_regions.py`.** `SwapRegions` (`:226`) is the analysis class. `_ring_of(prog,
hop, unit)` (`:104`) finds the ring depth by scanning for the first access on that hop whose `Ref`
names a `Gen`, defaulting to 1. `_requirements(blk, hop, unit, ring)` (`:116`) is the per-block
ordered `[(inst, required_generation)]`, computed **in the block's own chunk frame**: a loop-carried
`Ref` gives `(gdelta − blk.gen_rel) mod ring`, an absolute peel `Ref` gives `abs_gen mod ring`, and
a ring-less access contributes no requirement at all. Subtracting the block's own frame is what makes
the number comparable with any other block's once the edge's chunk delta is applied — computing
frame-free requirements *here* is what removed a spurious drain swap that came from reading a merged
generation as absolute. `_units(prog, hop)` (`:138`) lists the distinct pointer identities on a hop
in first-seen order (so the output is deterministic). `_topo(prog, fwd_succs, fwd_preds)` (`:178`) is
this module's own topological order; its docstring states why one pass suffices — with back edges
cut the CFG is a DAG, the loop header's incoming value comes from its preheader, and the back edge is
reconciled afterwards by the closure step, so no iteration to a fixpoint is needed. It is a *second
copy* of `gr_increment._topo` (`:255`) with a different docstring and the same body; the two should
be one function.

**`gir/analyses/lds_hazards.py`.** `Hazard.same_trip` (`:114`) is `distance == 0`: the two accesses
land on the same buffer in the **same** iteration, so the edge must be discharged *inside* the body —
by program order if same-agent, by a fence placed between them if not. Any non-zero distance is
purely loop-carried and **any** fence in the body separates trip *v* from trip *v+1*. A cross-block
pair has no trip distance at all (`distance is None`) and is therefore never `same_trip`.
`Hazard.in_program_order` (`:127`) is `producer.pos < consumer.pos` within one block; it is only
meaningful for a same-trip pair, and it is what distinguishes a legitimate same-agent in-place refill
from a violation of the copies-last rule that makes such a refill safe. `Unresolved` (`:138`) is the
frozen record of a pair whose frame could not be established — "reported, never silently dropped",
except that nothing production-side reads the report (§19.2.8, S3). `LdsHazardSet.__iter__` (`:152`)
and `__len__` (`:155`) make the result iterable and countable; `needing_fence()` (`:169`) returns the
cross-agent edges and its docstring flags it as **the only place the fence/no-fence decision is
made** — a same-agent edge is discharged by program order plus the completion counter, so fencing it
would be pure cost. `_ring_of(ref)` (`:180`) is `max(1, ref.gen.ring)` or 1.

`split_region_modes(prog)` (`gir/analyses/lds_hazards.py:185`) returns the per-operand region-axis
map with the axes of movements that have **one** region removed, and it is the fix to a token count
that was wrong on every kernel. The arithmetic: two matmul inputs split in two over a double-buffered
ring is `2 regions × 2 buffers = 4` tokens each, and the scale operands are never split, so they are
`1 × 2 = 2` each — twelve in total. Every emitted kernel named **sixteen**, because the
region-membership helper keyed on the axis tuple being non-empty and the scale tensors carry their
parent's axis. The tuple answers "which axis", never "how many"; the scales keep the axis
deliberately, because the register-rate derivation needs it broadcast, and removing it at the θ source
drove one scale operand's rate from 2 to 4 and cost 26 kernels. So the *count* must come from the
per-movement region count. Correcting it changed nothing on hardware (the same six cells failed
before and after): the four extra tokens named buffers no read consumed, and an unused def imposes no
ordering. They were removed because the count is arithmetic and sixteen was not it — not because a
kernel depended on the difference. An intermediate build showed a large regression and was briefly
blamed on this change; it was not, it also carried the θ-source experiment above. Two changes, one
build, one wrong conclusion. An operand absent from the per-movement map keeps its axes, so an
unknown count stays conservative.

`_regions_of(ref, operand, region_modes, extents)` (`:221`) returns, per region axis, the **set** of
region values an access may touch: a coordinate that pins the axis names one region, a coordinate
that does not mention it touches every region. The unknown is modelled as the full set and stays a
may-alias, because being conservative costs a fence while being optimistic **loses** one. The pin is
trusted on both hops, and that is the point — a region split is a *coordinate* fact.
`_disjoint_storage(a, b)` (`:267`) is the corresponding provable-disjointness test: different
operand ⇒ different tensor ⇒ different storage; same operand ⇒ disjoint iff some region axis has
non-overlapping possible value sets. Sets, not equality, so an access that pins nothing is disjoint
from nothing. `_shared_accesses(blk, region_modes, extents)` (`:278`) yields every shared-space touch
in program order — a `Move`'s shared destination is a write, its shared source is a read, and an
instruction may hold several (a fused cooperative copy carries one destination `Ref` per member),
each its own access on its own ring. `_reachable(prog)` (`:296`) is `{label: set of labels reachable
from it}`, by depth-first walk; **reachability, not dominance**, because a cross-block hazard exists
if *some* execution runs the producer before the consumer, and the first drain block is reachable
from the steady loop even though the steady loop does not dominate it (the degenerate path enters it
straight from the prologue). `_kind(producer, consumer)` (`:316`) is the four-line hazard classifier:
write→write is write-after-write, write→read is read-after-write, read→write is write-after-read,
read→read is not a hazard. `LdsHazards._provably_disjoint(p, c, reach)` (`:382`) is the cross-block
counterpart of `_disjoint_storage`, and it is deliberately weak: **only** a peel-to-peel pair in
absolute frames can be shown not to alias across blocks. A loop-carried access takes a different
generation on every trip, so comparing its block-entry (trip-0) value against another block's would
exclude pairs that genuinely alias on a later trip; and if either block's frame is *relative*, its
resolved generations are not comparable at all.

**`gir/analyses/loop_shape.py`.** `Linear.__add__(k)` (`:58`) shifts the constant term of the
`coeff·T + const` symbolic count — the whole reason `Linear` exists rather than a rendered string is
that the covering check must compare *integers*, and comparing rendered strings would make
`T - 2` and `T-2` different answers. `_does_work(blk)` (`:83`) is "does this block hold a `Move` or an
`Mma`" — a block that only tests does not. `_loop_blocks(prog, header, latch)` (`:88`, with the
nested `reach` `:93`) is the natural loop: blocks reachable from the header that can also reach the
latch. `_exit_tester(prog, blocks)` (`:106`) finds the block whose terminator leaves the loop, **and
it is not always the latch** — this is the distinction the whole analysis turns on. In a post-tested
loop the latch carries the exit test, so tester equals latch and the tester does work; in a pre-tested
loop the *header* carries it and the latch back-edges unconditionally, so tester ≠ latch and the
tester does no work. Looking only at the latch, as the first version did, finds no test at all in the
pre-tested shape and silently reports **no loop**, which is worse than being wrong.
`_test_position(prog, tester)` (`:124`) is therefore just `POST if _does_work(tester) else PRE`:
structural, no phase name, no flag, nothing declared. `_trips_from_node(t)` (`:133`) **reads** the
count off the `LoopBack` terminator rather than reconstructing it from the exit comparison plus the
test position — that reconstruction assumed the counter starts at 0 and steps by +1, assumptions the
backend does not share (its loop counter is initialized to the count and **decrements**), and
reconstructing across them is where an off-by-one lived. With the count held directly, the test
position no longer changes the answer and is purely an emission property.

**`gir/analyses/mem_tokens.py`.** `MemTokenSet.__len__` (`:90`) is the buffer count.
`MemTokenSet.tokens_for(ref)` (`:104`) returns the token id(s) a `Ref` touches, or `()` if it was
never assigned — **a tuple, not an int**, because an access that does not pin its region axis may
touch several buffers and must carry all of their ids, or the halves it does not name go unordered.
`MemTokenSet.id_of(buf)` (`:111`) is the reverse lookup. `_sort_key(buf)` (`:201`) is
`(operand, region, generation)`, which is what makes the id assignment **deterministic** across runs
— a non-deterministic numbering would make two builds of one kernel differ in their token operands
and defeat byte-comparison. `_expand(operand, regions, generation)` (`:205`) is the cross product of
the per-axis region sets: a pinned access yields one buffer, an access leaving an axis unpinned
yields one per value of that axis **and carries them all**, which is precisely the case where a split
tile's second-half load went unwaited.

**`gir/analyses/region_increment.py`.** `region_of(prog, ref)` (`:39`) reads the region coordinate
tuple straight off `Tile.coord`, returning `()` for an unsplit tile — a region split **is** a
coordinate, which is exactly why GIR can answer "which half" where the pre-existing scaffold cannot
(the scaffold's both-halves escape hatch exists because its split order and its loop order differ,
not because the fact is unknowable). `_n_regions(prog, unit)` (`:75`) reads the count θ derived from
the per-movement map, **not** from the axis tuple being non-empty: an operand can own a region axis
while being split into one region — the scale operands have exactly that shape — and treating the
axis as a walk asks such a movement for a coordinate value it correctly does not have.
`RegionIncrementRegions` (`:131`) is the analysis class; its `run` (`:138`) is a deliberate
**program-order scan** rather than a fixpoint, because the region walk is a sequence with a
statically known closing step, not a dataflow question. `_axis_delta(rms, frm, to)` (`:176`) turns a
flat region step into `{mode: delta}` over the non-zero axes, and the reason is arithmetic: `steps`
is the difference of two mixed-radix indices, so a byte displacement could only be recovered by
multiplying one stride — right while a single axis moves, wrong the moment two do. In a 2×2 region
grid the flat step `2 → 1` is `−1` on one axis and `+1` on the other, whose byte displacement is
`−D₁ + D₂`, not `−1 × D`. The per-axis form degenerates to the old scalar exactly when one axis is
live, which is every shape shipped so far — which is why the scalar looked correct for as long as it
did.

**`gir/analyses/short_path.py`.** `_groups(inst)` (`:121`) returns the register groups an instruction
touches, and it is **part of the correspondence identity, not decoration**: a split read puts two
instructions at the same `(operand, coordinate)`, distinguished only by which register groups they
fill (one half rotating a ring, the other in place). Without it the correspondence is ambiguous and
`_trace` raises — which is how the omission was found, rather than by silently pairing the wrong two.
`_entry_gens(prog)` (`:132`) collects `{gen.id: entry_val}` from the loop headers' phis; on the
folded path the steady loop takes **zero** trips (that is what the degenerate trip count means), so
every loop-carried generation still holds its phi's entry value and a drain `Ref`'s offset resolves
against that. This is the one place the folded path's semantics enter the resolution, and it is a
consequence of the branch being taken, not a convention. `_defs_uses(inst, entry, free_modes,
base=0)` (`:221`) produces the location keys the two arms are compared on — `('shared', operand,
generation)` and `('register', operand, group, slot, free-tile coord)` — and it registers a
quantum-wide read at **every** coordinate of its footprint via `covered_coords`, because one
definition fills many locations; otherwise a consumer at a non-leader coordinate looks unfed and the
arm is judged unable to stand alone. `pairing_cause(f_src, s_src)` (`:260`) classifies one
corresponded consumer's producer pair, returning `None` when the two frames agree and otherwise one
of three causes; the three spellings of "no producer reached here" are collected in `_UNSERVED`
(`:258`) so the classification cannot miss one. `Break` (`:359`) is the frozen per-consumer record —
which location, which producer on each side, and the cause. `FoldVerdict` (`:371`) is the analysis
result: the verdict string, a reason, the breaks, the short-arm keys absent from the folded path, the
short-arm consumers with no definition in the arm at all, a count of folded-path instructions with no
counterpart, the preconditions the *consumer* must satisfy, and the two block lists.
`FoldVerdict.foldable` (`:383`) is `verdict in (FOLD, VACUOUS)` — the vacuous case counts because the
arm is unreachable, so keeping it is pure code growth for a trip count no reduction has.
`FoldVerdict.causes()` (`:388`) is a histogram of break causes, which is what makes a matrix report
readable. `_arm_is_unreachable(prog)` (`:540`) decides the vacuous case **from the peel-validity
guard**, not from the peel depth: it used to be `M == 1`, justified by reasoning that was tied to a
non-strict guard, and the guard is now strict.

**`gir/analyses/uniform_placement.py`.** `Violation.__repr__` (`:87`) renders
`block[index] scope=…: reason at where` — the tests assert on this string
(`test_uniform_placement.py` checks for `role='producer'` in the repr), so it is a contract, not a
debug convenience. `_preds_of(term)` (`:91`) returns every `Pred` a terminator tests: one for a
two-way conditional, one per arm for a chain, and **none** for an unconditional jump, a sink, or a
counted loop — the last is the interesting case, because a `LoopBack` carries a trip *count* rather
than a comparison, and a count cannot discriminate agents. `_pred_symbols(pred)` (`:101`) returns the
symbols a predicate reads — its counter and its bound's variable, with a bare constant bound
contributing nothing — which is what gets matched against the declared agent-varying symbol set.
`_reachable_from(succ, start)` (`:110`) is the module's own forward reachability walk.

**`gir/analyses/value_placement.py`.** `ValuePlacementSolver._norm(v)` (`:114`) reduces a value
modulo the domain when there is one — `ℤ_ring` for a rotating buffer pointer, unbounded `ℤ` for a
global-read chunk index — and passes the two lattice sentinels through untouched. That single
parameter is the whole difference between the two problems the solver serves. `_fwd(v, p, b)` (`:119`)
re-expresses a value crossing an edge into the successor's frame by *subtracting* the edge's chunk
delta; `_bwd(v, b, s)` (`:123`) re-expresses a successor's demand back into the predecessor's frame by
*adding* it. The two are the reason the solver can be shared: everything frame-specific is in
`_delta`, supplied by the caller. `_exit_want(b, antic)` (`:149`) is the single value **all** of a
block's successors demand, expressed in that block's frame, or `None` — and `None` covers two cases
that have the same remedy: no successor demands anything, or they disagree. In both, one definition
at the block's exit cannot serve them, because there is one register and the branch comes after it.

**`gir/render.py` — the debug view.** None of these can fail the build (the whole renderer is
reached through `gir_text`, which swallows every exception into a comment), but several of them exist
*because* a dump that omitted a fact caused a wrong conclusion to survive, and that provenance is the
useful part.

- `_coord_str(coord)` (`:21`) joins `(axis, value)` pairs, skipping `None` values.
- `_gen_str(ref)` (`:25`) renders which buffer a `Ref` names: a loop-carried generation **identity**,
  an absolute generation **value**, or a register rotation slot. The two generation forms are
  deliberately spelled apart — they used to differ by one character, and an SSA identity read as a
  concrete value is exactly the confusion the peel-versus-steady split in `Ref` exists to prevent. It
  also emits *every* part that is present: an earlier chain of early returns hid a register residence
  whenever a generation was also present.
- `_covers_str(ref)` (`:55`) renders the absorbed movement-quantum axes. A dump showing only `coord`
  shows the *definition's* coordinate while every consumer's names more, so a wide read and a narrow
  one render identically — which is the shape of an entire class of confusion about why a consumer
  looks unfed.
- `_ref_str(ref)` (`:67`) composes the three above into one reference string.
- `_dep_str(inst)` (`:82`) renders the dependency obligations **with their hazard kind**. The kind is
  the one field that decides issue order — a write-after-read edge means the writer must be placed
  after its prior readers — and it was invisible here.
- `_token_str(mv)` (`:101`) renders the LDS memory tokens a movement touches. It prints the storage
  ids and the completion token **apart**, under different prefixes; an `elif` once made the
  completion token unreachable, and one prefix served two different quantities.
- `_move_line(mv)` (`:124`) is `copy`/`read` plus sources, destinations, tokens and dependencies —
  the hop kind is derived from whether any destination is in shared space, never from a flag.
- `_mma_line(mm)` (`:131`) renders `mma <dst> += <srcs>   # <block>` from the actual `Ref`s, so a
  microscaling or sparse instruction shows all of its operands rather than a fixed two.
- `_pred_str(p)` (`:137`) renders a terminator predicate **with its scaffold hint**, because the
  label is attached downstream and is the whole reason a consumer can route an arm — a dump that
  omits it makes every terminator look unroutable, which is indistinguishable from the labelling pass
  not having run.
- `_term_line(term)` (`:152`) is the per-terminator-kind dispatch; note it is a *fourth* place that
  switches on terminator type, though unlike the three in §19.4.1 it only formats and cannot cause a
  wrong analysis.
- `_short_loop_lines(prog)` (`:170`) reports what happened to the degenerate arm — folded or kept —
  and reads the guard's false-edge target **off the CFG** rather than asserting it, because on a kept
  verdict it targets the arm and on a folded one the drain. It also qualifies the recorded obligation
  by verdict, since the obligation tuple is built before the verdict is known and is a statement about
  the *folded* path.
- `_theta_facts_lines(prog)` (`:234`) prints the θ facts the blocks are derived from — which
  coordinates are regions, which regions are the agent's rather than the coordinate's, which operands
  share a fused movement. It exists because a wrong conclusion once survived a whole investigation
  purely because those facts were absent from every dump, and its text about agent-relative regions
  is now a *retraction* of an earlier claim, with a test asserting the retraction is present.

---

That closes the section. Every module in `Tensile/Lowering/` has at least one entry in the failure
catalogue (§19.2), the test map (§19.3) or this index (§19.8); every raise, assert and documented
degradation is enumerated with its trigger and its remedy; the four extension recipes name the
concrete symbols to touch; and the gaps in §19.5 are stated with what closing each would cost rather
than as a list of intentions.

If you read only one thing here before changing this code, make it §19.1: **refuse, report, or
degrade — and if you degrade, put it in the table.** Every defect this package has shipped came from
a place that answered when it should have refused.

---

### 20. Complexity, cost and optimisation opportunities

This section is about **compile time**: how many Python operations the `Tensile/Lowering/` stack
performs to turn one θ point into one finalized `Program` plus its emitted rocisa, where those
operations concentrate, and what a future maintainer should change first if the number gets in the
way. It is also the section that closes the coverage of the package: every definition in
`Tensile/Lowering/` that the earlier sections describe *functionally* is described here again in
**cost** terms — its asymptotic shape, the practical value of its `n`, and how often it runs.

Nothing here is estimated. Every millisecond figure below was measured by running the pure-Python
half of the stack (θ → LoopIR → GIR → emit plan; no `rocisa`, no GPU) under `time.perf_counter`
and `cProfile` on the five kernel shapes tabulated in §20.2, on the machine this report was written
on. Reproduce with the recipe in §20.22. Absolute numbers will move with the interpreter; the
*ratios* between stages are the durable content, and those held across every shape measured.

#### 20.1 The two cost regimes, and which one you are in

Kernel generation in TensileLite is embarrassingly parallel: `TensileCreateLibrary` fans kernels out
over joblib workers, one kernel per task. So the quantity that matters is **wall time per kernel**,
not aggregate throughput, and it matters twice:

* **The sweep regime.** A tuning matrix builds thousands of kernels. At 8 ms of GIR per kernel the
  lowering is invisible against assembly emission and the assembler; at 165 ms it is not, and a
  36-cell × 200-solution sweep pays about twenty CPU-minutes for the lowering alone.
* **The interactive regime.** A developer builds one kernel and reads its `.gir` dump. Here the
  total is under a fifth of a second at the very worst shape, and no optimisation in this section
  is worth its risk.

The measured envelope, for `build_gir(theta, mainloop=emit_mainloop(theta))` — the single entry
point `KernelWriter._loopModelGirProgram` calls (`KernelWriter.py:3788`) — is:

| shape | GIR body size | `emit_mainloop` (layer 1) | `build_gir` (lower + 7 passes + verify) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| bf16 NT KMN, MT32×32, DepthU 64, 1 wave | 96 instructions | 9 ms | 8 ms |
| same, 4 waves (fences live) | 96 | 9 ms | 9 ms |
| bf16, DepthU 256, 1 wave | 336 | 11 ms | 30 ms |
| bf16, MIWaveTile 4×4, DepthU 512, 1 wave | 1936 | 30 ms | 76 ms |
| bf16, MIWaveTile 4×4, DepthU 512, 4 waves | 1936 | 31 ms | **165 ms** |

**What the reproduction recipe in §20.22 does and does not cover.** The recipe times
`lower_to_gir` plus a manual pass loop rather than calling `build_gir`, so it reproduces a **strict
subset** of the third column: it omits `verify_gir` and the post-pipeline `_check_rotation_waw`
gate, which §20.11 measures at 19 ms and §11.13 at a further few. Read the recipe's numbers as
"lowering + passes", and expect them to come in roughly 20 ms low against this table at the large
shapes. That is deliberate — the recipe exists to attribute time *per pass*, which needs the loop
unrolled — but the two columns are not the same quantity and the difference is larger than several
of the optimisations ranked in §20.19.

Two facts to take from the table before any detail:

1. **The cost is superlinear in the unrolled body length, not in the CFG.** The CFG has 4–6 blocks
   at every shape in the table; it is fixed by the peel depth `M` and the fold verdict, and it never
   grows with `DepthU`. Every cost that grows is a cost *inside one block's body*.
2. **The multi-wave column is the whole story at the largest shape.** One wave: 76 ms. Four waves:
   165 ms. Nothing about the program changed except that `meta['agent_distributed']` became true, so
   every LDS hazard became cross-agent and `FenceRegions` (§20.6) had 1284 edges to cover instead of
   zero. That single analysis is 60 ms of the 165.

#### 20.2 What `n` actually is

Five quantities drive everything. Their measured values, on the same five shapes (the fold verdict
was FOLD everywhere except the two DepthU 64 rows, which kept a `short` arm before the fold pass and
lost it after):

| quantity | symbol | DU64 MT32 | DU256 | DU512 MIWT4 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| blocks in the CFG | `B` | 6 → 4 | 6 → 4 | 6 → 4 |
| instructions in all bodies, before the passes | `I` | 96 | 336 | 1936 |
| instructions in the longest body (`steady`) | `L` | 19 | 67 | 387 |
| shared-space `Ref`s (LDS accesses) in all bodies | `A` | 50 | 170 | 650 |
| shared accesses in the `steady` body alone | `A_s` | 10 | 34 | 130 |
| LDS hazard edges | `H` | 140 | 524 | 2064 |
| distinct memory-token ids | `T_id` | 4 | 4 | 4 |
| `PendingMark`s applied | `P` | 20 | 20 | 20 (26 at 4 waves) |

`I` is the product of the per-trip WMMA count (`MIWaveTile[0] × MIWaveTile[1] × DepthU/MatrixInstK`)
and the peel structure. It is the only quantity that can reach four digits, and at the largest shape
TensileLite ships it is under 2000. **`B` never exceeds about a dozen**, which is why not one of the
CFG walks in the package — `Program.walk_rpo`, `cfg.successors`, `_reachable`, `_separates`,
`_topo`, `_loop_blocks` — is worth a second thought. `T_id` is startlingly small: four buffers
(A and B, two generations each) at every unsplit shape, twelve at a two-way TDMSplit with MX scales.
Any data structure keyed on tokens is free.

The load-bearing consequence: **an algorithm that is quadratic in `A` or in `L` is the only kind
that can hurt, and the package contains exactly four of them** (§20.5, §20.6, §20.10, §20.12).

Per-pass timings, taken by running `pipeline()` (`gir/passes/pipeline.py:36`) one pass at a time with
`AnalysisManager.invalidate()` between them exactly as `run_pipeline` (`gir/passes/pipeline.py:61`)
does, then the two gates and the plan:

| stage | DU64 1w | DU64 4w | DU512 MIWT4 1w | DU512 MIWT4 4w |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `lower_to_gir` (`loopir_to_gir.py:484`) | 2.9 ms | 2.7 ms | 59 ms | 59 ms |
| `ScaffoldShapePass` (`gir/passes/scaffold_shape.py:47`) | 0.69 | 0.66 | 10.8 | 10.8 |
| `RegGenPass` (`gir/passes/reg_gen.py:24`) | 0.03 | 0.02 | 0.29 | 0.31 |
| `TokensPass` (`gir/passes/tokens.py:120`) | 0.47 | 0.39 | 5.3 | 5.4 |
| `CollectPendingMarksPass` (`gir/passes/collect_pending.py:24`) | 1.57 | 1.99 | 17.4 | **65.2** |
| `PlacementPass` (`gir/passes/placement.py:30`) | 0.03 | 0.04 | 0.15 | 0.20 |
| `ApplyMarksPass` (`gir/passes/apply_marks.py:19`) | 0.03 | 0.03 | 0.08 | 0.11 |
| `RecordUnemittedPass` (`gir/passes/record_unemitted.py:27`) | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| `verify_gir` (`gir/verify.py:422`) | 1.11 | 1.12 | 18.4 | 19.3 |
| `check_plan` (`gir/verify_dataflow.py:277`) | 0.64 | 0.58 | 16.8 | 13.0 |
| `plan_program` over all blocks (`gir/emit_plan.py:311`) | 0.30 | 0.30 | 6.0 | 6.0 |

Read as a budget for the worst shape (DU512 MIWT4, 4 waves, 165 ms end to end):

```
   CollectPendingMarksPass    65 ms   40%   ── FenceRegions 61, SwapRegions 3, GrInc 0.8, RegionInc 0.2
   loopir_to_gir              59 ms   36%   ── the tree walk + node construction (§20.15)
   verify_gir                 19 ms   12%   ── of which _check_tokens 14.6 (a RECOMPUTE, §20.11)
   check_plan                 13 ms    8%   ── of which ~12 is re-planning blocks (§20.10)
   ScaffoldShapePass          11 ms    7%   ── ShortPathFold is 0.02 ms; the 11 is _flatten-free
   TokensPass                  5 ms    3%
   everything else            <1 ms
```

And the individual analyses, each timed on a **fresh** `AnalysisManager` so the number is its full
cost with dependencies, at DU512 MIWT4 4 waves:

| analysis | path:line | cost | dominant term |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `GenReaching` | `gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py:114` | 0.78 ms | one RPO pass over `I` refs |
| `LdsHazards` | `gir/analyses/lds_hazards.py:326` | 10.3 ms | `O(A_s²)` + `O(B²·A²)` |
| `MemTokenAssignment` | `gir/analyses/mem_tokens.py:130` | 3.3 ms | `O(A)` with a sort |
| `ShortPathFold` | `gir/analyses/short_path.py:395` | 0.02 ms | *the arm was already folded* |
| `UniformPlacement` | `gir/analyses/uniform_placement.py:121` | 0.10 ms | `O(F·B)` |
| `SwapRegions` | `gir/analyses/swap_regions.py:226` | 3.0 ms | `O(U_hop · I)` rescans |
| `GrIncrementRegions` | `gir/analyses/gr_increment.py:104` | 0.83 ms | `O(U · I)` rescans |
| `RegionIncrementRegions` | `gir/analyses/region_increment.py:131` | 0.24 ms | `O(I)` |
| `FenceRegions` | `gir/analyses/fence_regions.py:257` | **60.8 ms** | greedy set cover, §20.6 |
| `Dominators` / `BackEdges` | `gir/analyses/cfg.py:23`, `:95` | <0.05 ms | `O(B²)` on `B ≈ 4` |
| `LoopShape` | `gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:144` | <0.05 ms | `O(B²)` |
| `RegBandAnalysis` | `gir/analyses/reg_band.py:38` | 0.29 ms | `O(I)` |
| `DepDefuseAnalysis` | `gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py:43` | ~0.2 ms | `O(I)` |

The `ShortPathFold` figure needs a caveat that is itself a cost fact: it is 0.02 ms *because it was
asked after the fold pass had already deleted the arm*, so it returns `NA` at
`gir/analyses/short_path.py:401` without tracing anything. Asked before the fold — which is when
`FoldShortPathPass` (`gir/passes/fold_short_path.py:58`) actually asks it — it runs `_trace`
(`gir/analyses/short_path.py:291`) twice over `M+1` blocks and costs a few milliseconds at the large
shape. That is inside the 10.8 ms `ScaffoldShapePass` figure.

#### 20.4 The fixpoints, and how many rounds they actually run

Four things in this package are iterative. All four converge in a number of rounds bounded by the
CFG depth, which is 4 to 6.

**`Dominators.run` (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:27`).** The textbook iterative dominator-set computation:
initialise `dom(entry) = {entry}` and everything else to the full block set, then repeat
`dom(n) = {n} ∪ ⋂_{p ∈ preds(n)} dom(p)` until no set changes.

```
    dom[b] := (b == entry) ? {entry} : ALL
    repeat until no change:
        for b in blocks, b != entry:
            new := {b} ∪ intersection over known preds p of dom[p]
            if new != dom[b]: dom[b] := new; changed
```

Worst case `O(B²)` rounds × `O(B²)` set work = `O(B⁴)`, which for `B ≤ 12` is at most twenty
thousand set-element operations and measures below 50 µs. It visits blocks in `prog.blocks` insertion
order rather than reverse postorder, which costs an extra round or two and is not worth fixing.
`successors(prog)` (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:17`) is the plain helper it builds the predecessor map from:
`{label: [successor labels that exist as blocks]}`, `O(B + E)`, filtering the `'end'` pseudo-target.
It is not an `Analysis`, so it is **recomputed at every call site** — `Dominators`, `BackEdges`
indirectly, `lds_hazards._reachable`, `fence_regions.FenceRegions.run`, `swap_regions.SwapRegions.run`,
`gr_increment.GrIncrementRegions.run`, `uniform_placement.UniformPlacement.run`,
`loop_shape._loop_blocks`. Eight recomputations of an `O(B)` dictionary per pipeline run: measurable
in a profile, invisible in a clock.

**`BackEdges.run` (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:99`).** Not iterative at all: it asks `Dominators` once and
then tests every CFG edge `src → tgt` for `tgt ∈ dom(src)`, `O(E)`. Each hit becomes a `BackEdge`
(`gir/analyses/cfg.py:59`, constructed at `:63`) carrying `src`, `header`, and *the source block's
`GenXfer` list*, so a consumer keys the generation transfer per back edge rather than assuming
`xfers[0]`. The result is a `BackEdgeSet` (`gir/analyses/cfg.py:69`, `__init__` at `:70`) with four
`O(E)` linear-scan accessors: `__iter__` (`:73`), `leaving(label)` (`:76`, filters on `be.src`),
`entering(label)` (`:87`, filters on `be.header`), and `is_back_edge(src, target)` (`:91`). Every one
is a scan of a list whose length is the number of back edges — **one**, in every program this package
has ever built. Indexing them would be pure ceremony.

**`GenReaching.run` (`gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py:115`) is not a fixpoint at all, and that is a
deliberate cost choice worth naming.** It makes exactly one pass in reverse postorder
(`Program.walk_rpo`, `gir/nodes.py:487`, whose recursive helper is `visit` at `:495`), merging each
block's entry generations from predecessors already visited and then resolving every `Ref` in the
body. `O(I)` total. Iterating to a fixpoint would be the textbook thing to do; it is unnecessary
because the only cyclic edge is the back edge, and the back edge's contribution is *not* merged into
the header — it is recorded separately as a transfer (`by_xfer`, keyed `(block_label, gen.id)`),
because the header's phi declares its own entry value. That is the whole reason the analysis costs
0.78 ms instead of five rounds of that.

The single pass has a price, paid in precision rather than time, and the module is explicit about it
(`gir/analyses/gen_reaching.py:51`, `_resolve_phi_entry`): keying on the declared `entry_val` pins a
**representative trip**, not an invariant. The supporting cast:

* `_entry_of(blk, entries, relative)` (`:69`) — the real merge. A header returns its phi map and
  `is_relative=False`. Otherwise it collects the known predecessors' maps, and for each `Gen`: if
  every predecessor supplies it and they agree, that is the merged value; otherwise it is
  `RELATIVE_BASE = 0` (`:66`) and the block is flagged relative. Relativity is transitive — a block
  whose predecessor is relative is relative — which is checked with `any(p in relative …)` at `:103`.
  Cost `O(preds × gens)`, both single digits.
* `Reaching` (`:22`, `__init__` at `:26`) — the result object. `of(ref)` (`:32`) is a dict lookup on
  `id(ref)`; `is_relative(block_label)` (`:41`) a frozenset membership; `xfer(block_label, gen)`
  (`:46`) a dict lookup on `(label, gen.id)`. All `O(1)`. The **`id(ref)` keying** is the one
  structural cost hazard in the module: the result holds `prog` alive precisely so those identities
  stay valid, and any pass that *replaces* a `Ref` object silently orphans its entry. Nothing does
  today (passes insert `Mark`s, never rebuild `Ref`s), but it is the reason a future
  `Ref`-rewriting pass must bump `prog.version` rather than mutate in place.

**`ValuePlacementSolver` (`gir/analyses/value_placement.py:92`) is the only genuine two-fixpoint
solver, and it is run once per (hop, unit) pair.** Its shape:

```
    antic():                                   # backward, gir/analyses/value_placement.py:128
        inn[b] := first access's value, or BOTTOM
        repeat until stable:
            for each accessless b:
                inn[b] := meet over successors s of bwd(inn[s], b, s)

    avail(antic):                              # forward, :164
        repeat until stable:
            for each b:
                a_in[b]  := meet over preds p of fwd(leave[p], p, b)   (seeded at entry)
                body[b]  := last access's value, else a_in[b]
                leave[b] := the successors' agreed demand if any, else body[b]

    solve(on_conflict):                        # :193
        intra-block defs  : between consecutive accesses with different values
        head defs         : a_in[b] != antic[b]  (single-pred: place; multi-pred: report)
        exit defs         : body[b] != the successors' agreed value
```

with `meet` (`:56`) the three-point lattice (`BOTTOM` identity, equal values agree, disagreement is
`TOP`), `_norm` (`:114`) applying the modulus (`ℤ_ring` for a rotating pointer, `ℤ` for the
monotonically-advancing global address), `_fwd` (`:119`) / `_bwd` (`:123`) re-expressing a value
across an edge via the caller's `edge_delta`, and `_exit_want` (`:149`) returning the single value
every successor demands or `None`. `Access` (`:68`) is a frozen `(block, node, value)`; `Placement`
(`:76`) is a frozen `(block, after, before, from_value, to_value, at_exit)` — the window, with the
point deliberately left to `PlacementPass`.

Both loops are "sweep every block, repeat while anything changed", so a round is `O(B)` and the
round count is bounded by the length of the longest chain of accessless blocks, which is 1 or 2 in
every real program (only the loop header and, occasionally, a drain step lack accesses for a given
pointer). Measured: `SwapRegions` calls it four times (read hop × {A,B}, copy hop × {A,B}) and the
whole analysis is 3.0 ms at the largest shape — **and almost none of that is the solver**. The next
subsection says where it goes instead.

#### 20.5 Quadratic #1 — `LdsHazards`, `O(A_s²)` within a block and `O(B²·A²)` across

`LdsHazards.run` (`gir/analyses/lds_hazards.py:329`) is the second-largest single analysis and the
input to the largest. Structurally:

```
    by_block[b] := list(_shared_accesses(b))          # O(A)
    for each block b:                                  # SAME-BLOCK: every unordered pair
        for i < j over by_block[b]:  _pair(a_i, a_j)   # O(|by_block[b]|^2)
    _cross_block(...)                                  # CROSS-BLOCK: every ordered block pair
```

`_shared_accesses(blk, region_modes, extents)` (`:278`) walks the body once, yielding an `Access`
(`:77`) per shared `Ref`, with `regions` computed by `_regions_of` (`:221`). `Access.gdelta` (`:88`)
and `Access.storage` (`:92`) are trivial property accessors; `storage` returns `(operand, regions)`
and is what makes a TDMSplit tile's two halves distinguishable.

The same-block loop is the textbook `n²/2`. With `A_s = 130` in the DU512 steady body that is 8385
`_pair` calls; the profiler counted 23,719 `_pair` invocations across all blocks and 76,127 `_kind`
calls at that shape. `_pair` (`:391`) is cheap and short-circuits hard: `_kind(a, b)` (`:316`)
returns `None` for read→read and is checked first; `_disjoint_storage(a, b)` (`:267`) returns True
for different operands, which halves the survivors immediately. `_ring_of(ref)` (`:180`) is a two-
attribute lookup. Surviving pairs go to `_emit` (`:433`), which appends **both** directions with
distances `d` and `(-d) mod S` — that is why the edge count `H` is roughly twice the surviving pair
count.

`_cross_block` (`:345`) is the term with the frightening exponent: for every ordered pair of blocks
`(pb, cb)` where `cb` is reachable from `pb`, it takes the full cross product of their accesses.
That is `O(B² · (A/B)²) = O(A²)` in the worst case, and with `B = 4` and the accesses concentrated in
`steady` and the two drains it really is a few times `A²/2`. `_provably_disjoint` (`:382`) is the
only pruning: it returns True only for a peel↔peel pair in absolute frames with different
generations, so a loop-carried access on either side keeps the pair. Measured, this whole function
is 10 ms of the 10.3 ms analysis at DU512 — it *is* `LdsHazards`.

The result wrapper adds no cost of its own but does add **repeated linear scans**, which matter
because its consumer calls one of them per block. `LdsHazardSet` (`:145`, `__init__` at `:148`)
stores a tuple; `__iter__` (`:152`) and `__len__` (`:155`) are trivial; `edges(kind=, block=,
cross_agent=)` (`:158`) filters the whole tuple per call; `needing_fence()` (`:169`) is
`edges(cross_agent=True)`, i.e. a full `O(H)` scan; `unresolved()` (`:176`) returns the tuple of
`Unresolved` records (`:138`). `FenceRegions.run` calls `needing_fence()` **once per block** inside
its RPO loop (`gir/analyses/fence_regions.py:275`), so at `H = 1284` and `B = 4` that is 5136
predicate evaluations plus four list constructions of 1284 elements each. Small against the 60 ms
that follows, but it is the cheapest thing on the fix list: hoist it out of the loop.

Two helpers in this module are pure `meta` arithmetic and run once each:

* `split_region_modes(prog)` (`:185`) — `region_modes` with the axes of one-region movements
  removed, so an operand that carries a region *axis* but has only one region (the MX scales) does
  not get a phantom region dimension. `O(operands × axes)`; the reason the token count at a
  two-way-split MX kernel is twelve and not sixteen.
* `_regions_of(ref, operand, region_modes, extents)` (`:221`) — per region axis, the *set* of region
  values the access may touch. A pinned coordinate gives a singleton; an unpinned one, or one the
  `Ref.covers` quantum spans, gives the full range. Called once per shared access from
  `_shared_accesses` and again from `mem_tokens`, `O(axes)` each, building a `frozenset` per axis.
  At `A = 650` that is 650 small frozenset allocations, twice. Negligible, but it is one of the two
  places (`covered_coords` is the other) where the package allocates a container per instruction.

`_reachable(prog)` (`:296`) is a from-every-block forward closure, `O(B·(B+E))`, and is computed
**twice per pipeline run** — once inside `LdsHazards._cross_block` and once inside
`FenceRegions.run` (`:264`), which imports it directly. At `B = 4` the duplication is free; it is
listed here because it is the clearest example of the pattern that *would* cost if `B` ever grew
(persistent / grid-stride loops as an outer time level would do exactly that).

`Hazard` (`:103`) is a frozen record with two derived properties, both `O(1)`: `same_trip` (`:114`,
`distance == 0`) and `in_program_order` (`:127`, same block and `producer.pos < consumer.pos`).
They are re-evaluated on every `_admissible_slots` call, i.e. once per hazard per candidate block —
a property lookup, not a computation, and correctly left as one.

#### 20.6 Quadratic #2 — `FenceRegions`, and the 242,310 integers

This is the bottleneck. 60.8 ms of a 165 ms build at the worst shape; 1.99 ms at the common one.
The cost is entirely in the greedy set cover and its input representation, and both are fixable
without touching the algorithm's answer.

**What it computes.** For each block in reverse postorder, take the cross-agent hazards whose
consumer is in that block (plus same-block ones), drop those a fence in an earlier block already
covers, then choose the fewest *slots* — a slot `i` meaning "immediately before `body[i]`", with
slot `len(body)` at the end — such that every remaining hazard has a fence between its two ends.

**`_admissible_slots(hazard, n_slots, block)` (`gir/analyses/fence_regions.py:51`)** materialises,
as a `frozenset` of Python ints, every slot at which one fence discharges one hazard:

| hazard shape | admissible set | size |
|---|---|---|
| cross-block, `block` is the consumer's | `{s : s ≤ consumer.pos}` | `consumer.pos + 1` |
| cross-block, otherwise | `∅` | 0 |
| same-trip, producer before consumer | `{s : a < s ≤ b}` | `b − a` |
| loop-carried (or producer after consumer) | `{s : s > a or s ≤ b}` | `n_slots − a + b` |

The last row is the expensive one and it is the *common* one: a loop-carried pair admits nearly every
slot in the body. **Measured at DU512 MIWT4 4 waves: 1284 cross-agent hazards, `n_slots = 388`, and
the total number of set elements constructed is 242,310.** At DU64 the same figure is 784. That is
a factor of 309 for a factor of 20 in body length — the product of "more hazards" and "each hazard
admits more slots", i.e. genuinely `Θ(H · L)`.

**`_cover(hazards, n_slots, block)` (`:75`)** is greedy set cover over those sets:

```
    admissible[i] := _admissible_slots(hazards[i], n_slots, block)     # O(H·L) total
    if any admissible[i] is empty: RAISE   (the emitted order is undischargeable)
    remaining := {0..H-1}
    while remaining:
        best := argmax over s in 0..n_slots of  |{i in remaining : s in admissible[i]}|
                (ties to the EARLIEST slot, via the -s secondary key)
        chosen[best] := hazards covered by best
        remaining -= covered
```

The `argmax` line is `O(n_slots · |remaining|)` per round. The profiler shows 247,774 evaluations of
the inner generator at `:100` and 1568 `sum` calls — i.e. **four rounds**, `n_slots ≈ 390`, and about
400 remaining hazards averaged over the rounds. Greedy set cover is `O(rounds · n_slots · H)`, and
because a loop-carried hazard admits nearly everything, `rounds` is tiny (the measured fence count is
**6** for 1284 edges, across four blocks). So the asymptotic villain is not the greedy loop count —
it is the constant factor of doing membership tests against `H` Python frozensets `n_slots` times per
round.

The rest of the module is cheap and is where the *correctness* lives:

* `_already_fenced(hazard, block, fenced, doms, reachable, succ)` (`:107`) — is a fence in an
  already-processed block on every path from producer to consumer? `O(|fenced| · (B+E))` via
  `_separates`. `doms` and `reachable` are accepted and, since the separator rewrite, no longer
  read — see §20.18 for the dead-parameter note.
* `_separates(x, pb, cb, succ)` (`:161`) — delete `x` from the graph and ask whether `cb` is still
  reachable from `pb`'s successors. `O(B+E)`, called 1104 times in the profiled run (once per
  candidate hazard per already-fenced block).
* `_touched(blk, tokens)` (`:183`) — `[(body index, {token ids})]` for one block, `O(L)`. Computed
  once for **every** block up front at `:267`, which is the right call: `_tokens_across` needs every
  block's footprint, not just its own.
* `_tokens_across(blk, slot, touched, reachable, tokens, covered)` (`:196`) — plain liveness: the
  tokens touched on some path *into* the point intersected with those touched on some path *out of*
  it, unioned with the ends of the covered edges. `O(B + L + |covered|)` per fence. With six fences
  and `T_id = 4` this is nothing, and it is worth stressing **why** it is nothing: the token space is
  tiny, so the union/intersection sets never exceed a dozen elements even when the body has 387
  instructions.
* `_region_at(body, slot)` (`:247`) — a degenerate one-slot `Region`, `O(1)`.
* `FenceRegions.run` (`:260`) itself — RPO over blocks, per block: build `mine` (the `O(H)` scan
  noted above), call `_cover`, and emit one `PendingMark` per chosen slot with its `buffers`,
  `tokens`, `scope`, `kinds` and `edges` payload.

#### 20.7 The repeated whole-program rescan: the two pointer analyses

`SwapRegions` costs 3.0 ms and `GrIncrementRegions` 0.83 ms at the largest shape. Almost none of
that is the `ValuePlacementSolver` fixpoint (§20.4). It is **rescanning every instruction in the
program, once per pointer, three times over.**

`SwapRegions.run` (`gir/analyses/swap_regions.py:227`) does, for each of the two hops:

```
    for unit in _units(prog, hop):          # scan #1: O(I) to enumerate the pointers
        _flow(prog, hop, unit, ...):
            ring  := _ring_of(prog, hop, unit)          # scan #2: O(I), stops at first match
            reqs  := {b: _requirements(b, hop, unit)}   # scan #3: O(I), full
            solve
```

* `_hop_access(inst, hop)` (`:77`) is the shared predicate: `(unit, shared_ref)` or `None`. For the
  read hop it calls `read_operand` (`gir/refs.py:95`) and `first_shared_ref` (`gir/refs.py:32`); for
  the copy hop, `copy_unit` (`gir/refs.py:58`). It is invoked from all three scans, so the true
  count is `3 × U_hop × I` calls, with `U_hop` = 2 (A and B) on each hop. At `I = 1936` that is
  ~23,000 `_hop_access` calls, each of which does an `isinstance`, a space test over the `Ref`
  tuples, and for the copy hop a `copy_unit` that builds a set of rotation states.
* `_units(prog, hop)` (`:138`) returns the distinct pointer identities in first-seen order — an
  `O(I)` scan with an `O(U)` membership test against a *list*, which is correct precisely because a
  list preserves order and `U ≤ 4`.
* `_ring_of(prog, hop, unit)` (`:104`) scans until it finds the first `Ref` of that unit carrying a
  `Gen`, then returns its ring. Early-exits, so in practice `O(L_prologue)`, but the loop is written
  over the whole program.
* `_requirements(blk, hop, unit, ring)` (`:116`) is the real per-block scan: for each matching
  instruction, the frame-free requirement `(gdelta − blk.gen_rel) mod ring`, or `abs_gen mod ring`
  for a peel `Ref`. `O(L)` per block per unit.

The CFG plumbing around it is all `O(B+E)` and runs once per `run`, not per unit:
`_unemitted_edges(prog, headers)` (`:150`) — the edges into `model_only` blocks, the only paths
placement may ignore; `_topo(prog, fwd_succs, fwd_preds)` (`:178`) — Kahn's algorithm with back
edges cut, `O(B+E)` (note it uses `ready.pop(0)` on a list, an `O(B)` operation, giving `O(B²)`; at
`B = 4` this is four comparisons and is not worth a `deque`); `_edge_delta(prog, src, dst,
back_pairs)` (`:203`) — the chunk-frame conversion for one edge, `O(1)`, but called by the solver
`O(rounds × E)` times as a **Python closure** rather than a precomputed table. `SwapRegions._flow`
(`:263`) builds that closure and the `on_conflict` reporter (`:286`) fresh per unit.

`GrIncrementRegions` (`gir/analyses/gr_increment.py:104`) has the same shape and the same rescans:
`cache_key` (`:119`) pins the name; `run` (`:122`) builds the two filtered CFGs and calls `_flow`
(`:196`) per unit; `_units` (`:155`) is the `O(I)` enumeration; `_reqs` (`:166`) the `O(L)` per-block
requirement list; `_copy_of(inst)` (`:66`) the predicate (a copy is a `Move` with a `global` source
and a shared destination); `_chunk_of(blk, ref, peel_seq)` (`:84`) the `O(1)` chunk derivation, which
for a peel `Ref` uses the **positional** index rather than `abs_gen` because `abs_gen` is a ring slot
and equals the chunk only while the ring is at least as deep as the peel. `_flow`'s two closures,
`delta` (`:226`) and `on_conflict` (`:232`), and the module-level `_topo` (`:255`) — a second copy of
`swap_regions._topo`, differing only in that it always appends the unordered remainder — round it
out. That duplication is a maintenance hazard rather than a cost one (§20.18).

It costs a quarter of `SwapRegions` for two reasons: one hop instead of two, and `_reqs` divides the
peel counter by `_n_regions` (imported from `region_increment`, deliberately not re-derived) rather
than doing extra work.

**`RegionIncrementRegions` (`gir/analyses/region_increment.py:131`) is 0.24 ms and is explicitly not
a fixpoint.** `run` (`:138`) is a single program-order scan per block maintaining `at[unit]` (the
region the descriptor sits on) and emitting a `PendingMark` whenever a copy's own region differs,
plus a closing step back to region 0 at the block exit. `O(I)`. Its helpers:
`region_of(prog, ref)` (`:39`) reads the region coordinate straight off `Tile.coord`, `O(axes)`;
`_flat(region, prog, operand)` (`:52`) mixed-radix-combines it to one integer, returning `None` for
an unpinned axis; `_n_regions(prog, unit)` (`:75`) is a `meta['unit_regions']` lookup;
`_axis_delta(rms, frm, to)` (`:176`) is the per-axis step vector, `O(axes)`; `_split_copies(prog,
blk)` (`:85`) is the `O(L × members)` producer that also *checks* the by-index pairing precondition
across a fused group's members. `walk_violations(prog)` (`:188`) replays the same walk over the
finalized body for `G-WALK` — a second `O(I)` pass, run from `verify._check_walk`
(`gir/verify.py:213`), measured at 0.31 ms.

#### 20.8 Token assignment and stamping: `O(A)` with a sort, and a hidden expansion

`MemTokenAssignment.run` (`gir/analyses/mem_tokens.py:133`) is 3.3 ms. Its loop is over
`shared_refs(prog)` (`:115`) — a generator yielding `(block, inst, ref, is_write)` for every
shared-space touch, `O(I)` to walk and `O(A)` to yield — and per access it does:

```
    gen := reach.of(ref)                          # O(1)
    regions := _regions_of(ref, ...)              # O(axes), allocates frozensets
    if read and operand is agent-relative: widen regions to every value
    if the block's frame is RELATIVE: gens := every generation of the ring   # a MAY-set
    keys := sorted(_expand(operand, regions, g) for g in gens)               # the expansion
```

`_expand(operand, regions, generation)` (`:205`) is the **cross product of the per-axis region
sets**, so its output size is `∏|regions[i]|` — one `Buffer` for a pinned access, `nsplit` for an
agent-relative or unpinned one, times the ring depth when the frame is relative. The worst realistic
case is an agent-relative two-way split in a relative-frame block: `2 × 2 = 4` `Buffer` objects for
one `Ref`. `Buffer` (`:64`) is a frozen `(operand, region, generation)` triple with a `render()`
(`:77`) used only by diagnostics. The `sorted(..., key=_sort_key)` (`:190`, `_sort_key` at `:201`) is
`O(k log k)` on `k ≤ 4`. The final dense numbering sorts the *global* set of wanted buffers, `O(T_id
log T_id)` on `T_id = 4`.

So the 3.3 ms is not the algorithm — it is `A = 650` iterations of a Python loop that allocates
several small frozensets and tuples each. The result API is all `O(1)`: `MemTokenSet` (`:82`,
`__init__` at `:85`), `__len__` (`:90`), `buffers` (`:94`, copies the dict — `O(T_id)`),
`unresolved` (`:99`), `tokens_for(ref)` (`:104`, another `id(ref)` dict lookup), `id_of(buf)`
(`:111`).

`TokensPass.run` (`gir/passes/tokens.py:121`) costs 5.3 ms — more than the analysis it consumes,
which is worth explaining because it is *entirely* per-instruction constant work over `I = 1936`
instructions. Per `Move` it calls `_lds_ref(inst, side)` (`:44`, an `O(|refs|)` scan for the shared
`Ref`), `reach.of` (`O(1)`), `_completion_unit(prog, operand)` (`:66`) which calls `_unit_key(prog,
operand)` (`:52`) — **an `O(|unit_regions|)` linear scan of a dict's keys, per instruction**, to find
the canonical fuse-group key containing this operand — then `_region_key(prog, ref)` (`:74`), which
does a *second* `_unit_key` scan plus a set construction over `region_modes`, and finally
`_storage_ids(inst, tokens)` (`:35`), an `O(|refs|)` union plus a `sorted`. `_generation(ref, gen)`
(`:97`) is the one-line `(int(gen),)`. Four dict lookups, two linear scans, three small container
allocations, times 1936. That is the 5.3 ms, and it is the cleanest cache win in the package: the
`_unit_key` map is a pure function of `prog.meta` and could be built once as `{operand: key}` at the
top of `run`.

`DepDefuseAnalysis` (`gir/analyses/dep_defuse.py:43`, `cache_key` at `:45`, `run` at `:48`) is
`O(I)` and builds a `DepDefuse` (`:24`, `__init__` at `:25`) whose `add(inst)` (`:29`) splits the
inherited `(dep, counter, kind)` triples into RAW and WAR lists keyed on `id(inst)`, with `raw`
(`:36`) and `war` (`:39`) as `O(1)` lookups. `TokensPass` requests it (`gir/passes/tokens.py:124`)
"for consistency" and **nothing reads the result** — a full `O(I)` pass whose output is discarded.
Deleting that line is a free ~0.2 ms; keeping it is defensible only as a validation that the
`is_war` classification does not raise, which it cannot.

`RegBandAnalysis` (`gir/analyses/reg_band.py:38`, `cache_key` at `:40`, `run` at `:43`) is `O(I)`:
one dict write per register destination `Ref`, raising `RegBandError` (`:23`) if one
`(operand, group)` ever carries two different `reg_ring` widths. `RegBand` (`:27`, `__init__` at
`:28`) exposes `width(operand, group)` (`:31`) and `items()` (`:34`, copies the dict). `RegGenPass`
(`gir/passes/reg_gen.py:24`, `run` at `:25`) asks for it and then makes its **own** second `O(I)`
pass to assert every register read `Ref` has a concrete slot — 0.29 ms for two full walks that could
trivially be one. It is validation-only and mutates nothing.

#### 20.9 The leaves: per-instruction work in `emit_plan`, `refs` and `quantum`

`plan_block(prog, phase)` (`gir/emit_plan.py:296`) is 2.0 ms for the 387-instruction steady body,
6.0 ms for all four blocks. That is ~3 µs per instruction, and it is all constant-factor:

* `_plan_move(prog, inst, actions)` (`:92`) re-fetches five `prog.meta` dictionaries **per
  instruction** (`reduction_modes`, `free_modes`, `inner_order`, `mode_extents`, and for a split read
  `operand_regions` and `region_modes`), constructs `coord` as a fresh dict from the `Ref`'s
  coordinate tuple, builds two or three fresh `set`s (`freeset`, `rmodes`, `set(red) - rmodes`), and
  then calls `_project` **five times** — for `tile`, `region`, `tile_flat`, `k` and `k_flat`. Each
  `_project(coord, modes, inner_order, extents)` (`:62`) itself rebuilds `present = [m for m in
  inner_order if m in modes]` and walks it in reverse accumulating a mixed-radix index, `O(|ord|)`
  with `|ord| ∈ [3, 6]`. So one read act costs roughly 5 × 6 = 30 dict probes plus half a dozen
  container allocations.
* `_plan_mma(prog, inst, actions)` (`:193`) is worse per call: three `_project`s, then the
  **`scale_of` derivation** (`:222`) which, for every non-input register source, compares
  `set(free_modes[op])` against `set(free_modes[in0])` and `set(free_modes[in1])` — four set
  constructions and two comparisons per scale source, rebuilt for every one of the 1280 `Mma` nodes
  at the largest shape even though the answer is a constant of `prog.meta`.
* `_coord_val(tile, mode)` (`:52`) is a linear scan of the coordinate tuple for one mode, `O(|coord|)`
  — currently unreferenced from `_plan_move`/`_plan_mma` (both build a dict instead) but exported
  and used by tests.
* `_shared_ref(refs)` (`:78`) and `_register_dst(refs)` (`:85`) are two-element scans.
* `_plan_mark(inst, actions)` (`:274`) copies the `Mark.at` dict into an `EmitAction` (`:47`) per
  Mark, `O(|at|)`, 20–26 times per program.
* `plan_program(prog)` (`:311`) is `{phase: plan_block(...)}` over every block.

The `refs` helpers on this path are all trivially bounded: `shared_refs(refs)` (`gir/refs.py:27`),
`first_shared_ref(refs)` (`:32`), `_rotation_state(ref)` (`:44`), `copy_unit(inst)` (`:58`, `O(|dsts|)`
plus a set of at most two rotation states), `read_operand(inst)` (`:95`), and `covered_coords(ref,
extent=None)` (`:105`), whose output is `∏ extents` over the covered axes — **1 for A and B, 2 for a
merged scale read** — so the "cross product" is never larger than two elements in practice.
`_tile_axis_of(coord)` (`:142`) and `_extent_hint(ref)` (`:150`) are dead (unreferenced anywhere in
the package) and cost nothing; they are listed in §20.18 with the other removals.

`plan_quantum(acts, quantum_of, extent_of=None)` (`gir/quantum.py:149`) runs once per emitted block
inside `GirToRocisa.emit_block` (`gir_to_rocisa.py:139`). Two passes over the acts: the first buckets
read acts by `(tc, region, k, k_flat, carrier_of(tile))` — one θ-supplied `Expr` evaluation per read;
the second walks the buckets and, per bucket, calls `carrier_tile_of(q, carrier, n)`
(`gir/quantum.py:138`), which **linearly scans tile indices `0..n-1` calling `q.carrier_of(u)` until
it finds a match** — `O(n)` `Expr` evaluations per group, with `n` the operand's tile extent. For
A/B, `quantum_of` returns `None` and the whole loop is skipped, so this only ever runs on merged
scale reads where `n` is small. `_generation(at)` (`:101`) normalises `(token_ids, reg_buf, group)`
into a comparable key; `Decision` (`:71`) and `QuantumPlan` (`:115`, `__init__` at `:121`,
`decision(index)` at `:125`, `merged` at `:133`) are `O(1)` accessors over a list indexed by act
position — deliberately *not* an `id(act)` map, which is the right call for both correctness and
cost.

#### 20.10 The semantic gate: `check_plan`, and 12 ms of avoidable re-planning

`check_plan(prog, plans=None)` (`gir/verify_dataflow.py:277`) is called from
`KernelWriter.py:3803` with `plans` left `None`. Measured at DU512 MIWT4:

```
    check_plan(prog)                 17.1 ms
    check_plan(prog, plans=cached)    4.8 ms      # plan_program precomputed
```

The 12.3 ms difference is `plan_block` being run **five times** on the same blocks:
`check_region_coverage` (`:145`) plans `steady`; `check_source_coverage` (`:187`) plans `steady`
again; `check_register_dataflow` (`:119`) plans `prologue` once and `steady` **twice** (deliberately
— the second pass exposes the loop-carried edge that a single pass accepts because the first trip's
own reads already filled the file). The `plans` parameter exists precisely to avoid this and the
production call site does not use it.

Inside the checks, the per-act work:

* `_walk(prog, phase, regs, viol, acts)` (`gir/verify_dataflow.py:78`) simulates one block's plan
  against an abstract register file. Per `read` act: one `_reg_name(at)` (`:53`) tuple build and one
  dict write. Per `wmma` act: for each of the two inputs, `_expected(prog, at, which)` (`:61`) —
  which calls `_wmma_inputs(prog)` (`:47`), rebuilding a list from `prog.meta` **per input per
  instruction**, i.e. 2560 times at the largest shape — then a **linear scan of the whole register
  file** (`cand = [n for n in regs.slots if …]`, `:69`) to find the live register matching this
  operand, slot and tile index. The register file holds `O(tiles × W)` entries, which at
  `MIWaveTile 4×4` with `W = 2` is a few dozen; so this is `O(|regfile|)` per wmma input, roughly
  `1280 × 2 × 40 = 100k` tuple comparisons. That is the bulk of the 4.8 ms floor.
  `_RegFile` (`:68`, `__init__` at `:71`) is a plain dict; `snapshot()` (`:74`) marks everything used
  and is currently unreferenced from the checks (it exists for a caller that wants to prime a file).
* `check_source_coverage` (`:187`) contains a genuine, if small, `O(n²)`: `dups = sorted({c for c in
  seq if seq.count(c) > 1})` (`:214`) calls `list.count` once per element, so it is `O(|seq|²)` in
  the number of read acts for one operand — 130 at DU512, hence ~17k comparisons per operand. A
  `collections.Counter` makes it linear; the win is under a millisecond but the fix is one line.
* `check_region_coverage` (`:145`) is `O(acts)` with a per-operand set, plus the agent-relative
  exemption (`:169`) that scopes the check to over-coverage for an operand whose region is chosen by
  the wave rather than by the coordinate.
* `check_address_keys(prog, packed, phase, acts, force_within)` (`:230`) is `O(acts)` with one dict
  probe per read; it is **not** part of `check_plan` and is invoked only from tests, because it needs
  a `packed(operand)` callable that only the LDS-layout layer can supply.

#### 20.11 The verifier: 19 ms, of which 15 is a recomputation

`verify_gir(prog, expect_steady_loops="one")` (`gir/verify.py:422`) creates a **fresh
`AnalysisManager`** at `:432` and then runs twelve checks. Measured at DU512 MIWT4 4 waves:

| check | path:line | cost | why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `_check_term` | `gir/verify.py:351` | 0.02 ms | `O(B)`; `_term_targets` (`:337`) per block |
| `_check_cfg` | `:157` | 0.03 ms | `O(B)` phase counting + one `BackEdges` |
| `_check_walk` | `:213` | 0.31 ms | `region_increment.walk_violations`, `O(I)` |
| `_check_tokens` | `:230` | **14.55 ms** | recomputes `MemTokenAssignment` **and** `LdsHazards` |
| `_check_emit` | `:303` | 0.00 ms | `O(marks in model-only blocks)` |
| `_check_uniform_placement` | `:321` | 0.12 ms | `UniformPlacement`, `O(F·B)` |
| `_check_trip` | `:331` | 0.05 ms | `LoopShape` + `reduction_coverage_violations` |
| `_check_gen_ssa` | `:110` | 0.52 ms | two `O(I)` passes over refs |
| `_check_noiter` | `:135` | 2.04 ms | `O(I × |coord|)`; `bad` (`:136`) scans every coord |
| `_check_semantic` | `:149` | 0.44 ms | six `hasattr` probes per instruction |
| `_check_operands` | `:381` | 0.50 ms | two `O(I)` passes building a `(operand, space)` set |
| `_check_marks` | `:398` | 0.14 ms | `O(marks)` against `_MARK_SCHEMA` |

`_check_tokens` is three quarters of the verifier and the reason is structural, not algorithmic: the
fresh manager means `MemTokenAssignment` (3.3 ms) and `LdsHazards` (10.3 ms) are computed **a second
time**, having already been computed by `TokensPass` and `FenceRegions` moments earlier. `run_pipeline`
then calls `_check_rotation_waw(prog, am)` (`gir/passes/pipeline.py:74`) with the pipeline's own
manager — which `run_pipeline` invalidated after the last pass at `:67` — so `MemTokenAssignment` is
computed a **third** time. Three full computations of the same pure function of an unmutated program.

The fresh manager is not gratuitous: `verify_gir` is called mid-pipeline and directly on
un-piped `lower_to_gir` output by the tests, so it cannot assume a caller-supplied manager is
consistent with the program in front of it. But the *keying already solves that*: `AnalysisManager.get`
(`gir/analysis.py:48`) keys on `(analysis.cache_key, prog.version)`, so passing the caller's manager
is safe by construction — a stale entry is unreachable. Accepting an optional `am` parameter would
recover ~14 ms per kernel with no correctness argument against it.

The two `O(I)`-per-attribute walks are also worth naming. `_all_insts(prog)` (`:98`) is the shared
generator; `_refs_of(inst)` (`:104`) returns `srcs + dsts`. `_check_noiter` builds a generator
expression over every coordinate entry of every `Ref` **and** every `Mma.coord`, which is the 2 ms;
`_check_semantic` does six `hasattr` calls per instruction, which is 11,616 attribute probes at the
largest shape for an invariant that is structurally guaranteed by the dataclasses having no such
fields. Both are cheap insurance and neither is on the critical path, but if the verifier ever needs
to be fast they are the two to fuse into one pass over `_all_insts`.

`LoopShape` (`gir/analyses/loop_shape.py:144`, `run` at `:147`) and its supporting cast cost under
0.05 ms because they are `O(B²)` on `B = 4`: `_loop_blocks(prog, header, latch)` (`:88`) computes
`reach` (`:93`) from the header and from every candidate block, `O(B·(B+E))`; `_exit_tester(prog,
blocks)` (`:106`) scans the loop's blocks for the terminator with a target outside the set;
`_test_position(prog, tester)` (`:124`) asks `_does_work(blk)` (`:83`), an `O(L)` scan for any
`Move`/`Mma` — the one term that touches the body, and it early-exits on the first instruction;
`_trips_from_node(t)` (`:133`) reads the count off the `LoopBack` node. `Loop` (`:72`) is the frozen
result record and `Linear` (`:54`) the exact `coeff·T + const` count with `__add__` (`:58`),
`scaled(k)` (`:61`) and `render(sym)` (`:64`). `reduction_coverage_violations(prog, loops)` (`:180`)
is `O(B + |loops|)`.

`UniformPlacement.run` (`gir/analyses/uniform_placement.py:124`) is 0.10 ms but contains the one
avoidable `O(F · B)` in the verifier: it precomputes `fwd = {lab: _reachable_from(succ, lab)}`
(`:110`) once, correctly — and then, **inside the per-fence loop**, rebuilds `on_path` by iterating
over every block (`:145`). Since `on_path` depends only on the enclosing block label, not on the
fence, hoisting it out of the inner loop is a two-line change. The rest is `O(1)` per check:
`_preds_of(term)` (`:91`) returns the `Pred`s a terminator tests, `_pred_symbols(pred)` (`:101`) the
symbols it reads, and `Violation` (`:75`, `__init__` at `:80`, `__repr__` at `:87`) is a `__slots__`
record. The analysis is **inert in production** — `Block.role` is `'all'` everywhere and
`meta['agent_varying_symbols']` is written nowhere — so its cost is a fixed 0.1 ms of walking that
can never report anything until those two facts become live.

`ShortPathFold.run` (`gir/analyses/short_path.py:398`) is the most expensive thing in
`ScaffoldShapePass` when the arm exists, and free when it does not. Its cost is `_trace` (`:291`)
run twice — once over `(prologue,) + drains`, once over the `short` chain — each a single program-
order walk maintaining `last` (a location → value map) and `reach` (a consumer key → {location:
value} map). `O(I_folded + I_short)` with a constant factor of several tuple builds per instruction:
`_kind` (`:101`), `_operands` (`:110`), `_coord` (`:117`), `_groups` (`:121`), `_defs_uses` (`:221`)
which calls `_generation` (`:171`), `_free_coord` (`:186`) and `covered_coords` per destination.
`_entry_gens(prog)` (`:132`) and `_frame_base(blk)` (`:146`) are `O(B)` and `O(1)`. The verdict
phase is `O(|consumer keys|)` for F1 (`missing`), F0 (`unbound`) and F2 (the pairing loop calling
`_folded_producer` (`:517`) — which does a dict probe and, on a miss, an `O(|f_map|)` scan for the
same space and operand — and `pairing_cause` (`:260`)). `_arm_is_unreachable(prog)` (`:540`) is
`O(1)`. `FoldVerdict` (`:371`) with `foldable` (`:383`) and `causes()` (`:388`), and `Break` (`:359`),
are records. Nothing here is asymptotically interesting; it is measured at a few milliseconds on the
largest shape and only ever runs once.

#### 20.12 Quadratic #3 — anchor resolution by linear scan

`PlacementPass` (0.20 ms) and `ApplyMarksPass` (0.11 ms) are the two cheapest passes in the table,
